email_papers.title: The Sharp Directions Are Against You: Curvature Analysis of Activation Steering
email_papers.abstract: Activation steering adds a vector to a language model's internal representations at inference time. It is a lightweight alternative to fine-tuning for behavioral control. The standard construction, contrastive activation addition (CAA), is fragile, as on many inputs it shifts behavior in the wrong direction. To explain this fragility, we first study the geometry of the steering vector. We introduce steering Hessian, the matrix of second order derivative of the model's behavioral loss with respect to the steering vector. It captures the output behavior response sensitivity of the model under small perturbations of the steering vector along each direction. Its top eigenvectors are sharp directions: tiny perturbations along them can cause large, erratic, input-dependent behavioral swings. Bottom eigenvectors are flat directions: behavior is robust along them. Removing the sharp component of a steering vector approximately preserves its direction and magnitude (cosine > 0.974, norm reduction < 3% for typical settings) while reducing the vector's directional curvature by up to 12x (median 4x across 36 conditions). We evaluate on three model families (Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B), with four behavioral tasks, and 36 token-level conditions. Steering along sharp directions reverses the intended behavior in every condition tested, with anti-steer rates of 53-100%. Sharp directions account for only 1-5% of the CAA vector's squared norm. However, they drive a disproportionate share of the gap between the steered and unsteered next-token distributions during autoregressive generation. We term this one-line correction as sharp removal; it outperforms standard CAA in open-ended generation across all 25 conditions tested. A jailbreaking experiment further shows that sharp directions act as noise rather than signal: they disrupt coherent behavioral control regardless of steering polarity.

Introduction
Large language models (LLMs) generate fluent text across many domains, but controlling their behavior remains a central challenge.
Activation steering
(
Turner et al., 2023
;
Zou et al., 2023a
)
is a training-free approach to behavioral control. A
steering vector
𝐯

ℝ
d

is added to the model’s internal activations at a chosen layer during the forward pass, inducing targeted behavioral changes (e.g., increased honesty or reduced toxicity) without modifying any model parameters.
The standard recipe for building a steering vector is
contrastive activation addition
(CAA)
(
Rimsky et al., 2024
)
, which takes the mean activation difference between positive and negative behavioral exemplars. CAA is simple but fragile in well-documented ways:
•
Anti-steering.
On 30–50% of inputs, the CAA vector shifts behavior in the
opposite
direction from intended
(
Tan et al., 2024
)
.
•
Coefficient sensitivity.
Effectiveness depends on the scaling coefficient
α
\alpha
, with a narrow effective range before behavior degrades
(
Braun et al., 2025
)
.
•
Behavioral inversion.
As we show in §
5.3
, on three of four tested tasks, the CAA vector has the wrong sign at most layers, steering the model toward the
opposite
of the intended behavior.
These failures are typically treated as empirical nuisances. We give a geometric explanation for why they occur and a low-cost method to fix them.
Key insight.
Steering vectors live in a high-dimensional activation space, but not all directions in that space behave the same way. Some are catastrophically sensitive to perturbation. Most are not. CAA’s fragility comes from this anisotropy. The mean-difference construction does not distinguish the catastrophic directions from the stable ones, so a small fraction of the CAA vector’s squared norm (typically 1–5%, the
sharp energy fraction
ε
\varepsilon
) lies along the catastrophic directions. That small fraction drives most of CAA’s misbehavior at generation time. Identifying these directions and removing them turns a fragile vector into a robust one, with no retraining and no change to the downstream model.

7
Conclusions
We introduced the steering Hessian, a curvature object that decomposes a model’s activation space into directions that are sensitive or robust to perturbation of the steering vector. Five findings hold across all tested conditions: the spectrum of the steering Hessian is strongly anisotropic; sharp eigenvectors reverse intended behavior; the small sharp component in CAA drives a disproportionate share of the steered-vs-unsteered distributional gap during generation; removing the sharp component improves generation; and sharp directions disrupt coherent behavioral control regardless of steering polarity, acting as noise rather than signal. Where prior work on activation steering asks
which direction
to steer, the steering Hessian asks
which directions are safe to steer along
. The answer is determined by the model’s computational geometry, not by the behavioral concept alone.

The choice of single target token is a design decision. Different tokens give different Hessian matrices, but we find empirically that the resulting sharp/flat decomposition is robust to this choice. This pattern reflects that different behavioral concepts become geometrically separable from surface features at different depths. Appendix I
Why Does CAA Invert?
The mean-difference construction (Eq.
3
) captures the direction of maximal activation variance between contrastive contexts. By Proposition
1
, the sharp subspace corresponds to directions along which the downstream Jacobian most strongly translates perturbations into logit changes. These directions are sensitive to input-specific variation (lexical patterns, response format) rather than to the underlying behavioral disposition. When input-dependent features correlate with behavior in the
opposite
direction from the target disposition, CAA inverts. The flat subspace lies in the approximate nullspace of the Jacobian. It is insensitive to such input-specific variation and isolates the dispositional signal.

However, if there is a direct path to any negative applications, the authors should point it out. For example, it is legitimate to point out that an improvement in the quality of generative models could be used to generate Deepfakes for disinformation. On the other hand, it is not needed to point out that a generic algorithm for optimizing neural networks could enable people to train models that generate Deepfakes faster.
•
The authors should consider possible harms that could arise when the technology is being used as intended and functioning correctly, harms that could arise when the technology is being used as intended but gives incorrect results, and harms following from (intentional or unintentional) misuse of the technology.
•
If there are negative societal impacts, the authors could also discuss possible mitigation strategies (e.g., gated release of models, providing defenses in addition to attacks, mechanisms for monitoring misuse, mechanisms to monitor how a system learns from feedback over time, improving the efficiency and accessibility of ML).
11.
Safeguards
Question: Does the paper describe safeguards that have been put in place for responsible release of data or models that have a high risk for misuse (e.g., pre-trained language models, image generators, or scraped datasets)?
Answer:
[N/A]
Justification: The paper releases no new pretrained models or scraped datasets. All studied models and datasets are already publicly available, and harmful qualitative examples are restricted to illustrating safety findings under a content warning.
Guidelines:
•
The answer
[N/A]
means that the paper poses no such risks.
•
Released models that have a high risk for misuse or dual-use should be released with necessary safeguards to allow for controlled use of the model, for example by requiring that users adhere to usage guidelines or restrictions to access the model or implementing safety filters.
•
Datasets that have been scraped from the Internet could pose safety risks. The authors should describe how they avoided releasing unsafe images.
•
We recognize that providing effective safeguards is challenging, and many papers do not require this, but we encourage authors to take this into account and make a best faith effort.
12.
Licenses for existing assets
Question: Are the creators or original owners of assets (e.g., code, data, models), used in the paper, properly credited and are the license and terms of use explicitly mentioned and properly respected?
Answer:
[Yes]
Justification: All used models (Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B), datasets (RealToxicityPrompts, AdvBench, XSTest, WikiText-2), classifiers, and prior steering methods are properly cited.
Guidelines:
•
The answer
[N/A]
means that the paper does not use existing assets.
•
The authors should cite the original paper that produced the code package or dataset.
•
The authors should state which version of the asset is used and, if possible, include a URL.
•
The name of the license (e.g., CC-BY 4.0) should be included for each asset.
•
For scraped data from a particular source (e.g., website), the copyright and terms of service of that source should be provided.
•
If assets are released, the license, copyright information, and terms of use in the package should be provided. For popular datasets,
paperswithcode.com/datasets
has curated licenses for some datasets. Their licensing guide can help determine the license of a dataset.
•
For existing datasets that are re-packaged, both the original license and the license of the derived asset (if it has changed) should be provided.
•
If this information is not available online, the authors are encouraged to reach out to the asset’s creators.
13.
New assets
Question: Are new assets introduced in the paper well documented and is the documentation provided alongside the assets?
Answer:
[N/A]
Justification: No new assets are released.
Guidelines:
•
The answer
[N/A]
means that the paper does not release new assets.
•
Researchers should communicate the details of the dataset/code/model as part of their submissions via structured templates. This includes details about training, license, limitations, etc.
•
The paper should discuss whether and how consent was obtained from people whose asset is used.
•
At submission time, remember to anonymize your assets (if applicable). You can either create an anonymized URL or include an anonymized zip file.
14.
Crowdsourcing and research with human subjects
Question: For crowdsourcing experiments and research with human subjects, does the paper include the full text of instructions given to participants and screenshots, if applicable, as well as details about compensation (if any)?
Answer:
[N/A]
Justification: This paper does not involve crowdsourcing nor research with human subjects.
Guidelines:
•
The answer
[N/A]
means that the paper does not involve crowdsourcing nor research with human subjects.
•
Including this information in the supplemental material is fine, but if the main contribution of the paper involves human subjects, then as much detail as possible should be included in the main paper.
•
According to the NeurIPS Code of Ethics, workers involved in data collection, curation, or other labor should be paid at least the minimum wage in the country of the data collector.
15.
Institutional review board (IRB) approvals or equivalent for research with human subjects
Question: Does the paper describe potential risks incurred by study participants, whether such risks were disclosed to the subjects, and whether Institutional Review Board (IRB) approvals (or an equivalent approval/review based on the requirements of your country or institution) were obtained?

[N/A]

•
Depending on the country in which research is conducted, IRB approval (or equivalent) may be required for any human subjects research. If you obtained IRB approval, you should clearly state this in the paper.
•
We recognize that the procedures for this may vary significantly between institutions and locations, and we expect authors to adhere to the NeurIPS Code of Ethics and the guidelines for their institution.
•
For initial submissions, do not include any information that would break anonymity (if applicable), such as the institution conducting the review.
16.
Declaration of LLM usage

not

article.headline: 剔除锐方向：用曲率修复激活引导
article.lede: 作者提出steering Hessian，发现CAA中仅1–5%能量的锐方向会导致反向引导，减去该分量可提升生成。
article.problem: 对比激活加法（CAA）是常用的免训练行为控制方法，但它在不少输入上会把行为推向相反方向，且对引导系数敏感。作者指出，这类失败此前多被当作经验性问题，缺少几何解释。
article.method: 作者将行为损失对引导向量求二阶导，定义steering Hessian，并用Lanczos迭代估计顶部特征向量，得到高曲率的锐子空间。随后把CAA向量投影到该子空间并减去其分量，得到v_cleaned，即sharp removal；单层Hessian约40秒，全流程不到2分钟。
article.results: 在3个模型、4个任务、36个token级条件下，steering Hessian条件数为50–3,727；沿顶部锐方向引导在36/36条件中反向，anti-steer率53–100%。锐方向仅占CAA平方范数的1–5%，剔除后余弦相似度>0.974、范数下降<3%，方向曲率降低1.7–12×（中位数4×）。生成层面，sharp removal在25/25条件优于CAA；拒绝任务中CAA把Qwen拒绝率从78%降到36–44%、Llama从62%降到24–52%，sharp removal恢复到Qwen 88–98%、Llama 74–76%。
article.why_it_matters: 这项工作把激活引导的失败归因于激活空间曲率各向异性，并给出无需训练的一行后处理，可作为现有引导向量的通用清理步骤。锐方向还能在没有对抗优化的情况下暴露削弱安全对齐的方向，因此sharp energy fraction有潜力作为引导向量的安全审计指标。
article.limitations: 局限在于steering Hessian是(v_CAA, α=1.0)处的局部二次近似，大α下高阶项可能主导；实验只覆盖4个任务和3个7–8B指令模型，估计子空间在分布偏移下是否迁移仍未知。
article.figure_caption_zh: 图1：steering Hessian框架概览——激活空间中的行为损失呈各向异性，CAA向量含少量锐方向分量，剔除后得到避开高曲率区的v_cleaned；Llama-3.1-8B第16层真实谱跨三个数量级（κ=3,727）。

figure.caption: {Overview of the steering Hessian framework.} % {(a)}~The behavioral loss landscape is anisotropic in activation space. The CAA vector (gray) has a small component along the sharp eigenvectors (red dashed). Removing this component gives $ _{ {cleaned}}$ (green), which avoids the high-curvature region. % {(b)}~Real eigenspectrum from Llama-3.1-8B, sycophancy, layer 16: eigenvalues span three orders of magnitude ($ = 3{,}727$). The top-$k$ sharp eigenvectors (red, $ {S}_k$) are the component removed from CAA. %% (c) .... % {(d)}~The full pipeline. Sharp removal (step 4, highlighted) is a one-line operation after Hessian computation. Total: approximately 90 seconds per layer.

email_papers.title: DNAlign: Dynamic Null-Space Safe Alignment for LLMs
email_papers.abstract: Ensuring the safe and reliable deployment of large language models (LLMs) remains a fundamental challenge. Existing safety alignment approaches either incur high computational cost or unintentionally disrupt the model's core knowledge, leading to degraded fluency and factual accuracy on benign tasks. This reveals a persistent trade-off between safety and utility. We propose DNAlign, a lightweight alignment framework that integrates control-theoretic optimization with null-space projection. By treating the LLM as a dynamic system, the proposed framework introduces controllable perturbations to steer generation toward safe behavior. A key component is the projection module, which restricts these perturbations to the harmful-related subspace derived from neutral hidden states, thereby preserving general knowledge and response quality. A value function trained on human preference data adaptively optimizes the control signals to align with human safety preferences. Extensive evaluations across multiple LLM backbones demonstrate that our framework consistently reduces harmful outputs while maintaining fluency, coherence, and factual utility. It achieves superior overall performance compared to prior alignment baselines without sacrificing generation diversity. These results indicate that the proposed framework provides an effective and practically deployable solution for safe LLM alignment. Code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/DNAlign.

Safe Alignment for LLMs

Abstract
Ensuring the safe and reliable deployment of large language models (LLMs) remains a fundamental challenge. Existing safety alignment approaches either incur high computational cost or unintentionally disrupt the model’s core knowledge, leading to degraded fluency and factual accuracy on benign tasks. This reveals a persistent trade-off between safety and utility.
We propose
DNAlign
, a lightweight alignment framework that integrates control-theoretic optimization with null-space projection. By treating the LLM as a dynamic system, the proposed framework introduces controllable perturbations to steer generation toward safe behavior. A key component is the projection module, which restricts these perturbations to the harmful-related subspace derived from neutral hidden states, thereby preserving general knowledge and response quality. A value function trained on human preference data adaptively optimizes the control signals to align with human safety preferences.
Extensive evaluations across multiple LLM backbones demonstrate that our framework consistently reduces harmful outputs while maintaining fluency, coherence, and factual utility. It achieves superior overall performance compared to prior alignment baselines without sacrificing generation diversity. These results indicate that the proposed framework provides an effective and practically deployable solution for safe LLM alignment. Code is available at
https://anonymous.4open.science/r/DNAlign
.
Index Terms:
Large language models, safety alignment, null-space projection, control theory, knowledge preservation, human preference learning.
I
Introduction
Ensuring the safety of Large Language Models (LLMs) is crucial for their reliable deployment in real-world applications. While LLMs have shown strong performance across fields like healthcare
[
19
,
22
]
, finance
[
4
]
, and education
[
1
]
, they also present significant risks by generating harmful or biased content. For example, chatbots may provide harmful instructions or reinforce negative stereotypes
[
3
]
, undermining trust and potentially causing societal harm
[
2
,
23
]
. Thus, two challenges must be addressed: aligning model outputs with human values (safety alignment) and preserving the model’s pre-trained knowledge for factual, fluent responses to benign queries.
Fig. 1:
Comparison of LLMs with/without DNAlign alignment. Unedited models forget security-related knowledge, while our proposed framework preserves safe responses.
Achieving robust safety alignment has led to methods like Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF)
[
32
,
5
]
and Direct Preference Optimization (DPO)
[
18
]
. While these approaches guide models toward safer outputs, they require extensive human labeling, risk overfitting to specific scenarios
[
6
]
, and struggle with balancing safety across diverse real-world prompts. Test-time interventions such as prompt engineering
[
13
]
and controlled decoding
[
10
,
9
]
offer a lightweight alternative, but their robustness remains limited: slight changes in phrasing, domain, or prompt structure often weaken their effect. Existing dynamic intervention methods, although more flexible, can still degrade fluency or factual accuracy on benign tasks, illustrating the difficulty of achieving safety without harming utility.
The second challenge is preserving LLMs’ core knowledge. Safety alignment methods often interfere with models’ ability to generate accurate, fluent responses to benign queries. Full fine-tuning
[
29
,
30
]
or static representation editing can overwrite valuable knowledge
[
8
,
16
]
, while continual learning techniques like Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC)
[
11
]
do not scale well to large models
[
13
]
.
Current efforts to integrate safety alignment and knowledge preservation are fragmented. Post-editing strategies like RLHF after knowledge editing
[
24
]
may overwrite edited parameters, and knowledge-aware prompting
[
26
]
improves accuracy but is sensitive to prompt variations and model biases
[
27
]
. These methods lack a unified framework to optimize both safety and knowledge retention in a single process.
We propose DNAlign, a novel LLM safety alignment method that uses control theory and null-space projection to unify safety alignment and knowledge preservation. Our framework models LLMs as dynamic systems, introducing control signals to direct outputs toward safety while ensuring these signals only affect harmful content, preserving pre-trained knowledge. By training a lightweight value function on human preference data, the proposed method optimizes safety alignment while minimizing interference with the model’s core knowledge. These observations highlight the need for a unified mechanism that jointly addresses safety and knowledge preservation, rather than treating them as separate objectives. Our contributions are as follows:
•
We introduce a unified framework, DNAlign, that unifies efficient safety alignment and knowledge preservation, resolving the trade-off between the two goals.
•
Grounded in control theory, we design dynamic control signals and null-space constraints to suppress harmful content without interfering with pre-trained knowledge, validated through rigorous experiments.
•
We test our method on multiple 7B-scale LLMs (Vicuna-7B and Qwen-7B) and show that it outperforms unedited models and other safety alignment methods in both safety (average reward) and core performance (coherence, diversity), with strong generalization to new harmful scenarios.
II
Related Work
LLMs have shown remarkable utility across domains, but balancing their safety and core knowledge retention remains a critical unresolved issue. Existing research tends to address these two goals in isolation, leading to trade-offs that limit real-world applicability. This section reviews relevant work from three perspectives, safety alignment, knowledge preservation, and their integration, and clarifies the gaps our framework aims to address.
II-A
Safety Alignment for LLMs
To mitigate the inherent risks associated with Large Language Models generating harmful, biased, or unethical content, researchers have developed various alignment methodologies. These approaches can be broadly classified into two categories: pre-training/fine-tuning-based methods which directly modify model parameters, and test-time intervention-based approaches which impose constraints on the output generation process without altering the pre-trained weights.Pre-training and fine-tuning strategies typically leverage extensive human preference data to reshape model behavior. Representative examples include RLHF
[
5
,
32
]
and DPO
[
18
]
. RLHF involves training a reward model using human evaluations of model outputs, subsequently fine-tuning the LLM via reinforcement learning to maximize this learned reward signal
[
17
]
. DPO simplifies this pipeline by directly optimizing the model to align with human preference rankings, thereby obviating the need for an explicit reward model. While effective in enhancing safety, these methods face critical limitations: they require substantial, high-quality human labeling, rendering the process resource-intensive and unscalable.
Moreover, existing methods frequently suffer from overfitting to specific training prompt distributions, resulting in a lack of adaptability to the diverse, unstructured prompts encountered in real-world deployment
[
6
]
. A more profound concern is their reliance on the LLM’s existing knowledge base, which may lead to compliant but factually inaccurate responses in complex domains
[
23
]
. Test-time interventions offer a lighter alternative by directly adjusting outputs. Techniques such as prompt engineering
[
13
]
involve appending safety instrsctions (e.g., avoid harmful advice) to the input prompt, while controlled decoding
[
10
,
9
]
modifies token sampling (e.g., penalizing harmful tokens) to suppress unsafe outputs. These approaches are straightforward to implement but critically lack robustness. Prompt engineering is highly sensitive to subtle rephrasing, which can easily bypass safety constraints. Controlled decoding, conversely, struggles to adapt to the dynamically varying safety needs across different scenarios (e.g., the differential tolerance standards required for educational versus healthcare contexts). Even sophisticated dynamic intervention methods, which model LLMs as dynamic systems, often fail to strike an adequate balance between safety and utility, frequently resulting in degraded fluency or accuracy on benign tasks
[
28
]
.
II-B
Preservation of LLMs’ Core Knowledge
The ability of LLMs to generate fluent, factual responses to benign queries (e.g., general knowledge retrieval or daily tasks) is fundamentally dependent on the vast knowledge accumulated during their pre-training phase. However, the safety alignment process often interferes with this core knowledge, leading to a noticeable performance degradation in domains unrelated to safety
[
8
,
16
]
. Existing knowledge preservation methods face distinct limitations corresponding to their technical methodologies. Early efforts primarily focused on full-model fine-tuning
[
29
,
30
]
, where all LLM parameters are updated by retraining on new, task-specific data. Although this can partially retain pre-trained knowledge, it is computationally demanding and highly susceptible to catastrophic forgetting, where newly introduced data overwrites previously critical information
[
11
]
. To mitigate this, continual learning techniques like EWC
[
11
]
and memory replay
[
20
]
were developed. EWC penalizes updates to parameters deemed critical for old tasks, while memory replay reinforces pre-trained knowledge by resampling and replaying historical task examples.
Unfortunately, existing solutions are ill-suited for modern LLMs with billions of parameters. EWC requires tracking and storing parameter importance estimates, leading to computationally prohibitive overhead, and memory replay necessitates the storage of massive, potentially sensitive, historical datasets
[
13
]
. In contrast, targeted knowledge editing methods offer greater precision by modifying only specific components linked to the knowledge being updated. Some approaches like ROME
[
14
]
and MEMIT
[
15
]
employ causal tracing to precisely identify knowledge neurons or attention patterns associated with specific facts (e.g., Earth’s orbit) and edit these localized structures to update or correct knowledge. More recently, null-space projection methods
[
16
]
have emerged, attempting to protect unrelated knowledge by projecting parameter perturbations into a subspace orthogonal to neutral knowledge representations (e.g., benign prompt features). However, these null-space techniques are predominantly focused on the issue of factual updating and largely neglect behavioral alignment. Consequently, LLMs might retain accurate knowledge but still exhibit harmful behavior, for instance, correctly explaining chemical principles yet providing inappropriate guidance for dangerous experiments.
II-C
Integration of Safety and Knowledge Preservation
Despite substantial progress made in the separate domains of safety alignment and knowledge preservation, the effective and unified integration of these two critical goals remains highly fragmented and largely ineffective. Current attempts predominantly fall into two categories: sequential pipelines and prompt-based methods. Sequential approaches, such as performing knowledge editing followed by subsequent RLHF alignment
[
24
,
25
]
, frequently suffer from detrimental parameter interference, where later alignment updates inadvertently overwrite the earlier knowledge corrections, thus failing to maintain factual accuracy. Prompt-based strategies
[
26
]
provide a lightweight, non-intrusive alternative but suffer from extreme brittleness to prompt rephrasings and are fundamentally incapable of addressing the deeper, harmful associations intrinsically embedded within the model’s learned representations
[
27
]
. These limitations collectively expose a significant gap in the literature: current methods treat safety and knowledge as distinct, independent objectives rather than optimizing them jointly and holistically within a unified, integrated process.
III
Preliminary
To establish a theoretical foundation for DNAlign, this section first elaborates on the generation mechanism of LLMs and then formalizes the mathematical framework for knowledge retention, two core pillars that underpin the design of our safety alignment method.

To address the trade-off between large language model safety alignment and core knowledge preservation, we propose

IV-A
Dynamical System Formulation for LLMs
To address the inherent trade-off between safety alignment and core knowledge preservation in LLMs, we formalize LLMs as discrete-time dynamic systems. This approach is rooted in control theory and explicitly captures the sequential evolution of internal states during token generation. This formalization enables controllable safety guidance by modeling state transitions and control signal interactions, while strictly preserving the LLM’s pre-trained generation logic such as contextual coherence and semantic fluency. Unlike existing safety methods that modify model weights or truncate outputs, which often lead to knowledge degradation, our dynamic system framework restricts interventions to transient state adjustments, ensuring neutral knowledge encoding remains unaltered.

IV-B
Null-Space Constraints for Knowledge Preservation
A critical challenge in LLM safety alignment is avoiding unintended disruptions to pre-trained neutral knowledge. Such knowledge underpins fluent and factual responses to benign queries, and modifications to it often lead to semantic incoherence or factual errors in non-harmful generation scenarios. To address this, we introduce null-space projection constraints. These constraints explicitly restrict the action scope of safety-oriented control signals to subspaces that are mathematically orthogonal to the subspaces encoding neutral knowledge, ensuring that safety interventions only target harmful content without altering the LLM’s native ability to process neutral prompts.

V
Experiments
The efficacy and robustness of the proposed DNAlign methodology are rigorously evaluated through a set of comprehensive experiments designed to address four core research questions (
RQ
s):
RQ1 (Safety Alignment).
Does the DNAlign intervention effectively reduce the generation of harmful, toxic, or unethical content, achieving superior safety performance compared to state-of-the-art baselines?
RQ2 (Utility Preservation).
Can DNAlign successfully preserve the LLM’s core knowledge and maintain high output quality and fluency when performing harmless or neutral tasks, thereby avoiding the common safety-utility trade-off?
RQ3 (Generalization Capability).
Does the method demonstrate strong generalization to diverse and novel harmful scenarios, specifically those beyond the specific datasets used for constructing the projection space and training the initial value function?
RQ4 (Practical Deployment Efficiency).
Is DNAlign computationally efficient enough for practical, real-world deployment, and how do the key hyperparameters (e.g., step size, number of iterations) influence the resulting safety and utility performance metrics?
To validate the efficacy of our method in achieving a crucial balance between stringent safety alignment and the preservation of core LLM knowledge, we perform comprehensive experiments leveraging the detailed design specifications and data from referenced materials. The subsequent sections systematically elaborate on the research workflow, precise experimental setup, and configurations of established baselines. Following this, we present detailed analyses focusing on six critical experimental aspects. Firstly, performance comparison against established safety baselines. Secondly hyperparameter sensitivity studies (focusing on step size and gradient ascent iterations). Thirdly inference time and computational overhead analysis. Fourthly ablation studies investigating the impact of projection-matrix sample size. Rigorous generalization testing across external harmful benchmarks. Last, detailed impact analysis on a diverse suite of harmless datasets. These structured evaluations provide empirical evidence supporting the method’s superiority and practical viability.
V-A
Research Workflow
The experiment follows a four-stage sequential workflow to ensure systematic validation:
1) Preparatory Stage
. We construct the null-space projection matrix using neutral prompts from SHP and train the value function on HH-RLHF under reward-model supervision.
2) Initialization Stage
. All backbone models (Vicuna-7B and Qwen-7B) and baseline methods are configured with unified random seeds and hyperparameters to ensure fair and consistent comparison.
3) Inference and Data Collection Stage
. Our method and all baseline methods are applied to multiple datasets including HH-RLHF, SHP, harmful benchmarks, and harmless benchmarks, to generate outputs and compute the four core evaluation metrics.
4) Result Analysis Stage
. Performance across datasets is aggregated to examine the safety–utility trade-off and to support extended studies such as hyperparameter sensitivity, inference-time evaluation, and projection-matrix ablations.

. The comprehensive quality score provides an overall assessment of model performance by integrating multiple aspects, including helpfulness, accuracy, fluency, and safety. This metric complements the individual metrics by capturing trade-offs between different performance dimensions, such as whether improved safety affects fluency. It uses DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B

A score of 1 indicates poor quality (e.g., harmful or inaccurate), while 10 reflects exceptional quality (e.g., safe, accurate, fluent). DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B has a 0.82 correlation with human evaluator scores, making it a reliable tool for capturing nuanced quality differences. V-D
Performance Comparison on HH-RLHF and SHP
The efficacy of our proposed methodology is comprehensively validated across two distinct yet complementary human-preference benchmarks: HH-RLHF and SHP. This dual-benchmark strategy allows for a robust assessment of two critical research objectives, including RQ1, focusing on safety alignment, and RQ2, pertaining to capability preservation in general-purpose interactions. The HH-RLHF dataset, characterized by its mixture of harmful and benign prompts, serves as a crucial testbed for evaluating safety-oriented performance.
Our proposed approach consistently demonstrates superior safety alignment compared to the RE-Control baseline and other tested systems, across both the Vicuna-7B and Qwen-7B foundational models. Specifically, with the Vicuna-7B backbone, our method achieves a substantially higher average reward (1.2258 vs. 0.9614 for RE-Control), alongside notably improved coherence (0.4325 vs. 0.3887), and better comprehensive quality (6.16 vs. 5.94), while maintaining comparable diversity. A similar positive pattern is evident under the Qwen-7B backbone, where our method significantly increases the average reward from 0.7218 to 0.9430 and registers the highest comprehensive quality. These compelling quantitative results collectively demonstrate that a more stringent safety alignment (RQ1) can be effectively realized without compromising the fluency or content richness of the generated responses in mixed harmful–benign scenarios.
To rigorously verify capability preservation (RQ) under general-purpose, non-adversarial conditions, we employ the SHP dataset, which predominantly consists of harmless, everyday human-model queries. In this context, our method successfully maintains or actively enhances the core model’s utility. For the Vicuna-7B model, both the average reward (1.0756) and comprehensive quality (6.97) metrics exceed those of the RE-Control baseline, with diversity and coherence remaining stable.
The experimental results under the Qwen-7B backbone exhibit the same positive pattern, definitively confirming that the introduced intervention strategy does not erode general-purpose performance. Taken together, the consistent performance improvements across these two structurally different datasets underscore that the proposed approach offers a balanced and synergistic enhancement. It simultaneously elevates both safety-oriented and utility-oriented metrics while diligently preserving broad output diversity. This demonstrated robustness, spanning performance and generalizability, suggests that the method is highly suitable for real-world deployments where the simultaneous requirement for uncompromising safety and high-fidelity response quality is a necessity.

V-F
Inference Time Analysis
Beyond effectiveness and hyperparameter robustness, we further quantify the computational overhead introduced by our method to evaluate its deployment practicality (RQ4).
To assess the practical deployment of the proposed framework, we evaluate inference time using the Qwen-7B backbone with 1,000 samples from the HH-RLHF dataset. The experiment compares DNAlign against the RE-Control model and the unedited base model, analyzing the impact of training batches (ranging from 1 to 10) on inference time.
Results show that the base model’s inference time decreases as batch size increases, from 51.059 minutes with 1 batch to 10.556 minutes with 10 batches. The RE-Control model exhibits a similar trend, dropping from 71.518 minutes (1 batch) to 10.617 minutes (10 batches). DNAlign, initially slower (123.734 minutes with 1 batch), also improves as batch size increases, reaching 12.447 minutes with 10 batches, only 1.891 minutes longer than the base model and 1.83 minutes longer than RE-Control.This higher initial overhead is due to DNAlign’s null-space projection module, critical for safety and knowledge preservation. However, the inference time gap narrows significantly with more batches, with DNAlign showing improved efficiency in larger batch sizes due to batch processing optimization. The precomputed projection matrix introduces negligible runtime overhead (less than 0.1% of total inference time), as it is loaded during inference rather than computed on the fly.
Importantly, our method maintains high output quality despite the additional inference time. It achieves a coherence score of 0.4250, surpassing both the base model (0.4192) and the RE-Control model (0.4203). This demonstrates that DNAlign successfully balances safety alignment, knowledge retention, and inference efficiency.
In conclusion, while the safety mechanisms of our method introduce some initial inference overhead, the gap diminishes as batch size increases, with a manageable difference of 1.891 minutes at 10 batches. Combined with superior performance, DNAlign proves feasible for real-world deployment scenarios requiring both efficiency and quality.

V-G
Research on Sample Parameters of Projection Matrix
To justify the design choices underlying the null-space projection module in our framework, we ablate the number of samples used to construct the projection matrix and analyze its impact on numerical stability and approximation error.
The selection of 20,000 samples for computing the projection matrix with Vicuna-7B is determined as the optimal engineering solution, supported by detailed empirical data and systematic experimental validation. As illustrated by the experimental results, the error exhibits distinct variation patterns across different sample size ranges. When the sample size is within 1 to 100, the model falls into the overfitting region, with errors maintaining at a low level (0.0000035 for 1 sample and 0.00258 for 100 samples) but lacking generalizability due to insufficient data diversity. As the sample size increases to the range of 500 to 3,000, a critical numerical instability region emerges, where the error fluctuates drastically. Specifically, the error rises to 0.587 at 500 samples, drops to 0.0415 at 1000 samples, then surges again to 1.757 at 1500 samples and reaches the peak of 2.923 at 3000 samples. This severe instability makes sample sizes in this range unsuitable for projection matrix construction.
When the sample size exceeds 3000 and enters the convergence region (5000 to 20000 samples), the error stabilizes at a low level and shows minimal fluctuations. At 5000 samples, the error is 0.0105. At 10000 samples, it decreases slightly to 0.00929. At 15000 samples, it rises marginally to 0.00949. And at 20000 samples, it stabilizes at 0.0094. Notably, the 20,000 sample solution not only achieves a stable and low error (0.0094) but also performs comparably to the 50,000 sample variant (error 0.0100) while significantly reducing computational costs. Additionally, the 20,000 sample size far exceeds the model’s hidden dimension (4096), ensuring the projection matrix is built on a complete orthogonal basis that meets the full-rank condition, thus guaranteeing mathematical rigor and excellent generalization ability. This selection also aligns with the sample size used in earlier experiments on Qianwen-7B, enabling fair cross-model comparisons.
In summary, the 20,000 sample approach achieves an optimal balance across four key dimensions: reliability (avoiding the numerical instability region), efficiency (reducing computational costs), performance (maintaining stable low errors in the convergence region), and scientific rigor (supporting cross-model comparisons). It is therefore confirmed as a fully validated and ideal solution for projection matrix computation with Vicuna-7B.

V-H
Generalization Testing
The critical third research question, RQ3, mandates the evaluation of the proposed DNAlign methodology’s generalization capability, specifically, its performance when facing harmful prompts that lie outside the scope of its original training distribution. This assessment is crucial for validating the robustness required for real-world deployment. To this end, we benchmark DNAlign against the base model (Qwen-7B) and the RE-Control baseline across three distinct external harmful datasets: RealToxicityPrompts, ToxiGen, and CategoricalHarmfulQA. These datasets represent diverse facets of safety risks, ranging from general toxicity to highly specific categorical harms. Our evaluation employs four rigorous metrics: diversity, coherence, comprehensive quality, and, critically, average reward for safety alignment. Across all three generalization datasets, DNAlign consistently demonstrates superior performance, particularly in fulfilling the stringent requirements of RQ3. For example, on the RealToxicityPrompts benchmark, which tests responses to model-generated toxic seeds, DNAlign achieves an average reward of 0.7999. This represents a dramatic improvement, showcasing a 137.1% increase over the base Qwen-7B model’s score of 0.3374. Importantly, this substantial safety gain is realized while maintaining highly competitive generative metrics, with diversity at 0.9241 and coherence at 0.4648, thereby mitigating the typical trade-off between safety and utility.
The effectiveness of DNAlign is further substantiated when tested against the extreme toxicity profiles in the ToxiGen dataset. Here, DNAlign’s average reward rises to 0.5465, an extraordinary 229.4% increase relative to the base model. This significant leap underscores the method’s exceptional capability in neutralizing high-risk, targeted harmful content. Even in this high-toxicity context, the fundamental quality of the generated text remains robust, evidenced by a coherence score of 0.2251 and a high diversity score of 0.9615. While acknowledging that DNAlign’s comprehensive quality score may be marginally lower than that of the unedited backbone on some specific datasets, a minor consequence of its stringent safety filtering, the overwhelming and consistent gains observed in the safety alignment metric (average reward) confirm its superior overall contribution. These collective results confirm that the DNAlign approach successfully maintains strong and reliable generalization across a wide spectrum of diverse harmful content. By demonstrating enhanced safety alignment without compromising the model’s core generative capabilities, DNAlign proves its robustness and its capacity to successfully balance the dual requirements of safety and utility, making it exceptionally well-suited for high-stakes, real-world deployment scenarios.

VI
Conclusion
DNAlign is a framework that effectively balances LLM safety alignment with core knowledge preservation, addressing the trade-off seen in existing methods. By integrating dynamic control theory and null-space projection, the proposed framework ensures targeted safety interventions without disrupting the model’s inherent capabilities. Experimental results demonstrate the superiority of our method across multiple datasets, outperforming baseline models like RE-Control in key metrics such as average reward, coherence, and comprehensive quality. Taken together, these findings provide affirmative answers to our four guiding research questions on safety, utility preservation, generalization, and practicality, positioning our framework as a promising solution for reliable and high-quality LLM deployment.

article.headline: DNAlign：在零空间里做安全对齐
article.lede: DNAlign 把 LLM 建模为动态系统，用零空间投影隔开安全干预与预训练知识，宣称在 7B 模型上同时提升安全奖励与
article.problem: 现有安全对齐路线各有代价：RLHF、DPO 需要大量人工标注并可能过拟合特定场景，测试时的提示工程与受控解码又不够稳健，动态干预还常在良性任务上损伤流畅度和事实性。核心难题是安全与效用之间的权衡：既要压住有害输出，又不想动模型已学到的中性知识。
article.method: 作者把 LLM 的逐 token 生成写成离散时间动态系统，状态由各层 KV 缓存和最终层 pre-logit 向量组成，再用梯度上升优化一个瞬态控制信号来提升安全奖励。关键一步是用 SHP 中性提示的最终层隐藏状态做 SVD，构建零空间投影矩阵 P，把控制信号投影到与中性知识子空间正交的方向，理论上避免扰动中性知识。价值函数是 3 层 MLP，在 HH-RLHF 数据上、以 UltraRM-13B 的奖励作为监督训练得到；推理时每个 token 做 100 次梯度上升，投影矩阵离线预计算，加载开销低于总推理时间的 0.1%。
article.results: 在 Vicuna-7B 的 HH-RLHF 上平均奖励为 1.2258，高于 RE-Control 的 0.9614；Qwen-7B 上从基线 0.7218 升到 0.9430。外部有害集上，RealToxicityPrompts 的平均奖励由基线 0.3374 升到 0.7999，论文报告提升 137.1%；ToxiGen 上达到 0.5465，报告提升 229.4%。效率上，Qwen-7B、1000 条样本单 batch 推理需 123.734 分钟，基线为 51.059 分钟；10 个 batch 时降到 12.447 分钟，基线为 10.556 分钟。投影矩阵构建用 20000 条样本，误差稳定在 0.0094。
article.why_it_matters: 若结论成立，这是一条不改权重、在推理时即插即用的对齐路径，对开源模型的安全部署和“安全干预不伤知识”的工程需求有直接参考价值。
article.limitations: 评测主要依赖自动指标：TF-IDF 余弦相似度、UltraRM-13B 奖励和 DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B 打分，缺人工评测，且只验证了 7B 规模骨干。单 batch 推理时间约为基线的 2.4 倍，部分数据集上综合质量还略低于未编辑基线，作者也承认零空间约束是“近似”保护而非严格保证。
article.figure_caption_zh: DNAlign 流程：先从输入提示算出初始状态 s0，再加载离线预计算的零空间投影矩阵 P，把梯度优化得到的控制信号 u_t 投影到零空间后更新系统状态，并据此采样下一个 token。

figure.caption: The sequential process begins by computing the initial state $s_0=\{h_0, o_0\}$ from the input prompt. It then loads the pre-computed null-space projection matrix $P$. In the core step, a gradient-optimized control signal $u_t$ is projected by $P$ to enforce safety alignment while minimally affecting neutral knowledge. Finally, the projected signal $P u_t$ updates the system state $s_{t+1}$, enabling token generation $y_t$.

email_papers.title: Reading, Writing, Sharing, and Interacting with the World through Video
email_papers.abstract: Video foundation models have advanced rapidly in understanding and generating visual sequences, while video world models seek to capture the underlying dynamics of the world they depict. Despite their different objectives, both concern the relationship between video observations and an evolving world. This survey adopts world modeling as a unifying lens for examining these developments. Viewing an observed video as a partial, lossy, and temporally ordered projection of a latent temporal world, we organize the literature around four complementary operations: reading infers world properties from observed video; writing synthesizes video from specified or learned world conditions; sharing integrates understanding and generation through common modeling mechanisms; and interacting predicts and updates world states under actions and evolving observations. This perspective distinguishes temporal coherence in observed or generated sequences from consistency in the underlying world state. Across tasks, representations, models, datasets, and benchmarks, we trace a shift in emphasis from clip-level recognition and perceptual fidelity toward persistent state, controllable evolution, physical and causal validity, and evaluation grounded in interaction and downstream decisions, and we distill the open challenges that follow.
email_papers.content:
Abstract
Video foundation models have advanced rapidly in understanding and generating visual sequences, while video world models seek to capture the underlying dynamics of the world they depict.
Despite their different objectives, both concern the relationship between video observations and an evolving world.
This survey adopts world modeling as a unifying lens for examining these developments.
Viewing an observed video as a partial, lossy, and temporally ordered projection of a latent temporal world, we organize the literature around four complementary operations:
reading
infers world properties from observed video;
writing
synthesizes video from specified or learned world conditions;
sharing
integrates understanding and generation through common modeling mechanisms; and
interacting
predicts and updates world states under actions and evolving observations.
This perspective distinguishes temporal coherence in observed or generated sequences from consistency in the underlying world state.
Across tasks, representations, models, datasets, and benchmarks, we trace a shift in emphasis from clip-level recognition and perceptual fidelity toward persistent state, controllable evolution, physical and causal validity, and evaluation grounded in interaction and downstream decisions, and we distill the open challenges that follow.

Beyond perceptual fidelity and local coherence, claims about the world require state that survives occlusion, revisits, and long horizons; controllable action effects; valid responses to interventions; and, for closed-loop use, latency within the control budget.
Stochastic futures also require coverage and calibration, unified models require matched evidence that information transfers between reading and writing, and systems built for training, planning, or evaluation must improve decisions in controlled environments or real tasks.
Meeting these requirements would move the field from rendering convincing video to modeling how the world changes.

article.headline: 综述：用世界模型视角统一视频理解与生成
article.lede: 综述提出以世界模型为统一视角，用读、写、共享、交互四种操作梳理视频理解与生成，并重新界定评测标准。
article.problem: 视频基础模型在理解与生成视觉序列上进展迅速，视频世界模型则试图刻画视频所描绘世界的底层动力学。两者目标不同，但都涉及视频观测与不断演变的世界之间的关系，此前文献往往分头叙述。
article.method: 该综述把世界建模作为统一透镜，将一段观测到的视频视为某个潜在时序世界的部分、有损、按时间排列的投影。围绕这一视角，作者把文献组织为四种互补操作：reading（从视频推断世界属性）、writing（按指定或学到的世界条件合成视频）、sharing（用共同建模机制打通理解与生成）、interacting（在动作与演化观测下预测并更新世界状态）。
article.results: 这是综述文章，论文未给出具体数字或实验结果；其组织方式是「读、写、共享、交互」四类操作，并以 2×3 的网格（原文图 10、第 8 节）逐格汇总各研究分支的代表性工作，同时给出表 2 作为「更强证据」的评测要求清单。作者据此指出，领域重心正从片段级识别与感知保真度，转向持久状态、可控演化、物理与因果有效性，以及基于交互和下游决策的评测。
article.why_it_matters: 它明确区分了「观测或生成序列的时间连贯性」与「底层世界状态的一致性」，把评价焦点从画面是否逼真推向模型是否真的跟踪世界状态。这对需要闭环决策与规划的下游使用尤为关键。
article.limitations: 作为综述，文章提出的是概念框架与评测建议，本身不含新实验，四类操作与 2×3 网格的划分是作者主张，覆盖面和可操作性仍需实证检验。文中也提到 Gemini 这类闭源系统虽展示了强长上下文视频与音频结果，但公开的设计细节很少，相关比较难以深入。
article.figure_caption_zh: 原文未给出图注；图 2 把四类操作展开为并行的研究分支，并列出各章考察的代表性工作。

email_papers.title: A Fix for Softmax and Cross-Entropy
email_papers.abstract: Standard implementations of softmax, log-softmax, and cross-entropy have two numerical bugs. The first bug, Softmax Collapse, rounds the target logit's gradient to zero if that one logit is much larger than the others, resulting in gradients that no longer sum to zero. The second bug, Softmax Cancellation, occurs when student logits are close to teacher logits, and produces non-zero gradients even when the student and teacher logits are equal. We present simple implementations of log-softmax, softmax, and cross-entropy that fix both bugs. Our fix eliminates the previously-observed "Slingshot" phenomenon, speeds up grokking with weight decay, prevents accuracy collapse without weight decay, stops student networks from drifting away from the teacher during distillation, and shows that after memorization, logit growth is bounded by an equilibrium between weight decay and Adam's $ε$ hyperparameter.

Conclusion
We have presented simple fixes for two numerical bugs in standard
implementations of softmax, log-softmax, and cross-entropy:
Softmax Collapse
, which zeroes out the dominant logit’s gradient at high
confidence while leaving non-dominant gradients non-zero, and
Softmax
Cancellation
, which loses precision when student logits approach teacher logits
in soft-target distillation.

,
expm1

, and
log1p

fp32, and fp64 without internally casting to higher
precision.

student networks from drifting away from the teacher during distillation, and
reveals that logit margins under AdamW and weight decay naturally converge to

experiments are uncommon in standard large-scale training, our fixed functions

slowdown, and may prove useful whenever models make high-confidence predictions

article.headline: Softmax 与交叉熵的两个数值 bug 及修复
article.lede: DeepMind 作者指出标准 softmax 与交叉熵存在两个数值缺陷，并给出可直接替换的对数空间实现。
article.problem: 标准实现先把 logit 减去最大值再取指数，虽然避免了溢出，却留下两个数值 bug。其一是 Softmax Collapse：当目标 logit 远大于其他 logit 时，目标梯度会被舍入为零，而非目标梯度仍为正，导致梯度之和不再为零。其二是 Softmax Cancellation：在软标签蒸馏中，学生与教师 logit 接近时，分别计算两个 softmax 再相减会损失精度，即使两者相等也留下非零梯度。
article.method: 作者把 log-softmax 与交叉熵改写成在对数空间中计算：不再把 e^{-m} 加到 1.0 上，而是用 softplus(-m) 表示损失，并把目标类从 log-sum-exp 中排除，让目标梯度由非目标梯度取负求和得到。针对软标签蒸馏，则直接用学生的 logit 与学生和教师 logit 之差 δ 构造 log(q/p)，并借助 expm1、log1p 计算 q−p，最后减去均值以保证梯度之和为零。论文给出了 JAX 实现，并称不改变精度，也就是不内部提升到 fp64。
article.results: 论文给出的精度悬崖为 bf16 约 5.5、fp32 约 16.6、fp64 约 36.7，一旦 logit margin 超过对应阈值，标准实现就会把目标梯度舍入为零。修复后 margin 能平滑越过这些悬崖，并在 AdamW 加权重衰减时停在 ε 决定的平衡点 log(1/ε)：ε=10⁻⁸ 时约 18.4，ε=10⁻¹² 约 27.6，ε=10⁻¹⁶ 约 36.8。在 a+b mod 31（λ=1，ε=10⁻⁸）上，标准交叉熵为 94.3±5.4% 测试准确率，修复版为 100.0±0.0%；bf16 下分别为 93.3±7.4% 与 100.0±0.1%。在 a²+b² mod 97（λ=0）上，标准交叉熵在约第 1250 步 margin 触及 16.6 时出现一次尖峰，测试准确率从 61% 掉到 23%，而修复版继续平滑升到 85%；a³+b mod 97 上则是从 60% 掉到 21%。蒸馏实验中，教师权重初始化学生、T=4、ε=10⁻⁸ 时，修复版在 bf16、fp32、fp64 下都保持在 KL=0 与 100% 准确率，标准版在 bf16 下会把约 10⁻³ 的残差梯度放大成参数漂移。
article.why_it_matters: 这两个 bug 是库级实现问题，而不是模型设计问题，修复只需替换几个算子就能消除 grokking 中的 Slingshot 尖峰、避免无权重衰减时的准确率崩塌，并让蒸馏中的学生不再被舍入噪声推离教师。论文还给出 margin 收敛到 log(1/ε) 的解析解释，把 Adam 的 ε 从“数值防零小量”提升为控制 logit 增长的实际超参数。
article.limitations: 实验集中在模运算 grokking 基准上的 1 层 Transformer 与 2 层 MLP，论文本身也承认如此大的 margin 与如此接近的师生 logit 差距在大规模常规训练中并不常见，方法在真实大模型上的收益尚未验证。此外，margin 平衡点的推导依赖权重衰减与 Adam 平稳点假设，且需要用 LaProp 并直接更新 v 才能覆盖 ε→0 的极端情形。
article.figure_caption_zh: 在 ε=10⁻⁸ 下，归一化 Adam 步长与 logit margin 的关系：修复版在 margin 约 18.4（即 log(1/ε)）附近平滑衰减，而标准交叉熵在 bf16 的 5.5 与 fp32 的 16.6 处直接把目标梯度归零。

email_papers.title: UniFlowWAM: A Unified World-Action Model with Visual Semantics and 4D Geometry
email_papers.abstract: Robot demonstrations record what the robot saw and what it did. They do not specify how the 3D world changed in between. Scene-level 3D flow describes it by tracking 3D scene points, providing the world representation with 4D geometry. Prior work has used flow to improve robot policies. Flow served as an intermediate prediction that a separate model converts into actions, as a prior injected at inference time, or as an extra output learned together with the action. In all of these designs, flow stays outside the policy, as a separate module or as an extra prediction head. We introduce UniFlowWAM, a Unified World-Action Model that makes 3D scene flow a third modality on par with vision and action. Its world representation therefore covers both visual semantics, through future visual features, and 4D geometry, through 3D flow, and flow receives its own supervision. UniFlowWAM is a diffusion transformer with one expert per modality, and the three experts exchange information through joint attention. We train UniFlowWAM under a ten-objective role grid, where each objective assigns every modality exactly one of three roles, namely target, condition, or absent. The same model thus serves as a policy, as forward and inverse dynamics, and as a predictor of future visual features or 3D flow. We evaluate UniFlowWAM on RoboCasa-GR1, LIBERO, and LIBERO-Plus in simulation, and on four real-world bimanual manipulation tasks. On RoboCasa-GR1, UniFlowWAM raises the success rate of its base model without flow from 52.1% to 56.4%. It preserves in-distribution success on LIBERO at 98.1% and reaches 87.7% zero-shot on LIBERO-Plus. On the real robot, it achieves 87.0% average success, compared with 68.5% for the strongest baseline.

every modality exactly one of three roles, namely target, condition, or absent.
The same model thus serves as a policy, as forward and inverse dynamics, and as a
predictor of future visual features or 3D flow.
We evaluate UniFlowWAM on RoboCasa-GR1, LIBERO, and LIBERO-Plus in simulation, and
on four real-world bimanual manipulation tasks.
On RoboCasa-GR1, UniFlowWAM raises the success rate of its base model without flow
from 52.1% to 56.4%.
It preserves in-distribution success on LIBERO at 98.1% and reaches 87.7%
zero-shot on LIBERO-Plus.
On the real robot, it achieves 87.0% average success, compared with 68.5%
for the strongest baseline.

1
Introduction
A robot manipulates objects by moving its own body. Its action labels only record the commands that its joints or end-effector execute. What those commands do to the scene is left unwritten. A mug pushed across the table and a mug lifted and set back down can end in the same pose. The action labels do not describe how the mug translates or rotates along the way. Among possible world representations in a world–action model, a goal image describes the resulting state, but not the transition. A video sequence captures this process visually, but does not describe how scene points move in 3D. Scene-level 3D flow makes the effects of robot commands on the scene explicit: it describes how each scene point is displaced in 3D over time, providing a 4D geometric representation of this process.
Prior work has used scene-level flow to improve robot policies. Flow served as intermediate representations that were predicted first and then converted into actions in a separate stage
[
38
,
42
]
. A learned 3D scene-flow prior sharpened a vision-language-action policy when injected at inference
[
34
]
. Concurrent work trains sparse 3D keypoint flow jointly with the action
[
18
]
. These results establish flow as a useful control signal and as a variable that can be learned with actions.
Unified future-image–action models learn actions together with predictions of the future. UWM
[
50
]
and UVA
[
17
]
train the policy together with forward and inverse dynamics and visual forecasting, so that both action-labeled and actionless data contribute. Latent-dynamics variants adopt the features of a frozen visual encoder
[
29
]
as the future-state target and scale to large robotic datasets
[
24
]
. The same model learns both to anticipate the visual consequences of actions and to infer actions from future visual features.
Those features capture the semantics in the future goal image, but do not explicitly describe how the 3D scene evolves to reach that state.
We ask:
can a pretrained visual–action model learn where the 3D points of the scene go, and, more importantly, does learning this improve the actions it predicts?
We explicitly supervise the 3D displacement of scene points, beyond the geometric state that depth-based targets supervise.
We introduce
UniFlowWAM
, a Unified World–Action Model whose world representation joins future visual semantics from DINOv3
[
29
]
with 4D geometry from scene-level 3D flow.
Actions, visual semantics, and flow are co-equal modalities of one diffusion transformer.
Following UWM
[
50
]
and UVA
[
17
]
, we call the model
unified
, as one model that is trained jointly on the three modalities serves as a policy, as forward and inverse dynamics, and as a predictor of future world state.
Unlike the flow-based policies above, flow here is neither a separate module nor a tracked input, but a modality inside the model. From the same demonstration clips used for policy learning, we extract point maps and scene flow offline with a monocular 3D tracker
[
22
]
and encode them with a frozen 4D VAE
[
51
]
. Each modality has its own expert, and the three exchange information only through shared joint attention. We add flow to a pretrained visual–action model during mid-training and post-training. The visual and action experts start from the pretrained weights, while the flow expert is trained from scratch. All three experts are then trained jointly, so the pretrained representations adapt to the new modality.
Each function of the model corresponds to one training objective. Ten objectives form a role grid, which assigns each modality the role of
target
,
condition
, or
absent
. With one target per objective, the grid covers all four combinations of flow and future visual features being present or absent for action prediction, and retains three objectives each for flow and visual prediction. This deliberate asymmetry design prioritizes the conditioning choices for the control variable. The four objectives without flow recover the pretrained model’s task set. Under the direct policy objective, the flow stream carries learned placeholders, so deployment requires no scene-flow extraction or flow encoding.
We evaluate UniFlowWAM in simulation on RoboCasa-GR1
[
25
]
, LIBERO, and LIBERO-Plus, and on four real-world bimanual tasks. On RoboCasa-GR1, adding flow to the base model improves the average success rate by 4.3 percentage points. The gain is largest on the tasks where the base model is weakest (Sec.
4.2
). On LIBERO, UniFlowWAM preserves in-distribution success at 98.1%, and it reaches 87.7% zero-shot on LIBERO-Plus under out-of-distribution perturbations. On the real robot, UniFlowWAM achieves an average success rate of 87.0%, compared with 68.5% for
π
0.5
\pi_{0.5}
[
27
]
, the strongest baseline (Sec.
4.3
). Ablations show where the flow objectives matter. On the real robot, post-training with the full ten-objective grid outperforms policy-only post-training by 12 to 18 points on every task, and the gap is largest on object placements at the edge of the demonstrated region.
Contributions.
(i) We make scene-level 3D flow a co-equal modality of a unified visual–action model, added to a pretrained model through a dedicated expert and joint mid-training and post-training on the same demonstrations. (ii) We organize actions, 3D flow, and future visual features through ten role-conditioned objectives, allowing flow to serve as a target or a condition while retaining a direct policy that needs no flow input. (iii) We show manipulation gains on RoboCasa-GR1 and improved robustness on LIBERO-Plus while retaining in-distribution performance on LIBERO.

3.5
Training Strategy
We initialize the visual–action backbone from the publicly released pretrained checkpoint of LDA
[
24
]
. We then perform
mid-training
to incorporate scene-level 3D flow into the model, jointly optimizing the ten objectives in Sec.
3.4
over actions, future visual features, and 3D flow. This stage extends the pretrained visual–action model to support 3D flow as both a prediction target and a conditioning modality. The resulting model is subsequently post-trained on demonstrations from each downstream domain.
4
Experiments
Our experiments assess manipulation performance, robustness to distribution shifts, and the contribution of scene-level 3D flow. We evaluate UniFlowWAM on RoboCasa-GR1, LIBERO, and LIBERO-Plus in simulation, and on an ALOHA-style robot for real-world bimanual manipulation.
4.1
Experimental Setup
Mid-training data.
We use a filtered mixture of three public robot-demonstration datasets; all are robot-camera recordings. RoboCOIN
[
36
]
is a bimanual manipulation dataset collected on 15 robot platforms in residential, commercial, and industrial settings; we use 47,050 episodes from six of these platforms. RoboMIND 2.0
[
11
]
is a dual-arm and mobile manipulation dataset collected on six robot embodiments; we use 140,231 episodes from three of them, including Franka and UR arms. MolmoAct2-BimanualYAM
[
8
]
is AllenAI’s teleoperated bimanual dataset collected on a single low-cost platform, the YAM arms; we use 27,162 episodes. The combined corpus covers ten embodiments, with 214,443 episodes and 133.0 million frames. We sample 16-step chunks at three-frame intervals, yielding around 42 million training windows. We extract scene-level 3D flow offline with frozen Track4World
[
22
]
and encode its point maps and flow into latents using a frozen MotionCrafter 4D VAE
[
51
]
.
Model and training.
Starting from LDA’s released pretrained checkpoint
[
24
]
, our model UniFlowWAM adds a dedicated 3D flow expert to the MMDiT backbone to incorporate flow as a third modality. Qwen3-VL-4B supplies visual–language conditioning through cross-attention, while DINOv3 provides visual prediction targets. Both encoders remain frozen during mid-training. We train on 48 NVIDIA H200 GPUs with a global batch size of 1,536.

4.3
Real-World Experiments on ALOHA
Hardware.
We use AgileX Cobot Magic, an ALOHA-style platform with two 6-DoF PiPER arms and parallel-jaw grippers. A top-mounted camera provides the main view, and two wrist cameras provide the wrist views. Both the proprioceptive state and the action command are 14-dimensional, with six joint positions and one gripper position per arm.
Demonstrations.
We consider four tasks that differ in what they demand of the two arms (Fig.
3
).
Chili transfer
repeats a single pick-and-place primitive, moving two chilies onto a plate.
Cabbage transfer
chains distinct primitives instead of repeating one, placing a cabbage into a pot and then covering the pot with a lid.
Pen manipulation
adds an articulated object and asymmetric arm roles, as one arm holds the drawer steady while the other places two pens into it in succession, after which the drawer is pushed closed.
Towel folding
replaces the rigid objects with a deformable one that has no pose to track, requiring two successive folds. After preprocessing, we retain 50 demonstrations per task and post-train a separate model for each task. At inference, each model uses the policy mode to predict 16-step action chunks.

Evaluation.
For model with full objective setup as our default model, each policy is evaluated for 50 trials per task. We fix the starting conditions in advance instead of drawing them at random. Within a task we change one thing at a time, in equal steps. For chili transfer we keep the chili at the same spot on the table and turn it about the vertical axis to five fixed orientations. Each orientation is run the same number of times, and the plate position varies slightly across trials. The other three tasks follow the same idea along the factor that matters for them. All conditions stay inside the area the demonstrations cover. Every policy sees the same starting conditions, so the differences we report come from the policies and not from where the objects happened to start. We report full-task success rate and a process score, the fraction of milestones completed, scaled to 100. The milestones are those in Fig.
3
, four for cabbage (grasp, place in pot, grasp lid, close) and chili (grasp and place each chili), six for pen (pick and place each pen, support the drawer with the right gripper, push it closed), and five for towel (grasp, lift, fold in half, fold again, press flat). Milestones are scored independently, so a trial that fails one but recovers on a later one still earns credit for the later one. Both metrics are averaged over trials, then over tasks.

Post-training objectives.
We first ask what the objective grid contributes on its own, varying the objectives used in LIBERO post-training while holding the mid-trained initialization and the demonstration data fixed. The four variants form a nested ladder. The full grid uses all ten objectives, with 3D flow as both a target and a condition. The flow-as-condition variant drops the three objectives that predict flow and keeps the other seven. The no-flow variant also drops flow conditioning and keeps the four visual–action objectives of the base model. Policy-only training keeps the single action-prediction objective. Every variant acts through the direct policy objective and takes no flow input at test time, so the differences come from training rather than from the inference path.
All four objective sets are first post-trained on the same 120k-step schedule. The reduced sets level off within this budget, whereas the full ten-objective grid is still improving at 120k steps. We therefore extend the full grid alone to a 200k-step schedule, and at 170k steps it reaches 87.0% on LIBERO-Plus. More objectives thus call for a longer schedule rather than lowering the attainable success rate. Because the simulated benchmark separates the objective sets mainly by training speed, we compare them on the real robot below, where at equal training steps the full grid clearly outperforms policy-only training.

Objectives on the real robot.
On the real robot, the four variants differ noticeably in success rate (Table
4
). Policy-only post-training reaches 76% on chili transfer, 76% on pen manipulation, and 72% on towel folding, while the full ten-objective grid reaches 94%, 90%, and 84%, a gain of 12 to 18 points on every task. The no-flow variant, which keeps the four visual–action objectives, closes most of this gap on chili transfer (92%), but the gap largely remains on pen manipulation (80%), where the two variants that use 3D flow reach 88% and 90%. On all three tasks, success rate improves overall as objectives are added. Relative to the no-flow variant, the 3D flow objectives add 10 points on pen manipulation and 8 on towel folding, the two more demanding tasks, but only 2 on chili transfer, the simplest one.
Where the failures fall.
The losses concentrate in one place. Chili transfer splits its trials evenly into five orientation groups, and 4 of the 6 failures of policy-only post-training fall in the sideways
90
∘
90^{\circ}
group alone. In that group, policy-only post-training succeeds in only 1 of its 5 trials, a success rate of 20%, against 76% over the whole task. The full grid succeeds in 80% of its trials in the same group. Although the group contains few trials, a gap of 20% against 80% is large enough that we read it as a real difference rather than as sampling noise.
Why that group is hard is visible in the training data. Fig.
5
shows that the demonstrations are far from uniform. Most chili grasps cluster near the lengthwise placement, so the sideways orientation is the condition the model has seen least, and it is where policy-only post-training fails most. In the pen demonstrations, most pens start in the middle of a compact region, and few start near its edge. When the pens start near this edge, policy-only post-training succeeds less often.
The two variants differ in one respect. Policy-only post-training never sees 3D flow, neither as a conditioning input nor as a prediction target, whereas the full grid uses it as both. Initialization, data, schedule, and the deployment path are identical, and neither takes flow as input at test time, so the difference at the edge of the demonstrated region is attributable to the flow objectives themselves.
Position encoding.
Removing MM-RoPE lowers LIBERO-Plus at every evaluated checkpoint, by 1.1–2.8 points and by 2.5 at the best checkpoint, with the loss concentrated under robot-initial-state perturbations. Removing the absolute embedding costs 1.5 points at the best checkpoint and up to 4.4 at matched steps, with the gap narrowing as training proceeds. We keep both. Observation and flow tokens lie on the image grid, while action tokens have no image location. We tested two placements for the action tokens, the grid origin and the grid center. The origin is better by less than one point in the best LIBERO success rate. We therefore adopt the grid origin, while considering the difference between the two placements to be small.
4.5
Discarded Designs
While developing joint training with 3D flow, we tried several designs that did not work well. The two below were not run as controlled ablations, but each bears on a natural design choice.
Encoding flow with an image VAE.
Im2Flow2Act
[
38
]
wrote 2D point tracks into image channels and encoded them with a Stable Diffusion autoencoder. Our first version extended this idea to 3D. It mapped the displacement

of each tracked point, relative to its position in the first frame of the clip, directly to the R, G, and B channels and encoded the result with the frozen SDXL image VAE. The VAE reconstructs these images faithfully, and the flow denoising loss decreases normally. The generated flow, however, is nearly the same for every input, so the model has collapsed to an average flow over the dataset. Revising the training data and the patch embedding reduced the collapse but never produced usable flow. We later replaced the image VAE with the 4D VAE of MotionCrafter
[
51
]
, which is trained on geometry and flow.
Gating the flow modality.
To preserve what the LDA backbone learned in pretraining, we first admitted flow gradually through a per-layer gate on the attention logits from the existing tokens to the flow tokens. The gate starts closed and opens on a fixed fast or slow schedule. On RoboCasa-GR1, neither schedule helps. The faster one trails the ungated model by 3.3 points in mean success rate over 21 seeds. All later experiments, including every UniFlowWAM result in this paper, therefore use no gate.
5
Limitations
Flow tracking noise and representation shift.
We use Track4World to generate offline 3D flow pseudo-labels from demonstration videos. These labels can contain temporal inconsistencies, such as an isolated reversal of flow direction within a continuous trajectory. In our pipeline, we use SAM-based segmentation to separate the manipulation foreground from the background and retain only foreground 3D flow for latent encoding. The pretrained 4D VAE
[
51
]
remains effective at compressing these foreground-only inputs.
Limited flow pretraining.
Our 3D flow mid-training uses approximately 1,200 hours of demonstrations, substantially less than the EI-30k corpus used for LDA pretraining
[
24
]
. The added flow expert has not been pretrained alongside the visual–action backbone on that scale.
As tracking models continue to improve, flow extraction is expected to become faster and more accurate, making flow easier to scale for robot training in the same way as video. We leave larger-scale joint pretraining to future work.
