article.headline: 3D场景流成为机器人的第三模态
article.lede: 上交MVIG与上海创智学院等提出UniFlowWAM，把场景级3D流当作与视觉、动作并列的模态，放进同一个扩散Trans
article.problem: 机器人示教只记录「看到了什么」和「做了什么」，却不记录三维场景在这两者之间如何位移：目标图像给出末态而非过程，视频捕捉外观却不描述场景点在3D中怎么移动。此前工作把3D流当作独立模块、推理期注入的先验或额外的预测头，流始终留在策略之外。
article.method: 作者在LDA视觉-动作骨干上为3D流新增一个独立专家，三个专家各自保留归一化、Q/K/V投影与前馈网络，只通过联合自注意力交换信息，并用MM-RoPE把动作、流、视觉token统一到同一时空坐标系。训练使用10个「角色网格」目标，每个目标给三种模态分别指定target、condition或absent，使同一模型同时充当策略、前向/逆动力学与未来状态预测器。流由Track4World离线提取、经冻结的MotionCrafter 4D VAE编码为latent；部署时走直接策略目标，流槽位填学习到的占位符，无需提取流。
article.results: 在RoboCasa-GR1的11个共享评测种子上，带mid-training的UniFlowWAM把成功率从LDA的52.11%提到56.38%（+4.27点），在基线低于50%的10个任务上平均提升6.47点。LIBERO保持98.05%，LIBERO-Plus零样本达87.65%，相机扰动下为96.9%，而该类别最强基线为76.6%。真实ALOHA双臂平台上平均成功率87.0%、过程分92.3，π0.5为68.5%和77.0。真机消融中，全目标网格相对仅策略训练在每个任务高12到18点（如毛巾折叠84%对72%）。
article.why_it_matters: 它给出了一条把几何世界表示内化进策略、而非外挂成模块的可行路线，且推理时不依赖流输入，不增加部署开销。对做世界-动作模型的人来说，这种「多模态角色网格」的训练组织方式可以直接迁移到其他感知模态。
article.limitations: 3D流标签是Track4World从单目视频生成的伪标签，论文自己承认可能存在流动方向反转一类的时间不一致；流mid-training只用了约1200小时示教，远少于LDA预训练所用的EI-30k，新加的流专家从零训练，未与骨干同规模预训练。此外RoboCasa上的绝对提升有限，表中OpenWAM-α公布值为60.5%，高于本文跨种子最好成绩58.9%，而LIBERO已接近饱和，作者也称该基准上1个百分点的差异不具信息量。
article.figure_caption_zh: 网络架构：动作、场景级3D流与未来视觉特征分属三个专家，仅在联合自注意力中交互，由训练目标决定谁是被加噪的预测目标、谁是干净条件，预测出的流latent再由4D VAE解码为点图与场景流。

figure.caption: {Network architecture.} Actions, scene-level 3D flow, and future visual features are three modalities of one diffusion transformer, each processed by its own expert; the experts exchange information only through joint self-attention. The objective decides which modalities are noised targets and which are clean conditions. Predicted flow latents are decoded by the 4D VAE into point maps and scene flow.

email_papers.content:
Abstract
Recent world action models provide visual foresight and future prediction for robot manipulation, but lack explicit mechanisms for compositional skill reuse. Agentic robotics combines code-based planning and reasoning with reusable skills, but often lacks predictive grounding in physical dynamics.

Introduction
Learning-based robotic manipulation has progressed from small task-specific visuomotor policies over a decade ago
to broadly supervised foundation models that connect perception, language, and action
(
Levine et al., 2016
;
Zitkovich et al., 2023
;
Kim et al., 2024
;
Niu et al., 2024
;
Black et al., 2024
;
Bjorck et al., 2025
;
Niu et al., 2025
;
Liu et al., 2025
;
Black et al., 2025
;
Liu et al., 2026
)
.
In parallel, self-supervised video prediction has long been valued as a learning signal to model the world: image inpainting extended to video prediction led to action-conditioned video predictors that can imagine the future before committing to an action
(
Pathak et al., 2016
;
He et al., 2021
;
Tong et al., 2022
;
Finn et al., 2016
;
Assran et al., 2025
;
Ye et al., 2026
)
.
World Action Models (WAMs) couple visual prediction with visuomotor policies, grounding control in representations of how the physical world evolves
(
Ye et al., 2026
;
Kim and others, 2026
;
Yuan and others, 2026
)
.
This predictive grounding is particularly valuable for complex manipulation, where successful execution depends on anticipating object motion, contact, and the consequences of low-level actions. Yet predicted video and action chunks do not by themselves specify how a long-horizon task should be decomposed: which reusable skills to invoke, how to parameterize them, or how to compose them across subtasks.
Predicting the world and/or actions in general can also be expensive, especially as it can be difficult to establish limits on how many degrees of freedom need to be “world modeled” (or teleoperated, in the supervised setting).
Agentic robot systems provide complementary structure to WAMs: a programmatic harness that selects reusable skills and tools, binds them to the current scene, tracks progress, and replans as observations change
(
Liang et al., 2023
;
Fu et al., 2026
;
Zhang et al., 2026
;
Xiao et al., 2026
;
Lu et al., 2026
)
. This programmatic representation makes the structure of multi-step tasks explicit, specifying which skills and tools to invoke, with what arguments, and in what sequence.
Yet agentic robotics often lacks predictive grounding in real-world physical dynamics and does not leverage a learned model of how the world will change as the robot acts.
We advocate for an architecture that combines the foresight and action execution of WAMs with the cognitive efficiency, reusable skills, and potential for future self-improvement of agentic robotics.

Experiments
We evaluate AW-0 on RoboTwin 2.0
(
Chen et al., 2025
)
and 8 real-world tasks spanning parallel-gripper and dexterous-hand embodiments, assessing language following, semantic reasoning, and skill execution, as well as the robustness benefits of hybrid execution in variant scenarios.
Baselines.
We compare four baselines: (1)
π
0.5
\pi_{0.5}
(
Black et al., 2025
)
, a state-of-the-art VLA with strong semantic reasoning; (2) EgoScale
(
Zheng et al., 2026
)
, a VLA pretrained on large-scale egocentric human data; (3) DreamZero
(
Ye et al., 2026
)
, a WAM jointly generating future video and actions; and (4) WLA
(
Yang et al., 2026
)
, an autoregressive model jointly predicting textual subtasks, subgoal images, and actions.
All baselines and the default AW-0 configuration use the same task-specific demonstrations for post-training and follow the same evaluation protocol. The simulation hybrid configuration uses separately collected CaP-generated demonstrations, as described below. Baseline implementation details are provided in Appendix
C
.
3.1

Simulation Experiment
Benchmarks.
We evaluate AW-0 on RoboTwin 2.0.
Following the training-data requirements specified on the official RoboTwin 2.0 leaderboard
1
1
1
https://robotwin-platform.github.io/leaderboard
, we train on 50 clean demonstrations per task (2,500 episodes in total) and evaluate under the benchmark’s two settings:
clean
, with a clean tabletop, plain background, fixed lighting, and no distractors; and
random
, with domain randomization over background and tabletop textures, lighting, tabletop height, and distractor objects. We report the mean success rate over 50 rollouts per task.
Hybrid Evaluation.
We additionally evaluate AW-0 in the hybrid mode, in which the training demonstrations are collected by executing CaP programs written against a set of CaP-X-style
(
Fu et al., 2026
)
primitive APIs that we develop for RoboTwin 2.0. The programs are written automatically by Claude Opus 4.8, following the agentic framework of ASPIRE
(
Lu et al., 2026
)
.

Method

Average Scores from Table
1
.
Main Results.

Table
1
and Figure
4
report the results on RoboTwin 2.0. The two inference modes exhibit complementary strengths.
Overall, AW-0 achieves the highest average success rate of 50.7% across both settings, outperforming all baselines including models designed for broad generalization.
The advantage comes mostly from the clean setting, where AW-0 reaches 80.8%, exceeding the strongest baseline WLA (64.8%) by 16.0 points. Under visual randomization, performance drops to 20.6%, consistent with the challenges of pixel-level O.O.D prediction discussed in prior work
(
Yan et al., 2026
)
. It falls below the VLA baseline
π

\pi_{0.5}
(27.7%) but still outperforms the strongest WAM baseline DreamZero (17.6%) and remains far ahead of EgoScale (2.9%) and WLA (3.6%).
We further observe that hybrid execution improves robustness under distribution shift. In the random setting, it raises the success rate from 20.6% to 29.2%, outperforming all baselines including the strong VLA baseline
π

(27.7%). Relative to its clean-setting performance, the hybrid mode retains
46

of its success rate under randomization, compared with 25% for the default mode. This robustness comes at a cost in the clean setting, where the hybrid mode reaches 63.1%, on par with the strongest baseline, but 17.7 points below the default mode. For further analysis, see Appendix
J
.
3.2
Real-world Experiment
Robot Platforms and Action Space.
We conduct real-world experiments on two platforms: the YAM station, a fixed-base bimanual setup with two 6-DoF arms and parallel grippers, and the Tianji–Sharpa platform, a bimanual robot with two 22-DoF Sharpa dexterous hands.
Both platforms observe three RGB views and act in the unified 64-D state–action space defined in Appendix
A
. Further details on the robot setups are provided in Appendix
D
.
Evaluation Protocol and Metrics.
We use 100 demonstrations per task for post-training and evaluate on the 8 real-world tasks in Table
2
, 4 on each platform, with
3

rollouts per task (3 training seeds, 16 evaluation rollouts per seed) under randomized initial object poses. Task definitions, evaluation settings, and per-task scoring rubrics are provided in Appendix

.

Method

Conclusion
We present AW-0, an agentic world action model that integrates code-based skill planning with predictive dynamics and continuous control. Through joint denoising, the code expert provides structured semantic guidance for video and action generation. An automated annotation pipeline enables learning this planning interface from large-scale robot and human demonstrations. Experiments on RoboTwin 2.0 and real-world manipulation with YAM and dexterous hands demonstrate improvements in language following, semantic reasoning, and skill execution, with hybrid execution further enhancing robustness. These results establish a unified foundation for future work on skill reuse and iterative interaction between programmatic planning, world prediction, and execution, providing a potential agentic system foundation that continually interacts with and learns from environments.

Appendix G
Additional Analysis on Real-world Results
G.1
Impact of Code Expert on Language Following Capability
We further examine whether code-based planning improves the alignment of predicted visual dynamics with task semantics. As shown in Figure
33
, we compare the video generation quality of the right wrist camera of AW-0 with a natural-language subgoal variant (Subgoal) and a model without a planning stream (AW-0 w/o code), under the instruction
“Arrange the fruits so that finally there is only mango in the left bowl.”
This task requires identifying the intended object and grounding the desired outcome in an appropriate interaction. The three variants are evaluated under the same task and scene configuration, with similar but non-identical initial observations from separate rollouts.
The predicted futures reveal distinct differences in task understanding: AW-0 directs the interaction toward the mango, whereas Subgoal exhibits ambiguous targeting between the apple and mango, and AW-0 w/o code targets the apple. These observations suggest that structured skill calls and explicit object arguments provide a more specific planning condition for video prediction than a natural-language subgoal alone. By connecting instruction semantics to concrete interactions, the code stream helps align predicted dynamics with the intended task. Since the action expert also conditions on predictive video representations, this alignment provides a pathway for improving language following, complementing the execution results in our main experiments.

in the first row, the target fruit lies close to the basket rim. As the gripper approaches, its left jaw moves outside the basket, causing the closing motion to grasp the basket wall rather than only the fruit. This case highlights the need to account for surrounding geometry when selecting a grasp. Explicitly estimating the rim geometry and checking clearance along both the approach and closing paths could help reject obstructed grasps and select a more accurate approach direction.

Successful tool use requires coordinating the tool’s opening with its approach trajectory, in addition to holding and positioning the tool itself. Explicitly tracking the tong tips and opening width could help condition actions on the tool’s state. A feedback check that the tips are open and positioned on opposite sides of the fruit before closing could further reduce unsuccessful contact.

article.headline: AW-0：代码规划接入世界动作模型
article.lede: AW-0 以代码、视频、动作三专家联合去噪，在 RoboTwin 2.0 平均成功率 50.7%，随机场景混合执行达 2
article.problem: 近期的世界动作模型能预测视觉未来并生成动作，却缺少组合式技能复用的显式机制；agentic robotics 能用代码规划调用可复用技能，却常缺少对物理动力学的预测基础。AW-0 试图把程序化规划与预测性世界模型接起来。
article.method: AW-0 采用 Mixture-of-Transformers 主干，代码、视频、动作三个专家联合去噪：视频与动作走连续流匹配，代码走离散掩码扩散。自动化标注管线从大规模机器人与人类演示中学习规划接口；推理时可在默认模式与基于 CaP 程序的混合执行间切换。
article.results: 在 RoboTwin 2.0 上，AW-0 跨干净与随机两种设置的平均成功率为 50.7%，高于所有基线。干净设置达 80.8%，比最强基线 WLA 的 64.8% 高 16.0 个百分点；随机设置降到 20.6%，低于 π0.5 的 27.7%，但高于 DreamZero 的 17.6%、EgoScale 的 2.9% 和 WLA 的 3.6%。混合执行把随机设置提升到 29.2%，超过 π0.5 的 27.7%，并保留干净设置的 46%，默认模式仅保留 25%；代价是干净设置降至 63.1%，比默认模式低 17.7 个百分点。真实实验覆盖 2 种 embodiment 的 8 个任务，每任务用 100 条演示、3×16 次 rollout 评估，但材料未给出真实任务的具体分数。
article.why_it_matters: 把程序化规划、世界预测与底层控制放进同一模型，为长程操作的技能复用和持续交互学习提供了可检验的路线；混合执行在分布偏移下的增益也直接指向部署鲁棒性。
article.limitations: 随机场景成功率仅 20.6%，仍低于 π0.5 的 27.7%，说明像素级 OOD 预测仍是短板；混合执行把随机场景提升到 29.2%，却让干净场景从 80.8% 降到 63.1%。此外，真实实验只覆盖 2 种 embodiment、8 个任务，且材料未给出真实任务的具体分数。

email_papers.title: QK-Edit: Revisiting Attention-based Injection in MM-DiT for Image and Video Editing
email_papers.abstract: Multimodal Diffusion Transformers (MM-DiTs) have recently emerged as a powerful framework for unified text-vision synthesis, surpassing traditional U-Net architectures in generative tasks. One key innovation lies in its Multimodal Self-Attention (MM-SA) interaction, where image and text tokens are concatenated and processed via self-attention. However, this mechanism poses significant challenges for editing, rendering conventional U-Net-based attention manipulation methods ineffective. To address this limitation, we propose QK-Edit, a training-free framework that exploits the unique attention dynamics of MM-DiTs for precise text-guided image and video editing. By introducing a novel query-key manipulation strategy, our method isolates and adjusts critical attention components to achieve an optimal balance between prompt fidelity and structural consistency. This enables seamless edits across various tasks, including object addition, object removal, object replacement, changing background, changing material, changing color, and style transformation. Notably, it can be easily implemented with feature replacement in inference. QK-Edit demonstrates superior editing performance on state-of-the-art models, such as FLUX and HunyuanVideo, effectively bridging the gap between generative power and editable flexibility in MM-DiTs, and paving the way for scalable multimodal content creation.

Abstract
Multimodal Diffusion Transformers (MM-DiTs) have recently emerged as a powerful framework for unified text-vision synthesis, surpassing traditional U-Net architectures in generative tasks. One key innovation lies in its Multimodal Self-Attention (MM-SA) interaction where image and text tokens are concatenated and processed via self-attention.
However, this mechanism poses significant challenges for editing, rendering conventional U-Net-based attention manipulation methods ineffective. To address this limitation, we propose QK-Edit, a training-free framework that exploits the unique attention dynamics of MM-DiTs for precise text-guided image and video editing. By introducing a novel query-key manipulation strategy, our method isolates and adjusts critical attention components to achieve an optimal balance between prompt fidelity and structural consistency. This enables seamless edits across various tasks, including object addition, object removal, object replacement, changing background, changing material, changing color, and style transformation.
Notably, it can be easily implemented with feature replacement in inference.
QK-Edit demonstrates superior editing performance on state-of-the-art models, such as FLUX and HunyuanVideo, effectively bridging the gap between generative power and editable flexibility in MM-DiTs, and paving the way for scalable multimodal content creation.

QK-Edit: A training-free, text-guided framework for high-fidelity image and video editing.
Our method leverages strategic query-key manipulation within the vision components of Multimoda Self-Attention (MM-SA) in MM-DiTs to seamlessly perform diverse edits (
e.g
.

), while preserving structural consistency and visual details. Please refer to the supplementary material for more video results at higher resolutions (1K), different aspect ratios (landscape and portrait formats) and longer lengths (129 frames).
1
Introduction
The emergence of Transformer-based diffusion models
[
50
]
, particularly Multimodal Diffusion Transformers (MM-DiTs)
[
5
,
16
,
34
,
70
]
, has redefined the landscape of generative models for image and video synthesis.
Unlike U-Net architectures
[
55
]
, which separate text-vision Cross-Attention (CA) and vision-vision Self-Attention (SA), MM-DiTs leverage a Multimodal Self-Attention (MM-SA) mechanism to process multimodal inputs in a unified embedding space.
MM-SA concatenates text and vision embeddings and computes self-attention on the joint embedding
1
1
1
In this paper, “vision” refers to video or image data.
. This integration enables nuanced and coherent outputs, making MM-DiTs a cornerstone in models such as FLUX
[
5
]
, Stable Diffusion 3.0
[
16
]
, HunyuanVideo
[
34
]
, and CogVideo-X
[
70
]
. However, MM-SA introduces complexities that challenge existing editing paradigms based on attention manipulation
[
22
,
61
]
.
Specifically, due to the joint attention mechanism, textual and visual interactions become deeply intertwined within a single attention matrix, complicating the independent manipulation of textual and visual information. As a result, such editing methods for U-Net models become ineffective in Fig.
2
.
These complexities arise because such previous editing methods rely heavily on the modular nature of U-Net architectures
[
54
]
, where cross-attention facilitates precise text-guided modifications, and self-attention ensures spatial consistency. In contrast, MM-DiTs integrate these attention mechanisms into a unified structure, making it challenging to independently control text-vision and vision-vision interactions without one adversely affecting the other.
A naive solution is to decompose the MM-SA map into four quadrants, each representing a specific interaction between text and vision embeddings and directly apply previous CA-based or SA-based editing techniques such as P2P
[
22
]
or PnP
[
61
]
to the respective attention maps. However, this often leads to undesirable outputs, as illustrated in Fig.
2
.
Through systematic analysis, we observe: (1) text-to-vision attention has negligible impact on the final generation, (2) vision-to-text attention relates vision region to the text token, and finally (3) vision-vision attention defines both spatial and temporal consistency within visual embeddings.
As a result, simultaneous replacement of vision-to-text and vision-to-vision attention is necessary to enable precise control over spatial and temporal properties while adhering to the target prompt. Building upon these insights, we propose QK-Edit, a training-free editing framework that manipulates the attention quadrants of MM-DiTs to achieve high-fidelity edits. In practice, we leverage the fact that text-to-vision attention has minimal impact on the generation and replace the vision component in query and key embeddings of the target image or video with that of the source image or video during the denoising process.
In practice, our proposed strategy is straightforward to implement, requiring only minimal code modifications.

Our QK-Edit can be seamlessly extended to image and video domains, demonstrating its versatility in various generative tasks.
Extensive experiments validate the effectiveness of QK-Edit on state-of-the-art models such as FLUX

Notably, our method enables high-resolution, long-frame video editing with spatio-temporal consistency, overcoming the limitations of previous editing approaches.
Furthermore, the training-free nature of QK-Edit ensures computational efficiency and broad applicability.
QK-Edit represents a pivotal step in bridging the gap between the generative power and editable flexibility of Transformer-based diffusion models.

5
Conclusion
In this work, we present QK-Edit, a simple yet effective training-free framework that exploits the unique attention dynamics of MM-DiTs for precise text-guided image and video editing. Extensive experiments demonstrate the versatility of QK-Edit across a wide range of editing tasks,
e.g
.
, object addition, object removal, object replacement, changing background, changing material, changing color, and style transformation
etc
. More importantly, it can be easily implemented with a few lines of code.
Limitation and future work.
While QK-Edit significantly advances training-free text-guided editing for MM-DiTs, it still exhibits several limitations. First, the accuracy of real video inversion remains challenging, particularly in complex scenes with intricate motions, which can compromise subsequent editing results. Second, QK-Edit inevitably introduces minor unintended modifications in regions that should remain unaltered; future work could incorporate masks to better preserve these areas. Third, as a training-free approach, QK-Edit inherits the limitations of its base generative model, such as suboptimal text rendering and structural deficiencies in handling complex motions (e.g., gymnastic videos). These issues might be alleviated by employing more advanced generative models, which we leave as a promising direction for future research.

article.headline: 在 MM-DiT 上做免训练编辑：只换 QK
article.lede: 不训练、不改架构，只把多模态自注意力里视觉侧的 Q、K 换成源视频的，就能在 FLUX 与 HunyuanVideo 上
article.problem: MM-DiT（如 FLUX、HunyuanVideo）把文本与视觉 token 拼接后在同一个自注意力里计算，文本-视觉与视觉-视觉的交互被揉进同一张注意力图，U-Net 时代靠分别操纵 cross-attention 和 self-attention 的编辑方法（P2P、PnP）因此失效。直接把 MM-SA 拆成四个象限、再套用旧的 CA/SA 编辑策略，往往得到不可用的结果。
article.method: 作者逐块、逐组件地做消融分析：跳过 MM-SA 会显著改变空间布局，跳过 FFN 几乎无影响；把四个注意力象限分别置零后发现，第 2 象限（text-to-vision）影响可忽略，第 3 象限（vision-to-text）决定文本-视觉对应关系，第 4 象限（vision-vision）决定空间与时间一致性。据此，QK-Edit 在去噪过程中记录源图像/视频的视觉侧 Q、K，并在生成目标时替换掉目标侧的对应分量；由于第 2 象限影响微弱，这一替换等价于同时操纵第 3、4 象限，且只需在推理时做特征替换，不必改动被 flash-attention 封装的注意力图。图像编辑在前 30% 推理步内施加替换，视频编辑用前 20% 步。
article.results: 在 PIE-Bench 真实图像编辑上，QK-Edit 取得 CLIP-T 0.264、DINO 0.776、PickScore 22.33，均高于 RF-Solver 的 0.257/0.769/21.98。在 TGVE+ 的生成式视频编辑设定下，对比同样基于 HunyuanVideo 的 DiTCtrl，CLIP_frames 0.951 对 0.904、PickScore 21.24 对 20.01、ViCLIP_dir 0.217 对 0.141、ViCLIP_out 0.268 对 0.242。真实视频编辑设定下为 ViCLIP_out 0.258、CLIP_frames 0.921、PickScore 20.52；作者另建含 43 条、分辨率超过 1K、长度超过 100 帧的 HiLo-Benchmark，QK-Edit 得 CLIP_frames 0.908、PickScore 20.08，优于 KV_concat 的 0.896/19.87。视频实验覆盖 320×320、65 帧到 1280×720、129 帧，均在 NVIDIA A100 上完成。
article.why_it_matters: 它把「编辑能力」从重新训练或额外适配器，降格成推理时的几行 Q、K 替换代码，让新一代 MM-DiT 生成模型可以低成本复用到图像与视频编辑任务上。对后续工作而言，四象限的功能划分本身也是一份可复用的机理解读。
article.limitations: 论文自述的局限包括：真实视频反演在复杂运动场景下仍不准确，会拖累后续编辑；本应保持不变的区域仍会出现轻微意外改动，作者建议未来引入 mask；作为免训练方法，它继承了基座模型的缺陷（文字渲染、体操类复杂运动等）。此外，表 3 中 Flatten 的 ViCLIP_dir 为 0.204，高于 QK-Edit 的 0.196，与正文「在所有指标上超过所有基线」的表述并不完全一致，该结论需打折看待。

VideoMaMa++: Temporally Consistent Video Matting via Preserve-and-Refine Tokens
Sangbeom Lim
Affiliation:
Korea University
Seoung Wug Oh
Affiliation:
Adobe Research
Heeji Yoon
Affiliation:
KAIST AI
https://cvlab-kaist.github.io/VideoMaMa-PlusPlus
Seungryong Kim
Joon-Young Lee
Abstract
Diffusion-based video matting has recently emerged as a leading approach, leveraging video diffusion priors from internet-scale pretraining to achieve strong zero-shot generalization from limited synthetic data. However, the heavy compute of these diffusion backbones limits inference to a short chunk of just 6–24 frames, so even ordinary videos span multiple chunks. Because each chunk is matted independently from coarse mask guidance, existing methods fail to maintain consistency across chunk boundaries, producing flickering edges and discontinuous transparency.
We address this with a mask-guided diffusion-matting framework built on two ideas. The RGB and mask conditioning are represented as separate token streams that interact through full spatio-temporal self-attention, letting the model adaptively combine fine RGB texture with coarse mask layout rather than committing to a fixed channel-wise fusion. On top of this, we propose a novel pair of learnable embeddings, the
preserve token
and the
refine token
, that act as a per-frame conditioning interface and enable a sliding-window inference scheme in which already-generated mattes are propagated across chunk boundaries for local temporal consistency, complemented by a globally shared
reference anchor
at every chunk to prevent error accumulation in long sequences without any additional training.
Across standard video matting benchmarks and in-the-wild long footage, our framework outperforms prior diffusion-based methods in both fine-detail accuracy and temporal consistency, and uniquely maintains consistency across chunk boundaries on long videos.
†
†

, a mask-guided video matting framework that recovers fine-grained details (e.g., hair strands) and scales reliably to long videos.
(a) Per-frame qualitative results on diverse in-the-wild videos.

1
Introduction
Video matting, the task of extracting foreground objects with pixel-level precision from video, is a fundamental component of video editing applications such as background replacement
Zeng et al. (2025)
;
Gao et al. (2025)
;
Ren et al. (2024)
, visual composition
Dalva et al. (2024)
;
Yang et al. (2025a)
, and relighting
Chaturvedi et al. (2025)
;
Ren et al. (2024)
;
Wang et al. (2025)
;
Choi et al. (2025)
. Producing convincing composites in these settings requires alpha mattes that capture fine structures such as hair strands and motion-blurred edges, and that remain temporally consistent across the entire video.
Recent video matting methods leverage priors from video object segmentation models
Huynh et al. (2024)
;
Yang et al. (2025b)
.
However, these methods still rely on dedicated matting annotations and offer limited zero-shot generalization, with most existing methods restricted to human portraits due to the scarcity of matting labels for other categories.
A more recent line of work instead leverages video diffusion priors
Lim et al. (2026)
;
Ge et al. (2025)
, transferring generative knowledge obtained from internet-scale pretraining to close the train–test gap that arises when models are trained only on synthetic matting data.
In particular, VideoMaMa
Lim et al. (2026)
demonstrates that a mask-to-matte diffusion model trained on synthetic data alone can generalize to non-human categories and to in-the-wild video footage.
However, applying diffusion-based matting to real videos exposes a fundamental limitation that hinders general video processing. Diffusion backbones are computationally heavy and cannot process arbitrarily long sequences in a single forward pass; existing methods are therefore chunk-based, handling only 6–24 frames at a time. As a result, even ordinary videos must be split into multiple chunks and processed sequentially. When each chunk is matted independently from its coarse mask guidance, the resulting mattes drift across chunk boundaries, producing flickering edges and discontinuous transparency, as illustrated in Figure
1
(b). The root cause is the inherent ambiguity of coarse mask guidance: a single binary mask admits many plausible fine-grained refinements at object boundaries, and independently processed chunks settle on different ones.
In this work, we present a novel mask-guided diffusion-matting framework designed for long, high-resolution video. At its core, we represent the two guidance modalities, the RGB frames and the coarse mask, as separate token streams alongside the noisy matte tokens, and let them interact through full spatio-temporal self-attention. This design replaces the channel concatenation used in prior U-Net-based diffusion matting
Lim et al. (2026)
and preserves each modality’s distinct structure. The high-frequency RGB texture carries hair and edge cues, while the binary mask provides a coarse but spatially anchored foreground extent, and attention adaptively composes the two at every layer and spatial location. As a result, the model leans on RGB at object boundaries where the mask is unreliable, and on the mask in the interior where it confidently localizes the foreground. We instantiate this on a Diffusion Transformer (DiT)
Peebles and Xie (2023)
;
Wan et al. (2025)
with Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE)
Su et al. (2024)
, which naturally accommodates diverse resolutions and frame counts.
To resolve the chunk-boundary inconsistency described above, we introduce a novel pair of learnable token embeddings, the
preserve token
and the
refine token
, a new conditioning interface for consistent video matting. The preserve token marks a frame whose guidance is already a fine matte, previously generated or ground truth, and tells the model to keep it as a reference. The refine token marks a frame with only a coarse mask and asks the model to refine it into a fine matte consistent with the preserve-tagged references via DiT’s full self-attention. We employ these tokens in a sliding-window inference scheme in which each chunk overlaps a few preserve-tagged frames with the previous chunk, so that already-generated mattes propagate across chunk boundaries and maintain local temporal consistency. To further guard against error accumulation over long sequences, we additionally supply a globally reliable matte as a
reference anchor
at every chunk through the same preserve token, without any additional training.
We validate our framework through extensive experiments on standard video matting benchmarks and in-the-wild footage. Our method outperforms existing video matting approaches on VideoMatte
Lin et al. (2021)
, YoutubeMatte
Yang et al. (2025b)
, and V-HIM60
Huynh et al. (2024)
in both fine-detail accuracy and temporal consistency, and achieves state-of-the-art performance on long-video matting where prior diffusion-based methods fail to maintain consistency across chunk boundaries. The same preserve mechanism also gives users direct control at inference time, for example to interactively correct erroneous outputs by re-tagging specific frames as refine while keeping trusted neighbors as preserve.
Our contributions can be summarized as follows.
•
A mask-guided diffusion-matting framework with
token-level guidance representation
, where the RGB frames and the coarse mask are kept as separate token streams adaptively composed by full spatio-temporal self-attention, rather than fused via channel concatenation as in prior works.
•
A novel
preserve
and
refine
token mechanism that enables chunk-consistent matting through sliding-window inference with overlap-based propagation, complemented by a globally shared
reference anchor
that prevents error accumulation in long sequences without any additional training.
•
State-of-the-art performance on standard video matting benchmarks and in-the-wild long-video footage, with substantial gains in fine-detail accuracy and temporal consistency over prior diffusion-based methods that process video chunk-wise.
2
Related Work
Video matting.
Video matting methods can be broadly categorized into auxiliary-free and auxiliary-guided approaches
Park et al. (2023)
;
Huang et al. (2025a)
. Auxiliary-free methods
Lin et al. (2022)
;
Ke et al. (2022)
;
Li et al. (2024)
typically focus on portrait matting, restricting their applicability to human-centric scenarios. Auxiliary-guided approaches relax this restriction by accepting additional conditioning at the cost of an extra annotation. Trimap-guided methods
Huang and Lee (2023)
;
Seong et al. (2022)
require manual trimap annotations and cannot easily leverage modern segmentation models such as the SAM family
Kirillov et al. (2023)
;
Ravi et al. (2024)
;
Carion et al. (2025)
. More recent mask-guided methods reduce this burden by accepting only a coarse binary mask. MaGGIe
Huynh et al. (2024)
decouples target tracking from matting but struggles to generalize to in-the-wild videos, while MatAnyone
Yang et al. (2025b)
;
Yang et al. (2026)
propagates target-assigned mattes through a memory-augmented architecture trained on dedicated matting datasets such as VM800
Yang et al. (2025b)
and VMReal
Yang et al. (2026)
. Despite these advances, all of these methods remain constrained by predominantly synthetic and human-centric training data, leaving in-the-wild generalization to non-human categories largely unsolved.
Diffusion priors for perception.
Diffusion priors from internet-scale pretraining have been transferred to dense perception tasks. Marigold
Ke et al. (2024)
pioneered this direction by adapting Stable Diffusion
Rombach et al. (2022)
for depth estimation, and the same recipe extends to a range of video perception tasks
Bin et al. (2025)
;
Shao et al. (2025)
;
Hu et al. (2025)
;
Xu et al. (2025b)
, with more recent works
Xu et al. (2025a)
;
Zhang et al. (2026)
extending it to DiT-based backbones.
Diffusion long-video inference.
Diffusion backbones, however, are computationally heavy and limited to short chunks, so applying them to long videos requires a chunk-wise inference scheme. ChronoDepth
Shao et al. (2025)
and DepthCrafter
Hu et al. (2025)
adopt sliding-window inference with overlapping frames between adjacent chunks for local temporal smoothness, but offer no global anchor against drift. A parallel line of work tackles this through auto-regressive generation
Huang et al. (2025b)
;
Chen et al. (2024)
;
Yin et al. (2025)
;
Liu et al. (2025)
;
Cui et al. (2025)
;
Yang et al. (2025c)
;
Ma et al. (2026)
, where each chunk is conditioned on the previous chunk via causal attention with KV-cache reuse. While effective for free-form video generation, this hidden-state propagation does not naturally compose with explicit external conditioning such as a guide mask. Our work instead propagates fully-formed reference mattes between chunks through the preserve token, keeping each chunk fully conditioned on its own user-supplied mask.
Diffusion-based video matting.
In the matting domain, recent diffusion-based methods transfer video diffusion priors to video matting using only synthetic data. The auxiliary-free GVM
Ge et al. (2025)
and the mask-guided VideoMaMa
Lim et al. (2026)
both demonstrate that this prior generalizes to non-human categories and in-the-wild footage, but both inherit the chunk-wise inference limitation of prior diffusion-based perception models. VideoMaMa, the closest mask-guided baseline, additionally fuses RGB, mask, and noise via channel concatenation, entangling the guidance modalities and limiting fine-detail recovery. Our work departs from this design by representing the two guidance modalities as separate token streams, and by introducing the preserve and refine tokens that maintain chunk-wise consistency through globally shared reference anchors and overlap-based local smoothing.

We adopt a mask-guided formulation that decomposes video matting into two subproblems: foreground tracking and boundary refinement. Tracking a target object across a video is itself a demanding task, and entangling it with matte generation forces a single model to simultaneously localize objects and resolve pixel-level matting. By conditioning on a binary mask, we decouple these two challenges and allow our model to focus on generating fine-grained matting details such as hair strands and motion blur, while inheriting localization capabilities from off-the-shelf segmentation models
Ravi et al. (2024)

Carion et al. (2025)

Cheng and Schwing (2022)
;

.
We design an end-to-end pipeline for long-video matting that takes a video and a single user prompt on the first frame as input, and produces a temporally consistent alpha matte across the entire sequence. The pipeline operates in three stages, illustrated in Figure
2
. First, we obtain a per-frame foreground signal by propagating the user prompt across all frames using an off-the-shelf video segmentation model such as Segment Anything
Ravi et al. (2024)
;
Carion et al. (2025)
. Second, the resulting binary mask track is passed to our Diffusion Transformer (DiT) backbone together with the RGB frames to generate fine-grained alpha mattes (Section
3.2
). Finally, long sequences are handled by a chunk-wise inference scheme equipped with preserve and refine tokens (Section
3.3
), which propagates information across chunk boundaries to maintain temporal consistency throughout the video.

3.3
Preserve and Refine Tokens
The formulation above operates on a single clip, while video matting in practice requires handling long sequences. DiT backbones are computationally heavy and cannot process long videos in a single forward pass. A natural solution is chunk-wise inference, where the video is split into fixed-length clips and each clip is processed independently. However, when each chunk is refined from its guidance in isolation, the resulting mattes drift across chunk boundaries, producing flickering edges and discontinuous transparency.
To address this, we introduce two learnable token embeddings, a
preserve token
and a
refine token
, which assign each frame a per-frame mode that determines whether its matte is carried through unchanged or generated from coarse guidance. The preserve token marks anchor frames whose alpha mattes should be retained, while the refine token marks frames that should be converted from coarse guidance into fine-grained alpha mattes. DiT’s full self-attention propagates information from preserve frames to refine frames, yielding mattes that remain consistent across chunks.
Why not auto-regressive diffusion?
We chose to propagate fully-formed reference mattes through the preserve token rather than reuse the previous chunk’s key-value (KV) cache as in auto-regressive diffusion approaches
Huang et al. (2025b)
;
Yin et al. (2025)
. Hidden-state propagation implicitly turns the model into a propagation-based matting framework, where each chunk’s prediction is determined more by the previous chunk’s internal state than by its own mask guidance. This re-entangles localization and fine-detail recovery, the two subproblems we explicitly decoupled by adopting mask-guided conditioning. The preserve token instead exposes the previous chunk’s contribution as an explicit alpha matte, so each chunk remains fully grounded in its own mask guidance while still receiving long-range temporal context through self-attention.
Training.
We train both tokens jointly within a single clip. For each training clip, we randomly select a subset of frames as preserve frames, replace their guide input with the ground-truth alpha matte, and add the preserve token embedding to those frames. The remaining frames receive the refine token together with the standard binary mask guide input. The model is supervised against the ground-truth matte at all frames through the pixel-level supervision, learning to reconstruct the supplied matte at preserve frames and to generate fine-grained mattes from coarse guidance at refine frames. Joint training within a single clip is essential, as it forces the DiT to learn a unified representation in which preserve and refine frames interact through self-attention, rather than treating them as two disjoint tasks.
3.4
Temporally Consistent Inference
We deploy the preserve and refine tokens at inference through two complementary mechanisms: a sliding-window scheme that propagates mattes between adjacent chunks for local consistency, and a reference anchor that supplies a globally reliable matte at every chunk to prevent long-range drift.
Sliding window.
At inference, we apply a sliding-window scheme in which consecutive chunks share an overlap region. The overlapping frames receive the previous chunk’s predicted matte as input together with the preserve token, so that their mattes are passed through unchanged, while the remaining frames receive the guide signal together with the refine token. Although the preserve token is applied only to the overlap frames, DiT’s full attention allows them to condition the generation of every other frame in the chunk, transferring temporal context across the chunk boundary and producing chunk-consistent mattes.
Reference anchor.
The sliding-window scheme alone is vulnerable to error accumulation, since a corrupted overlap frame, e.g., due to occlusion, tracking drift, or other video artifacts, propagates through the preserve token to all subsequent chunks and cascades local failures through the rest of the video. To prevent this, we introduce a
reference anchor
, a globally reliable frame whose matte is supplied as preserve input alongside the local overlap frames at every chunk, providing a stable, error-free signal that the model can attend to throughout inference while the overlap frames continue to carry short-range temporal context. Crucially, this capability emerges directly from the preserve token without any additional training: because the preserve token already learns to treat its inputs as anchors, any user-supplied matte can serve as an anchor for the rest of the video.
This design gives users explicit control over which frame anchors the inference. By default, we reuse the matte predicted at the first chunk as the reference anchor throughout the video, which we find sufficient for most sequences. When the first frame is unreliable due to heavy occlusion, motion blur, or partial visibility, the user can instead select a later frame with cleaner foreground appearance as the reference, allowing the entire sequence to be conditioned on the most informative anchor available.
4
Experiments
4.1
Implementation Details
We build VideoMaMa++ on top of the Wan 2.1 (1.3B)
Wan et al. (2025)
model, training on a combination of image and video matting datasets. To preserve the generative prior, we adapt the DiT to the video matting task using LoRA
Hu et al. (2022)
rather than fine-tuning the full backbone. Training uses 3-frame clips at
1024
×
1024
1024\times 1024
resolution, which provides sufficient capacity for both spatial detail and temporal modeling. At inference, we process the video in chunks of 6 frames with a 2-frame overlap between consecutive chunks, where one of the overlap frames is the reference anchor.
Although the training and inference settings differ in both frame count and chunking behavior, the model generalizes across them due to RoPE’s
Su et al. (2024)
relative position encoding, which removes the dependence on absolute resolution and clip length present in fixed positional embeddings.

The preserve and refine tokens also enable selective refinement of individual frames within a chunk. Given an initial prediction, we identify the frame with the largest error against the ground-truth matte, mark it with the refine token, and mark the remaining frames with the preserve token. 5
Conclusion
We introduce VideoMaMa++, a diffusion transformer model that leverages generative priors for robust video matting, overcoming data scarcity. VideoMaMa++ introduces preserve and refine tokens that enable temporally consistent matting on long videos, addressing a fundamental limitation of diffusion-based approaches confined to short clips. We demonstrate that VideoMaMa++ achieves state-of-the-art performance across diverse benchmarks while producing fine-grained, temporally consistent results on long in-the-wild videos. An annotation-free analysis further shows that our chunk-wise inference exhibits no measurable discontinuity at chunk boundaries, unlike VideoMaMa processing chunks independently. Nevertheless, VideoMaMa++ is more computationally demanding than feed-forward models and, like all mask-guided methods, depends on the upstream mask track; reducing the DiT inference cost and benchmarking temporal smoothness on real footage are promising future directions.
We believe VideoMaMa++ provides a scalable framework bridging the gap between short-clip generation and real-world long-video applications.

Appendix Overview
This supplementary material provides additional details on implementation, evaluation, and qualitative results that could not be included in the main paper due to space constraints.
The document is organized as follows:
•
Section
A
provides additional implementation details, including the training configuration and the list of datasets used to train VideoMaMa++.
•
Section
B
presents qualitative results for the interactive refinement experiment, illustrating how VideoMaMa++ progressively improves its own predictions across iterations through the preserve and refine token mechanism.
•
Section
C
reports zero-shot evaluation of VideoMaMa++ on image matting benchmarks, demonstrating that our model generalizes effectively beyond video to single-image settings.
•
Section
D
discusses annotation noise in the AM-2K benchmark and explains why MAD-T provides a more reliable measure of matting quality than MAD on this dataset.
•
Section
E
describes the guidance-mask generation protocol shared by all mask-guided methods and reports a single evaluation exception on the YouTubeMatte static_0017 sequence, where SAM3
Carion et al. (2025)
must be re-initialized at a later frame to capture an object that enters the scene partway through the video, together with results under first-frame initialization
•
Section
F
introduces an annotation-free test for chunk-boundary discontinuities, which quantifies temporal consistency on in-the-wild videos without ground truth, and validates it on YouTubeMatte.
•
Section
G
reports the computational cost of VideoMaMa++ and prior methods, including a per-stage runtime breakdown and end-to-end throughput with mask generation.
•
Section
H
details the reference-anchor experiments, including the anchor-refresh setting and the corruption protocol used to test robustness to a degraded anchor.
•
Section
I
discusses the limitations of this work: its dependence on the upstream mask track, and the absence of a video matting benchmark that can rigorously evaluate temporal smoothness on real-world footage.
•
Section
J
discusses the positive and negative societal impacts of mask-guided video matting.

Appendix D
AM-2K Justification
We observe that the AM-2K
Li et al. (2022)
ground-truth annotations contain systematic errors that disproportionately penalize fine-detail predictions under the MAD metric. As illustrated in Figure
6
, the AM-2K ground truth often lacks detail within foreground regions, despite the predictions correctly recovering them. Because MAD averages absolute differences over the entire image, these annotation gaps inflate the reported error even when the predicted matte is visually superior. MAD-T, by contrast, restricts the evaluation to the transition region defined by the ground-truth trimap, isolating the boundary detail where matting quality matters most. Under this more reliable metric, VideoMaMa++ achieves state-of-the-art performance against all comparison methods, indicating that the apparent MAD gap on AM-2K reflects annotation noise rather than a true performance deficit.

Initializing SAM3
Carion et al. (2025)
on the first frame fails to track a sheet of paper that the subject begins holding mid-sequence, since the object is not yet visible at initialization. Initializing on a later frame where both are simultaneously visible recovers the correct mask track.
Re-initialized sequence.
For all evaluations, the input masks are obtained automatically without human intervention, with one exception. The static_0017 sequence from YouTubeMatte
Yang et al. (2025b)
presents a granularity ambiguity at the first frame: a sheet of paper that becomes part of the foreground only enters the scene partway through the video, and is therefore not visible at the moment of mask initialization. As a result, when SAM3
Carion et al. (2025)
is prompted on the first frame, the resulting mask track captures only the subject and cannot recover the paper once it appears, as shown in Figure
7
. Because mask-guided matting models, including MaGGIe
Huynh et al. (2024)
, VideoMaMa
Lim et al. (2026)
, and ours, faithfully follow the granularity defined by the input mask, the paper is consequently excluded from the predicted alpha matte. To resolve this without manual annotation, we initialize SAM3 on a later frame (frame 60) where both the subject and the paper are simultaneously visible, and propagate the prompt across the entire sequence. This re-initialized track is used for all mask-guided methods. We note that the MatAnyone
Yang et al. (2025b)
;
Yang et al. (2026)
series is not affected by this issue, as it does not rely on an external mask track. We report this exception in the interest of full transparency.

Appendix H
Reference Anchor Analysis Details
This section details the reference-anchor experiments of Table
3
, all conducted on V-HIM60
Huynh et al. (2024)
.
Anchor choice and refresh.
The first frame may not be representative of later frames. We therefore replace it as the anchor with a random frame or the last frame of the first chunk, which leaves performance nearly unchanged across all metrics. Because the foreground may also change in appearance over long sequences, we further re-anchor to a recent frame every 3 chunks. V-HIM60 sequences contain substantial pose, scale, and appearance variation, yet refreshing yields nearly identical quality to the default setting, so a first-frame anchor does not become stale on this benchmark. Refreshing nevertheless remains available at negligible cost for footage whose appearance changes more drastically.
Corruption protocol.
We corrupt the input of the first frame, which serves as the anchor, rather than the propagated matte. Because the anchor is the model’s own first-frame prediction, a corrupted input yields a degraded anchor matte that is propagated to all later chunks. We consider three corruptions:
•
Poor guidance mask.
We erode (under-segmentation, E) or dilate (over-segmentation, D) the first-frame guidance mask using grayscale morphology with a square kernel of
k
∈
{
5
,
21
}
k\in\{5,21\}
px.
•
Motion blur.
We apply a horizontal motion-blur kernel of
k
∈
{
7
,
15
,
25
}
k\in\{7,15,25\}
px to the first-frame RGB (B), so the model must matte a motion-blurred appearance.
•
Occlusion.
We composite a real animal foreground from AM-2K
Li et al. (2022)
over the subject using its ground-truth matte, enlarging it until at least 99% of the subject is covered, and zero the occluded region of the guidance mask so that it remains consistent with the now-invisible subject (Occ.).
We exclude the corrupted first frame from evaluation, so the metrics measure how the degraded anchor propagates to the rest of the video. This matters most under occlusion, where the input RGB and the ground-truth matte of the first frame disagree. It is also why the clean baseline in Table
3
b differs slightly from the main results: the only difference is the excluded clean first frame.
Results.
Across all corruptions, performance degrades only marginally relative to the clean baseline. Full occlusion is the most severe case, followed by motion blur and poor guidance masks, and larger kernels generally lead to slightly larger degradation. Even with a fully occluded anchor, the model remains close to its clean-anchor performance, indicating that a degraded anchor has only a limited effect on the rest of the video.
Appendix I
Limitation
Dependence on the mask track.
VideoMaMa++ deliberately separates tracking, delegated to a mask generator such as SAM3
Carion et al. (2025)
, from matting, so its robustness is bounded by the quality of the mask track. Errors confined to individual frames of a chunk, such as missing thin structures or drift under motion blur, can be corrected through cross-frame attention to neighboring frames or through interactive refinement (Section
B
). However, if the tracker locks onto the wrong object for an entire sequence, the matte follows that wrong track. This limitation is shared by all mask-guided matting methods.
Evaluating temporal smoothness on real video.
A key limitation of this work, and of video matting research more broadly, is the absence of a benchmark that can rigorously evaluate temporal smoothness on real video. Existing benchmarks
Lin et al. (2021)
;
Yang et al. (2025b)
;
Lim et al. (2026)
are constructed by compositing per-frame foregrounds onto random backgrounds, which provides accurate per-frame ground truth but does not capture the temporal dynamics of naturally captured footage.
As a result, temporal consistency on real-world videos is still largely assessed qualitatively. The annotation-free seam test of Section
F
quantifies one specific failure mode, discontinuities at chunk boundaries, without ground truth. However, it measures neither per-frame accuracy nor flicker within a chunk, and it applies only to methods that process video in chunks, so it cannot compare the overall temporal behavior of arbitrary methods.
Developing a benchmark with reliable ground-truth temporal smoothness, ideally captured rather than composited, remains an open problem for the community.
Appendix J
Societal Impact
Positive Societal Impact.
Our mask-guided video matting framework can substantially benefit creative industries, education, and communication. By reducing the manual effort required for high-quality video matting, the method lowers the barrier to professional-grade video production, enabling independent creators, educators, and small studios to produce polished content without specialized expertise or costly proprietary software. In film and visual effects, it can accelerate labor-intensive rotoscoping workflows, allowing artists to focus on creative decisions rather than frame-by-frame manual labeling. The technology also improves the quality of background replacement in video conferencing and virtual classrooms, supporting remote collaboration and accessibility-oriented applications such as isolating speakers or interpreters in educational content.
Negative Societal Impact.
Despite these benefits, high-quality video matting can be misused. As a core component in video manipulation pipelines, improved matting may facilitate the creation of more convincing deepfakes and manipulated media, contributing to misinformation and the erosion of public trust in video evidence.

article.headline: 给扩散模型加保留/精炼令牌，长视频抠像不再跳变
article.lede: VideoMaMa++ 用分离的 RGB 与掩码令牌流，加上保留、精炼令牌，把扩散抠像推广到长视频，块边界不再闪烁。
article.problem: 扩散式视频抠像依赖互联网规模预训练的生成先验，零样本泛化强，但扩散主干算力开销大，单次推理只能处理 6–24 帧，普通视频也要切成多块。各块仅凭粗糙二值掩码独立生成，而同一掩码对应多种合理的边界细化结果，于是块与块之间会漂移，出现边缘闪烁和透明度不连续。
article.method: 作者在 DiT 主干上把 RGB 帧与引导掩码表示为两条独立令牌流，与噪声令牌一起经完整时空自注意力交互，取代此前 U-Net 式的通道拼接融合。在此基础上引入一对可学习嵌入——保留令牌（preserve）和精炼令牌（refine）：前者标记「已是成品 matte、需保持」的帧，后者标记「只有粗掩码、需细化」的帧。推理时采用滑动窗口，让相邻块共享若干带保留令牌的重叠帧以传递局部时序信息，并在每个块额外送入一个全局参考锚帧，防止长序列上的误差累积，无需额外训练。
article.results: 在 VideoMatte240K、YouTubeMatte 与 V-HIM60 (Hard) 三个基准上，所有指标均为最优：VideoMatte 上 MAD 3.86、Grad 1.79、dtSSD 0.82，对照 VideoMaMa 分别为 4.34、4.06、1.21；YouTubeMatte 上 MAD 1.15（VideoMaMa 1.41）；V-HIM60 (Hard) 上 MAD 1.69（VideoMaMa 2.30）。块边界一致性专项实验中，开启保留令牌后重叠帧两次预测的 MAD 从 0.7128 降至 0.2583，Gradient 从 0.6811 降至 0.1235。无标注接缝检测显示，YouTubeMatte 上 VideoMaMa 有 62/64（MAX）与 63/64（fg-mean）片段在块接缝处变化超出内部帧，而本方法仅 18/64；16 段真实视频上为 14/16 对 7/16。代价是速度：1024×1024 下单卡 H100 为 1.17 FPS、峰值显存 11.3 GB，VideoMaMa 为 3.41 FPS、7.9 GB。
article.why_it_matters: 它把「扩散先验能给出精细发丝级 matte」和「长视频需要跨块一致」这两件事第一次同时做到，且保留了 6 帧推理即可、无需为长视频额外训练的可扩展形式。对视频后期、背景替换这类真正按分钟计的实际管线，块边界闪烁一直是扩散方法落地的直接障碍。
article.limitations: 方法仍依赖上游掩码跟踪：若跟踪器整段锁定到错误目标，matte 会跟着错，这是所有掩码引导方法的共同局限。此外它比前馈模型慢得多（1024² 下 1.17 FPS），且目前缺少能在真实拍摄视频上严格评估时序平滑度的基准，接缝检测只覆盖块边界这一种失效模式。

email_papers.title: GAD: Geometry Attention Distillation for Consistent Video Generation
email_papers.abstract: Video diffusion models generate visually compelling short-term sequences but often struggle to preserve scene geometry and object structure over time. In this paper, we first demonstrate that current video attention cannot identify reliable correspondences across frames, with responses dispersed across multiple regions even after recognizable scene structure has emerged. We argue that reliable cross-frame associations are essential for information exchange as scene structure forms in video generation. Thus, we introduce Geometry Attention Distillation (GAD), which transfers correspondences from a frozen geometry model's attention to video attention. Extracted from clean videos, these correspondences link the same static surface or moving object across frames. Since structure formation begins in deeper layers at higher noise and shallower layers at lower noise, we apply attention distillation at a student layer selected according to the noise timestep. After training, video attention focuses more consistently on corresponding locations. Experiments across all three video backbones demonstrate improved long-range scene consistency and dynamic temporal consistency, with geometric gains across generation lengths. On Wan2.2 5B, GAD improves cross-frame matching accuracy by at least 30% over the Wan baseline on both long-range benchmarks. Notably, GAD achieves these gains without additional inference modules, offering a promising approach to efficient and consistent video-based world simulation. Project page: https://fantasy-amap.github.io/GAD/.

After training, video attention focuses more consistently on corresponding locations.

Notably,

1  Introduction
Recent video diffusion models
[

generate visually compelling sequences from text and images, yet struggle to preserve scene geometry over time and maintain coherent object structure during motion. Such consistency is essential for interactive world modeling
[
68

49

, robotic planning
[
17
,
32
]
, and autonomous driving simulation
[
21
,
64
]
, where generated videos must represent temporally coherent environments.
To improve consistency, existing approaches employ camera-aware positional encoding
[
36
,
72
]
, explicit geometric conditioning
[
53
,
6
,
25
]

[
37
,
78

[
65
,
23

.
However, such guidance does not ensure that video models reliably associate observations of the same scene element across frames, a capability essential for consistent video generation.
To understand how cross-frame associations develop, we examine attention patterns in video models and the emergence of scene structure across noise levels and network depths.
Our analysis shows that video attention cannot reliably identify the same scene element across frames: its responses are often dispersed across multiple regions, even after recognizable scene structure has emerged.
Such ambiguous associations can mix information from unrelated regions, undermining the preservation of scene geometry and object structure across frames.
Ideally, cross-frame attention should connect observations of the same scene element, enabling information exchange that supports consistent structure formation. We further observe that recognizable scene structure begins to emerge in deeper layers at higher noise and shallower layers at lower noise. This suggests guiding video attention where structure and cross-frame associations are beginning to form, with the guidance depth adapted to the noise level. For a source of this guidance, we turn to geometry foundation models
[
35
,
58
]
with promising multi-view matching capabilities.
Probing VGGT-
Ω
\Omega
[
59
]
reveals attention responses that associate the same static surface or moving object across frames, providing geometric correspondence targets for guiding video attention.
Building on these insights, we introduce Geometry Attention Distillation (
GAD
), an attention distillation framework that guides cross-frame associations during structure formation. During training, we extract correspondence targets from the attention of a frozen geometry model on clean videos. The total attention each source token assigns to a target frame serves as a reliability cue for weighting its supervision. We select the student layer for attention distillation according to the noise timestep, guiding cross-frame associations as scene structure forms. At the selected layer, pairwise supervision encourages spatial discrimination within frame pairs, while trackwise supervision extends temporal coverage by matching a common source to multiple target frames. These complementary distillation objectives are optimized jointly with the original video generation loss, transferring cross-frame relations while preserving the flexibility of video representations. After training, video attention focuses more consistently on corresponding regions across frames, while generated videos better preserve scene geometry and moving-object structure.
We evaluate
GAD
on camera-controlled video generation using RealEstate10K and DL3DV-10K for long-range scene consistency and OmniWorld-Game for dynamic consistency.
Across all three video backbones,
GAD
improves geometric consistency in long-range generation and temporal consistency in dynamic generation.
Geometric improvements across generation lengths further support the applicability of
GAD
across backbone configurations and video durations.
Notably, with Wan2.2 5B,
GAD
delivers at least a 30% relative improvement in cross-frame matching accuracy on both long-range benchmarks, without additional inference modules or computations.
Our main contributions are summarized as follows:
•
We analyze cross-frame associations in video models, revealing persistent geometric ambiguities in attention and a noise-dependent shift in the depth at which scene structure begins to form. These observations motivate geometry attention distillation at layers where structure is emerging.
•
We propose
GAD
, an attention distillation framework that transfers geometric correspondence knowledge to video attention for improved cross-frame consistency.
•
Extensive experiments demonstrate that
GAD
improves long-range scene consistency and dynamic temporal consistency across all three video backbones, with consistent improvements across generation lengths and no additional inference modules.

3  Analysis and Motivation
3.1  Attention Patterns in Video Models
Cross-frame consistency requires associating the same scene element across viewpoint changes or object motion. We examine how video attention establishes these associations across noise levels and network depths.
In
Fig.
2(a)
, we fix a source query and a target frame within a single video generation trajectory, and visualize the target frame’s intermediate token features using PCA alongside query-to-target attention responses. The PCA visualizations reveal recognizable scene structure, while the attention maps show whether responses concentrate near the reference correspondence or favor other regions. Further visualization details are provided in
Section
E.1
.
This joint analysis reveals two key findings. First, video attention cannot reliably identify the same scene element across frames. Its responses can remain dispersed across multiple regions, including those with similar appearance or semantics, even after recognizable scene structure has emerged in the PCA features. Second, the emergence of scene structure and cross-frame associations depends on both noise level and network depth. We distinguish three qualitative regimes.
In the
noise-dominated region
, PCA features show little recognizable scene structure, while attention responses remain scattered rather than concentrated around the corresponding region.
In the
structure-formation region
(red boxes in
Fig.
2(a)
), recognizable scene structure begins to emerge, and attention starts to respond to corresponding regions across frames, although competing responses remain. This region occurs in deeper layers at higher noise and shallower layers at lower noise.
In the
structure-established region
, scene layout is more clearly defined in the PCA features and cross-frame associations are more apparent, but they are not necessarily geometrically accurate.
These observations motivate explicitly guiding video attention toward geometrically corresponding regions to help preserve scene and object structure across frames.
Furthermore, the three observed regimes suggest that the placement of this guidance matters. In the noise-dominated region, weak structural evidence may make correspondence supervision difficult to exploit; in the structure-established region, additional guidance may have less opportunity to shape associations that have already formed.
The structure-formation region offers an intermediate stage where correspondence learning has a structural basis while the associations are still developing. We therefore hypothesize that geometric guidance is most effective in this region. Since this region emerges at different depths depending on noise, we adapt the supervision layer to the noise timestep.

5.3  Ablations
Using Wan2.2 5B on DL3DV-10K, we ablate the noise-timestep routing schedule, confidence-aware teacher weighting, and pairwise and trackwise supervision to assess their contributions.
Noise-dependent supervision.
As shown in
Table
4
, fixed-layer supervision (R2–R4) already improves geometric metrics over the Wan baseline (R1), while the proposed noise-timestep routing (R8) outperforms all other configurations (R1–R7); complete metrics appear in
Table
6
. Thus, correspondence targets are useful on their own, while their placement determines how effectively they guide generation. The lower performance of R5–R7 compared with R2–R4 further suggests that varying supervision with noise is insufficient without an appropriate layer choice.
These results support the motivation in
Section
3
: supervision should adapt to the noise timestep to target the structure-formation region rather than constrain a fixed layer throughout denoising.
Contributions of distillation components.
Table
5
shows that transferring teacher correspondences indiscriminately is insufficient: without confidence weighting, matching hit rate falls below the Wan baseline despite modest improvements in camera error. This supports accounting for uncertainty in teacher matches rather than treating every target equally. With confidence weighting, either pairwise or trackwise supervision improves all geometric metrics, while their combination performs best across all seven metrics. The joint gains are consistent with their complementary roles: pairwise supervision discriminates spatial matches within a target frame, whereas trackwise supervision extends correspondence coverage across time.
6  Conclusion
We have presented
GAD
, an attention distillation framework that transfers geometric correspondence knowledge from a frozen geometry teacher to video attention.
Motivated by geometric ambiguities in video attention and the noise-dependent emergence of scene structure,
GAD
guides cross-frame associations during structure formation while preserving the video model’s representational flexibility.
Experiments show that
GAD
consistently focuses attention on corresponding regions and improves long-range scene consistency and dynamic temporal consistency across all three video backbones, with geometric improvements across generation lengths. These gains require no additional inference modules. Our findings highlight geometric correspondence transfer through attention as a promising approach to consistent video generation and video-based world simulation.

Appendix A
Loss and Sampling Details
Sampling source–target relations.
Pairwise supervision samples valid directed frame pairs without replacement, excluding pairs within the same frame. Within each selected pair, source tokens are sampled uniformly without replacement from those with valid cached correspondences. Each selected query is compared with all spatial keys in its target frame. If fewer valid pairs or queries are available than the sampling budget, the remaining entries are masked out.
Trackwise supervision first samples one source frame containing eligible source tokens, then samples tokens that have valid correspondences in at least two other frames. Each source is matched to all of its valid target frames, excluding its own frame. For each target frame, the candidate set contains the Gaussian positive neighborhood and uniformly sampled spatial negatives without replacement from outside that neighborhood. Both schemes resample their relations during training; confidence weights affect the loss reduction rather than the probability of selecting a valid relation.

Appendix B
Implementation Details
B.1  Teacher Targets and Alignment
Reference correspondences for head selection.
We select the teacher layer–head pair using reference correspondences from both static and dynamic scenes. For the static set, we randomly sample 50 DL3DV scenes and estimate per-view depth and camera parameters with VGGT-
Ω
\Omega
, retaining only high-confidence depth estimates. Inspired by CAMEO
[
34
]
, we construct correspondence labels through cycle projection. A sampled source pixel is unprojected into 3D using its depth and camera parameters, then projected into a target view and assigned to a target token. We unproject the center of that target token using the target-view depth and project it back into the source view. A correspondence is retained only if the projections remain in bounds, the projected and estimated depths agree in both directions, and the return location is sufficiently close to the source sample. When multiple samples within a source token pass these checks, we retain the correspondence with the smallest cycle error. These are geometry-derived reference labels, rather than manually annotated ground truth. For the dynamic set, we use the provided ground-truth point correspondences from 30 dynamic scenes in TAPVid-DAVIS
[
15
]
.
Layer–head evaluation and selection.
We randomly sample query tokens from the input frame of each video and examine every global-attention layer–head pair. For each query, we extract the maximum-response location in each subsequent view and its target-frame attention mass, following
Eq.
1
. We compare the predicted locations with the reference correspondences to measure correspondence error and examine the associated attention masses as reliability cues. Considering correspondence consistency across both static and dynamic tokens, we select layer 13, head 10, which provides the best overall performance in this evaluation. All layer and head indices here are zero-based, and this single pair is used for training-label extraction in all experiments.
The evaluation also reveals substantial specialization across heads. For example, layer 13, head 0 captures static-token correspondences well but fails to reliably associate dynamic tokens, whereas layer 12, head 12 captures dynamic-token correspondences well but performs poorly on static tokens. Other pairs exhibit little correspondence consistency for either type of token. These observations motivate selecting a pair using both static and dynamic scenes, rather than relying on either set alone.
Limitations of projection-based labels.
The depth-and-camera cycle projection above assumes a static scene and therefore cannot directly recover correspondences for moving scene elements. We also observe substantial errors around thin structures and closely spaced surfaces, where depth errors and token discretization can associate different surfaces. These limitations can affect methods that rely on such projection-derived supervision, including CAMEO. Extracting correspondences from VGGT-
Ω
\Omega
attention instead exploits the model’s learned cross-view consistency without imposing a static-scene projection constraint. In our observations, this alleviates these failure cases and also supports correspondences for dynamic scene elements.

Human visibility annotations.
We determine the sigmoid mapping from human visibility annotations on DL3DV, using attention labels computed in an 81-frame teacher context. The annotated subset contains 55 scenes: 48 randomly sampled scenes and seven manually selected challenging scenes involving thin structures, occlusions, or out-of-view content. Each annotation page shows one source token and seven target frames sampled from seven temporal intervals, independently of attention mass. Annotators judge whether the source-token content is visible, not visible, or uncertain in each target frame; attention statistics are hidden during annotation. Of 803 judgments, we exclude 230 uncertain cases and retain 573 source-token/target-frame pairs, comprising 401 visible and 172 not-visible cases. These labels assess visibility rather than the localization accuracy of the attention maximum.

The OmniWorld-Game adapters cover the same 0–5-second interval. Voyager and Uni3C use one 81-frame segment, with Voyager retaining its internal prefix mechanism. Camera-scale adaptation.
Warping-based methods are sensitive to camera scale because their explicit scene initialization and geometric conditioning depend on depth estimated from the first frame. Camera translations must therefore be expressed at a scale consistent with this depth; a mismatch produces an inconsistent initial scene and incorrect warps, which can propagate errors into subsequent predictions. This dependence on depth–camera scale calibration is a practical limitation of these explicit geometric methods. To provide suitable geometric inputs for a fair comparison, we carefully align camera translations with the depth scale used by each baseline, using the dataset- and model-specific corrections described below. PCA projection.
For each inspected layer and denoising step, we collect the target frame’s block-output features and project the spatial tokens onto three principal components. PCA is fitted independently for each layer–step pair, with a fixed random seed and deterministic component signs. Each projected channel is scaled using its first and 99th percentiles for RGB display. Because each projection is fitted independently, we compare the spatial organization of regions within each visualization rather than matching colors across cells. As discussed in
Section
3.1
, these maps reveal where recognizable scene structure emerges across noise levels and network depth: little coherent structure is visible in the noise-dominated region, scene regions begin to take shape in the structure-formation region, and the scene layout becomes more clearly defined in the structure-established region. The onset of recognizable structure occurs in deeper layers at higher noise and in shallower layers at lower noise. Viewed alongside the attention maps, the PCA features help distinguish the emergence of scene structure from the development of cross-frame associations, showing that attention can still favor competing regions even when the scene layout is recognizable. This joint analysis motivates placing correspondence supervision near the structure-formation stage and adapting the supervised layer to the noise timestep.
Attention readout.
At the same layer and step, we extract queries and keys after normalization and rotary positional encoding. For the fixed source query, each head’s dot-product scores are softmax-normalized over all video keys. We then retain the target-frame slice and average the resulting probabilities over heads. This readout differs from both the block-output features used for PCA and the learned aggregation MLP used during training. Target-frame responses are displayed after normalization by each map’s maximum, with color mapping and interpolation used only for visualization. Thus, the color scale indicates relative spatial response within a map, not an absolute probability shared across layers or noise levels.
The denoising axis uses the actual model noise timesteps along the sampled inference trajectory. The noise-dependent shift in structure formation motivates our layer-routing schedule, whose generation performance is evaluated against fixed-layer and alternative schedules in

Section
B.1
. For these visualizations, source queries are mapped to the

Heatmaps are normalized within each target frame and displayed with contrast adjustment to highlight the spatial concentration of attention responses. The examples illustrate that selected heads can associate observations of static surfaces and moving object parts.
Appendix F
Limitations and Future Work
GAD
improves scene and dynamic consistency across all three video backbones by transferring geometric correspondences during training, while preserving the original inference procedure. Its current design suggests three directions for further improvement.
More reliable correspondence targets.
Our results demonstrate that attention distillation with geometric correspondence targets improves video consistency. The current implementation extracts these targets from VGGT-
Ω
\Omega
attention, making their quality dependent on the teacher’s matching ability and spatial resolution. This raises a natural question: can more reliable correspondences further improve the effectiveness of attention distillation? Stronger correspondence estimators or complementary sources of matching evidence could provide more accurate and complete supervision, particularly for ambiguous appearance, occlusion, and moving objects. The correspondence-based formulation of
GAD
provides a basis for exploring such alternatives to the current geometry teacher.
Adaptive supervision placement.
Our noise-timestep routing improves geometric metrics over fixed-layer supervision, demonstrating the value of adapting supervision depth to the denoising state. The current layer assignment depends only on the noise timestep and remains fixed throughout training. As the video model learns, the layers that benefit most from correspondence supervision may also change. Conditioning routing jointly on noise timestep and training progress could better match supervision to the model’s evolving representations, extending the current mechanism while preserving the original inference procedure.
Extension to autoregressive video generation.
GAD
improves static and dynamic consistency in Wan’s bidirectional video models. Autoregressive video generation offers a natural next setting, where preserving scene identity over long rollouts and maintaining coherent object motion remain important challenges. The principle of guiding attention with correspondences also applies to associations between newly generated content and preceding frames. Adapting the distillation objectives to the available temporal context under causal attention could help autoregressive models retain scene structure and moving-object identity as generation proceeds. This offers a promising route to extending the benefits demonstrated here to autoregressive generation.
