article.headline: 把几何模型的注意力蒸馏进视频生成注意力
article.lede: 研究者发现视频模型的跨帧注意力常常对不准同一场景元素，于是用冻结的几何模型 VGGT-Ω 的注意力作为对应关系监督，在不
article.problem: 视频扩散模型能生成视觉上连贯的短视频，却难以在时间上保持场景几何与物体结构。作者分析了 Wan2.2 5B 的注意力，发现即使 PCA 特征里已经出现可辨认的场景结构，跨帧注意力响应仍分散在多个区域，无法稳定指向同一场景元素。他们还观察到场景结构的形成与噪声水平和网络深度相关：高噪声时出现在较深层，低噪声时出现在较浅层。
article.method: GAD 从冻结的 VGGT-Ω（1B）第 13 层第 10 个头上提取干净视频的跨帧对应关系，并以源 token 分配给目标帧的总注意力质量作为可靠性权重，对可能不可靠的匹配降权。训练时按噪声时间步选择学生层（t<850 用 L5，850≤t<950 用 L15，t≥950 用 L25），在该层用成对监督和轨迹监督两种交叉熵损失约束注意力的匹配分布，并与原流匹配目标联合优化。教师、对应关系缓存和头聚合 MLP 都只用于训练，推理时仅使用训练后的视频模型。
article.results: 在 RealEstate10K 与 DL3DV-10K 的 15 秒长程生成上，三个骨干的七项指标均优于各自 Wan 基线；Wan2.2 5B 上跨帧匹配命中率在两个数据集都取得至少 30% 的相对提升（RealEstate10K 从 0.263 到 0.350，DL3DV-10K 从 0.257 到 0.335），旋转距离从 6.705 度降到 4.335 度。Wan2.1 14B 在两个数据集全部七项指标上为最优，匹配命中率从 0.413 升到 0.476。OmniWorld-Game 的 5 秒动态生成中，主体一致性从 0.825 升到 0.853、背景一致性从 0.900 升到 0.913；推理峰值显存维持 34.85 GB 不变，运行时间 69.60 秒对 70.44 秒。在 DL3DV-10K 上按 5/10/15 秒分别训练时，各时长的四项几何指标均有改善（如 5 秒命中率 0.529 到 0.571），层路由消融中逐步加深的 R8 方案旋转距离为 4.890 度，优于任意固定层的 6.540 度。
article.why_it_matters: 它把「跨帧该看哪里」作为可监督的训练信号而非推理期外挂模块，为需要时间一致环境的视频世界模型提供了一条不增加推理成本的路径。
article.limitations: 监督质量受制于教师 VGGT-Ω 的匹配能力与空间分辨率，论文也承认该教师的注意力在目标元素被遮挡或缺失时仍可能出现峰值。层路由只依赖噪声时间步、训练全程固定，且方法仅在 Wan 这类双向模型上验证，自回归生成尚未测试；5 秒和 10 秒设定下还出现小幅 FID 或 FVD 折衷。

Abstract
Humanoid mobility over complex terrain requires accurate foot placement and coordinated whole-body motion capable of robust adaptation. Reinforcement learning (RL) policies trained without motion references generalize well across terrains, yet eliciting effective whole-body coordination through reward design and exploration alone remains challenging. In contrast, reference-based methods yield natural motions but struggle to adapt beyond the predefined trajectories in their training data. We introduce a learning framework that bridges these two approaches by using motion data strictly as a training prior. An explicit, self-supervised, attention-based contact planner predicts future body–environment contacts, while a contact-conditioned tracker translates these plans into coordinated whole-body motion. Together, they establish contact as an interface between sensory observations and control actions. This abstraction allows the policy to internalize the contact-aware structure of locomotion rather than directly replicating kinematics. Consequently, a single policy can exploit data-driven motion priors for natural whole-body coordination while retaining the flexibility to discover environment-dependent behaviors through reinforcement learning. Building on the learned contact planner and tracker, a subsequent fine-tuning stage bootstraps their acquired capabilities to explore environment variations beyond those covered by the original motion data. Operating entirely from onboard observations without any reference inputs at deployment, this framework enables versatile humanoid mobility in challenging environments.
Introduction
Deploying humanoid robots in human-centric environments requires capabilities well beyond stable bipedal walking. Traversing cluttered and geometrically constrained environments often demands stepping across sparse footholds, climbing onto obstacles, crawling through confined spaces, or leveraging the upper body for support. These multi-contact behaviors fundamentally diverge from conventional locomotion. Instead of adhering to a prescribed pattern of foot contacts, the robot must continuously determine the spatial, temporal, and anatomical distribution of its environmental interactions. Achieving this capability while remaining robust to disturbances and generalizing to previously unseen terrain remains a central challenge for humanoid mobility.
Reinforcement learning (RL) has proven highly effective for teaching quadrupedal and bipedal robots to swiftly navigate rough
[

, sparse
[

, and even parkour

terrains without reference motions. Similar principles have increasingly been applied to humanoids, enabling robust behaviors that adapt well to terrain variations
[
35
,

]
. However, extending this paradigm to whole-body motion control introduces a massive combinatorial space. The robot must simultaneously determine which anatomical parts establish contact, the precise spatial and temporal distribution of those contacts, and the coordinated kinematics of the remaining degrees of freedom. Encoding these complex interactions indirectly through task objectives requires extensive reward shaping, where minor adjustments can yield drastically different contact strategies
[
48
]
. Consequently, while pure RL provides a powerful mechanism for robustness, reward signals alone offer insufficient structure for efficiently discovering complex whole-body behaviors.
Figure 1
:
Agile and robust humanoid mobility in diverse environments.
Our holistic controller enables a humanoid robot (the Unitree G1) to dynamically traverse diverse and challenging environments, including (a) ladder climbing, (b,j) stage climbing, (c) crawling, (d) vaulting over thin walls, (e) stair climbing, (f) standing up from the ground, (g) jumping down, (h) walking over stepping stones, and (i) sitting down, using a single generalist policy.
An alternative is to provide this structure directly through reference motions. Motion-imitation methods such as DeepMimic
[
34
]
reframe behavior discovery as a constrained tracking problem, enabling highly dynamic and coordinated whole-body motions. More recent systems extend this idea to humanoids using large motion datasets, retargeting, and learned motion priors
[
9
,
13
,
51
,
57
,
22
,
2
,
23
,
54
,

,

]
. Such approaches naturally produce coordinated and human-like behaviors because the reference specifies not only the desired task outcome but also how the entire body should achieve it. Yet a tracking controller can only execute a suitable motion if an appropriate reference can first be generated for the current environment. During deployment in previously unseen environments, this shifts the central problem from control to reference generation.
One solution is therefore to generate these references online. Model-based approaches can use trajectory planners to provide dynamically feasible motions that are subsequently tracked by a learned controller
[
15
,
19
]
, given a user-specified velocity or goal command. This decomposition combines explicit reasoning about environmental geometry with the robustness of learned control. Yet it also makes deployment dependent on a whole-body planner, which can be computationally expensive and inherits the modeling assumptions and failure modes of the planning system. For highly dynamic locomotion with intermittent multi-contact interactions, generating accurate full-body trajectories in real time remains particularly challenging.
Recent work has consequently begun replacing model-based reference generation with learned motion generators or planners
[
52
,
61
,
47
]
. These methods provide a promising route toward more expressive whole-body behaviors by learning the distribution of feasible motions from data. Nevertheless, generating complete motion trajectories remains a high-dimensional prediction problem. Generalization to environment configurations not represented in the motion data often requires substantial data augmentation, and small trajectory errors can become consequential when steppable or contactable regions are sparse. In such environments, producing a motion that is kinematically plausible is insufficient: the predicted interaction with the environment must also be physically accurate.
A related line of work attempts to close the gap between reference-based training and autonomous deployment by composing, augmenting, or distilling reference motions into perceptive policies
[
49
,
43
,
45
,
46
,
3
]
. Wu et al.
[
49
]
, for example, use motion matching to compose retargeted human skills into obstacle-adaptive reference trajectories, train tracking experts, and subsequently distill these behaviors into a vision-based policy. Wang et al.
[
43
]
introduce a generalist humanoid locomotion framework that trains multiple specialist policies for diverse skills and distills their expertise into a single vision-based policy through case-adaptive specialist selection, enabling unified locomotion control without reference motions at deployment. Wang et al.
[
45
,
46
]
propose a hybrid imitation learning framework that combines reference motion tracking with adversarial imitation learning, enabling a unified controller to preserve the naturalness of motion data while improving skill composition and adaptation to procedurally generated environments. Chen et al.
[
3
]
introduce a single perceptive whole-body policy that autonomously transitions between conventional locomotion and parkour skills without reference motions or skill labels at deployment, using terrain-conditioned reference augmentation during training to acquire diverse whole-body behaviors from a small set of motion seeds. These approaches demonstrate that motion data can provide valuable priors for highly dynamic humanoid behaviors. However, they require machinery for adapting and composing full-body motions across environmental variations. As the diversity and required geometric precision of the terrain increase, constructing references that cover the relevant combinations of obstacle geometry, contact location, and skill transition becomes increasingly difficult. This raises a fundamental question: how much of a reference motion does a robot actually need in order to learn generalizable whole-body locomotion?
We argue that the essential information lies not in the complete kinematic-space trajectory, but in its interaction with the environment. Consider how humans traverse irregular natural terrains. Human locomotion does not rely solely on reacting to the terrain immediately beneath the feet; instead, visual information is gathered prospectively to determine suitable future interactions with the environment. Matthis et al.
[
28
]
studied gaze and full-body kinematics during walking over natural outdoor terrain and showed that humans adapt their gaze behavior according to terrain complexity while maintaining a consistent temporal look-ahead strategy. Their findings reveal a tight coupling between perception of the upcoming terrain and the subsequent decisions on contact positions. These observations suggest that successful locomotion over geometrically constrained terrain depends critically on identifying where future contacts should occur, rather than prescribing the complete body trajectory leading to them.
The importance of contact has also been recognized in recent learning-based control methods. Zhang et al.
[
59
]
condition whole-body humanoid control on sequential contact objectives, demonstrating that contact specifications can effectively coordinate diverse whole-body behaviors. Omar et al.
[
32
]
use contact-centric representations to facilitate multi-task robot learning. More recently, Chen et al.
[
5
]
incorporate scene-interaction contacts as prompts for general humanoid whole-body motion tracking. Yu et al.
[
56
]
introduce contact flow, combining key body trajectories with temporal contact signals, as a shared interface for executing and composing long-horizon humanoid loco-manipulation skills. Together, these works demonstrate that contacts provide a compact and effective abstraction for specifying complex robot behaviors.
This perspective becomes even more relevant for whole-body mobility. When traversing sparse and complex terrain, the critical decisions extend beyond selecting footholds: the robot must determine which parts of the body should interact with the environment and where these interactions should occur. Once these contacts are specified, however, there may exist many valid whole-body trajectories that realize them. A hand contact on the top of a ledge, for example, constrains an essential interaction with the environment without uniquely determining the trajectories of the arms, torso, and legs. We therefore propose contact as an intermediate representation between terrain perception and whole-body control. Compared with a full-body reference trajectory, contacts retain the geometrically critical information required for terrain interaction while leaving the policy freedom to adapt the motion connecting them.
This representation also changes the role of motion data. Rather than using demonstrations as trajectories that the robot must reproduce, we use them as training-time guidance for learning which body–environment interactions are useful. Reference motions provide examples of effective contacts during training, while reinforcement learning determines how those contacts should be realized under different robot states and terrain configurations. The resulting policy is therefore not required to remain close to a reference trajectory. More importantly, the reference is removed entirely at deployment: given only the robot state, terrain observation, and a user-specified goal, the policy must autonomously determine appropriate contacts and execute the corresponding whole-body motion. In this way, demonstrations provide structure to the otherwise difficult exploration problem of whole-body locomotion without constraining the policy to the distribution of full-body trajectories contained in the dataset.

(B)

Training follows a backward curriculum: the robot is initialized at progressively earlier states along the reference trajectory, advancing to an earlier state only after the current one has been successfully learned.

In the goal-reaching environment, the contact planner predicts contact plans from map scans, robot proprioception, and the goal command; the whole-body controller executes these plans and is fine-tuned with RL using task (

) rewards. Successful rollouts are stored in the fine-tuning buffer and subsequently used as additional supervision for the contact planner, forming a bootstrapping loop in which planner-generated contacts are executed, validated through successful interaction, and recycled to improve the planner. Reference trajectories are sampled proportionally from the original dataset during fine-tuning to retain the previously learned tracking behaviors.
To autonomously infer these contacts from terrain observations, we build upon attention-based map encoding (AME)
[
12
,
58
]
. AME uses robot proprioception to condition attention over a local terrain representation, allowing the policy to selectively extract terrain features relevant to its current locomotion state. In previous work, this mechanism was learned implicitly and was shown to focus on steppable terrain regions associated with future footholds. Here, we exploit an alternative capability of this architecture: attention provides a natural interface for explicit contact planning. Rather than using attention only to encode terrain into a latent representation for control, we use it to identify task-relevant contact locations on the terrain map. Specifically, our contact planner attends to terrain points conditioned on the robot’s proprioception and a user-specified goal and predicts explicit contact locations directly on the map. This formulation tightly couples when and where the robot should interact with the environment to its evolving physical state. The planner can therefore shift its attention as the robot moves, selecting different terrain regions for feet, hands, and other body contacts according to both local geometry and the current proprioceptive state. This design is particularly suited to sparse terrain, where a small error in a predicted contact can distinguish a feasible interaction from a failure. At the same time, predicting contacts rather than complete whole-body trajectories substantially reduces the dimensionality of the planning problem.
Based on these insights, we introduce a framework that uses an explicit, self-supervised attention-based contact representation as the interface between perception and whole-body control. During training, reference motion data guides the discovery of effective body-environment interactions. Rather than tracking full reference trajectories, the system abstracts the motion data into a task-relevant contact structure. The policy then leverages RL to physically realize these target contacts while optimizing for broader locomotion objectives. This formulation preserves the primary advantage of motion data by providing structured guidance for coordinated whole-body behavior without restricting the agent to strict kinematic reproduction.
This contact-centric representation has several important properties. First, it reduces the dimensionality of the guidance compared to full-body trajectory tracking. Because multiple dynamically feasible motions can realize the same contact objective, the contact representation constrains only the task-relevant interactions while leaving the policy free to explore and optimize the whole-body motion between contacts. Second, contact locations are expressed directly with respect to the environment, providing the geometric precision needed when feasible support regions are sparse. Third, training remains simple: instead of constructing rewards that separately induce climbing, crawling, stepping, and other behaviors, reference contacts can be incorporated through a common contact-tracking objective. Finally, because reference trajectories are used only as training-time guidance, deployment requires neither motion retrieval nor a model- or learning-based motion generator. Terrain diversity can therefore be explored directly through RL rather than covered through exhaustive manual augmentation of reference trajectories.
To obtain diverse and physically feasible whole-body references for training, we use a motion-retargeting pipeline
[
61
]
. It transfers human motion data to the target humanoid while accounting for kinematic constraints. The resulting trajectories, together with their body–environment contact labels and positions, provide contact-aware references as training-time guidance for learning whole-body locomotion.
In summary, this paper introduces a three-stage training framework that progressively transfers knowledge from motion data to a whole-body control policy, with the following contributions:
1)
A contact-informed whole-body tracking training pipeline where the policy is conditioned on contact plans instead of whole-body trajectories.
2)
A supervised learning formulation for contact planning, leveraging human motion data to capture rich and diverse contact strategies, and an attention-based contact planner (ACP) that predicts contact plans for nine body parts (hands, elbows, knees, feet, and pelvis) on rough and discontinuous terrain given a user-specified goal.
3)
An RL fine-tuning stage bootstrapping on planner-generated contact plans that bridges data-driven imitation and reward-driven exploration, enabling generalization to unseen terrains.
4)
A LiDAR-based neural mapping framework that accurately captures fine-grained geometry, including small and thin structures such as ladder rungs, for precise whole-body locomotion.
Through three training stages – contact tracking, contact planning, and RL fine-tuning – our framework progressively reduces its reliance on motion data while preserving the coordinated whole-body behaviors acquired from demonstrations. By isolating task-relevant contact structure, this framework yields a unified generalist policy capable of versatile, coordinated whole-body motion control in previously unseen environments using only onboard sensing (Figure
1
). Figures
2
and
3
provide a visual overview of the method.
Results
0.1
Agile and generalized whole-body locomotion
We tested our unified generalist policy on the Unitree G1 humanoid robot through extensive real-world experiments (Figures
1
and
4
) across a diverse range of challenging indoor and outdoor terrains. Operating without reference motions at deployment, the controller achieves precise, coordinated whole-body locomotion by autonomously adapting its contact strategy to the perceived terrain. The resulting behaviors include stair, ladder, and box climbing, sitting down, standing up from the ground, sparse and composite terrain traversal, and other whole-body interactions.
Importantly, successful execution requires more than recognizing the surrounding geometry: the policy must also select an appropriate interaction strategy according to user-specified goal. Consequently, the same environment can elicit substantially different whole-body behaviors depending on the desired goal position and orientation as well as the geometry. For example, as shown in Figure
5
A, when approaching a box, a forward-facing goal behind the robot can let the robot sit down (a), whereas a forward-facing goal in front of the robot on top of a low box prompts the robot to step onto it (b). If the box is too high, the policy instead leverages a whole-body climbing strategy that uses the hands for additional support (c). When the desired orientation points to the left or right, the policy reorients its body and performs a sideways climbing maneuver (d). When the goal is located farther across the top surface, the robot climbs onto the box, crawls forward toward the target, and then stands up (e). If the goal is on the other side of the box, the robot climbs up, crawls forward, then steps down (f). Similarly, different motions can be generated for getting down from a box given different heights and goal commands (g-i). These examples demonstrate that our unified generalist policy does not simply associate a terrain category with a fixed motion primitive, but jointly interprets environment geometry and goal commands to synthesize appropriate contact patterns and whole-body motions online.
The unified policy further generalizes to unseen and composite terrains, where multiple terrain types and interaction modes are encountered sequentially, as shown in Figure
5
B. In these scenarios, the robot must not only execute individual skills but also autonomously determine how to connect them as the terrain and goal evolve. The policy synthesizes appropriate motion transitions between behaviors without manually designed transition motions, explicit skill-switching mechanisms, or augmentation of the motion dataset for specific terrain compositions. For example, it can transition continuously from walking to climbing, crawling, standing, or other contact-rich behaviors as required by the local geometry and the user-specified goal. In Figures
5
B-a and
5
B-b, only one goal is specified. For the unstructured terrains shown in Figures
5
B-c and
5
B-d, these goals are provided as manually specified intermediate waypoints to guide local traversal. (Global navigation is beyond the scope of this work.) The resulting policy successfully traverses diverse unseen terrains while maintaining its original ability without requiring additional reference motions or terrain-specific motion augmentation. This capability allows a single policy to compose previously learned interaction strategies into continuous whole-body locomotion over terrain configurations not represented in the original motion dataset. Together, these results demonstrate precise, robust, and goal-conditioned whole-body humanoid locomotion that generalizes beyond both the motions and terrain configurations encountered during training. Detailed simulation-based analysis is provided in Section
0.3
.
Figure 4
:
Compositional whole-body motion control.
(a)
Walking - ladder climbing - jumping down.
(b)
Walking - stairs climbing - jumping down.
(c)
Stairs climbing up - stepping stones - stairs climbing down.
(d)
Stairs climbing up - stairs climbing down - box climbing up - jumping down.
(e)
Walking - vaulting - box climbing up.
(f)
Stairs climbing up - beam - jumping down. All motions deployed with a single generalist policy.
Figure 5
:
Simulation results.
The red dots indicate contact plans; the sphere and arrow indicate goal position and orientation.
(A)
The robot selects different interaction strategies on the same type of terrain depending on the desired goal position and orientation.
(B)
The fine-tuned policy generalizes to composite terrains and unseen terrains.
0.2
Failure Recovery
Our learned policy demonstrates strong robustness and emergent failure-recovery capabilities on the real robot, as shown in Figure
6
. Figure
6
A shows that, after an unsuccessful stand-up attempt on uneven terrain, the policy autonomously makes repeated attempts until it successfully recovers to a standing configuration. Figures
6
B and
6
C demonstrate recovery from unexpected falls: when the robot fails to land a jump-down maneuver or is tipped over because of a perception failure, the policy recovers from the ground and resumes locomotion. Figure
6

Simulation-based Evaluations
We use simulation to examine whether contact commands provide sufficient guidance for whole-body tracking, how learned contact plans transfer beyond the reference terrains, and how goal-reaching RL fine-tuning and attention-based planning contribute to this generalization (Figure

We distinguish three terrain groups by their usage in different training stages.
Reference-anchored terrains
are associated with reference motions used in Stage 1/2, and test retention of demonstrated behaviors.
Goal-reaching terrains
are the procedurally generated terrains used for reference-free fine-tuning in Stage 3 and provide a zero-shot transfer test for Stage-2 policies.
Unseen terrains
introduce obstacle composition, task-irrelevant distractors, and surface roughness to test skill transitions, rejection of irrelevant geometry, and traversal of irregular support surfaces, respectively.
The first two groups each contain four categories, defined by support density and the body parts required for support. Dense foot-only terrains provide continuous support for walking, such as stairs and slopes; sparse foot-only terrains require precise foot placement, as on stepping stones and narrow beams. Dense whole-body terrains provide broad surfaces for additional hand or knee support, as in box climbing and get-up transitions; sparse whole-body terrains offer only discrete contacts for multiple links, as in ladder climbing and vaulting. This division distinguishes the placement precision required by sparse support from the multi-limb coordination required by whole-body interactions. and

,

Category-level comparisons pool 3,000 episodes per method and category across three evaluation seeds. The terrain-specific comparisons in Figure

E use 1,000 episodes per method and radar axis, with the ladder axis pooling four variants. The eight curated composite courses are evaluated separately from the unseen-terrain benchmark. For category-level evaluations, success requires reaching within 0.5 m of the active goal horizontally; for sitting, standing, and get-up transitions, the criterion is instead a vertical error below 0.1 m. On the curated courses, success additionally requires reaching the target height and passing through the prescribed course without entering the pit or leaving the traversal lane.
Contact placement error measures the Euclidean distance between commanded and realized contact positions at contact onset, averaged over valid contact events. We report Wilson 95% confidence intervals for success and episode-cluster-robust 95% intervals for contact error. These quantify evaluation uncertainty rather than variability across training runs. Episodes with invalid policy outputs count as failures and are excluded from contact error. Sensor noise, physics randomization, and action delay are disabled to isolate terrain-dependent performance.

Discussion
Our results suggest that contact can serve as a general interface for humanoid mobility, bridging motion data, sensory observation, and whole-body control. Unlike full-body trajectories, contacts only specify where, when, and with which body part the robot should interact with the environment without prescribing how the entire motion should be executed. This abstraction allows demonstrations to provide structured guidance during training while leaving reinforcement learning the flexibility to explore behaviors on new terrain. As a result, a single policy can compose and transition between diverse whole-body behaviors without reference trajectories, skill labels, or manually designed transitions at deployment.
The attention-based contact planner plays an important role in terms of the generalization capability of our framework. Building on attention-based map encoding
[
12
,
58
]
, the planner selectively attends to terrain regions relevant to future contacts conditioned on proprioception and goal commands. Rather than coupling a particular terrain configuration to a specific motion, the policy learns to reason about the local geometry that supports each interaction. This allows contact strategies acquired from demonstrated motions to adapt to new terrain geometries and to be recombined on unseen terrain compositions. Goal conditioning further enables different contact strategies to emerge on the same terrain depending on the desired position and orientation. Together, selective terrain attention and explicit contact prediction provide a structured representation that helps transfer whole-body behaviors beyond the terrain in the reference data encountered during training.
Several limitations remain. First, our current perception and contact representations primarily target terrain-centric 2.5-D interactions. Although the LiDAR-based mapping pipeline captures fine geometric structures such as ladder rungs, more general interactions including overhead contacts, hanging, and manipulation will require richer 3D perception and contact representations. Second, the current system also addresses only local goal-conditioned locomotion rather than global navigation. Additionally, the current pipeline cannot handle aerial motions that do not have distinguishable contact sequences. For example, the contact sequences of a backflip and a vertical jump are essentially the same, despite their substantially different whole-body motions, and therefore cannot be distinguished by our current contact representation.
Future work could extend the contact interface to vision-based and general 3D scene representations, allowing contacts with arbitrary surrounding structures rather than predominantly terrain surfaces. Combining such representations with semantic or global planners could enable humanoids to autonomously select goals and interaction strategies over larger environments. Semantic task inputs could also complement the contact representation in cases where different behaviors share indistinguishable contact sequences, providing additional information to specify the intended motion. Ultimately, walking, climbing, crawling, recovery, and manipulation can all be viewed as different sequences of body-environment interactions. Contact therefore offers a common physical abstraction through which humanoids may compose known interaction strategies into new behaviors in previously unseen environments.
Materials and Methods
Motivation
Developing generalizable whole-body motion control exposes a fundamental tradeoff. Pure RL excels at robust, foot-dominant locomotion, but scaling it to whole-body interactions requires complex reward engineering. Conversely, reference-tracking methods provide strong kinematic priors but bind the policy to the source data, necessitating online trajectory generation during deployment. This dependency creates a bottleneck on sparse or unstructured terrains, where precise environmental interactions must rapidly adapt to unseen geometric constraints.
Bridging these approaches does not require transferring complete reference trajectories. Inspired by biological studies showing that human visual attention prospectively targets future foot placements
[
28
]
, we propose that the essential information lies strictly in the spatial, temporal, and anatomical distribution of environmental interactions. Contact thus serves as a compact intermediate representation. It retains the geometrically critical structure of demonstrated motions while leaving the high-dimensional kinematics underconstrained, allowing a single contact sequence to specify highly complex behaviors.
Motivated by this, we use future whole-body contacts as the interface between perception, planning, and control (Figure
2
A). During training, motion data exposes the robot to coordinated interaction strategies, which an attention-based contact planner learns to predict directly from terrain geometry, robot proprioception, and goal commands. Subsequent RL fine-tuning randomizes the terrain without requiring corresponding reference augmentation. This formulation strictly separates what interactions should occur from how the robot should realize them. The contact planner provides geometrically precise, goal-dependent interaction targets, while RL synthesizes the robust motion required between contacts. Consequently, reference motions act solely as training guidance and are entirely eliminated at deployment, enabling a single onboard-sensing policy to autonomously execute and transition between diverse whole-body behaviors.
To support this framework, we developed two enabling pipelines. First, a constrained motion-retargeting tool extracts diverse contact strategies from human data, preserving key environmental interactions while respecting the robot’s kinematic limits. Second, because precise contact planning on sparse structures like ladder rungs demands high-fidelity perception, we introduce a LiDAR-based neural mapping pipeline that reconstructs detailed local geometry to provide the planner with a consistent terrain representation. Together, these components provide diverse contact-rich training data and sufficiently detailed terrain observations for precise whole-body contact planning in real-world environments.
Contact-Informed Whole-Body Tracker
To provide whole-body reference motions for training, we utilize contact-aware motion retargeting
[
61
]
. It transfers recorded human behaviors to the target humanoid while accounting for differences in morphology, kinematic constraints, and, importantly, body–environment interactions. Direct joint-angle mapping is generally infeasible because human motion data and the robot differ substantially in their kinematic structures and body proportions, often resulting in joint-limit violations, ground penetration, and physically inconsistent contacts. Such artifacts are particularly problematic for contact-rich behaviors such as climbing, crawling, vaulting, etc where the semantics of the motion are largely determined by which body part establishes contact, when the contact occurs, and where it occurs in the environment. We therefore explicitly extract the contact sequence together with the robot kinematics from the dataset.
This retargeting tool first converts human motions from different sources into a unified floating-base and Cartesian landmark representation, followed by spatial rescaling and temporal normalization. For each frame, it solves a nonlinear IK problem over the robot base pose and joint configuration. Position objectives track corresponding body landmarks, including the hips, knees, ankles, toes, shoulders, elbows, hands, chest, and head, while orientation objectives align individual robot limb segments with the corresponding directions in the human skeleton. The optimization additionally constrains the robot within its joint limits and enforces unilateral ground constraints on the feet to prevent penetration. For motions involving richer environmental interactions, minimum-distance constraints against the robot and environment geometry further prevent physically invalid intersections with obstacles such as boxes, stairs, and ladder rungs. Temporal regularization toward the previous solution suppresses frame-to-frame discontinuities, producing smooth trajectories while maintaining consistent contact configurations over time.
In parallel with kinematic retargeting, we explicitly detect and record body–environment contacts at every frame, involving the pelvis, knees, feet, elbows, and hands, which are identified from the simulated contact geometry and associated with the corresponding environmental objects. We record both the active contact sequence and contact locations in the world frame, preserving the temporal contact schedule and spatial relationship between the robot and the environment.

For each body the plan gives a target contact position, expressed in a gravity-aligned frame centered at the robot base and rotated with its yaw so that it is invariant to the robot’s world position and heading, together with a binary occupancy flag indicating whether that body is expected to establish a new contact within the planning horizon.

LiDAR-based Neural Mapping
To provide the controller with accurate height map observations, we design a
LiDAR-based neural mapping pipeline, illustrated in
Figure
8
. The pipeline builds on the depth-based neural
mapping method of Zhang et al.
[
58
]
, adapted to the sensing characteristics of
LiDAR to handle perception noise. We convert each frame’s point cloud into
local grids and use a neural network to predict local elevations with
associated uncertainty. The predictions are fused into a global map, which
the locomotion controller queries during deployment.
Network design.
The main difference from Zhang et al.
[
58
]
lies in the network design. Unlike
depth cameras, which provide a roughly fixed region of interest, our
head-mounted MID-360
[
24
]
LiDAR provides a panoramic view
with sparse hits. Rather than directly predicting a dense reconstruction,
we have the network select one of three modes for each grid:
keep the exact measured height, use the average of the neighborhood, or
discard the value and leave the grid empty. This allows the model to
generalize to arbitrary scan sparsity. Moreover, the disagreement among
the mode logits, interpreted as probabilities for sampling modes, serves
as an uncertainty estimate that accounts for sensing noise. Only non-empty
predictions are processed during fusion.
Fusion prior for overhanging structures.
Since the mapping must handle overhanging structures such as ladders, we
introduce a heuristic prior in the global fusion. When a new prediction falls in the
same grid as an existing confident prediction (uncertainty
<
0.15
<0.15
m) and lies more than 0.15 m
below it, the new point is discarded unless its elevation angle is above
−
40
∘
-40^{\circ}
. This ensures that if an earlier scan observes an
overhanging ladder rung while a later close-by scan only observes the floor beneath
it, the rung is not erased from the global map. Despite this ladder-targeted prior, the mapping module stays effective for all tested terrains.
Training and implementation.
We train on the same meshes as Zhang et al.
[
58
]
, augmented with random
overhanging bars and random ladders leaning against boxes to ensure
performance on sparse overhanging structures. We also simulate per-point
positional noise and ray-divergence
noise
[
33
]
according to the
LiDAR specifications. Since training is formulated as mode
classification, we derive labels from the ground truth and the generated
noisy grids, and train the CNN with a cross-entropy loss. Local grids
cover
[
−
3
,
3
]
[-3,3]
m in
x
x
and
[
−
1.5
,
1.5
]
[-1.5,1.5]
m in
y
y
in the gravity-aligned LiDAR frame,
with a grid resolution of 3 cm. The pipeline runs onboard on the
Jetson Orin NX CPU, updating within 30 ms per 10-Hz LiDAR scan (20000 points).
It is also worth noting that, since the LiDAR is head-mounted, occlusion is
considerably less severe than on the platforms used by Zhang et al.

Overview of the LiDAR-based neural mapping pipeline for height map observations. (A) At each frame, LiDAR points are projected into x-y grid cells and the highest point per cell is retained, producing a 2D local grid map. A neural network then predicts local elevations with associated uncertainty, and the predictions are fused into the global map using odometry. (B) The network uses CNNs to predict per-grid logits over three fill modes: the exact measured value, the neighborhood average, or leaving the grid empty. The mode with the highest logit determines the grid’s elevation prediction, while the disagreement among modes and logits yields the uncertainty estimate. Stage 1 requires approximately 1 day using 3 NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPUs. Stage 2 requires approximately 1 day and 21 hours using 2 RTX 4090 GPUs, and Stage 3 requires approximately 2 days and 6 hours using 4 RTX 4090 GPUs. Planner optimization settings are listed in Table

.
Domain Randomization
At simulation startup we sample, independently per environment, the friction and restitution coefficients, torso mass and center-of-mass offset, joint stiffness and damping scales, and per-joint default-position offsets, from uniform ranges listed in the supplementary methods; each environment retains its sampled values throughout training. At every control step, uniform noise is added to all non-privileged (actor) observations; the height scan additionally receives Gaussian noise per step and a per-episode elevation offset to emulate elevation-mapping drift. These randomizations are active across all three training stages. Details are summarized in Table
S2
.
Terrains and Curriculum
Stages 1 and 2 use
reference-anchored
terrains spatially aligned with the motion-capture clips (stairs of varying step height, gaps, stepping stones, climbing obstacles, balance beams). In Stage 1 the tracker is initialized by Curriculum State Initialization (CSI): each episode begins at a curriculum-set phase of the reference motion, starting near the end of each clip (initial phase
0.9
0.9
) and widening backward toward the start as tracking improves — so the tracker first learns to finish each clip before being asked to execute it from the beginning. Stage 2 disables this phase curriculum and samples initial phases uniformly over each clip. Stage 3 adds
goal-reaching
terrains from a procedurally generated suite (platforms, stepping stones, gaps, balance beams, ladders, pallets), each paired with reachable target patches sampled at reset. These terrains span ten difficulty levels set by step height, gap width, or stone spacing; following the curriculum of
[
38
]
, an environment is promoted a level when it reaches within
0.5
​
m
0.5\,\mathrm{m}
horizontally of its goal at the required height and completes the episode without early termination (gated by an exponentially smoothed per-environment success rate) and demoted when its minimum qualifying goal distance during the episode exceeds
1.0
​
m
1.0\,\mathrm{m}
. The initialization and curriculum-update parameters are summarized in Table
S4
.
Deployment
We deploy the trained generalist policy on the Unitree G1 using its onboard NVIDIA Jetson Orin, with all perception, state estimation, mapping, and policy inference running entirely onboard. The G1’s Livox LiDAR provides point-cloud measurements to DLIO
[
4
]
, which estimates the robot root state and produces a deskewed point cloud. The deskewed point cloud is subsequently processed by our neural mapping pipeline to generate the local height scan used as terrain observation by the policy. The neural mapping module, DLIO, and the learned policy run concurrently on the Jetson Orin, enabling fully onboard perception and control without external computation or sensing.

Network architectures
The tracker and both value networks use three hidden layers with
512, 256, and 128 units and ELU activations.
The contact-conditioned tracker receives 468 features:
375 proprioceptive-history features, 63 height samples,
27 contact-target coordinates, and a three-dimensional goal command.
The kinematics-conditioned variant adds 52 reference features.
Both trackers output commands for 23 joints.
The reference-following and goal-reaching critics receive
353 and 298 features, respectively.
Table
S3
specifies the planner architectures.
The attention planner uses ELU activations in its terrain encoder
and ReLU activations in its context, FiLM, and occupancy MLPs.
The MLP baseline uses two 285-unit hidden layers with ELU activations,
followed by separate terrain-weight and occupancy heads.
Terrain weights are normalized separately for each body,
and occupancy outputs are passed through a sigmoid.
The attention and MLP planners contain 786,993 and 833,322
parameters, respectively.

article.headline: 把接触当接口：人形机器人全身运动新框架
article.lede: ETH团队提出三阶段学习框架，用注意力接触规划器替代全身参考轨迹，单一策略让Unitree G1完成爬梯、钻爬与翻越。
article.problem: 纯强化学习训练的人形机器人策略泛化性好，但要诱导出爬、钻、撑等全身协调动作，靠奖励塑形和探索非常困难且奖励微调就会改变接触策略。基于参考动作的方法动作自然，却只能执行已有轨迹，部署到新环境时还得先在线生成全身参考，在稀疏支撑面上小误差即失败。
article.method: 作者把接触作为感知与控制之间的中间表示：用人体动作重定向数据提取九个身体部位（双手、双肘、双膝、双脚与骨盆）的接触位置与占用标签，先训练一个以接触为条件的全身跟踪器，再训练一个基于地形注意力、以本体感受和目标指令为条件的接触规划器。第三阶段在程序化生成、无参考动作的地形上用强化学习微调，成功回合的接触经事后标注回灌给规划器，形成自举循环；部署时仅依赖机载LiDAR神经建图，不使用任何参考输入。
article.results: 仿真中仅给接触命令的跟踪器在全部地形类别成功率至少98.5%，额外输入参考运动学没有带来一致提升；强化学习微调后，稀疏全身接触地形的成功率提升54.8个百分点，参考锚定地形上的表现仍保持。与最接近的前作MGMT相比，该方法在全部11个地形类别上成功率更高，8条人工组合赛道上平均成功率92.5%，MGMT为58.8%。真机上单一策略完成爬楼梯、爬梯子、钻爬、翻墙、跳下与跌倒后起身；机载LiDAR建图在Jetson Orin NX上处理每帧10 Hz、20000点的扫描耗时在30 ms以内。
article.why_it_matters: 它把「演示数据怎么用」从复现轨迹改成学习交互结构，使动作先验在训练时提供引导、在部署时被完全丢弃，为单一策略组合多种全身技能提供了可扩展路径。
article.limitations: 感知与接触表示目前主要面向地形中心的2.5维交互，悬空抓握、悬挂与操作需要更丰富的三维表示；系统只做局部目标条件运动而非全局导航，且接触序列无法区分后空翻与垂直跳这类空中动作。与PHP、LLP等方法的比较仅为定性表格，作者也承认因平台、数据与感知模态差异，未做同设定定量复现。

page_papers.title: The Sharp Directions Are Against You: Curvature Analysis of Activation Steering
page_papers.abstract: Activation steering adds a vector to a language model's internal representations at inference time. It is a lightweight alternative to fine-tuning for behavioral control. The standard construction, contrastive activation addition (CAA), is fragile, as on many inputs it shifts behavior in the wrong direction. To explain this fragility, we first study the geometry of the steering vector. We introduce steering Hessian, the matrix of second order derivative of the model's behavioral loss with respect to the steering vector. It captures the output behavior response sensitivity of the model under small perturbations of the steering vector along each direction. Its top eigenvectors are sharp directions: tiny perturbations along them can cause large, erratic, input-dependent behavioral swings. Bottom eigenvectors are flat directions: behavior is robust along them. Removing the sharp component of a steering vector approximately preserves its direction and magnitude (cosine > 0.974, norm reduction < 3% for typical settings) while reducing the vector's directional curvature by up to 12x (median 4x across 36 conditions). We evaluate on three model families (Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B), with four behavioral tasks, and 36 token-level conditions. Steering along sharp directions reverses the intended behavior in every condition tested, with anti-steer rates of 53-100%. Sharp directions account for only 1-5% of the CAA vector's squared norm. However, they drive a disproportionate share of the gap between the steered and unsteered next-token distributions during autoregressive generation. We term this one-line correction as sharp removal; it outperforms standard CAA in open-ended generation across all 25 conditions tested. A jailbreaking experiment further shows that sharp directions act as noise rather than signal: they disrupt coherent behavioral control regardless of steering polarity.

Introduction
Large language models (LLMs) generate fluent text across many domains, but controlling their behavior remains a central challenge.
Activation steering
(
Turner et al., 2023
;
Zou et al., 2023a
)
is a training-free approach to behavioral control. A
steering vector

is added to the model’s internal activations at a chosen layer during the forward pass, inducing targeted behavioral changes (e.g., increased honesty or reduced toxicity) without modifying any model parameters.
The standard recipe for building a steering vector is
contrastive activation addition
(CAA)
(
Rimsky et al., 2024
)
, which takes the mean activation difference between positive and negative behavioral exemplars. CAA is simple but fragile in well-documented ways:
•
Anti-steering.
On 30–50% of inputs, the CAA vector shifts behavior in the
opposite
direction from intended
(
Tan et al., 2024
)
.
•
Coefficient sensitivity.
Effectiveness depends on the scaling coefficient
α
\alpha

(
Braun et al., 2025
)
.
•
Behavioral inversion.
As we show in §
5.3

opposite
of the intended behavior.
These failures are typically treated as empirical nuisances. We give a geometric explanation for why they occur and a low-cost method to fix them.
Key insight.
Steering vectors live in a high-dimensional activation space, but not all directions in that space behave the same way. Some are catastrophically sensitive to perturbation. Most are not. CAA’s fragility comes from this anisotropy. The mean-difference construction does not distinguish the catastrophic directions from the stable ones, so a small fraction of the CAA vector’s squared norm (typically 1–5%, the
sharp energy fraction
ε
\varepsilon

Findings 1–2: Anisotropic Hessian, sharp directions are adversarial (36/36)
The steering Hessian is strongly anisotropic at every condition (condition numbers 50–3,727), and steering along its top eigenvectors reverses behavior in all 36 conditions, with zero exceptions. On safety-critical tasks, sharp directions reverse safety-aligned behavior on 100% of inputs at the best layers.

7
Conclusions
We introduced the steering Hessian, a curvature object that decomposes a model’s activation space into directions that are sensitive or robust to perturbation of the steering vector. Five findings hold across all tested conditions: the spectrum of the steering Hessian is strongly anisotropic; sharp eigenvectors reverse intended behavior; the small sharp component in CAA drives a disproportionate share of the steered-vs-unsteered distributional gap during generation; removing the sharp component improves generation; and sharp directions disrupt coherent behavioral control regardless of steering polarity, acting as noise rather than signal. Where prior work on activation steering asks
which direction
to steer, the steering Hessian asks
which directions are safe to steer along
. The answer is determined by the model’s computational geometry, not by the behavioral concept alone.

Appendix I
Why Does CAA Invert?
The mean-difference construction (Eq.
3
) captures the direction of maximal activation variance between contrastive contexts. By Proposition
1
, the sharp subspace corresponds to directions along which the downstream Jacobian most strongly translates perturbations into logit changes. These directions are sensitive to input-specific variation (lexical patterns, response format) rather than to the underlying behavioral disposition. When input-dependent features correlate with behavior in the
opposite
direction from the target disposition, CAA inverts. The flat subspace lies in the approximate nullspace of the Jacobian. It is insensitive to such input-specific variation and isolates the dispositional signal.

We used general-purpose LLM assistants only for writing, editing, formatting, and presentation support.

article.headline: 剔除锐方向：用曲率修复激活引导
article.lede: 作者提出steering Hessian，发现CAA中仅1–5%能量的锐方向会导致反向引导，减去该分量可提升生成。
article.problem: 对比激活加法（CAA）是常用的免训练行为控制方法，但它在不少输入上会把行为推向相反方向，且对引导系数敏感。作者指出，这类失败此前多被当作经验性问题，缺少几何解释。
article.method: 作者将行为损失对引导向量求二阶导，定义steering Hessian，并用Lanczos迭代估计顶部特征向量，得到高曲率的锐子空间。随后把CAA向量投影到该子空间并减去其分量，得到v_cleaned，即sharp removal；单层Hessian约40秒，全流程不到2分钟。
article.results: 在3个模型、4个任务、36个token级条件下，steering Hessian条件数为50–3,727；沿顶部锐方向引导在36/36条件中反向，anti-steer率53–100%。锐方向仅占CAA平方范数的1–5%，剔除后余弦相似度>0.974、范数下降<3%，方向曲率降低1.7–12×（中位数4×）。生成层面，sharp removal在25/25条件优于CAA；拒绝任务中CAA把Qwen拒绝率从78%降到36–44%、Llama从62%降到24–52%，sharp removal恢复到Qwen 88–98%、Llama 74–76%。
article.why_it_matters: 这项工作把激活引导的失败归因于激活空间曲率各向异性，并给出无需训练的一行后处理，可作为现有引导向量的通用清理步骤。锐方向还能在没有对抗优化的情况下暴露削弱安全对齐的方向，因此sharp energy fraction有潜力作为引导向量的安全审计指标。
article.limitations: 局限在于steering Hessian是(v_CAA, α=1.0)处的局部二次近似，大α下高阶项可能主导；实验只覆盖4个任务和3个7–8B指令模型，估计子空间在分布偏移下是否迁移仍未知。
article.figure_caption_zh: 图1：steering Hessian框架概览——激活空间中的行为损失呈各向异性，CAA向量含少量锐方向分量，剔除后得到避开高曲率区的v_cleaned；Llama-3.1-8B第16层真实谱跨三个数量级（κ=3,727）。

figure.caption: {Overview of the steering Hessian framework.} % {(a)}~The behavioral loss landscape is anisotropic in activation space. The CAA vector (gray) has a small component along the sharp eigenvectors (red dashed). Removing this component gives $ _{ {cleaned}}$ (green), which avoids the high-curvature region. % {(b)}~Real eigenspectrum from Llama-3.1-8B, sycophancy, layer 16: eigenvalues span three orders of magnitude ($ = 3{,}727$). The top-$k$ sharp eigenvectors (red, $ {S}_k$) are the component removed from CAA. %% (c) .... % {(d)}~The full pipeline. Sharp removal (step 4, highlighted) is a one-line operation after Hessian computation. Total: approximately 90 seconds per layer.

page_papers.title: DNAlign: Dynamic Null-Space Safe Alignment for LLMs
page_papers.abstract: Ensuring the safe and reliable deployment of large language models (LLMs) remains a fundamental challenge. Existing safety alignment approaches either incur high computational cost or unintentionally disrupt the model's core knowledge, leading to degraded fluency and factual accuracy on benign tasks. This reveals a persistent trade-off between safety and utility. We propose DNAlign, a lightweight alignment framework that integrates control-theoretic optimization with null-space projection. By treating the LLM as a dynamic system, the proposed framework introduces controllable perturbations to steer generation toward safe behavior. A key component is the projection module, which restricts these perturbations to the harmful-related subspace derived from neutral hidden states, thereby preserving general knowledge and response quality. A value function trained on human preference data adaptively optimizes the control signals to align with human safety preferences. Extensive evaluations across multiple LLM backbones demonstrate that our framework consistently reduces harmful outputs while maintaining fluency, coherence, and factual utility. It achieves superior overall performance compared to prior alignment baselines without sacrificing generation diversity. These results indicate that the proposed framework provides an effective and practically deployable solution for safe LLM alignment. Code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/DNAlign.

DNAlign: Dynamic Null-Space
Safe Alignment for LLMs

Bimei Wang
Tiantian Rao

Hong Peng, Bin Hu,  , Tat-Seng Chua

Abstract
Ensuring the safe and reliable deployment of large language models (LLMs) remains a fundamental challenge. Existing safety alignment approaches either incur high computational cost or unintentionally disrupt the model’s core knowledge, leading to degraded fluency and factual accuracy on benign tasks. This reveals a persistent trade-off between safety and utility.
We propose
DNAlign
, a lightweight alignment framework that integrates control-theoretic optimization with null-space projection. By treating the LLM as a dynamic system, the proposed framework introduces controllable perturbations to steer generation toward safe behavior. A key component is the projection module, which restricts these perturbations to the harmful-related subspace derived from neutral hidden states, thereby preserving general knowledge and response quality. A value function trained on human preference data adaptively optimizes the control signals to align with human safety preferences.
Extensive evaluations across multiple LLM backbones demonstrate that our framework consistently reduces harmful outputs while maintaining fluency, coherence, and factual utility. It achieves superior overall performance compared to prior alignment baselines without sacrificing generation diversity. These results indicate that the proposed framework provides an effective and practically deployable solution for safe LLM alignment. Code is available at
https://anonymous.4open.science/r/DNAlign
.
Index Terms:
Large language models, safety alignment, null-space projection, control theory, knowledge preservation, human preference learning.
I
Introduction
Ensuring the safety of Large Language Models (LLMs) is crucial for their reliable deployment in real-world applications. While LLMs have shown strong performance across fields like healthcare
[
19
,
22
]
, finance
[
4
]
, and education
[
1
]
, they also present significant risks by generating harmful or biased content. For example, chatbots may provide harmful instructions or reinforce negative stereotypes
[
3
]
, undermining trust and potentially causing societal harm
[
2
,
23
]
. Thus, two challenges must be addressed: aligning model outputs with human values (safety alignment) and preserving the model’s pre-trained knowledge for factual, fluent responses to benign queries.
Fig. 1:
Comparison of LLMs with/without DNAlign alignment. Unedited models forget security-related knowledge, while our proposed framework preserves safe responses.
Achieving robust safety alignment has led to methods like Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF)
[
32
,
5
]
and Direct Preference Optimization (DPO)
[
18
]
. While these approaches guide models toward safer outputs, they require extensive human labeling, risk overfitting to specific scenarios
[
6
]
, and struggle with balancing safety across diverse real-world prompts. Test-time interventions such as prompt engineering
[
13
]
and controlled decoding
[
10
,
9
]
offer a lightweight alternative, but their robustness remains limited: slight changes in phrasing, domain, or prompt structure often weaken their effect. Existing dynamic intervention methods, although more flexible, can still degrade fluency or factual accuracy on benign tasks, illustrating the difficulty of achieving safety without harming utility.
The second challenge is preserving LLMs’ core knowledge. Safety alignment methods often interfere with models’ ability to generate accurate, fluent responses to benign queries. Full fine-tuning
[
29
,
30
]
or static representation editing can overwrite valuable knowledge
[
8
,
16
]
, while continual learning techniques like Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC)
[
11
]
do not scale well to large models
[
13
]
.
Current efforts to integrate safety alignment and knowledge preservation are fragmented. Post-editing strategies like RLHF after knowledge editing
[
24
]
may overwrite edited parameters, and knowledge-aware prompting
[
26
]
improves accuracy but is sensitive to prompt variations and model biases
[
27
]
. These methods lack a unified framework to optimize both safety and knowledge retention in a single process.
We propose DNAlign, a novel LLM safety alignment method that uses control theory and null-space projection to unify safety alignment and knowledge preservation. Our framework models LLMs as dynamic systems, introducing control signals to direct outputs toward safety while ensuring these signals only affect harmful content, preserving pre-trained knowledge. By training a lightweight value function on human preference data, the proposed method optimizes safety alignment while minimizing interference with the model’s core knowledge. These observations highlight the need for a unified mechanism that jointly addresses safety and knowledge preservation, rather than treating them as separate objectives. Our contributions are as follows:
•
We introduce a unified framework, DNAlign, that unifies efficient safety alignment and knowledge preservation, resolving the trade-off between the two goals.
•
Grounded in control theory, we design dynamic control signals and null-space constraints to suppress harmful content without interfering with pre-trained knowledge, validated through rigorous experiments.
•
We test our method on multiple 7B-scale LLMs (Vicuna-7B and Qwen-7B) and show that it outperforms unedited models and other safety alignment methods in both safety (average reward) and core performance (coherence, diversity), with strong generalization to new harmful scenarios.
II
Related Work
LLMs have shown remarkable utility across domains, but balancing their safety and core knowledge retention remains a critical unresolved issue. Existing research tends to address these two goals in isolation, leading to trade-offs that limit real-world applicability. This section reviews relevant work from three perspectives, safety alignment, knowledge preservation, and their integration, and clarifies the gaps our framework aims to address.
II-A
Safety Alignment for LLMs
To mitigate the inherent risks associated with Large Language Models generating harmful, biased, or unethical content, researchers have developed various alignment methodologies. These approaches can be broadly classified into two categories: pre-training/fine-tuning-based methods which directly modify model parameters, and test-time intervention-based approaches which impose constraints on the output generation process without altering the pre-trained weights.Pre-training and fine-tuning strategies typically leverage extensive human preference data to reshape model behavior. Representative examples include RLHF
[
5
,
32
]
and DPO
[
18
]
. RLHF involves training a reward model using human evaluations of model outputs, subsequently fine-tuning the LLM via reinforcement learning to maximize this learned reward signal
[
17
]
. DPO simplifies this pipeline by directly optimizing the model to align with human preference rankings, thereby obviating the need for an explicit reward model. While effective in enhancing safety, these methods face critical limitations: they require substantial, high-quality human labeling, rendering the process resource-intensive and unscalable.
Moreover, existing methods frequently suffer from overfitting to specific training prompt distributions, resulting in a lack of adaptability to the diverse, unstructured prompts encountered in real-world deployment
[
6
]
. A more profound concern is their reliance on the LLM’s existing knowledge base, which may lead to compliant but factually inaccurate responses in complex domains
[
23
]
. Test-time interventions offer a lighter alternative by directly adjusting outputs. Techniques such as prompt engineering
[
13
]
involve appending safety instrsctions (e.g., avoid harmful advice) to the input prompt, while controlled decoding
[
10
,
9
]
modifies token sampling (e.g., penalizing harmful tokens) to suppress unsafe outputs. These approaches are straightforward to implement but critically lack robustness. Prompt engineering is highly sensitive to subtle rephrasing, which can easily bypass safety constraints. Controlled decoding, conversely, struggles to adapt to the dynamically varying safety needs across different scenarios (e.g., the differential tolerance standards required for educational versus healthcare contexts). Even sophisticated dynamic intervention methods, which model LLMs as dynamic systems, often fail to strike an adequate balance between safety and utility, frequently resulting in degraded fluency or accuracy on benign tasks
[
28
]
.
II-B
Preservation of LLMs’ Core Knowledge
The ability of LLMs to generate fluent, factual responses to benign queries (e.g., general knowledge retrieval or daily tasks) is fundamentally dependent on the vast knowledge accumulated during their pre-training phase. However, the safety alignment process often interferes with this core knowledge, leading to a noticeable performance degradation in domains unrelated to safety
[
8
,
16
]
. Existing knowledge preservation methods face distinct limitations corresponding to their technical methodologies. Early efforts primarily focused on full-model fine-tuning
[
29
,
30
]
, where all LLM parameters are updated by retraining on new, task-specific data. Although this can partially retain pre-trained knowledge, it is computationally demanding and highly susceptible to catastrophic forgetting, where newly introduced data overwrites previously critical information
[
11
]
. To mitigate this, continual learning techniques like EWC
[
11
]
and memory replay
[
20
]
were developed. EWC penalizes updates to parameters deemed critical for old tasks, while memory replay reinforces pre-trained knowledge by resampling and replaying historical task examples.
Unfortunately, existing solutions are ill-suited for modern LLMs with billions of parameters. EWC requires tracking and storing parameter importance estimates, leading to computationally prohibitive overhead, and memory replay necessitates the storage of massive, potentially sensitive, historical datasets
[
13
]
. In contrast, targeted knowledge editing methods offer greater precision by modifying only specific components linked to the knowledge being updated. Some approaches like ROME
[
14
]
and MEMIT
[
15
]
employ causal tracing to precisely identify knowledge neurons or attention patterns associated with specific facts (e.g., Earth’s orbit) and edit these localized structures to update or correct knowledge. More recently, null-space projection methods
[
16
]
have emerged, attempting to protect unrelated knowledge by projecting parameter perturbations into a subspace orthogonal to neutral knowledge representations (e.g., benign prompt features). However, these null-space techniques are predominantly focused on the issue of factual updating and largely neglect behavioral alignment. Consequently, LLMs might retain accurate knowledge but still exhibit harmful behavior, for instance, correctly explaining chemical principles yet providing inappropriate guidance for dangerous experiments.
II-C
Integration of Safety and Knowledge Preservation
Despite substantial progress made in the separate domains of safety alignment and knowledge preservation, the effective and unified integration of these two critical goals remains highly fragmented and largely ineffective. Current attempts predominantly fall into two categories: sequential pipelines and prompt-based methods. Sequential approaches, such as performing knowledge editing followed by subsequent RLHF alignment
[
24
,
25
]
, frequently suffer from detrimental parameter interference, where later alignment updates inadvertently overwrite the earlier knowledge corrections, thus failing to maintain factual accuracy. Prompt-based strategies
[
26
]
provide a lightweight, non-intrusive alternative but suffer from extreme brittleness to prompt rephrasings and are fundamentally incapable of addressing the deeper, harmful associations intrinsically embedded within the model’s learned representations
[
27
]
. These limitations collectively expose a significant gap in the literature: current methods treat safety and knowledge as distinct, independent objectives rather than optimizing them jointly and holistically within a unified, integrated process.
III
Preliminary
To establish a theoretical foundation for DNAlign, this section first elaborates on the generation mechanism of LLMs and then formalizes the mathematical framework for knowledge retention, two core pillars that underpin the design of our safety alignment method.

IV
Method
To address the trade-off between large language model safety alignment and core knowledge preservation, we propose
DNAlign
, a unified framework integrating control theory and null-space projection. This method models LLMs as discrete-time dynamic systems for targeted safety interventions, while leveraging null-space constraints to protect pre-trained neutral knowledge.
IV-A
Dynamical System Formulation for LLMs
To address the inherent trade-off between safety alignment and core knowledge preservation in LLMs, we formalize LLMs as discrete-time dynamic systems. This approach is rooted in control theory and explicitly captures the sequential evolution of internal states during token generation. This formalization enables controllable safety guidance by modeling state transitions and control signal interactions, while strictly preserving the LLM’s pre-trained generation logic such as contextual coherence and semantic fluency. Unlike existing safety methods that modify model weights or truncate outputs, which often lead to knowledge degradation, our dynamic system framework restricts interventions to transient state adjustments, ensuring neutral knowledge encoding remains unaltered.

IV-B
Null-Space Constraints for Knowledge Preservation
A critical challenge in LLM safety alignment is avoiding unintended disruptions to pre-trained neutral knowledge. Such knowledge underpins fluent and factual responses to benign queries, and modifications to it often lead to semantic incoherence or factual errors in non-harmful generation scenarios. To address this, we introduce null-space projection constraints. These constraints explicitly restrict the action scope of safety-oriented control signals to subspaces that are mathematically orthogonal to the subspaces encoding neutral knowledge, ensuring that safety interventions only target harmful content without altering the LLM’s native ability to process neutral prompts.

V
Experiments
The efficacy and robustness of the proposed DNAlign methodology are rigorously evaluated through a set of comprehensive experiments designed to address four core research questions (
RQ
s):
RQ1 (Safety Alignment).
Does the DNAlign intervention effectively reduce the generation of harmful, toxic, or unethical content, achieving superior safety performance compared to state-of-the-art baselines?
RQ2 (Utility Preservation).
Can DNAlign successfully preserve the LLM’s core knowledge and maintain high output quality and fluency when performing harmless or neutral tasks, thereby avoiding the common safety-utility trade-off?
RQ3 (Generalization Capability).
Does the method demonstrate strong generalization to diverse and novel harmful scenarios, specifically those beyond the specific datasets used for constructing the projection space and training the initial value function?
RQ4 (Practical Deployment Efficiency).
Is DNAlign computationally efficient enough for practical, real-world deployment, and how do the key hyperparameters (e.g., step size, number of iterations) influence the resulting safety and utility performance metrics?
To validate the efficacy of our method in achieving a crucial balance between stringent safety alignment and the preservation of core LLM knowledge, we perform comprehensive experiments leveraging the detailed design specifications and data from referenced materials. The subsequent sections systematically elaborate on the research workflow, precise experimental setup, and configurations of established baselines. Following this, we present detailed analyses focusing on six critical experimental aspects. Firstly, performance comparison against established safety baselines. Secondly hyperparameter sensitivity studies (focusing on step size and gradient ascent iterations). Thirdly inference time and computational overhead analysis. Fourthly ablation studies investigating the impact of projection-matrix sample size. Rigorous generalization testing across external harmful benchmarks. Last, detailed impact analysis on a diverse suite of harmless datasets. These structured evaluations provide empirical evidence supporting the method’s superiority and practical viability.

Research Workflow
The experiment follows a four-stage sequential workflow to ensure systematic validation:
1) Preparatory Stage
. We construct the null-space projection matrix using neutral prompts from SHP and train the value function on HH-RLHF under reward-model supervision.
2) Initialization Stage
. All backbone models (Vicuna-7B and Qwen-7B) and baseline methods are configured with unified random seeds and hyperparameters to ensure fair and consistent comparison.
3) Inference and Data Collection Stage
. Our method and all baseline methods are applied to multiple datasets including HH-RLHF, SHP, harmful benchmarks, and harmless benchmarks, to generate outputs and compute the four core evaluation metrics.
4) Result Analysis Stage
. Performance across datasets is aggregated to examine the safety–utility trade-off and to support extended studies such as hyperparameter sensitivity, inference-time evaluation, and projection-matrix ablations.

. The comprehensive quality score provides an overall assessment of model performance by integrating multiple aspects, including helpfulness, accuracy, fluency, and safety. A score of 1 indicates poor quality (e.g., harmful or inaccurate), while 10 reflects exceptional quality (e.g., safe, accurate, fluent). DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B has a 0.82 correlation with human evaluator scores, making it a reliable tool for capturing nuanced quality differences. Together with the other metrics, this provides a rigorous, objective evaluation framework for assessing DNAlign’s safety alignment and knowledge preservation.
V-D
Performance Comparison on HH-RLHF and SHP
The efficacy of our proposed methodology is comprehensively validated across two distinct yet complementary human-preference benchmarks: HH-RLHF and SHP. This dual-benchmark strategy allows for a robust assessment of two critical research objectives, including RQ1, focusing on safety alignment, and RQ2, pertaining to capability preservation in general-purpose interactions. The HH-RLHF dataset, characterized by its mixture of harmful and benign prompts, serves as a crucial testbed for evaluating safety-oriented performance.
Our proposed approach consistently demonstrates superior safety alignment compared to the RE-Control baseline and other tested systems, across both the Vicuna-7B and Qwen-7B foundational models. Specifically, with the Vicuna-7B backbone, our method achieves a substantially higher average reward (1.2258 vs. 0.9614 for RE-Control), alongside notably improved coherence (0.4325 vs. 0.3887), and better comprehensive quality (6.16 vs. 5.94), while maintaining comparable diversity. A similar positive pattern is evident under the Qwen-7B backbone, where our method significantly increases the average reward from 0.7218 to 0.9430 and registers the highest comprehensive quality. These compelling quantitative results collectively demonstrate that a more stringent safety alignment (RQ1) can be effectively realized without compromising the fluency or content richness of the generated responses in mixed harmful–benign scenarios.
To rigorously verify capability preservation (RQ) under general-purpose, non-adversarial conditions, we employ the SHP dataset, which predominantly consists of harmless, everyday human-model queries. In this context, our method successfully maintains or actively enhances the core model’s utility. For the Vicuna-7B model, both the average reward (1.0756) and comprehensive quality (6.97) metrics exceed those of the RE-Control baseline, with diversity and coherence remaining stable.
The experimental results under the Qwen-7B backbone exhibit the same positive pattern, definitively confirming that the introduced intervention strategy does not erode general-purpose performance. Taken together, the consistent performance improvements across these two structurally different datasets underscore that the proposed approach offers a balanced and synergistic enhancement. It simultaneously elevates both safety-oriented and utility-oriented metrics while diligently preserving broad output diversity. This demonstrated robustness, spanning performance and generalizability, suggests that the method is highly suitable for real-world deployments where the simultaneous requirement for uncompromising safety and high-fidelity response quality is a necessity.

V-F
Inference Time Analysis
Beyond effectiveness and hyperparameter robustness, we further quantify the computational overhead introduced by our method to evaluate its deployment practicality (RQ4).
To assess the practical deployment of the proposed framework, we evaluate inference time using the Qwen-7B backbone with 1,000 samples from the HH-RLHF dataset. The experiment compares DNAlign against the RE-Control model and the unedited base model, analyzing the impact of training batches (ranging from 1 to 10) on inference time.
Results show that the base model’s inference time decreases as batch size increases, from 51.059 minutes with 1 batch to 10.556 minutes with 10 batches. The RE-Control model exhibits a similar trend, dropping from 71.518 minutes (1 batch) to 10.617 minutes (10 batches). DNAlign, initially slower (123.734 minutes with 1 batch), also improves as batch size increases, reaching 12.447 minutes with 10 batches, only 1.891 minutes longer than the base model and 1.83 minutes longer than RE-Control.This higher initial overhead is due to DNAlign’s null-space projection module, critical for safety and knowledge preservation. However, the inference time gap narrows significantly with more batches, with DNAlign showing improved efficiency in larger batch sizes due to batch processing optimization. The precomputed projection matrix introduces negligible runtime overhead (less than 0.1% of total inference time), as it is loaded during inference rather than computed on the fly.
Importantly, our method maintains high output quality despite the additional inference time. It achieves a coherence score of 0.4250, surpassing both the base model (0.4192) and the RE-Control model (0.4203). This demonstrates that DNAlign successfully balances safety alignment, knowledge retention, and inference efficiency.
In conclusion, while the safety mechanisms of our method introduce some initial inference overhead, the gap diminishes as batch size increases, with a manageable difference of 1.891 minutes at 10 batches. Combined with superior performance, DNAlign proves feasible for real-world deployment scenarios requiring both efficiency and quality.
