V-G
Research on Sample Parameters of Projection Matrix
To justify the design choices underlying the null-space projection module in our framework, we ablate the number of samples used to construct the projection matrix and analyze its impact on numerical stability and approximation error.
The selection of 20,000 samples for computing the projection matrix with Vicuna-7B is determined as the optimal engineering solution, supported by detailed empirical data and systematic experimental validation. As illustrated by the experimental results, the error exhibits distinct variation patterns across different sample size ranges. When the sample size is within 1 to 100, the model falls into the overfitting region, with errors maintaining at a low level (0.0000035 for 1 sample and 0.00258 for 100 samples) but lacking generalizability due to insufficient data diversity. As the sample size increases to the range of 500 to 3,000, a critical numerical instability region emerges, where the error fluctuates drastically. Specifically, the error rises to 0.587 at 500 samples, drops to 0.0415 at 1000 samples, then surges again to 1.757 at 1500 samples and reaches the peak of 2.923 at 3000 samples. This severe instability makes sample sizes in this range unsuitable for projection matrix construction.
When the sample size exceeds 3000 and enters the convergence region (5000 to 20000 samples), the error stabilizes at a low level and shows minimal fluctuations. At 5000 samples, the error is 0.0105. At 10000 samples, it decreases slightly to 0.00929. At 15000 samples, it rises marginally to 0.00949. And at 20000 samples, it stabilizes at 0.0094. Notably, the 20,000 sample solution not only achieves a stable and low error (0.0094) but also performs comparably to the 50,000 sample variant (error 0.0100) while significantly reducing computational costs. Additionally, the 20,000 sample size far exceeds the model’s hidden dimension (4096), ensuring the projection matrix is built on a complete orthogonal basis that meets the full-rank condition, thus guaranteeing mathematical rigor and excellent generalization ability. This selection also aligns with the sample size used in earlier experiments on Qianwen-7B, enabling fair cross-model comparisons.
In summary, the 20,000 sample approach achieves an optimal balance across four key dimensions: reliability (avoiding the numerical instability region), efficiency (reducing computational costs), performance (maintaining stable low errors in the convergence region), and scientific rigor (supporting cross-model comparisons). It is therefore confirmed as a fully validated and ideal solution for projection matrix computation with Vicuna-7B.

V-H
Generalization Testing
The critical third research question, RQ3, mandates the evaluation of the proposed DNAlign methodology’s generalization capability, specifically, its performance when facing harmful prompts that lie outside the scope of its original training distribution. This assessment is crucial for validating the robustness required for real-world deployment. To this end, we benchmark DNAlign against the base model (Qwen-7B) and the RE-Control baseline across three distinct external harmful datasets: RealToxicityPrompts, ToxiGen, and CategoricalHarmfulQA. These datasets represent diverse facets of safety risks, ranging from general toxicity to highly specific categorical harms. Our evaluation employs four rigorous metrics: diversity, coherence, comprehensive quality, and, critically, average reward for safety alignment. Across all three generalization datasets, DNAlign consistently demonstrates superior performance, particularly in fulfilling the stringent requirements of RQ3. For example, on the RealToxicityPrompts benchmark, which tests responses to model-generated toxic seeds, DNAlign achieves an average reward of 0.7999. This represents a dramatic improvement, showcasing a 137.1% increase over the base Qwen-7B model’s score of 0.3374. Importantly, this substantial safety gain is realized while maintaining highly competitive generative metrics, with diversity at 0.9241 and coherence at 0.4648, thereby mitigating the typical trade-off between safety and utility.
The effectiveness of DNAlign is further substantiated when tested against the extreme toxicity profiles in the ToxiGen dataset. Here, DNAlign’s average reward rises to 0.5465, an extraordinary 229.4% increase relative to the base model. This significant leap underscores the method’s exceptional capability in neutralizing high-risk, targeted harmful content. Even in this high-toxicity context, the fundamental quality of the generated text remains robust, evidenced by a coherence score of 0.2251 and a high diversity score of 0.9615. While acknowledging that DNAlign’s comprehensive quality score may be marginally lower than that of the unedited backbone on some specific datasets, a minor consequence of its stringent safety filtering, the overwhelming and consistent gains observed in the safety alignment metric (average reward) confirm its superior overall contribution. These collective results confirm that the DNAlign approach successfully maintains strong and reliable generalization across a wide spectrum of diverse harmful content. By demonstrating enhanced safety alignment without compromising the model’s core generative capabilities, DNAlign proves its robustness and its capacity to successfully balance the dual requirements of safety and utility, making it exceptionally well-suited for high-stakes, real-world deployment scenarios.

VI
Conclusion
DNAlign is a framework that effectively balances LLM safety alignment with core knowledge preservation, addressing the trade-off seen in existing methods. By integrating dynamic control theory and null-space projection, the proposed framework ensures targeted safety interventions without disrupting the model’s inherent capabilities. Experimental results demonstrate the superiority of our method across multiple datasets, outperforming baseline models like RE-Control in key metrics such as average reward, coherence, and comprehensive quality. Taken together, these findings provide affirmative answers to our four guiding research questions on safety, utility preservation, generalization, and practicality, positioning our framework as a promising solution for reliable and high-quality LLM deployment.

article.headline: DNAlign：在零空间里做安全对齐
article.lede: DNAlign 把 LLM 建模为动态系统，用零空间投影隔开安全干预与预训练知识，宣称在 7B 模型上同时提升安全奖励与
article.problem: 现有安全对齐路线各有代价：RLHF、DPO 需要大量人工标注并可能过拟合特定场景，测试时的提示工程与受控解码又不够稳健，动态干预还常在良性任务上损伤流畅度和事实性。核心难题是安全与效用之间的权衡：既要压住有害输出，又不想动模型已学到的中性知识。
article.method: 作者把 LLM 的逐 token 生成写成离散时间动态系统，状态由各层 KV 缓存和最终层 pre-logit 向量组成，再用梯度上升优化一个瞬态控制信号来提升安全奖励。关键一步是用 SHP 中性提示的最终层隐藏状态做 SVD，构建零空间投影矩阵 P，把控制信号投影到与中性知识子空间正交的方向，理论上避免扰动中性知识。价值函数是 3 层 MLP，在 HH-RLHF 数据上、以 UltraRM-13B 的奖励作为监督训练得到；推理时每个 token 做 100 次梯度上升，投影矩阵离线预计算，加载开销低于总推理时间的 0.1%。
article.results: 在 Vicuna-7B 的 HH-RLHF 上平均奖励为 1.2258，高于 RE-Control 的 0.9614；Qwen-7B 上从基线 0.7218 升到 0.9430。外部有害集上，RealToxicityPrompts 的平均奖励由基线 0.3374 升到 0.7999，论文报告提升 137.1%；ToxiGen 上达到 0.5465，报告提升 229.4%。效率上，Qwen-7B、1000 条样本单 batch 推理需 123.734 分钟，基线为 51.059 分钟；10 个 batch 时降到 12.447 分钟，基线为 10.556 分钟。投影矩阵构建用 20000 条样本，误差稳定在 0.0094。
article.why_it_matters: 若结论成立，这是一条不改权重、在推理时即插即用的对齐路径，对开源模型的安全部署和“安全干预不伤知识”的工程需求有直接参考价值。
article.limitations: 评测主要依赖自动指标：TF-IDF 余弦相似度、UltraRM-13B 奖励和 DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B 打分，缺人工评测，且只验证了 7B 规模骨干。单 batch 推理时间约为基线的 2.4 倍，部分数据集上综合质量还略低于未编辑基线，作者也承认零空间约束是“近似”保护而非严格保证。
article.figure_caption_zh: DNAlign 流程：先从输入提示算出初始状态 s0，再加载离线预计算的零空间投影矩阵 P，把梯度优化得到的控制信号 u_t 投影到零空间后更新系统状态，并据此采样下一个 token。

figure.caption: The sequential process begins by computing the initial state $s_0=\{h_0, o_0\}$ from the input prompt. It then loads the pre-computed null-space projection matrix $P$. In the core step, a gradient-optimized control signal $u_t$ is projected by $P$ to enforce safety alignment while minimally affecting neutral knowledge. Finally, the projected signal $P u_t$ updates the system state $s_{t+1}$, enabling token generation $y_t$.

page_papers.title: Reading, Writing, Sharing, and Interacting with the World through Video
page_papers.abstract: Video foundation models have advanced rapidly in understanding and generating visual sequences, while video world models seek to capture the underlying dynamics of the world they depict. Despite their different objectives, both concern the relationship between video observations and an evolving world. This survey adopts world modeling as a unifying lens for examining these developments. Viewing an observed video as a partial, lossy, and temporally ordered projection of a latent temporal world, we organize the literature around four complementary operations: reading infers world properties from observed video; writing synthesizes video from specified or learned world conditions; sharing integrates understanding and generation through common modeling mechanisms; and interacting predicts and updates world states under actions and evolving observations. This perspective distinguishes temporal coherence in observed or generated sequences from consistency in the underlying world state. Across tasks, representations, models, datasets, and benchmarks, we trace a shift in emphasis from clip-level recognition and perceptual fidelity toward persistent state, controllable evolution, physical and causal validity, and evaluation grounded in interaction and downstream decisions, and we distill the open challenges that follow.
page_papers.content:
Abstract
Video foundation models have advanced rapidly in understanding and generating visual sequences, while video world models seek to capture the underlying dynamics of the world they depict.
Despite their different objectives, both concern the relationship between video observations and an evolving world.
This survey adopts world modeling as a unifying lens for examining these developments.
Viewing an observed video as a partial, lossy, and temporally ordered projection of a latent temporal world, we organize the literature around four complementary operations:
reading
infers world properties from observed video;
writing
synthesizes video from specified or learned world conditions;
sharing
integrates understanding and generation through common modeling mechanisms; and
interacting
predicts and updates world states under actions and evolving observations.
This perspective distinguishes temporal coherence in observed or generated sequences from consistency in the underlying world state.
Across tasks, representations, models, datasets, and benchmarks, we trace a shift in emphasis from clip-level recognition and perceptual fidelity toward persistent state, controllable evolution, physical and causal validity, and evaluation grounded in interaction and downstream decisions, and we distill the open challenges that follow.

Beyond perceptual fidelity and local coherence, claims about the world require state that survives occlusion, revisits, and long horizons; controllable action effects; valid responses to interventions; and, for closed-loop use, latency within the control budget.
Stochastic futures also require coverage and calibration, unified models require matched evidence that information transfers between reading and writing, and systems built for training, planning, or evaluation must improve decisions in controlled environments or real tasks.
Meeting these requirements would move the field from rendering convincing video to modeling how the world changes.

article.headline: 综述：用世界模型视角统一视频理解与生成
article.lede: 综述提出以世界模型为统一视角，用读、写、共享、交互四种操作梳理视频理解与生成，并重新界定评测标准。
article.problem: 视频基础模型在理解与生成视觉序列上进展迅速，视频世界模型则试图刻画视频所描绘世界的底层动力学。两者目标不同，但都涉及视频观测与不断演变的世界之间的关系，此前文献往往分头叙述。
article.method: 该综述把世界建模作为统一透镜，将一段观测到的视频视为某个潜在时序世界的部分、有损、按时间排列的投影。围绕这一视角，作者把文献组织为四种互补操作：reading（从视频推断世界属性）、writing（按指定或学到的世界条件合成视频）、sharing（用共同建模机制打通理解与生成）、interacting（在动作与演化观测下预测并更新世界状态）。
article.results: 这是综述文章，论文未给出具体数字或实验结果；其组织方式是「读、写、共享、交互」四类操作，并以 2×3 的网格（原文图 10、第 8 节）逐格汇总各研究分支的代表性工作，同时给出表 2 作为「更强证据」的评测要求清单。作者据此指出，领域重心正从片段级识别与感知保真度，转向持久状态、可控演化、物理与因果有效性，以及基于交互和下游决策的评测。
article.why_it_matters: 它明确区分了「观测或生成序列的时间连贯性」与「底层世界状态的一致性」，把评价焦点从画面是否逼真推向模型是否真的跟踪世界状态。这对需要闭环决策与规划的下游使用尤为关键。
article.limitations: 作为综述，文章提出的是概念框架与评测建议，本身不含新实验，四类操作与 2×3 网格的划分是作者主张，覆盖面和可操作性仍需实证检验。文中也提到 Gemini 这类闭源系统虽展示了强长上下文视频与音频结果，但公开的设计细节很少，相关比较难以深入。

page_papers.title: A Fix for Softmax and Cross-Entropy
page_papers.abstract: Standard implementations of softmax, log-softmax, and cross-entropy have two numerical bugs. The first bug, Softmax Collapse, rounds the target logit's gradient to zero if that one logit is much larger than the others, resulting in gradients that no longer sum to zero. The second bug, Softmax Cancellation, occurs when student logits are close to teacher logits, and produces non-zero gradients even when the student and teacher logits are equal. We present simple implementations of log-softmax, softmax, and cross-entropy that fix both bugs. Our fix eliminates the previously-observed "Slingshot" phenomenon, speeds up grokking with weight decay, prevents accuracy collapse without weight decay, stops student networks from drifting away from the teacher during distillation, and shows that after memorization, logit growth is bounded by an equilibrium between weight decay and Adam's $ε$ hyperparameter.

8
Conclusion
We have presented simple fixes for two numerical bugs in standard
implementations of softmax, log-softmax, and cross-entropy:
Softmax Collapse
, which zeroes out the dominant logit’s gradient at high
confidence while leaving non-dominant gradients non-zero, and
Softmax
Cancellation
, which loses precision when student logits approach teacher logits
in soft-target distillation.
Rewriting these functions in log space using
softplus
\operatorname{softplus}
,
expm1
\operatorname{expm1}
, and
log1p
\operatorname{log1p}
restores accurate, zero-sum gradients across bf16,
fp32, and fp64 without internally casting to higher
precision.
Fixing these bugs eliminates Slingshot loss spikes during grokking, prevents
student networks from drifting away from the teacher during distillation, and
reveals that logit margins under AdamW and weight decay naturally converge to
log
⁡
(
1
/
ϵ
)
\log(\nicefrac{{1}}{{\epsilon}})
.
Though the extreme margins and near-zero student–teacher gaps probed by our
experiments are uncommon in standard large-scale training, our fixed functions
are easy drop-in replacements that can be implemented without meaningful
slowdown, and may prove useful whenever models make high-confidence predictions
or distill from close teachers.

article.headline: Softmax 与交叉熵的两个数值 bug 及修复
article.lede: DeepMind 作者指出标准 softmax 与交叉熵存在两个数值缺陷，并给出可直接替换的对数空间实现。
article.problem: 标准实现先把 logit 减去最大值再取指数，虽然避免了溢出，却留下两个数值 bug。其一是 Softmax Collapse：当目标 logit 远大于其他 logit 时，目标梯度会被舍入为零，而非目标梯度仍为正，导致梯度之和不再为零。其二是 Softmax Cancellation：在软标签蒸馏中，学生与教师 logit 接近时，分别计算两个 softmax 再相减会损失精度，即使两者相等也留下非零梯度。
article.method: 作者把 log-softmax 与交叉熵改写成在对数空间中计算：不再把 e^{-m} 加到 1.0 上，而是用 softplus(-m) 表示损失，并把目标类从 log-sum-exp 中排除，让目标梯度由非目标梯度取负求和得到。针对软标签蒸馏，则直接用学生的 logit 与学生和教师 logit 之差 δ 构造 log(q/p)，并借助 expm1、log1p 计算 q−p，最后减去均值以保证梯度之和为零。论文给出了 JAX 实现，并称不改变精度，也就是不内部提升到 fp64。
article.results: 论文给出的精度悬崖为 bf16 约 5.5、fp32 约 16.6、fp64 约 36.7，一旦 logit margin 超过对应阈值，标准实现就会把目标梯度舍入为零。修复后 margin 能平滑越过这些悬崖，并在 AdamW 加权重衰减时停在 ε 决定的平衡点 log(1/ε)：ε=10⁻⁸ 时约 18.4，ε=10⁻¹² 约 27.6，ε=10⁻¹⁶ 约 36.8。在 a+b mod 31（λ=1，ε=10⁻⁸）上，标准交叉熵为 94.3±5.4% 测试准确率，修复版为 100.0±0.0%；bf16 下分别为 93.3±7.4% 与 100.0±0.1%。在 a²+b² mod 97（λ=0）上，标准交叉熵在约第 1250 步 margin 触及 16.6 时出现一次尖峰，测试准确率从 61% 掉到 23%，而修复版继续平滑升到 85%；a³+b mod 97 上则是从 60% 掉到 21%。蒸馏实验中，教师权重初始化学生、T=4、ε=10⁻⁸ 时，修复版在 bf16、fp32、fp64 下都保持在 KL=0 与 100% 准确率，标准版在 bf16 下会把约 10⁻³ 的残差梯度放大成参数漂移。
article.why_it_matters: 这两个 bug 是库级实现问题，而不是模型设计问题，修复只需替换几个算子就能消除 grokking 中的 Slingshot 尖峰、避免无权重衰减时的准确率崩塌，并让蒸馏中的学生不再被舍入噪声推离教师。论文还给出 margin 收敛到 log(1/ε) 的解析解释，把 Adam 的 ε 从“数值防零小量”提升为控制 logit 增长的实际超参数。
article.limitations: 实验集中在模运算 grokking 基准上的 1 层 Transformer 与 2 层 MLP，论文本身也承认如此大的 margin 与如此接近的师生 logit 差距在大规模常规训练中并不常见，方法在真实大模型上的收益尚未验证。此外，margin 平衡点的推导依赖权重衰减与 Adam 平稳点假设，且需要用 LaProp 并直接更新 v 才能覆盖 ε→0 的极端情形。

page_papers.title: UniFlowWAM: A Unified World-Action Model with Visual Semantics and 4D Geometry
page_papers.abstract: Robot demonstrations record what the robot saw and what it did. They do not specify how the 3D world changed in between. Scene-level 3D flow describes it by tracking 3D scene points, providing the world representation with 4D geometry. Prior work has used flow to improve robot policies. Flow served as an intermediate prediction that a separate model converts into actions, as a prior injected at inference time, or as an extra output learned together with the action. In all of these designs, flow stays outside the policy, as a separate module or as an extra prediction head. We introduce UniFlowWAM, a Unified World-Action Model that makes 3D scene flow a third modality on par with vision and action. Its world representation therefore covers both visual semantics, through future visual features, and 4D geometry, through 3D flow, and flow receives its own supervision. UniFlowWAM is a diffusion transformer with one expert per modality, and the three experts exchange information through joint attention. We train UniFlowWAM under a ten-objective role grid, where each objective assigns every modality exactly one of three roles, namely target, condition, or absent. The same model thus serves as a policy, as forward and inverse dynamics, and as a predictor of future visual features or 3D flow. We evaluate UniFlowWAM on RoboCasa-GR1, LIBERO, and LIBERO-Plus in simulation, and on four real-world bimanual manipulation tasks. On RoboCasa-GR1, UniFlowWAM raises the success rate of its base model without flow from 52.1% to 56.4%. It preserves in-distribution success on LIBERO at 98.1% and reaches 87.7% zero-shot on LIBERO-Plus. On the real robot, it achieves 87.0% average success, compared with 68.5% for the strongest baseline.

Abstract
Robot demonstrations record what the robot saw and what it did.
They do not specify how the 3D world changed in between.
Scene-level 3D flow describes it by tracking 3D scene points, providing the world representation with 4D geometry.
Prior work has used flow to improve robot policies.
Flow served as an intermediate prediction that a separate model converts
into actions, as a prior injected at inference time, or as an extra output
learned together with the action.
In all of these designs, flow stays outside the policy, as a separate module
or as an extra prediction head.
We introduce UniFlowWAM, a Unified World–Action Model that makes 3D scene flow a
third modality on par with vision and action.
Its world representation therefore covers both visual semantics, through future
visual features, and 4D geometry, through 3D flow, and flow receives its own
supervision.
UniFlowWAM is a diffusion transformer with one expert per modality, and the three
experts exchange information through joint attention.
We train UniFlowWAM under a ten-objective role grid, where each objective assigns
every modality exactly one of three roles, namely target, condition, or absent.
The same model thus serves as a policy, as forward and inverse dynamics, and as a
predictor of future visual features or 3D flow.
We evaluate UniFlowWAM on RoboCasa-GR1, LIBERO, and LIBERO-Plus in simulation, and
on four real-world bimanual manipulation tasks.
On RoboCasa-GR1, UniFlowWAM raises the success rate of its base model without flow
from 52.1% to 56.4%.
It preserves in-distribution success on LIBERO at 98.1% and reaches 87.7%
zero-shot on LIBERO-Plus.
On the real robot, it achieves 87.0% average success, compared with 68.5%
for the strongest baseline.
Figure 1:
UniFlowWAM overview
: UniFlowWAM couples visual features, scene-level 3D flow, and actions in one three-expert diffusion transformer, denoising the three jointly so that 3D flow carries scene displacement into the space where actions are executed. A grid of ten objectives assigns each modality the role of target, condition, or absent, so a single model covers policy, dynamics, and prediction, yet deploys as a direct policy that needs no flow at test time.
1
Introduction
A robot manipulates objects by moving its own body. Its action labels only record the commands that its joints or end-effector execute. What those commands do to the scene is left unwritten. A mug pushed across the table and a mug lifted and set back down can end in the same pose. The action labels do not describe how the mug translates or rotates along the way. Among possible world representations in a world–action model, a goal image describes the resulting state, but not the transition. A video sequence captures this process visually, but does not describe how scene points move in 3D. Scene-level 3D flow makes the effects of robot commands on the scene explicit: it describes how each scene point is displaced in 3D over time, providing a 4D geometric representation of this process.
Prior work has used scene-level flow to improve robot policies. Flow served as intermediate representations that were predicted first and then converted into actions in a separate stage
[
38
,
42
]
. A learned 3D scene-flow prior sharpened a vision-language-action policy when injected at inference
[
34
]
. Concurrent work trains sparse 3D keypoint flow jointly with the action
[
18
]
. These results establish flow as a useful control signal and as a variable that can be learned with actions.
Unified future-image–action models learn actions together with predictions of the future. UWM
[
50
]
and UVA
[
17
]
train the policy together with forward and inverse dynamics and visual forecasting, so that both action-labeled and actionless data contribute. Latent-dynamics variants adopt the features of a frozen visual encoder
[
29
]
as the future-state target and scale to large robotic datasets
[
24
]
. The same model learns both to anticipate the visual consequences of actions and to infer actions from future visual features.
Those features capture the semantics in the future goal image, but do not explicitly describe how the 3D scene evolves to reach that state.
We ask:
can a pretrained visual–action model learn where the 3D points of the scene go, and, more importantly, does learning this improve the actions it predicts?
We explicitly supervise the 3D displacement of scene points, beyond the geometric state that depth-based targets supervise.
We introduce
UniFlowWAM
, a Unified World–Action Model whose world representation joins future visual semantics from DINOv3
[
29
]
with 4D geometry from scene-level 3D flow.
Actions, visual semantics, and flow are co-equal modalities of one diffusion transformer.
Following UWM
[
50
]
and UVA
[
17
]
, we call the model
unified
, as one model that is trained jointly on the three modalities serves as a policy, as forward and inverse dynamics, and as a predictor of future world state.
Unlike the flow-based policies above, flow here is neither a separate module nor a tracked input, but a modality inside the model. From the same demonstration clips used for policy learning, we extract point maps and scene flow offline with a monocular 3D tracker
[
22
]
and encode them with a frozen 4D VAE
[
51
]
. Each modality has its own expert, and the three exchange information only through shared joint attention. We add flow to a pretrained visual–action model during mid-training and post-training. The visual and action experts start from the pretrained weights, while the flow expert is trained from scratch. All three experts are then trained jointly, so the pretrained representations adapt to the new modality.
Each function of the model corresponds to one training objective. Ten objectives form a role grid, which assigns each modality the role of
target
,
condition
, or
absent
. With one target per objective, the grid covers all four combinations of flow and future visual features being present or absent for action prediction, and retains three objectives each for flow and visual prediction. This deliberate asymmetry design prioritizes the conditioning choices for the control variable. The four objectives without flow recover the pretrained model’s task set. Under the direct policy objective, the flow stream carries learned placeholders, so deployment requires no scene-flow extraction or flow encoding.
We evaluate UniFlowWAM in simulation on RoboCasa-GR1
[
25

, LIBERO, and LIBERO-Plus, and on four real-world bimanual tasks. On RoboCasa-GR1, adding flow to the base model improves the average success rate by 4.3 percentage points. The gain is largest on the tasks where the base model is weakest (Sec.
4.2
). On LIBERO, UniFlowWAM preserves in-distribution success at 98.1%, and it reaches 87.7% zero-shot on LIBERO-Plus under out-of-distribution perturbations. On the real robot, UniFlowWAM achieves an average success rate of 87.0%, compared with 68.5% for

4.3
). Ablations show where the flow objectives matter. On the real robot, post-training with the full ten-objective grid outperforms policy-only post-training by 12 to 18 points on every task, and the gap is largest on object placements at the edge of the demonstrated region.
Contributions.
(i) We make scene-level 3D flow a co-equal modality of a unified visual–action model, added to a pretrained model through a dedicated expert and joint mid-training and post-training on the same demonstrations. (ii) We organize actions, 3D flow, and future visual features through ten role-conditioned objectives, allowing flow to serve as a target or a condition while retaining a direct policy that needs no flow input. (iii) We show manipulation gains on RoboCasa-GR1 and improved robustness on LIBERO-Plus while retaining in-distribution performance on LIBERO.

From optical flow to scene-level 3D flow.
Flow was classically estimated in 2D, between adjacent frames
[
30

How flow is used in policies.
In the most direct use, flow serves as an explicit interface between perception and control. NovaFlow
[
16
]
extracts 3D object flow from generated videos without training a flow predictor, and plans actions from it. Im2Flow2Act
[
38
]
and PointAction
[
31

[
46

[
15

[
26

34

[
48

and Track4Action
[
32

5

and ChronoFlow-Policy

18

3.5
Training Strategy
We initialize the visual–action backbone from the publicly released pretrained checkpoint of LDA
[
24
]
. We then perform
mid-training
to incorporate scene-level 3D flow into the model, jointly optimizing the ten objectives in Sec.
3.4
over actions, future visual features, and 3D flow. This stage extends the pretrained visual–action model to support 3D flow as both a prediction target and a conditioning modality. The resulting model is subsequently post-trained on demonstrations from each downstream domain.
4
Experiments
Our experiments assess manipulation performance, robustness to distribution shifts, and the contribution of scene-level 3D flow. We evaluate UniFlowWAM on RoboCasa-GR1, LIBERO, and LIBERO-Plus in simulation, and on an ALOHA-style robot for real-world bimanual manipulation.
4.1
Experimental Setup
Mid-training data.
We use a filtered mixture of three public robot-demonstration datasets; all are robot-camera recordings. RoboCOIN
[
36
]
is a bimanual manipulation dataset collected on 15 robot platforms in residential, commercial, and industrial settings; we use 47,050 episodes from six of these platforms. RoboMIND 2.0
[
11
]
is a dual-arm and mobile manipulation dataset collected on six robot embodiments; we use 140,231 episodes from three of them, including Franka and UR arms. MolmoAct2-BimanualYAM
[
8
]
is AllenAI’s teleoperated bimanual dataset collected on a single low-cost platform, the YAM arms; we use 27,162 episodes. The combined corpus covers ten embodiments, with 214,443 episodes and 133.0 million frames. We sample 16-step chunks at three-frame intervals, yielding around 42 million training windows. We extract scene-level 3D flow offline with frozen Track4World
[
22
]
and encode its point maps and flow into latents using a frozen MotionCrafter 4D VAE
[
51
]
.
Model and training.
Starting from LDA’s released pretrained checkpoint
[
24
]
, our model UniFlowWAM adds a dedicated 3D flow expert to the MMDiT backbone to incorporate flow as a third modality. Qwen3-VL-4B supplies visual–language conditioning through cross-attention, while DINOv3 provides visual prediction targets. Both encoders remain frozen during mid-training. We train on 48 NVIDIA H200 GPUs with a global batch size of 1,536.
4.2
Simulation Experiments
4.2.1
Benchmarks
RoboCasa
[
25
]
targets everyday household tasks for generalist robots. We use its GR-1 tabletop tasks: 24 tasks for a GR-1 humanoid with dexterous hands, observed by a single egocentric camera and controlled through 29 joint dimensions across the arms, hands, and waist. Each task comes with 1,000 demonstrations, 24,000 in total, or 6.0 million frames and 83.6 hours at 20 fps.
LIBERO
[
20
]
targets lifelong robot learning with a single Franka Panda arm. It contains 4 suites of 10 tasks each: Spatial varies the layout of the same objects, Object varies the objects to manipulate, Goal varies the goal within one scene, and Long collects long-horizon tasks. We use the no-noops release introduced by OpenVLA
[
14
]
. We evaluate in two settings. LIBERO itself is the in-distribution test. LIBERO-Plus

4.3
Real-World Experiments on ALOHA
Hardware.
We use AgileX Cobot Magic, an ALOHA-style platform with two 6-DoF PiPER arms and parallel-jaw grippers. A top-mounted camera provides the main view, and two wrist cameras provide the wrist views. Both the proprioceptive state and the action command are 14-dimensional, with six joint positions and one gripper position per arm.
Demonstrations.
We consider four tasks that differ in what they demand of the two arms (Fig.
3
).
Chili transfer
repeats a single pick-and-place primitive, moving two chilies onto a plate.
Cabbage transfer
chains distinct primitives instead of repeating one, placing a cabbage into a pot and then covering the pot with a lid.
Pen manipulation
adds an articulated object and asymmetric arm roles, as one arm holds the drawer steady while the other places two pens into it in succession, after which the drawer is pushed closed.
Towel folding
replaces the rigid objects with a deformable one that has no pose to track, requiring two successive folds. After preprocessing, we retain 50 demonstrations per task and post-train a separate model for each task. At inference, each model uses the policy mode to predict 16-step action chunks.
Figure 3:
Real-world manipulation tasks.
Instructions and scored milestones for four tasks:

Evaluation.
For model with full objective setup as our default model, each policy is evaluated for 50 trials per task. We fix the starting conditions in advance instead of drawing them at random. Within a task we change one thing at a time, in equal steps. For chili transfer we keep the chili at the same spot on the table and turn it about the vertical axis to five fixed orientations. Each orientation is run the same number of times, and the plate position varies slightly across trials. The other three tasks follow the same idea along the factor that matters for them. All conditions stay inside the area the demonstrations cover. Every policy sees the same starting conditions, so the differences we report come from the policies and not from where the objects happened to start. We report full-task success rate and a process score, the fraction of milestones completed, scaled to 100. The milestones are those in Fig.
3
, four for cabbage (grasp, place in pot, grasp lid, close) and chili (grasp and place each chili), six for pen (pick and place each pen, support the drawer with the right gripper, push it closed), and five for towel (grasp, lift, fold in half, fold again, press flat). Milestones are scored independently, so a trial that fails one but recovers on a later one still earns credit for the later one. Both metrics are averaged over trials, then over tasks.

Post-training objectives.
We first ask what the objective grid contributes on its own, varying the objectives used in LIBERO post-training while holding the mid-trained initialization and the demonstration data fixed. The four variants form a nested ladder. The full grid uses all ten objectives, with 3D flow as both a target and a condition. The flow-as-condition variant drops the three objectives that predict flow and keeps the other seven. The no-flow variant also drops flow conditioning and keeps the four visual–action objectives of the base model. Policy-only training keeps the single action-prediction objective. Every variant acts through the direct policy objective and takes no flow input at test time, so the differences come from training rather than from the inference path.
All four objective sets are first post-trained on the same 120k-step schedule. The reduced sets level off within this budget, whereas the full ten-objective grid is still improving at 120k steps. We therefore extend the full grid alone to a 200k-step schedule, and at 170k steps it reaches 87.0% on LIBERO-Plus. More objectives thus call for a longer schedule rather than lowering the attainable success rate. Because the simulated benchmark separates the objective sets mainly by training speed, we compare them on the real robot below, where at equal training steps the full grid clearly outperforms policy-only training.

Objectives on the real robot.
On the real robot, the four variants differ noticeably in success rate (Table
4
). Policy-only post-training reaches 76% on chili transfer, 76% on pen manipulation, and 72% on towel folding, while the full ten-objective grid reaches 94%, 90%, and 84%, a gain of 12 to 18 points on every task. The no-flow variant, which keeps the four visual–action objectives, closes most of this gap on chili transfer (92%), but the gap largely remains on pen manipulation (80%), where the two variants that use 3D flow reach 88% and 90%. On all three tasks, success rate improves overall as objectives are added. Relative to the no-flow variant, the 3D flow objectives add 10 points on pen manipulation and 8 on towel folding, the two more demanding tasks, but only 2 on chili transfer, the simplest one.
Where the failures fall.
The losses concentrate in one place. Chili transfer splits its trials evenly into five orientation groups, and 4 of the 6 failures of policy-only post-training fall in the sideways
90
∘
90^{\circ}
group alone. In that group, policy-only post-training succeeds in only 1 of its 5 trials, a success rate of 20%, against 76% over the whole task. The full grid succeeds in 80% of its trials in the same group. Although the group contains few trials, a gap of 20% against 80% is large enough that we read it as a real difference rather than as sampling noise.
Why that group is hard is visible in the training data. Fig.
5
shows that the demonstrations are far from uniform. Most chili grasps cluster near the lengthwise placement, so the sideways orientation is the condition the model has seen least, and it is where policy-only post-training fails most. In the pen demonstrations, most pens start in the middle of a compact region, and few start near its edge. When the pens start near this edge, policy-only post-training succeeds less often.
The two variants differ in one respect. Policy-only post-training never sees 3D flow, neither as a conditioning input nor as a prediction target, whereas the full grid uses it as both. Initialization, data, schedule, and the deployment path are identical, and neither takes flow as input at test time, so the difference at the edge of the demonstrated region is attributable to the flow objectives themselves.
Position encoding.
Removing MM-RoPE lowers LIBERO-Plus at every evaluated checkpoint, by 1.1–2.8 points and by 2.5 at the best checkpoint, with the loss concentrated under robot-initial-state perturbations. Removing the absolute embedding costs 1.5 points at the best checkpoint and up to 4.4 at matched steps, with the gap narrowing as training proceeds. We keep both. Observation and flow tokens lie on the image grid, while action tokens have no image location. We tested two placements for the action tokens, the grid origin and the grid center. The origin is better by less than one point in the best LIBERO success rate. We therefore adopt the grid origin, while considering the difference between the two placements to be small.
4.5
Discarded Designs
While developing joint training with 3D flow, we tried several designs that did not work well. The two below were not run as controlled ablations, but each bears on a natural design choice.
Encoding flow with an image VAE.
Im2Flow2Act
[
38
]
wrote 2D point tracks into image channels and encoded them with a Stable Diffusion autoencoder. Our first version extended this idea to 3D. It mapped the displacement

of each tracked point, relative to its position in the first frame of the clip, directly to the R, G, and B channels and encoded the result with the frozen SDXL image VAE. The VAE reconstructs these images faithfully, and the flow denoising loss decreases normally. The generated flow, however, is nearly the same for every input, so the model has collapsed to an average flow over the dataset. Revising the training data and the patch embedding reduced the collapse but never produced usable flow. We later replaced the image VAE with the 4D VAE of MotionCrafter
[
51
]
, which is trained on geometry and flow.
Gating the flow modality.
To preserve what the LDA backbone learned in pretraining, we first admitted flow gradually through a per-layer gate on the attention logits from the existing tokens to the flow tokens. The gate starts closed and opens on a fixed fast or slow schedule. On RoboCasa-GR1, neither schedule helps. The faster one trails the ungated model by 3.3 points in mean success rate over 21 seeds. All later experiments, including every UniFlowWAM result in this paper, therefore use no gate.
5
Limitations
Flow tracking noise and representation shift.
We use Track4World to generate offline 3D flow pseudo-labels from demonstration videos. These labels can contain temporal inconsistencies, such as an isolated reversal of flow direction within a continuous trajectory. In our pipeline, we use SAM-based segmentation to separate the manipulation foreground from the background and retain only foreground 3D flow for latent encoding. The pretrained 4D VAE
[
51
]
remains effective at compressing these foreground-only inputs.
Limited flow pretraining.
Our 3D flow mid-training uses approximately 1,200 hours of demonstrations, substantially less than the EI-30k corpus used for LDA pretraining
[
24
]
. The added flow expert has not been pretrained alongside the visual–action backbone on that scale.
As tracking models continue to improve, flow extraction is expected to become faster and more accurate, making flow easier to scale for robot training in the same way as video. We leave larger-scale joint pretraining to future work.

article.headline: 3D场景流成为机器人的第三模态
article.lede: 上交MVIG与上海创智学院等提出UniFlowWAM，把场景级3D流当作与视觉、动作并列的模态，放进同一个扩散Trans
article.problem: 机器人示教只记录「看到了什么」和「做了什么」，却不记录三维场景在这两者之间如何位移：目标图像给出末态而非过程，视频捕捉外观却不描述场景点在3D中怎么移动。此前工作把3D流当作独立模块、推理期注入的先验或额外的预测头，流始终留在策略之外。
article.method: 作者在LDA视觉-动作骨干上为3D流新增一个独立专家，三个专家各自保留归一化、Q/K/V投影与前馈网络，只通过联合自注意力交换信息，并用MM-RoPE把动作、流、视觉token统一到同一时空坐标系。训练使用10个「角色网格」目标，每个目标给三种模态分别指定target、condition或absent，使同一模型同时充当策略、前向/逆动力学与未来状态预测器。流由Track4World离线提取、经冻结的MotionCrafter 4D VAE编码为latent；部署时走直接策略目标，流槽位填学习到的占位符，无需提取流。
article.results: 在RoboCasa-GR1的11个共享评测种子上，带mid-training的UniFlowWAM把成功率从LDA的52.11%提到56.38%（+4.27点），在基线低于50%的10个任务上平均提升6.47点。LIBERO保持98.05%，LIBERO-Plus零样本达87.65%，相机扰动下为96.9%，而该类别最强基线为76.6%。真实ALOHA双臂平台上平均成功率87.0%、过程分92.3，π0.5为68.5%和77.0。真机消融中，全目标网格相对仅策略训练在每个任务高12到18点（如毛巾折叠84%对72%）。
article.why_it_matters: 它给出了一条把几何世界表示内化进策略、而非外挂成模块的可行路线，且推理时不依赖流输入，不增加部署开销。对做世界-动作模型的人来说，这种「多模态角色网格」的训练组织方式可以直接迁移到其他感知模态。
article.limitations: 3D流标签是Track4World从单目视频生成的伪标签，论文自己承认可能存在流动方向反转一类的时间不一致；流mid-training只用了约1200小时示教，远少于LDA预训练所用的EI-30k，新加的流专家从零训练，未与骨干同规模预训练。此外RoboCasa上的绝对提升有限，表中OpenWAM-α公布值为60.5%，高于本文跨种子最好成绩58.9%，而LIBERO已接近饱和，作者也称该基准上1个百分点的差异不具信息量。
article.figure_caption_zh: 网络架构：动作、场景级3D流与未来视觉特征分属三个专家，仅在联合自注意力中交互，由训练目标决定谁是被加噪的预测目标、谁是干净条件，预测出的流latent再由4D VAE解码为点图与场景流。

figure.caption: {Network architecture.} Actions, scene-level 3D flow, and future visual features are three modalities of one diffusion transformer, each processed by its own expert; the experts exchange information only through joint self-attention. The objective decides which modalities are noised targets and which are clean conditions. Predicted flow latents are decoded by the 4D VAE into point maps and scene flow.

page_papers.content:
Abstract
Recent world action models provide visual foresight and future prediction for robot manipulation, but lack explicit mechanisms for compositional skill reuse. Agentic robotics combines code-based planning and reasoning with reusable skills, but often lacks predictive grounding in physical dynamics.

Introduction
Learning-based robotic manipulation has progressed from small task-specific visuomotor policies over a decade ago
to broadly supervised foundation models that connect perception, language, and action
(
Levine et al., 2016
;
Zitkovich et al., 2023
;
Kim et al., 2024
;
Niu et al., 2024
;
Black et al., 2024
;
Bjorck et al., 2025
;
Niu et al., 2025
;
Liu et al., 2025
;
Black et al., 2025
;
Liu et al., 2026
)
.
In parallel, self-supervised video prediction has long been valued as a learning signal to model the world: image inpainting extended to video prediction led to action-conditioned video predictors that can imagine the future before committing to an action
(
Pathak et al., 2016
;
He et al., 2021
;
Tong et al., 2022
;
Finn et al., 2016
;
Assran et al., 2025
;
Ye et al., 2026
)
.
World Action Models (WAMs) couple visual prediction with visuomotor policies, grounding control in representations of how the physical world evolves
(
Ye et al., 2026
;
Kim and others, 2026
;
Yuan and others, 2026
)
.
This predictive grounding is particularly valuable for complex manipulation, where successful execution depends on anticipating object motion, contact, and the consequences of low-level actions. Yet predicted video and action chunks do not by themselves specify how a long-horizon task should be decomposed: which reusable skills to invoke, how to parameterize them, or how to compose them across subtasks.
Predicting the world and/or actions in general can also be expensive, especially as it can be difficult to establish limits on how many degrees of freedom need to be “world modeled” (or teleoperated, in the supervised setting).
Agentic robot systems provide complementary structure to WAMs: a programmatic harness that selects reusable skills and tools, binds them to the current scene, tracks progress, and replans as observations change
(
Liang et al., 2023
;
Fu et al., 2026
;
Zhang et al., 2026
;
Xiao et al., 2026
;
Lu et al., 2026
)
. This programmatic representation makes the structure of multi-step tasks explicit, specifying which skills and tools to invoke, with what arguments, and in what sequence.
Yet agentic robotics often lacks predictive grounding in real-world physical dynamics and does not leverage a learned model of how the world will change as the robot acts.
We advocate for an architecture that combines the foresight and action execution of WAMs with the cognitive efficiency, reusable skills, and potential for future self-improvement of agentic robotics.

Experiments
We evaluate AW-0 on RoboTwin 2.0
(
Chen et al., 2025
)
and 8 real-world tasks spanning parallel-gripper and dexterous-hand embodiments, assessing language following, semantic reasoning, and skill execution, as well as the robustness benefits of hybrid execution in variant scenarios.
Baselines.
We compare four baselines: (1)
π
0.5
\pi_{0.5}
(
Black et al., 2025
)
, a state-of-the-art VLA with strong semantic reasoning; (2) EgoScale
(
Zheng et al., 2026
)
, a VLA pretrained on large-scale egocentric human data; (3) DreamZero
(
Ye et al., 2026
)
, a WAM jointly generating future video and actions; and (4) WLA
(
Yang et al., 2026
)
, an autoregressive model jointly predicting textual subtasks, subgoal images, and actions.
All baselines and the default AW-0 configuration use the same task-specific demonstrations for post-training and follow the same evaluation protocol. The simulation hybrid configuration uses separately collected CaP-generated demonstrations, as described below. Baseline implementation details are provided in Appendix
C
.
3.1

Simulation Experiment
Benchmarks.
We evaluate AW-0 on RoboTwin 2.0.
Following the training-data requirements specified on the official RoboTwin 2.0 leaderboard
1
1
1
https://robotwin-platform.github.io/leaderboard
, we train on 50 clean demonstrations per task (2,500 episodes in total) and evaluate under the benchmark’s two settings:
clean
, with a clean tabletop, plain background, fixed lighting, and no distractors; and
random
, with domain randomization over background and tabletop textures, lighting, tabletop height, and distractor objects. We report the mean success rate over 50 rollouts per task.
Hybrid Evaluation.
We additionally evaluate AW-0 in the hybrid mode, in which the training demonstrations are collected by executing CaP programs written against a set of CaP-X-style
(
Fu et al., 2026
)
primitive APIs that we develop for RoboTwin 2.0. The programs are written automatically by Claude Opus 4.8, following the agentic framework of ASPIRE
(
Lu et al., 2026
)
.

Method

Average Scores from Table

.
Main Results.

Table
1
and Figure
4
report the results on RoboTwin 2.0. The two inference modes exhibit complementary strengths.
Overall, AW-0 achieves the highest average success rate of 50.7% across both settings, outperforming all baselines including models designed for broad generalization.
The advantage comes mostly from the clean setting, where AW-0 reaches 80.8%, exceeding the strongest baseline WLA (64.8%) by 16.0 points. Under visual randomization, performance drops to 20.6%, consistent with the challenges of pixel-level O.O.D prediction discussed in prior work
(
Yan et al., 2026
)
. It falls below the VLA baseline
π

\pi_{0.5}
(27.7%) but still outperforms the strongest WAM baseline DreamZero (17.6%) and remains far ahead of EgoScale (2.9%) and WLA (3.6%).
We further observe that hybrid execution improves robustness under distribution shift. In the random setting, it raises the success rate from 20.6% to 29.2%, outperforming all baselines including the strong VLA baseline
π

(27.7%). Relative to its clean-setting performance, the hybrid mode retains
46

of its success rate under randomization, compared with 25% for the default mode. This robustness comes at a cost in the clean setting, where the hybrid mode reaches 63.1%, on par with the strongest baseline, but 17.7 points below the default mode. For further analysis, see Appendix
J
.
3.2
Real-world Experiment
Robot Platforms and Action Space.
We conduct real-world experiments on two platforms: the YAM station, a fixed-base bimanual setup with two 6-DoF arms and parallel grippers, and the Tianji–Sharpa platform, a bimanual robot with two 22-DoF Sharpa dexterous hands.
Both platforms observe three RGB views and act in the unified 64-D state–action space defined in Appendix
A
. Further details on the robot setups are provided in Appendix
D
.
Evaluation Protocol and Metrics.
We use 100 demonstrations per task for post-training and evaluate on the 8 real-world tasks in Table

Method

Conclusion
We present AW-0, an agentic world action model that integrates code-based skill planning with predictive dynamics and continuous control. Through joint denoising, the code expert provides structured semantic guidance for video and action generation. An automated annotation pipeline enables learning this planning interface from large-scale robot and human demonstrations. Experiments on RoboTwin 2.0 and real-world manipulation with YAM and dexterous hands demonstrate improvements in language following, semantic reasoning, and skill execution, with hybrid execution further enhancing robustness. These results establish a unified foundation for future work on skill reuse and iterative interaction between programmatic planning, world prediction, and execution, providing a potential agentic system foundation that continually interacts with and learns from environments.

We conduct data collection and policy evaluation on two robot embodiments: the YAM station with parallel grippers and the Tianji–Sharpa station with dexterous hands. This section describes the robot hardware, visual observations, and teleoperation interfaces used in our experiments. Figure

Appendix G
Additional Analysis on Real-world Results
G.1
Impact of Code Expert on Language Following Capability
We further examine whether code-based planning improves the alignment of predicted visual dynamics with task semantics. As shown in Figure
33
, we compare the video generation quality of the right wrist camera of AW-0 with a natural-language subgoal variant (Subgoal) and a model without a planning stream (AW-0 w/o code), under the instruction
“Arrange the fruits so that finally there is only mango in the left bowl.”
This task requires identifying the intended object and grounding the desired outcome in an appropriate interaction. The three variants are evaluated under the same task and scene configuration, with similar but non-identical initial observations from separate rollouts.
The predicted futures reveal distinct differences in task understanding: AW-0 directs the interaction toward the mango, whereas Subgoal exhibits ambiguous targeting between the apple and mango, and AW-0 w/o code targets the apple. These observations suggest that structured skill calls and explicit object arguments provide a more specific planning condition for video prediction than a natural-language subgoal alone. By connecting instruction semantics to concrete interactions, the code stream helps align predicted dynamics with the intended task. Since the action expert also conditions on predictive video representations, this alignment provides a pathway for improving language following, complementing the execution results in our main experiments.

in the first row, the target fruit lies close to the basket rim. As the gripper approaches, its left jaw moves outside the basket, causing the closing motion to grasp the basket wall rather than only the fruit. This case highlights the need to account for surrounding geometry when selecting a grasp. Explicitly estimating the rim geometry and checking clearance along both the approach and closing paths could help reject obstructed grasps and select a more accurate approach direction.

Explicitly tracking the tong tips and opening width could help condition actions on the tool’s state. article.headline: AW-0：代码规划接入世界动作模型
article.lede: AW-0 以代码、视频、动作三专家联合去噪，在 RoboTwin 2.0 平均成功率 50.7%，随机场景混合执行达 2
article.problem: 近期的世界动作模型能预测视觉未来并生成动作，却缺少组合式技能复用的显式机制；agentic robotics 能用代码规划调用可复用技能，却常缺少对物理动力学的预测基础。AW-0 试图把程序化规划与预测性世界模型接起来。
article.method: AW-0 采用 Mixture-of-Transformers 主干，代码、视频、动作三个专家联合去噪：视频与动作走连续流匹配，代码走离散掩码扩散。自动化标注管线从大规模机器人与人类演示中学习规划接口；推理时可在默认模式与基于 CaP 程序的混合执行间切换。
article.results: 在 RoboTwin 2.0 上，AW-0 跨干净与随机两种设置的平均成功率为 50.7%，高于所有基线。干净设置达 80.8%，比最强基线 WLA 的 64.8% 高 16.0 个百分点；随机设置降到 20.6%，低于 π0.5 的 27.7%，但高于 DreamZero 的 17.6%、EgoScale 的 2.9% 和 WLA 的 3.6%。混合执行把随机设置提升到 29.2%，超过 π0.5 的 27.7%，并保留干净设置的 46%，默认模式仅保留 25%；代价是干净设置降至 63.1%，比默认模式低 17.7 个百分点。真实实验覆盖 2 种 embodiment 的 8 个任务，每任务用 100 条演示、3×16 次 rollout 评估，但材料未给出真实任务的具体分数。
article.why_it_matters: 把程序化规划、世界预测与底层控制放进同一模型，为长程操作的技能复用和持续交互学习提供了可检验的路线；混合执行在分布偏移下的增益也直接指向部署鲁棒性。
article.limitations: 随机场景成功率仅 20.6%，仍低于 π0.5 的 27.7%，说明像素级 OOD 预测仍是短板；混合执行把随机场景提升到 29.2%，却让干净场景从 80.8% 降到 63.1%。此外，真实实验只覆盖 2 种 embodiment、8 个任务，且材料未给出真实任务的具体分数。

page_papers.title: QK-Edit: Revisiting Attention-based Injection in MM-DiT for Image and Video Editing
page_papers.abstract: Multimodal Diffusion Transformers (MM-DiTs) have recently emerged as a powerful framework for unified text-vision synthesis, surpassing traditional U-Net architectures in generative tasks. One key innovation lies in its Multimodal Self-Attention (MM-SA) interaction, where image and text tokens are concatenated and processed via self-attention. However, this mechanism poses significant challenges for editing, rendering conventional U-Net-based attention manipulation methods ineffective. To address this limitation, we propose QK-Edit, a training-free framework that exploits the unique attention dynamics of MM-DiTs for precise text-guided image and video editing. By introducing a novel query-key manipulation strategy, our method isolates and adjusts critical attention components to achieve an optimal balance between prompt fidelity and structural consistency. This enables seamless edits across various tasks, including object addition, object removal, object replacement, changing background, changing material, changing color, and style transformation. Notably, it can be easily implemented with feature replacement in inference. QK-Edit demonstrates superior editing performance on state-of-the-art models, such as FLUX and HunyuanVideo, effectively bridging the gap between generative power and editable flexibility in MM-DiTs, and paving the way for scalable multimodal content creation.

Abstract
Multimodal Diffusion Transformers (MM-DiTs) have recently emerged as a powerful framework for unified text-vision synthesis, surpassing traditional U-Net architectures in generative tasks. One key innovation lies in its Multimodal Self-Attention (MM-SA) interaction where image and text tokens are concatenated and processed via self-attention.
However, this mechanism poses significant challenges for editing, rendering conventional U-Net-based attention manipulation methods ineffective. To address this limitation, we propose QK-Edit, a training-free framework that exploits the unique attention dynamics of MM-DiTs for precise text-guided image and video editing. By introducing a novel query-key manipulation strategy, our method isolates and adjusts critical attention components to achieve an optimal balance between prompt fidelity and structural consistency. This enables seamless edits across various tasks, including object addition, object removal, object replacement, changing background, changing material, changing color, and style transformation.
Notably, it can be easily implemented with feature replacement in inference.
QK-Edit demonstrates superior editing performance on state-of-the-art models, such as FLUX and HunyuanVideo, effectively bridging the gap between generative power and editable flexibility in MM-DiTs, and paving the way for scalable multimodal content creation.

Specifically, due to the joint attention mechanism, textual and visual interactions become deeply intertwined within a single attention matrix, complicating the independent manipulation of textual and visual information. As a result, such editing methods for U-Net models become ineffective in Fig.

These complexities arise because such previous editing methods rely heavily on the modular nature of U-Net architectures
[
54
]
, where cross-attention facilitates precise text-guided modifications, and self-attention ensures spatial consistency. In contrast, MM-DiTs integrate these attention mechanisms into a unified structure, making it challenging to independently control text-vision and vision-vision interactions without one adversely affecting the other.
A naive solution is to decompose the MM-SA map into four quadrants, each representing a specific interaction between text and vision embeddings and directly apply previous CA-based or SA-based editing techniques such as P2P
[
22
]
or PnP
[
61
]
to the respective attention maps. However, this often leads to undesirable outputs, as illustrated in Fig.
2
.
Through systematic analysis, we observe: (1) text-to-vision attention has negligible impact on the final generation, (2) vision-to-text attention relates vision region to the text token, and finally (3) vision-vision attention defines both spatial and temporal consistency within visual embeddings.
As a result, simultaneous replacement of vision-to-text and vision-to-vision attention is necessary to enable precise control over spatial and temporal properties while adhering to the target prompt. Building upon these insights, we propose QK-Edit, a training-free editing framework that manipulates the attention quadrants of MM-DiTs to achieve high-fidelity edits. In practice, we leverage the fact that text-to-vision attention has minimal impact on the generation and replace the vision component in query and key embeddings of the target image or video with that of the source image or video during the denoising process.
In practice, our proposed strategy is straightforward to implement, requiring only minimal code modifications.

5
Conclusion
In this work, we present QK-Edit, a simple yet effective training-free framework that exploits the unique attention dynamics of MM-DiTs for precise text-guided image and video editing. Extensive experiments demonstrate the versatility of QK-Edit across a wide range of editing tasks,
e.g
.
, object addition, object removal, object replacement, changing background, changing material, changing color, and style transformation
etc
. More importantly, it can be easily implemented with a few lines of code.
Limitation and future work.
While QK-Edit significantly advances training-free text-guided editing for MM-DiTs, it still exhibits several limitations. First, the accuracy of real video inversion remains challenging, particularly in complex scenes with intricate motions, which can compromise subsequent editing results. Second, QK-Edit inevitably introduces minor unintended modifications in regions that should remain unaltered; future work could incorporate masks to better preserve these areas. Third, as a training-free approach, QK-Edit inherits the limitations of its base generative model, such as suboptimal text rendering and structural deficiencies in handling complex motions (e.g., gymnastic videos). These issues might be alleviated by employing more advanced generative models, which we leave as a promising direction for future research.

), showcasing the flexibility of our method on both landscape and portrait formats.
9
Failure Cases and Artifacts
As a training-free method, our performance is inherently bounded by the capabilities of the base model. We have discussed some failure cases in the Limitation section. More failure cases are illustrated in Fig.
10
.

article.headline: 在 MM-DiT 上做免训练编辑：只换 QK
article.lede: 不训练、不改架构，只把多模态自注意力里视觉侧的 Q、K 换成源视频的，就能在 FLUX 与 HunyuanVideo 上
article.problem: MM-DiT（如 FLUX、HunyuanVideo）把文本与视觉 token 拼接后在同一个自注意力里计算，文本-视觉与视觉-视觉的交互被揉进同一张注意力图，U-Net 时代靠分别操纵 cross-attention 和 self-attention 的编辑方法（P2P、PnP）因此失效。直接把 MM-SA 拆成四个象限、再套用旧的 CA/SA 编辑策略，往往得到不可用的结果。
article.method: 作者逐块、逐组件地做消融分析：跳过 MM-SA 会显著改变空间布局，跳过 FFN 几乎无影响；把四个注意力象限分别置零后发现，第 2 象限（text-to-vision）影响可忽略，第 3 象限（vision-to-text）决定文本-视觉对应关系，第 4 象限（vision-vision）决定空间与时间一致性。据此，QK-Edit 在去噪过程中记录源图像/视频的视觉侧 Q、K，并在生成目标时替换掉目标侧的对应分量；由于第 2 象限影响微弱，这一替换等价于同时操纵第 3、4 象限，且只需在推理时做特征替换，不必改动被 flash-attention 封装的注意力图。图像编辑在前 30% 推理步内施加替换，视频编辑用前 20% 步。
article.results: 在 PIE-Bench 真实图像编辑上，QK-Edit 取得 CLIP-T 0.264、DINO 0.776、PickScore 22.33，均高于 RF-Solver 的 0.257/0.769/21.98。在 TGVE+ 的生成式视频编辑设定下，对比同样基于 HunyuanVideo 的 DiTCtrl，CLIP_frames 0.951 对 0.904、PickScore 21.24 对 20.01、ViCLIP_dir 0.217 对 0.141、ViCLIP_out 0.268 对 0.242。真实视频编辑设定下为 ViCLIP_out 0.258、CLIP_frames 0.921、PickScore 20.52；作者另建含 43 条、分辨率超过 1K、长度超过 100 帧的 HiLo-Benchmark，QK-Edit 得 CLIP_frames 0.908、PickScore 20.08，优于 KV_concat 的 0.896/19.87。视频实验覆盖 320×320、65 帧到 1280×720、129 帧，均在 NVIDIA A100 上完成。
article.why_it_matters: 它把「编辑能力」从重新训练或额外适配器，降格成推理时的几行 Q、K 替换代码，让新一代 MM-DiT 生成模型可以低成本复用到图像与视频编辑任务上。对后续工作而言，四象限的功能划分本身也是一份可复用的机理解读。
article.limitations: 论文自述的局限包括：真实视频反演在复杂运动场景下仍不准确，会拖累后续编辑；本应保持不变的区域仍会出现轻微意外改动，作者建议未来引入 mask；作为免训练方法，它继承了基座模型的缺陷（文字渲染、体操类复杂运动等）。此外，表 3 中 Flatten 的 ViCLIP_dir 为 0.204，高于 QK-Edit 的 0.196，与正文「在所有指标上超过所有基线」的表述并不完全一致，该结论需打折看待。

page_papers.content:
VideoMaMa++: Temporally Consistent Video Matting via Preserve-and-Refine Tokens
Sangbeom Lim
Affiliation:
Korea University
Seoung Wug Oh
Affiliation:
Adobe Research
Heeji Yoon
Affiliation:
KAIST AI
https://cvlab-kaist.github.io/VideoMaMa-PlusPlus
Seungryong Kim
Joon-Young Lee
Abstract
Diffusion-based video matting has recently emerged as a leading approach, leveraging video diffusion priors from internet-scale pretraining to achieve strong zero-shot generalization from limited synthetic data. However, the heavy compute of these diffusion backbones limits inference to a short chunk of just 6–24 frames, so even ordinary videos span multiple chunks. Because each chunk is matted independently from coarse mask guidance, existing methods fail to maintain consistency across chunk boundaries, producing flickering edges and discontinuous transparency.
We address this with a mask-guided diffusion-matting framework built on two ideas. The RGB and mask conditioning are represented as separate token streams that interact through full spatio-temporal self-attention, letting the model adaptively combine fine RGB texture with coarse mask layout rather than committing to a fixed channel-wise fusion. On top of this, we propose a novel pair of learnable embeddings, the
preserve token
and the
refine token
, that act as a per-frame conditioning interface and enable a sliding-window inference scheme in which already-generated mattes are propagated across chunk boundaries for local temporal consistency, complemented by a globally shared
reference anchor
at every chunk to prevent error accumulation in long sequences without any additional training.
Across standard video matting benchmarks and in-the-wild long footage, our framework outperforms prior diffusion-based methods in both fine-detail accuracy and temporal consistency, and uniquely maintains consistency across chunk boundaries on long videos.
†
†
footnotetext:
Co-corresponding authors.
Figure 1
:
We introduce
VideoMaMa++
, a mask-guided video matting framework that recovers fine-grained details (e.g., hair strands) and scales reliably to long videos.
(a) Per-frame qualitative results on diverse in-the-wild videos.
(b) Long-video matting results: VideoMaMa
Lim et al. (2026)
, which processes videos in chunks, fails to maintain consistency across chunk boundaries (red boxes), whereas VideoMaMa++ produces mattes that are both finely detailed and temporally consistent.
1
Introduction
Video matting, the task of extracting foreground objects with pixel-level precision from video, is a fundamental component of video editing applications such as background replacement
Zeng et al. (2025)
;
Gao et al. (2025)
;
Ren et al. (2024)
, visual composition
Dalva et al. (2024)
;
Yang et al. (2025a)
, and relighting
Chaturvedi et al. (2025)
;
Ren et al. (2024)
;
Wang et al. (2025)
;
Choi et al. (2025)
. Producing convincing composites in these settings requires alpha mattes that capture fine structures such as hair strands and motion-blurred edges, and that remain temporally consistent across the entire video.
Recent video matting methods leverage priors from video object segmentation models
Huynh et al. (2024)
;
Yang et al. (2025b)
.
However, these methods still rely on dedicated matting annotations and offer limited zero-shot generalization, with most existing methods restricted to human portraits due to the scarcity of matting labels for other categories.
A more recent line of work instead leverages video diffusion priors
Lim et al. (2026)
;
Ge et al. (2025)
, transferring generative knowledge obtained from internet-scale pretraining to close the train–test gap that arises when models are trained only on synthetic matting data.
In particular, VideoMaMa
Lim et al. (2026)
demonstrates that a mask-to-matte diffusion model trained on synthetic data alone can generalize to non-human categories and to in-the-wild video footage.
However, applying diffusion-based matting to real videos exposes a fundamental limitation that hinders general video processing. Diffusion backbones are computationally heavy and cannot process arbitrarily long sequences in a single forward pass; existing methods are therefore chunk-based, handling only 6–24 frames at a time. As a result, even ordinary videos must be split into multiple chunks and processed sequentially. When each chunk is matted independently from its coarse mask guidance, the resulting mattes drift across chunk boundaries, producing flickering edges and discontinuous transparency, as illustrated in Figure
1
(b). The root cause is the inherent ambiguity of coarse mask guidance: a single binary mask admits many plausible fine-grained refinements at object boundaries, and independently processed chunks settle on different ones.
In this work, we present a novel mask-guided diffusion-matting framework designed for long, high-resolution video. At its core, we represent the two guidance modalities, the RGB frames and the coarse mask, as separate token streams alongside the noisy matte tokens, and let them interact through full spatio-temporal self-attention. This design replaces the channel concatenation used in prior U-Net-based diffusion matting
Lim et al. (2026)
and preserves each modality’s distinct structure. The high-frequency RGB texture carries hair and edge cues, while the binary mask provides a coarse but spatially anchored foreground extent, and attention adaptively composes the two at every layer and spatial location. As a result, the model leans on RGB at object boundaries where the mask is unreliable, and on the mask in the interior where it confidently localizes the foreground. We instantiate this on a Diffusion Transformer (DiT)
Peebles and Xie (2023)
;
Wan et al. (2025)
with Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE)
Su et al. (2024)
, which naturally accommodates diverse resolutions and frame counts.
To resolve the chunk-boundary inconsistency described above, we introduce a novel pair of learnable token embeddings, the
preserve token
and the
refine token
, a new conditioning interface for consistent video matting. The preserve token marks a frame whose guidance is already a fine matte, previously generated or ground truth, and tells the model to keep it as a reference. The refine token marks a frame with only a coarse mask and asks the model to refine it into a fine matte consistent with the preserve-tagged references via DiT’s full self-attention. We employ these tokens in a sliding-window inference scheme in which each chunk overlaps a few preserve-tagged frames with the previous chunk, so that already-generated mattes propagate across chunk boundaries and maintain local temporal consistency. To further guard against error accumulation over long sequences, we additionally supply a globally reliable matte as a
reference anchor
at every chunk through the same preserve token, without any additional training.
We validate our framework through extensive experiments on standard video matting benchmarks and in-the-wild footage. Our method outperforms existing video matting approaches on VideoMatte
Lin et al. (2021)
, YoutubeMatte
Yang et al. (2025b)
, and V-HIM60
Huynh et al. (2024)
in both fine-detail accuracy and temporal consistency, and achieves state-of-the-art performance on long-video matting where prior diffusion-based methods fail to maintain consistency across chunk boundaries. The same preserve mechanism also gives users direct control at inference time, for example to interactively correct erroneous outputs by re-tagging specific frames as refine while keeping trusted neighbors as preserve.
Our contributions can be summarized as follows.
•
A mask-guided diffusion-matting framework with
token-level guidance representation
, where the RGB frames and the coarse mask are kept as separate token streams adaptively composed by full spatio-temporal self-attention, rather than fused via channel concatenation as in prior works.
•
A novel
preserve
and
refine
token mechanism that enables chunk-consistent matting through sliding-window inference with overlap-based propagation, complemented by a globally shared
reference anchor
that prevents error accumulation in long sequences without any additional training.
•
State-of-the-art performance on standard video matting benchmarks and in-the-wild long-video footage, with substantial gains in fine-detail accuracy and temporal consistency over prior diffusion-based methods that process video chunk-wise.
2
Related Work
Video matting.
Video matting methods can be broadly categorized into auxiliary-free and auxiliary-guided approaches
Park et al. (2023)
;
Huang et al. (2025a)
. Auxiliary-free methods
Lin et al. (2022)
;
Ke et al. (2022)
;
Li et al. (2024)
typically focus on portrait matting, restricting their applicability to human-centric scenarios. Auxiliary-guided approaches relax this restriction by accepting additional conditioning at the cost of an extra annotation. Trimap-guided methods
Huang and Lee (2023)
;
Seong et al. (2022)
require manual trimap annotations and cannot easily leverage modern segmentation models such as the SAM family
Kirillov et al. (2023)
;
Ravi et al. (2024)
;
Carion et al. (2025)
. More recent mask-guided methods reduce this burden by accepting only a coarse binary mask. MaGGIe
Huynh et al. (2024)
decouples target tracking from matting but struggles to generalize to in-the-wild videos, while MatAnyone
Yang et al. (2025b)
;
Yang et al. (2026)
propagates target-assigned mattes through a memory-augmented architecture trained on dedicated matting datasets such as VM800
Yang et al. (2025b)
and VMReal
Yang et al. (2026)
. Despite these advances, all of these methods remain constrained by predominantly synthetic and human-centric training data, leaving in-the-wild generalization to non-human categories largely unsolved.
Diffusion priors for perception.
Diffusion priors from internet-scale pretraining have been transferred to dense perception tasks. Marigold
Ke et al. (2024)
pioneered this direction by adapting Stable Diffusion
Rombach et al. (2022)
for depth estimation, and the same recipe extends to a range of video perception tasks
Bin et al. (2025)
;
Shao et al. (2025)
;
Hu et al. (2025)
;
Xu et al. (2025b)
, with more recent works
Xu et al. (2025a)
;
Zhang et al. (2026)
extending it to DiT-based backbones.
Diffusion long-video inference.
Diffusion backbones, however, are computationally heavy and limited to short chunks, so applying them to long videos requires a chunk-wise inference scheme. ChronoDepth
Shao et al. (2025)
and DepthCrafter
Hu et al. (2025)
adopt sliding-window inference with overlapping frames between adjacent chunks for local temporal smoothness, but offer no global anchor against drift. A parallel line of work tackles this through auto-regressive generation
Huang et al. (2025b)
;
Chen et al. (2024)
;
Yin et al. (2025)
;
Liu et al. (2025)
;
Cui et al. (2025)
;
Yang et al. (2025c)
;
Ma et al. (2026)
, where each chunk is conditioned on the previous chunk via causal attention with KV-cache reuse. While effective for free-form video generation, this hidden-state propagation does not naturally compose with explicit external conditioning such as a guide mask. Our work instead propagates fully-formed reference mattes between chunks through the preserve token, keeping each chunk fully conditioned on its own user-supplied mask.
Diffusion-based video matting.
In the matting domain, recent diffusion-based methods transfer video diffusion priors to video matting using only synthetic data. The auxiliary-free GVM
Ge et al. (2025)
and the mask-guided VideoMaMa
Lim et al. (2026)
both demonstrate that this prior generalizes to non-human categories and in-the-wild footage, but both inherit the chunk-wise inference limitation of prior diffusion-based perception models. VideoMaMa, the closest mask-guided baseline, additionally fuses RGB, mask, and noise via channel concatenation, entangling the guidance modalities and limiting fine-detail recovery. Our work departs from this design by representing the two guidance modalities as separate token streams, and by introducing the preserve and refine tokens that maintain chunk-wise consistency through globally shared reference anchors and overlap-based local smoothing.
3
Method

We adopt a mask-guided formulation that decomposes video matting into two subproblems: foreground tracking and boundary refinement. Tracking a target object across a video is itself a demanding task, and entangling it with matte generation forces a single model to simultaneously localize objects and resolve pixel-level matting. By conditioning on a binary mask, we decouple these two challenges and allow our model to focus on generating fine-grained matting details such as hair strands and motion blur, while inheriting localization capabilities from off-the-shelf segmentation models
Ravi et al. (2024)

Carion et al. (2025)

We design an end-to-end pipeline for long-video matting that takes a video and a single user prompt on the first frame as input, and produces a temporally consistent alpha matte across the entire sequence. The pipeline operates in three stages, illustrated in Figure

. First, we obtain a per-frame foreground signal by propagating the user prompt across all frames using an off-the-shelf video segmentation model such as Segment Anything
Ravi et al. (2024)
;

. Second, the resulting binary mask track is passed to our Diffusion Transformer (DiT) backbone together with the RGB frames to generate fine-grained alpha mattes (Section
3.2
). Finally, long sequences are handled by a chunk-wise inference scheme equipped with preserve and refine tokens (Section
3.3
), which propagates information across chunk boundaries to maintain temporal consistency throughout the video.

3.3
Preserve and Refine Tokens
The formulation above operates on a single clip, while video matting in practice requires handling long sequences. DiT backbones are computationally heavy and cannot process long videos in a single forward pass. A natural solution is chunk-wise inference, where the video is split into fixed-length clips and each clip is processed independently. However, when each chunk is refined from its guidance in isolation, the resulting mattes drift across chunk boundaries, producing flickering edges and discontinuous transparency.
To address this, we introduce two learnable token embeddings, a
preserve token
and a
refine token
, which assign each frame a per-frame mode that determines whether its matte is carried through unchanged or generated from coarse guidance. The preserve token marks anchor frames whose alpha mattes should be retained, while the refine token marks frames that should be converted from coarse guidance into fine-grained alpha mattes. DiT’s full self-attention propagates information from preserve frames to refine frames, yielding mattes that remain consistent across chunks.
Why not auto-regressive diffusion?
We chose to propagate fully-formed reference mattes through the preserve token rather than reuse the previous chunk’s key-value (KV) cache as in auto-regressive diffusion approaches
Huang et al. (2025b)
;
Yin et al. (2025)
. Hidden-state propagation implicitly turns the model into a propagation-based matting framework, where each chunk’s prediction is determined more by the previous chunk’s internal state than by its own mask guidance. This re-entangles localization and fine-detail recovery, the two subproblems we explicitly decoupled by adopting mask-guided conditioning. The preserve token instead exposes the previous chunk’s contribution as an explicit alpha matte, so each chunk remains fully grounded in its own mask guidance while still receiving long-range temporal context through self-attention.
Training.
We train both tokens jointly within a single clip. For each training clip, we randomly select a subset of frames as preserve frames, replace their guide input with the ground-truth alpha matte, and add the preserve token embedding to those frames. The remaining frames receive the refine token together with the standard binary mask guide input. The model is supervised against the ground-truth matte at all frames through the pixel-level supervision, learning to reconstruct the supplied matte at preserve frames and to generate fine-grained mattes from coarse guidance at refine frames. Joint training within a single clip is essential, as it forces the DiT to learn a unified representation in which preserve and refine frames interact through self-attention, rather than treating them as two disjoint tasks.
3.4
Temporally Consistent Inference
We deploy the preserve and refine tokens at inference through two complementary mechanisms: a sliding-window scheme that propagates mattes between adjacent chunks for local consistency, and a reference anchor that supplies a globally reliable matte at every chunk to prevent long-range drift.
Sliding window.
At inference, we apply a sliding-window scheme in which consecutive chunks share an overlap region. The overlapping frames receive the previous chunk’s predicted matte as input together with the preserve token, so that their mattes are passed through unchanged, while the remaining frames receive the guide signal together with the refine token. Although the preserve token is applied only to the overlap frames, DiT’s full attention allows them to condition the generation of every other frame in the chunk, transferring temporal context across the chunk boundary and producing chunk-consistent mattes.
Reference anchor.
The sliding-window scheme alone is vulnerable to error accumulation, since a corrupted overlap frame, e.g., due to occlusion, tracking drift, or other video artifacts, propagates through the preserve token to all subsequent chunks and cascades local failures through the rest of the video. To prevent this, we introduce a
reference anchor
, a globally reliable frame whose matte is supplied as preserve input alongside the local overlap frames at every chunk, providing a stable, error-free signal that the model can attend to throughout inference while the overlap frames continue to carry short-range temporal context. Crucially, this capability emerges directly from the preserve token without any additional training: because the preserve token already learns to treat its inputs as anchors, any user-supplied matte can serve as an anchor for the rest of the video.
This design gives users explicit control over which frame anchors the inference. By default, we reuse the matte predicted at the first chunk as the reference anchor throughout the video, which we find sufficient for most sequences. When the first frame is unreliable due to heavy occlusion, motion blur, or partial visibility, the user can instead select a later frame with cleaner foreground appearance as the reference, allowing the entire sequence to be conditioned on the most informative anchor available.
4
Experiments
4.1
Implementation Details
We build VideoMaMa++ on top of the Wan 2.1 (1.3B)
Wan et al. (2025)
model, training on a combination of image and video matting datasets. To preserve the generative prior, we adapt the DiT to the video matting task using LoRA
Hu et al. (2022)
rather than fine-tuning the full backbone. Training uses 3-frame clips at
