Although the training and inference settings differ in both frame count and chunking behavior, the model generalizes across them due to RoPE’s
Su et al. (2024)
relative position encoding, which removes the dependence on absolute resolution and clip length present in fixed positional embeddings.

We further quantify this observation with an annotation-free test for chunk-boundary discontinuities (Appendix

With both models run at identical seams, VideoMaMa’s matte change spikes at seams in-the-wild clips, whereas VideoMaMa++ stays at chance level. On YouTubeMatte, where ground truth is available, the same test detects VideoMaMa’s discontinuity and finds none in the ground-truth mattes, supporting its validity. Per clip, VideoMaMa’s seam contrast exceeds that of VideoMaMa++ at identical boundaries, and these conclusions are stable across difference statistics and detrending windows. Since the test targets only chunk-boundary discontinuities, it applies only to chunk-wise methods, which is why we compare against VideoMaMa.

The preserve and refine tokens also enable selective refinement of individual frames within a chunk. Given an initial prediction, we identify the frame with the largest error against the ground-truth matte, mark it with the refine token, and mark the remaining frames with the preserve token. Re-running the model under this configuration regenerates the marked frame while attending to the others as anchors, producing a refined matte that draws on temporal context from the rest of the chunk. We design a targeted experiment to verify that the preserve and refine tokens produce consistent mattes across chunk boundaries. Using a chunk size of 6 with an overlap of 2 frames, each overlap frame is generated twice: once as part of the preceding chunk and once as part of the following chunk. w/o preserve

w/ preserve

5
Conclusion
We introduce VideoMaMa++, a diffusion transformer model that leverages generative priors for robust video matting, overcoming data scarcity. VideoMaMa++ introduces preserve and refine tokens that enable temporally consistent matting on long videos, addressing a fundamental limitation of diffusion-based approaches confined to short clips. We demonstrate that VideoMaMa++ achieves state-of-the-art performance across diverse benchmarks while producing fine-grained, temporally consistent results on long in-the-wild videos. An annotation-free analysis further shows that our chunk-wise inference exhibits no measurable discontinuity at chunk boundaries, unlike VideoMaMa processing chunks independently. Nevertheless, VideoMaMa++ is more computationally demanding than feed-forward models and, like all mask-guided methods, depends on the upstream mask track; reducing the DiT inference cost and benchmarking temporal smoothness on real footage are promising future directions.
We believe VideoMaMa++ provides a scalable framework bridging the gap between short-clip generation and real-world long-video applications.

Appendix Overview
This supplementary material provides additional details on implementation, evaluation, and qualitative results that could not be included in the main paper due to space constraints.
The document is organized as follows:
•
Section
A
provides additional implementation details, including the training configuration and the list of datasets used to train VideoMaMa++.
•
Section
B
presents qualitative results for the interactive refinement experiment, illustrating how VideoMaMa++ progressively improves its own predictions across iterations through the preserve and refine token mechanism.
•
Section
C
reports zero-shot evaluation of VideoMaMa++ on image matting benchmarks, demonstrating that our model generalizes effectively beyond video to single-image settings.
•
Section
D
discusses annotation noise in the AM-2K benchmark and explains why MAD-T provides a more reliable measure of matting quality than MAD on this dataset.
•
Section
E
describes the guidance-mask generation protocol shared by all mask-guided methods and reports a single evaluation exception on the YouTubeMatte static_0017 sequence, where SAM3
Carion et al. (2025)
must be re-initialized at a later frame to capture an object that enters the scene partway through the video, together with results under first-frame initialization
•
Section
F
introduces an annotation-free test for chunk-boundary discontinuities, which quantifies temporal consistency on in-the-wild videos without ground truth, and validates it on YouTubeMatte.
•
Section
G
reports the computational cost of VideoMaMa++ and prior methods, including a per-stage runtime breakdown and end-to-end throughput with mask generation.
•
Section
H
details the reference-anchor experiments, including the anchor-refresh setting and the corruption protocol used to test robustness to a degraded anchor.
•
Section
I
discusses the limitations of this work: its dependence on the upstream mask track, and the absence of a video matting benchmark that can rigorously evaluate temporal smoothness on real-world footage.
•
Section
J
discusses the positive and negative societal impacts of mask-guided video matting.

Appendix D
AM-2K Justification
We observe that the AM-2K
Li et al. (2022)
ground-truth annotations contain systematic errors that disproportionately penalize fine-detail predictions under the MAD metric. As illustrated in Figure
6
, the AM-2K ground truth often lacks detail within foreground regions, despite the predictions correctly recovering them. Because MAD averages absolute differences over the entire image, these annotation gaps inflate the reported error even when the predicted matte is visually superior. MAD-T, by contrast, restricts the evaluation to the transition region defined by the ground-truth trimap, isolating the boundary detail where matting quality matters most. Under this more reliable metric, VideoMaMa++ achieves state-of-the-art performance against all comparison methods, indicating that the apparent MAD gap on AM-2K reflects annotation noise rather than a true performance deficit.

Initializing SAM3
Carion et al. (2025)
on the first frame fails to track a sheet of paper that the subject begins holding mid-sequence, since the object is not yet visible at initialization. Initializing on a later frame where both are simultaneously visible recovers the correct mask track.
Re-initialized sequence.
For all evaluations, the input masks are obtained automatically without human intervention, with one exception. The static_0017 sequence from YouTubeMatte
Yang et al. (2025b)
presents a granularity ambiguity at the first frame: a sheet of paper that becomes part of the foreground only enters the scene partway through the video, and is therefore not visible at the moment of mask initialization. As a result, when SAM3
Carion et al. (2025)
is prompted on the first frame, the resulting mask track captures only the subject and cannot recover the paper once it appears, as shown in Figure
7
. Because mask-guided matting models, including MaGGIe
Huynh et al. (2024)
, VideoMaMa
Lim et al. (2026)
, and ours, faithfully follow the granularity defined by the input mask, the paper is consequently excluded from the predicted alpha matte. To resolve this without manual annotation, we initialize SAM3 on a later frame (frame 60) where both the subject and the paper are simultaneously visible, and propagate the prompt across the entire sequence. This re-initialized track is used for all mask-guided methods. We note that the MatAnyone
Yang et al. (2025b)
;
Yang et al. (2026)
series is not affected by this issue, as it does not rely on an external mask track. We report this exception in the interest of full transparency.

Appendix H
Reference Anchor Analysis Details
This section details the reference-anchor experiments of Table
3
, all conducted on V-HIM60
Huynh et al. (2024)
.
Anchor choice and refresh.
The first frame may not be representative of later frames. We therefore replace it as the anchor with a random frame or the last frame of the first chunk, which leaves performance nearly unchanged across all metrics. Because the foreground may also change in appearance over long sequences, we further re-anchor to a recent frame every 3 chunks. V-HIM60 sequences contain substantial pose, scale, and appearance variation, yet refreshing yields nearly identical quality to the default setting, so a first-frame anchor does not become stale on this benchmark. Refreshing nevertheless remains available at negligible cost for footage whose appearance changes more drastically.
Corruption protocol.
We corrupt the input of the first frame, which serves as the anchor, rather than the propagated matte. Because the anchor is the model’s own first-frame prediction, a corrupted input yields a degraded anchor matte that is propagated to all later chunks. We consider three corruptions:
•
Poor guidance mask.
We erode (under-segmentation, E) or dilate (over-segmentation, D) the first-frame guidance mask using grayscale morphology with a square kernel of
k
∈
{
5
,
21
}
k\in\{5,21\}
px.
•
Motion blur.
We apply a horizontal motion-blur kernel of
k
∈
{
7
,
15
,
25
}
k\in\{7,15,25\}
px to the first-frame RGB (B), so the model must matte a motion-blurred appearance.
•
Occlusion.
We composite a real animal foreground from AM-2K
Li et al. (2022)
over the subject using its ground-truth matte, enlarging it until at least 99% of the subject is covered, and zero the occluded region of the guidance mask so that it remains consistent with the now-invisible subject (Occ.).
We exclude the corrupted first frame from evaluation, so the metrics measure how the degraded anchor propagates to the rest of the video. This matters most under occlusion, where the input RGB and the ground-truth matte of the first frame disagree. It is also why the clean baseline in Table
3
b differs slightly from the main results: the only difference is the excluded clean first frame.
Results.
Across all corruptions, performance degrades only marginally relative to the clean baseline. Full occlusion is the most severe case, followed by motion blur and poor guidance masks, and larger kernels generally lead to slightly larger degradation. Even with a fully occluded anchor, the model remains close to its clean-anchor performance, indicating that a degraded anchor has only a limited effect on the rest of the video.
Appendix I
Limitation
Dependence on the mask track.
VideoMaMa++ deliberately separates tracking, delegated to a mask generator such as SAM3
Carion et al. (2025)
, from matting, so its robustness is bounded by the quality of the mask track. Errors confined to individual frames of a chunk, such as missing thin structures or drift under motion blur, can be corrected through cross-frame attention to neighboring frames or through interactive refinement (Section
B
). However, if the tracker locks onto the wrong object for an entire sequence, the matte follows that wrong track. This limitation is shared by all mask-guided matting methods.
Evaluating temporal smoothness on real video.
A key limitation of this work, and of video matting research more broadly, is the absence of a benchmark that can rigorously evaluate temporal smoothness on real video. Existing benchmarks
Lin et al. (2021)
;
Yang et al. (2025b)
;
Lim et al. (2026)
are constructed by compositing per-frame foregrounds onto random backgrounds, which provides accurate per-frame ground truth but does not capture the temporal dynamics of naturally captured footage.
As a result, temporal consistency on real-world videos is still largely assessed qualitatively. The annotation-free seam test of Section
F
quantifies one specific failure mode, discontinuities at chunk boundaries, without ground truth. However, it measures neither per-frame accuracy nor flicker within a chunk, and it applies only to methods that process video in chunks, so it cannot compare the overall temporal behavior of arbitrary methods.
Developing a benchmark with reliable ground-truth temporal smoothness, ideally captured rather than composited, remains an open problem for the community.
Appendix J
Societal Impact
Positive Societal Impact.
Our mask-guided video matting framework can substantially benefit creative industries, education, and communication. By reducing the manual effort required for high-quality video matting, the method lowers the barrier to professional-grade video production, enabling independent creators, educators, and small studios to produce polished content without specialized expertise or costly proprietary software. In film and visual effects, it can accelerate labor-intensive rotoscoping workflows, allowing artists to focus on creative decisions rather than frame-by-frame manual labeling. The technology also improves the quality of background replacement in video conferencing and virtual classrooms, supporting remote collaboration and accessibility-oriented applications such as isolating speakers or interpreters in educational content.
Negative Societal Impact.
Despite these benefits, high-quality video matting can be misused. As a core component in video manipulation pipelines, improved matting may facilitate the creation of more convincing deepfakes and manipulated media, contributing to misinformation and the erosion of public trust in video evidence.

article.headline: 给扩散模型加保留/精炼令牌，长视频抠像不再跳变
article.lede: VideoMaMa++ 用分离的 RGB 与掩码令牌流，加上保留、精炼令牌，把扩散抠像推广到长视频，块边界不再闪烁。
article.problem: 扩散式视频抠像依赖互联网规模预训练的生成先验，零样本泛化强，但扩散主干算力开销大，单次推理只能处理 6–24 帧，普通视频也要切成多块。各块仅凭粗糙二值掩码独立生成，而同一掩码对应多种合理的边界细化结果，于是块与块之间会漂移，出现边缘闪烁和透明度不连续。
article.method: 作者在 DiT 主干上把 RGB 帧与引导掩码表示为两条独立令牌流，与噪声令牌一起经完整时空自注意力交互，取代此前 U-Net 式的通道拼接融合。在此基础上引入一对可学习嵌入——保留令牌（preserve）和精炼令牌（refine）：前者标记「已是成品 matte、需保持」的帧，后者标记「只有粗掩码、需细化」的帧。推理时采用滑动窗口，让相邻块共享若干带保留令牌的重叠帧以传递局部时序信息，并在每个块额外送入一个全局参考锚帧，防止长序列上的误差累积，无需额外训练。
article.results: 在 VideoMatte240K、YouTubeMatte 与 V-HIM60 (Hard) 三个基准上，所有指标均为最优：VideoMatte 上 MAD 3.86、Grad 1.79、dtSSD 0.82，对照 VideoMaMa 分别为 4.34、4.06、1.21；YouTubeMatte 上 MAD 1.15（VideoMaMa 1.41）；V-HIM60 (Hard) 上 MAD 1.69（VideoMaMa 2.30）。块边界一致性专项实验中，开启保留令牌后重叠帧两次预测的 MAD 从 0.7128 降至 0.2583，Gradient 从 0.6811 降至 0.1235。无标注接缝检测显示，YouTubeMatte 上 VideoMaMa 有 62/64（MAX）与 63/64（fg-mean）片段在块接缝处变化超出内部帧，而本方法仅 18/64；16 段真实视频上为 14/16 对 7/16。代价是速度：1024×1024 下单卡 H100 为 1.17 FPS、峰值显存 11.3 GB，VideoMaMa 为 3.41 FPS、7.9 GB。
article.why_it_matters: 它把「扩散先验能给出精细发丝级 matte」和「长视频需要跨块一致」这两件事第一次同时做到，且保留了 6 帧推理即可、无需为长视频额外训练的可扩展形式。对视频后期、背景替换这类真正按分钟计的实际管线，块边界闪烁一直是扩散方法落地的直接障碍。
article.limitations: 方法仍依赖上游掩码跟踪：若跟踪器整段锁定到错误目标，matte 会跟着错，这是所有掩码引导方法的共同局限。此外它比前馈模型慢得多（1024² 下 1.17 FPS），且目前缺少能在真实拍摄视频上严格评估时序平滑度的基准，接缝检测只覆盖块边界这一种失效模式。

page_papers.title: GAD: Geometry Attention Distillation for Consistent Video Generation
page_papers.abstract: Video diffusion models generate visually compelling short-term sequences but often struggle to preserve scene geometry and object structure over time. In this paper, we first demonstrate that current video attention cannot identify reliable correspondences across frames, with responses dispersed across multiple regions even after recognizable scene structure has emerged. We argue that reliable cross-frame associations are essential for information exchange as scene structure forms in video generation. Thus, we introduce Geometry Attention Distillation (GAD), which transfers correspondences from a frozen geometry model's attention to video attention. Extracted from clean videos, these correspondences link the same static surface or moving object across frames. Since structure formation begins in deeper layers at higher noise and shallower layers at lower noise, we apply attention distillation at a student layer selected according to the noise timestep. After training, video attention focuses more consistently on corresponding locations. Experiments across all three video backbones demonstrate improved long-range scene consistency and dynamic temporal consistency, with geometric gains across generation lengths. On Wan2.2 5B, GAD improves cross-frame matching accuracy by at least 30% over the Wan baseline on both long-range benchmarks. Notably, GAD achieves these gains without additional inference modules, offering a promising approach to efficient and consistent video-based world simulation. Project page: https://fantasy-amap.github.io/GAD/.

We argue that reliable cross-frame associations are essential for information exchange as scene structure forms in video generation.
Thus, we introduce Geometry Attention Distillation (
GAD
), which transfers correspondences from a frozen geometry model’s attention to video attention.
Extracted from clean videos, these correspondences link the same static surface or moving object across frames.
Since structure formation begins in deeper layers at higher noise and shallower layers at lower noise, we apply attention distillation at a student layer selected according to the noise timestep.
After training, video attention focuses more consistently on corresponding locations.
Experiments across all three video backbones demonstrate improved long-range scene consistency and dynamic temporal consistency, with geometric gains across generation lengths.
On Wan2.2 5B,
GAD
improves cross-frame matching accuracy by at least 30% over the Wan baseline on both long-range benchmarks.
Notably,
GAD

However, such guidance does not ensure that video models reliably associate observations of the same scene element across frames, a capability essential for consistent video generation.
To understand how cross-frame associations develop, we examine attention patterns in video models and the emergence of scene structure across noise levels and network depths.
Our analysis shows that video attention cannot reliably identify the same scene element across frames: its responses are often dispersed across multiple regions, even after recognizable scene structure has emerged.
Such ambiguous associations can mix information from unrelated regions, undermining the preservation of scene geometry and object structure across frames.
Ideally, cross-frame attention should connect observations of the same scene element, enabling information exchange that supports consistent structure formation. We further observe that recognizable scene structure begins to emerge in deeper layers at higher noise and shallower layers at lower noise. This suggests guiding video attention where structure and cross-frame associations are beginning to form, with the guidance depth adapted to the noise level. For a source of this guidance, we turn to geometry foundation models
[
35
,
58
]
with promising multi-view matching capabilities.
Probing VGGT-
Ω
\Omega
[
59
]
reveals attention responses that associate the same static surface or moving object across frames, providing geometric correspondence targets for guiding video attention.
Building on these insights, we introduce Geometry Attention Distillation (
GAD
), an attention distillation framework that guides cross-frame associations during structure formation. During training, we extract correspondence targets from the attention of a frozen geometry model on clean videos. The total attention each source token assigns to a target frame serves as a reliability cue for weighting its supervision. We select the student layer for attention distillation according to the noise timestep, guiding cross-frame associations as scene structure forms. At the selected layer, pairwise supervision encourages spatial discrimination within frame pairs, while trackwise supervision extends temporal coverage by matching a common source to multiple target frames. These complementary distillation objectives are optimized jointly with the original video generation loss, transferring cross-frame relations while preserving the flexibility of video representations. After training, video attention focuses more consistently on corresponding regions across frames, while generated videos better preserve scene geometry and moving-object structure.
We evaluate
GAD
on camera-controlled video generation using RealEstate10K and DL3DV-10K for long-range scene consistency and OmniWorld-Game for dynamic consistency.
Across all three video backbones,
GAD
improves geometric consistency in long-range generation and temporal consistency in dynamic generation.
Geometric improvements across generation lengths further support the applicability of
GAD
across backbone configurations and video durations.
Notably, with Wan2.2 5B,
GAD
delivers at least a 30% relative improvement in cross-frame matching accuracy on both long-range benchmarks, without additional inference modules or computations.
Our main contributions are summarized as follows:
•
We analyze cross-frame associations in video models, revealing persistent geometric ambiguities in attention and a noise-dependent shift in the depth at which scene structure begins to form. These observations motivate geometry attention distillation at layers where structure is emerging.
•
We propose
GAD
, an attention distillation framework that transfers geometric correspondence knowledge to video attention for improved cross-frame consistency.
•
Extensive experiments demonstrate that
GAD
improves long-range scene consistency and dynamic temporal consistency across all three video backbones, with consistent improvements across generation lengths and no additional inference modules.

3  Analysis and Motivation
3.1  Attention Patterns in Video Models
Cross-frame consistency requires associating the same scene element across viewpoint changes or object motion. We examine how video attention establishes these associations across noise levels and network depths.
In
Fig.
2(a)
, we fix a source query and a target frame within a single video generation trajectory, and visualize the target frame’s intermediate token features using PCA alongside query-to-target attention responses. The PCA visualizations reveal recognizable scene structure, while the attention maps show whether responses concentrate near the reference correspondence or favor other regions. Further visualization details are provided in
Section
E.1
.
This joint analysis reveals two key findings. First, video attention cannot reliably identify the same scene element across frames. Its responses can remain dispersed across multiple regions, including those with similar appearance or semantics, even after recognizable scene structure has emerged in the PCA features. Second, the emergence of scene structure and cross-frame associations depends on both noise level and network depth. We distinguish three qualitative regimes.
In the
noise-dominated region
, PCA features show little recognizable scene structure, while attention responses remain scattered rather than concentrated around the corresponding region.
In the
structure-formation region
(red boxes in
Fig.
2(a)
), recognizable scene structure begins to emerge, and attention starts to respond to corresponding regions across frames, although competing responses remain. This region occurs in deeper layers at higher noise and shallower layers at lower noise.
In the
structure-established region
, scene layout is more clearly defined in the PCA features and cross-frame associations are more apparent, but they are not necessarily geometrically accurate.
These observations motivate explicitly guiding video attention toward geometrically corresponding regions to help preserve scene and object structure across frames.
Furthermore, the three observed regimes suggest that the placement of this guidance matters. In the noise-dominated region, weak structural evidence may make correspondence supervision difficult to exploit; in the structure-established region, additional guidance may have less opportunity to shape associations that have already formed.
The structure-formation region offers an intermediate stage where correspondence learning has a structural basis while the associations are still developing. We therefore hypothesize that geometric guidance is most effective in this region. Since this region emerges at different depths depending on noise, we adapt the supervision layer to the noise timestep.

With Wan2.1 14B,

achieves the best results across all seven metrics on both datasets, indicating that its benefits extend to a larger backbone.
Qualitative comparisons in

4
and
7

GAD
better preserves scene layout and geometric structure throughout long-range camera-controlled sequences.
Dynamic video consistency.
Across all three backbones,
GAD
improves subject consistency, background consistency, and motion smoothness over the corresponding Wan baseline (
Table
2

Improvements in both subject and background scores suggest that correspondence supervision is useful beyond static scene content, consistent with transferring relations between moving objects rather than enforcing fixed spatial locations. Lower FID and FVD and higher CLIP scores further indicate that these gains coexist with improved generation quality and text alignment. Qualitative comparisons in

and

5.3  Ablations
Using Wan2.2 5B on DL3DV-10K, we ablate the noise-timestep routing schedule, confidence-aware teacher weighting, and pairwise and trackwise supervision to assess their contributions.
Noise-dependent supervision.
As shown in
Table
4
, fixed-layer supervision (R2–R4) already improves geometric metrics over the Wan baseline (R1), while the proposed noise-timestep routing (R8) outperforms all other configurations (R1–R7); complete metrics appear in
Table
6
. Thus, correspondence targets are useful on their own, while their placement determines how effectively they guide generation. The lower performance of R5–R7 compared with R2–R4 further suggests that varying supervision with noise is insufficient without an appropriate layer choice.
These results support the motivation in
Section
3
: supervision should adapt to the noise timestep to target the structure-formation region rather than constrain a fixed layer throughout denoising.
Contributions of distillation components.
Table
5
shows that transferring teacher correspondences indiscriminately is insufficient: without confidence weighting, matching hit rate falls below the Wan baseline despite modest improvements in camera error. This supports accounting for uncertainty in teacher matches rather than treating every target equally. With confidence weighting, either pairwise or trackwise supervision improves all geometric metrics, while their combination performs best across all seven metrics. The joint gains are consistent with their complementary roles: pairwise supervision discriminates spatial matches within a target frame, whereas trackwise supervision extends correspondence coverage across time.
6  Conclusion
We have presented
GAD
, an attention distillation framework that transfers geometric correspondence knowledge from a frozen geometry teacher to video attention.
Motivated by geometric ambiguities in video attention and the noise-dependent emergence of scene structure,
GAD
guides cross-frame associations during structure formation while preserving the video model’s representational flexibility.
Experiments show that
GAD
consistently focuses attention on corresponding regions and improves long-range scene consistency and dynamic temporal consistency across all three video backbones, with geometric improvements across generation lengths. These gains require no additional inference modules. Our findings highlight geometric correspondence transfer through attention as a promising approach to consistent video generation and video-based world simulation.

Appendix A
Loss and Sampling Details
Sampling source–target relations.
Pairwise supervision samples valid directed frame pairs without replacement, excluding pairs within the same frame. Within each selected pair, source tokens are sampled uniformly without replacement from those with valid cached correspondences. Each selected query is compared with all spatial keys in its target frame. If fewer valid pairs or queries are available than the sampling budget, the remaining entries are masked out.
Trackwise supervision first samples one source frame containing eligible source tokens, then samples tokens that have valid correspondences in at least two other frames. Each source is matched to all of its valid target frames, excluding its own frame. For each target frame, the candidate set contains the Gaussian positive neighborhood and uniformly sampled spatial negatives without replacement from outside that neighborhood. Both schemes resample their relations during training; confidence weights affect the loss reduction rather than the probability of selecting a valid relation.

Appendix B
Implementation Details
B.1  Teacher Targets and Alignment
Reference correspondences for head selection.
We select the teacher layer–head pair using reference correspondences from both static and dynamic scenes. For the static set, we randomly sample 50 DL3DV scenes and estimate per-view depth and camera parameters with VGGT-
Ω
\Omega
, retaining only high-confidence depth estimates. Inspired by CAMEO
[
34
]
, we construct correspondence labels through cycle projection. A sampled source pixel is unprojected into 3D using its depth and camera parameters, then projected into a target view and assigned to a target token. We unproject the center of that target token using the target-view depth and project it back into the source view. A correspondence is retained only if the projections remain in bounds, the projected and estimated depths agree in both directions, and the return location is sufficiently close to the source sample. When multiple samples within a source token pass these checks, we retain the correspondence with the smallest cycle error. These are geometry-derived reference labels, rather than manually annotated ground truth. For the dynamic set, we use the provided ground-truth point correspondences from 30 dynamic scenes in TAPVid-DAVIS
[
15
]
.
Layer–head evaluation and selection.
We randomly sample query tokens from the input frame of each video and examine every global-attention layer–head pair. For each query, we extract the maximum-response location in each subsequent view and its target-frame attention mass, following
Eq.
1
. We compare the predicted locations with the reference correspondences to measure correspondence error and examine the associated attention masses as reliability cues. Considering correspondence consistency across both static and dynamic tokens, we select layer 13, head 10, which provides the best overall performance in this evaluation. All layer and head indices here are zero-based, and this single pair is used for training-label extraction in all experiments.
The evaluation also reveals substantial specialization across heads. For example, layer 13, head 0 captures static-token correspondences well but fails to reliably associate dynamic tokens, whereas layer 12, head 12 captures dynamic-token correspondences well but performs poorly on static tokens. Other pairs exhibit little correspondence consistency for either type of token. These observations motivate selecting a pair using both static and dynamic scenes, rather than relying on either set alone.
Limitations of projection-based labels.
The depth-and-camera cycle projection above assumes a static scene and therefore cannot directly recover correspondences for moving scene elements. We also observe substantial errors around thin structures and closely spaced surfaces, where depth errors and token discretization can associate different surfaces. These limitations can affect methods that rely on such projection-derived supervision, including CAMEO. Extracting correspondences from VGGT-
Ω
\Omega
attention instead exploits the model’s learned cross-view consistency without imposing a static-scene projection constraint. In our observations, this alleviates these failure cases and also supports correspondences for dynamic scene elements.

Human visibility annotations.
We determine the sigmoid mapping from human visibility annotations on DL3DV, using attention labels computed in an 81-frame teacher context. The annotated subset contains 55 scenes: 48 randomly sampled scenes and seven manually selected challenging scenes involving thin structures, occlusions, or out-of-view content. Each annotation page shows one source token and seven target frames sampled from seven temporal intervals, independently of attention mass. Annotators judge whether the source-token content is visible, not visible, or uncertain in each target frame; attention statistics are hidden during annotation. Of 803 judgments, we exclude 230 uncertain cases and retain 573 source-token/target-frame pairs, comprising 401 visible and 172 not-visible cases. These labels assess visibility rather than the localization accuracy of the attention maximum.

Auxiliary computation and inference.
Pairwise supervision evaluates sampled queries against all spatial keys in their selected target frames. The OmniWorld-Game adapters cover the same 0–5-second interval. Voyager and Uni3C use one 81-frame segment, with Voyager retaining its internal prefix mechanism. These conversions change the temporal sampling of the output, not the evaluated camera interval.
Camera-scale adaptation.
Warping-based methods are sensitive to camera scale because their explicit scene initialization and geometric conditioning depend on depth estimated from the first frame. Camera translations must therefore be expressed at a scale consistent with this depth; a mismatch produces an inconsistent initial scene and incorrect warps, which can propagate errors into subsequent predictions. This dependence on depth–camera scale calibration is a practical limitation of these explicit geometric methods. To provide suitable geometric inputs for a fair comparison, we carefully align camera translations with the depth scale used by each baseline, using the dataset- and model-specific corrections described below. PCA projection.
For each inspected layer and denoising step, we collect the target frame’s block-output features and project the spatial tokens onto three principal components. PCA is fitted independently for each layer–step pair, with a fixed random seed and deterministic component signs. Each projected channel is scaled using its first and 99th percentiles for RGB display. Because each projection is fitted independently, we compare the spatial organization of regions within each visualization rather than matching colors across cells. As discussed in

The onset of recognizable structure occurs in deeper layers at higher noise and in shallower layers at lower noise. Viewed alongside the attention maps, the PCA features help distinguish the emergence of scene structure from the development of cross-frame associations, showing that attention can still favor competing regions even when the scene layout is recognizable. This joint analysis motivates placing correspondence supervision near the structure-formation stage and adapting the supervised layer to the noise timestep.
Attention readout.
At the same layer and step, we extract queries and keys after normalization and rotary positional encoding. For the fixed source query, each head’s dot-product scores are softmax-normalized over all video keys. We then retain the target-frame slice and average the resulting probabilities over heads. This readout differs from both the block-output features used for PCA and the learned aggregation MLP used during training. Target-frame responses are displayed after normalization by each map’s maximum, with color mapping and interpolation used only for visualization. Thus, the color scale indicates relative spatial response within a map, not an absolute probability shared across layers or noise levels.
The denoising axis uses the actual model noise timesteps along the sampled inference trajectory. The noise-dependent shift in structure formation motivates our layer-routing schedule, whose generation performance is evaluated against fixed-layer and alternative schedules in

Appendix F
Limitations and Future Work
GAD
improves scene and dynamic consistency across all three video backbones by transferring geometric correspondences during training, while preserving the original inference procedure. Its current design suggests three directions for further improvement.
More reliable correspondence targets.
Our results demonstrate that attention distillation with geometric correspondence targets improves video consistency. The current implementation extracts these targets from VGGT-
Ω
\Omega
attention, making their quality dependent on the teacher’s matching ability and spatial resolution. This raises a natural question: can more reliable correspondences further improve the effectiveness of attention distillation? Stronger correspondence estimators or complementary sources of matching evidence could provide more accurate and complete supervision, particularly for ambiguous appearance, occlusion, and moving objects. The correspondence-based formulation of
GAD
provides a basis for exploring such alternatives to the current geometry teacher.
Adaptive supervision placement.
Our noise-timestep routing improves geometric metrics over fixed-layer supervision, demonstrating the value of adapting supervision depth to the denoising state. The current layer assignment depends only on the noise timestep and remains fixed throughout training. As the video model learns, the layers that benefit most from correspondence supervision may also change. Conditioning routing jointly on noise timestep and training progress could better match supervision to the model’s evolving representations, extending the current mechanism while preserving the original inference procedure.
Extension to autoregressive video generation.
GAD
improves static and dynamic consistency in Wan’s bidirectional video models. Autoregressive video generation offers a natural next setting, where preserving scene identity over long rollouts and maintaining coherent object motion remain important challenges. The principle of guiding attention with correspondences also applies to associations between newly generated content and preceding frames. Adapting the distillation objectives to the available temporal context under causal attention could help autoregressive models retain scene structure and moving-object identity as generation proceeds. This offers a promising route to extending the benefits demonstrated here to autoregressive generation.

article.headline: 把几何模型的注意力蒸馏进视频生成注意力
article.lede: 研究者发现视频模型的跨帧注意力常常对不准同一场景元素，于是用冻结的几何模型 VGGT-Ω 的注意力作为对应关系监督，在不
article.problem: 视频扩散模型能生成视觉上连贯的短视频，却难以在时间上保持场景几何与物体结构。作者分析了 Wan2.2 5B 的注意力，发现即使 PCA 特征里已经出现可辨认的场景结构，跨帧注意力响应仍分散在多个区域，无法稳定指向同一场景元素。他们还观察到场景结构的形成与噪声水平和网络深度相关：高噪声时出现在较深层，低噪声时出现在较浅层。
article.method: GAD 从冻结的 VGGT-Ω（1B）第 13 层第 10 个头上提取干净视频的跨帧对应关系，并以源 token 分配给目标帧的总注意力质量作为可靠性权重，对可能不可靠的匹配降权。训练时按噪声时间步选择学生层（t<850 用 L5，850≤t<950 用 L15，t≥950 用 L25），在该层用成对监督和轨迹监督两种交叉熵损失约束注意力的匹配分布，并与原流匹配目标联合优化。教师、对应关系缓存和头聚合 MLP 都只用于训练，推理时仅使用训练后的视频模型。
article.results: 在 RealEstate10K 与 DL3DV-10K 的 15 秒长程生成上，三个骨干的七项指标均优于各自 Wan 基线；Wan2.2 5B 上跨帧匹配命中率在两个数据集都取得至少 30% 的相对提升（RealEstate10K 从 0.263 到 0.350，DL3DV-10K 从 0.257 到 0.335），旋转距离从 6.705 度降到 4.335 度。Wan2.1 14B 在两个数据集全部七项指标上为最优，匹配命中率从 0.413 升到 0.476。OmniWorld-Game 的 5 秒动态生成中，主体一致性从 0.825 升到 0.853、背景一致性从 0.900 升到 0.913；推理峰值显存维持 34.85 GB 不变，运行时间 69.60 秒对 70.44 秒。在 DL3DV-10K 上按 5/10/15 秒分别训练时，各时长的四项几何指标均有改善（如 5 秒命中率 0.529 到 0.571），层路由消融中逐步加深的 R8 方案旋转距离为 4.890 度，优于任意固定层的 6.540 度。
article.why_it_matters: 它把「跨帧该看哪里」作为可监督的训练信号而非推理期外挂模块，为需要时间一致环境的视频世界模型提供了一条不增加推理成本的路径。
article.limitations: 监督质量受制于教师 VGGT-Ω 的匹配能力与空间分辨率，论文也承认该教师的注意力在目标元素被遮挡或缺失时仍可能出现峰值。层路由只依赖噪声时间步、训练全程固定，且方法仅在 Wan 这类双向模型上验证，自回归生成尚未测试；5 秒和 10 秒设定下还出现小幅 FID 或 FVD 折衷。

Abstract
Humanoid mobility over complex terrain requires accurate foot placement and coordinated whole-body motion capable of robust adaptation. Reinforcement learning (RL) policies trained without motion references generalize well across terrains, yet eliciting effective whole-body coordination through reward design and exploration alone remains challenging. In contrast, reference-based methods yield natural motions but struggle to adapt beyond the predefined trajectories in their training data. We introduce a learning framework that bridges these two approaches by using motion data strictly as a training prior. An explicit, self-supervised, attention-based contact planner predicts future body–environment contacts, while a contact-conditioned tracker translates these plans into coordinated whole-body motion. Together, they establish contact as an interface between sensory observations and control actions. This abstraction allows the policy to internalize the contact-aware structure of locomotion rather than directly replicating kinematics. Consequently, a single policy can exploit data-driven motion priors for natural whole-body coordination while retaining the flexibility to discover environment-dependent behaviors through reinforcement learning. Building on the learned contact planner and tracker, a subsequent fine-tuning stage bootstraps their acquired capabilities to explore environment variations beyond those covered by the original motion data. Operating entirely from onboard observations without any reference inputs at deployment, this framework enables versatile humanoid mobility in challenging environments.
Introduction
Deploying humanoid robots in human-centric environments requires capabilities well beyond stable bipedal walking. Traversing cluttered and geometrically constrained environments often demands stepping across sparse footholds, climbing onto obstacles, crawling through confined spaces, or leveraging the upper body for support. These multi-contact behaviors fundamentally diverge from conventional locomotion. Instead of adhering to a prescribed pattern of foot contacts, the robot must continuously determine the spatial, temporal, and anatomical distribution of its environmental interactions. Achieving this capability while remaining robust to disturbances and generalizing to previously unseen terrain remains a central challenge for humanoid mobility.
Reinforcement learning (RL) has proven highly effective for teaching quadrupedal and bipedal robots to swiftly navigate rough

. However, extending this paradigm to whole-body motion control introduces a massive combinatorial space. The robot must simultaneously determine which anatomical parts establish contact, the precise spatial and temporal distribution of those contacts, and the coordinated kinematics of the remaining degrees of freedom. Encoding these complex interactions indirectly through task objectives requires extensive reward shaping, where minor adjustments can yield drastically different contact strategies
[
48
]
. Consequently, while pure RL provides a powerful mechanism for robustness, reward signals alone offer insufficient structure for efficiently discovering complex whole-body behaviors.
Figure 1
:
Agile and robust humanoid mobility in diverse environments.
Our holistic controller enables a humanoid robot (the Unitree G1) to dynamically traverse diverse and challenging environments, including (a) ladder climbing, (b,j) stage climbing, (c) crawling, (d) vaulting over thin walls, (e) stair climbing, (f) standing up from the ground, (g) jumping down, (h) walking over stepping stones, and (i) sitting down, using a single generalist policy.
An alternative is to provide this structure directly through reference motions. Motion-imitation methods such as DeepMimic
[
34
]
reframe behavior discovery as a constrained tracking problem, enabling highly dynamic and coordinated whole-body motions. More recent systems extend this idea to humanoids using large motion datasets, retargeting, and learned motion priors
[
9
,

. Such approaches naturally produce coordinated and human-like behaviors because the reference specifies not only the desired task outcome but also how the entire body should achieve it. Yet a tracking controller can only execute a suitable motion if an appropriate reference can first be generated for the current environment. During deployment in previously unseen environments, this shifts the central problem from control to reference generation.
One solution is therefore to generate these references online. Model-based approaches can use trajectory planners to provide dynamically feasible motions that are subsequently tracked by a learned controller
[
15
,
19
]
, given a user-specified velocity or goal command. This decomposition combines explicit reasoning about environmental geometry with the robustness of learned control. Yet it also makes deployment dependent on a whole-body planner, which can be computationally expensive and inherits the modeling assumptions and failure modes of the planning system. For highly dynamic locomotion with intermittent multi-contact interactions, generating accurate full-body trajectories in real time remains particularly challenging.
Recent work has consequently begun replacing model-based reference generation with learned motion generators or planners
[
52
,
61
,
47
]
. These methods provide a promising route toward more expressive whole-body behaviors by learning the distribution of feasible motions from data. Nevertheless, generating complete motion trajectories remains a high-dimensional prediction problem. Generalization to environment configurations not represented in the motion data often requires substantial data augmentation, and small trajectory errors can become consequential when steppable or contactable regions are sparse. In such environments, producing a motion that is kinematically plausible is insufficient: the predicted interaction with the environment must also be physically accurate.
A related line of work attempts to close the gap between reference-based training and autonomous deployment by composing, augmenting, or distilling reference motions into perceptive policies
[
49
,
43
,
45
,
46
,
3
]
. Wu et al.
[
49
]
, for example, use motion matching to compose retargeted human skills into obstacle-adaptive reference trajectories, train tracking experts, and subsequently distill these behaviors into a vision-based policy. Wang et al.
[
43
]
introduce a generalist humanoid locomotion framework that trains multiple specialist policies for diverse skills and distills their expertise into a single vision-based policy through case-adaptive specialist selection, enabling unified locomotion control without reference motions at deployment. Wang et al.
[
45
,
46
]
propose a hybrid imitation learning framework that combines reference motion tracking with adversarial imitation learning, enabling a unified controller to preserve the naturalness of motion data while improving skill composition and adaptation to procedurally generated environments. Chen et al.
[
3
]
introduce a single perceptive whole-body policy that autonomously transitions between conventional locomotion and parkour skills without reference motions or skill labels at deployment, using terrain-conditioned reference augmentation during training to acquire diverse whole-body behaviors from a small set of motion seeds. These approaches demonstrate that motion data can provide valuable priors for highly dynamic humanoid behaviors. However, they require machinery for adapting and composing full-body motions across environmental variations. As the diversity and required geometric precision of the terrain increase, constructing references that cover the relevant combinations of obstacle geometry, contact location, and skill transition becomes increasingly difficult. This raises a fundamental question: how much of a reference motion does a robot actually need in order to learn generalizable whole-body locomotion?
We argue that the essential information lies not in the complete kinematic-space trajectory, but in its interaction with the environment. Consider how humans traverse irregular natural terrains. Human locomotion does not rely solely on reacting to the terrain immediately beneath the feet; instead, visual information is gathered prospectively to determine suitable future interactions with the environment. Matthis et al.
[
28
]
studied gaze and full-body kinematics during walking over natural outdoor terrain and showed that humans adapt their gaze behavior according to terrain complexity while maintaining a consistent temporal look-ahead strategy. Their findings reveal a tight coupling between perception of the upcoming terrain and the subsequent decisions on contact positions. These observations suggest that successful locomotion over geometrically constrained terrain depends critically on identifying where future contacts should occur, rather than prescribing the complete body trajectory leading to them.
The importance of contact has also been recognized in recent learning-based control methods. Zhang et al.
[
59
]
condition whole-body humanoid control on sequential contact objectives, demonstrating that contact specifications can effectively coordinate diverse whole-body behaviors. Omar et al.
[
32
]
use contact-centric representations to facilitate multi-task robot learning. More recently, Chen et al.
[
5
]
incorporate scene-interaction contacts as prompts for general humanoid whole-body motion tracking. Yu et al.
[
56
]
introduce contact flow, combining key body trajectories with temporal contact signals, as a shared interface for executing and composing long-horizon humanoid loco-manipulation skills. Together, these works demonstrate that contacts provide a compact and effective abstraction for specifying complex robot behaviors.
This perspective becomes even more relevant for whole-body mobility. When traversing sparse and complex terrain, the critical decisions extend beyond selecting footholds: the robot must determine which parts of the body should interact with the environment and where these interactions should occur. Once these contacts are specified, however, there may exist many valid whole-body trajectories that realize them. A hand contact on the top of a ledge, for example, constrains an essential interaction with the environment without uniquely determining the trajectories of the arms, torso, and legs. We therefore propose contact as an intermediate representation between terrain perception and whole-body control. Compared with a full-body reference trajectory, contacts retain the geometrically critical information required for terrain interaction while leaving the policy freedom to adapt the motion connecting them.
This representation also changes the role of motion data. Rather than using demonstrations as trajectories that the robot must reproduce, we use them as training-time guidance for learning which body–environment interactions are useful. Reference motions provide examples of effective contacts during training, while reinforcement learning determines how those contacts should be realized under different robot states and terrain configurations. The resulting policy is therefore not required to remain close to a reference trajectory. More importantly, the reference is removed entirely at deployment: given only the robot state, terrain observation, and a user-specified goal, the policy must autonomously determine appropriate contacts and execute the corresponding whole-body motion. In this way, demonstrations provide structure to the otherwise difficult exploration problem of whole-body locomotion without constraining the policy to the distribution of full-body trajectories contained in the dataset.

Successful rollouts are stored in the fine-tuning buffer and subsequently used as additional supervision for the contact planner, forming a bootstrapping loop in which planner-generated contacts are executed, validated through successful interaction, and recycled to improve the planner. Reference trajectories are sampled proportionally from the original dataset during fine-tuning to retain the previously learned tracking behaviors.
To autonomously infer these contacts from terrain observations, we build upon attention-based map encoding (AME)
[
12
,
58
]
. AME uses robot proprioception to condition attention over a local terrain representation, allowing the policy to selectively extract terrain features relevant to its current locomotion state. In previous work, this mechanism was learned implicitly and was shown to focus on steppable terrain regions associated with future footholds. Here, we exploit an alternative capability of this architecture: attention provides a natural interface for explicit contact planning. Rather than using attention only to encode terrain into a latent representation for control, we use it to identify task-relevant contact locations on the terrain map. Specifically, our contact planner attends to terrain points conditioned on the robot’s proprioception and a user-specified goal and predicts explicit contact locations directly on the map. This formulation tightly couples when and where the robot should interact with the environment to its evolving physical state. The planner can therefore shift its attention as the robot moves, selecting different terrain regions for feet, hands, and other body contacts according to both local geometry and the current proprioceptive state. This design is particularly suited to sparse terrain, where a small error in a predicted contact can distinguish a feasible interaction from a failure. At the same time, predicting contacts rather than complete whole-body trajectories substantially reduces the dimensionality of the planning problem.
Based on these insights, we introduce a framework that uses an explicit, self-supervised attention-based contact representation as the interface between perception and whole-body control. During training, reference motion data guides the discovery of effective body-environment interactions. Rather than tracking full reference trajectories, the system abstracts the motion data into a task-relevant contact structure. The policy then leverages RL to physically realize these target contacts while optimizing for broader locomotion objectives. This formulation preserves the primary advantage of motion data by providing structured guidance for coordinated whole-body behavior without restricting the agent to strict kinematic reproduction.
This contact-centric representation has several important properties. First, it reduces the dimensionality of the guidance compared to full-body trajectory tracking. Because multiple dynamically feasible motions can realize the same contact objective, the contact representation constrains only the task-relevant interactions while leaving the policy free to explore and optimize the whole-body motion between contacts. Second, contact locations are expressed directly with respect to the environment, providing the geometric precision needed when feasible support regions are sparse. Third, training remains simple: instead of constructing rewards that separately induce climbing, crawling, stepping, and other behaviors, reference contacts can be incorporated through a common contact-tracking objective. Finally, because reference trajectories are used only as training-time guidance, deployment requires neither motion retrieval nor a model- or learning-based motion generator. Terrain diversity can therefore be explored directly through RL rather than covered through exhaustive manual augmentation of reference trajectories.
To obtain diverse and physically feasible whole-body references for training, we use a motion-retargeting pipeline
[
61
]
. It transfers human motion data to the target humanoid while accounting for kinematic constraints. The resulting trajectories, together with their body–environment contact labels and positions, provide contact-aware references as training-time guidance for learning whole-body locomotion.
In summary, this paper introduces a three-stage training framework that progressively transfers knowledge from motion data to a whole-body control policy, with the following contributions:
1)
A contact-informed whole-body tracking training pipeline where the policy is conditioned on contact plans instead of whole-body trajectories.
2)
A supervised learning formulation for contact planning, leveraging human motion data to capture rich and diverse contact strategies, and an attention-based contact planner (ACP) that predicts contact plans for nine body parts (hands, elbows, knees, feet, and pelvis) on rough and discontinuous terrain given a user-specified goal.
3)
An RL fine-tuning stage bootstrapping on planner-generated contact plans that bridges data-driven imitation and reward-driven exploration, enabling generalization to unseen terrains.
4)
A LiDAR-based neural mapping framework that accurately captures fine-grained geometry, including small and thin structures such as ladder rungs, for precise whole-body locomotion.
Through three training stages – contact tracking, contact planning, and RL fine-tuning – our framework progressively reduces its reliance on motion data while preserving the coordinated whole-body behaviors acquired from demonstrations. By isolating task-relevant contact structure, this framework yields a unified generalist policy capable of versatile, coordinated whole-body motion control in previously unseen environments using only onboard sensing (Figure
1
). Figures
2
and
3
provide a visual overview of the method.
Results
0.1
Agile and generalized whole-body locomotion
We tested our unified generalist policy on the Unitree G1 humanoid robot through extensive real-world experiments (Figures
1
and
4
) across a diverse range of challenging indoor and outdoor terrains. Operating without reference motions at deployment, the controller achieves precise, coordinated whole-body locomotion by autonomously adapting its contact strategy to the perceived terrain. The resulting behaviors include stair, ladder, and box climbing, sitting down, standing up from the ground, sparse and composite terrain traversal, and other whole-body interactions.
Importantly, successful execution requires more than recognizing the surrounding geometry: the policy must also select an appropriate interaction strategy according to user-specified goal. Consequently, the same environment can elicit substantially different whole-body behaviors depending on the desired goal position and orientation as well as the geometry. For example, as shown in Figure
5
A, when approaching a box, a forward-facing goal behind the robot can let the robot sit down (a), whereas a forward-facing goal in front of the robot on top of a low box prompts the robot to step onto it (b). If the box is too high, the policy instead leverages a whole-body climbing strategy that uses the hands for additional support (c). When the desired orientation points to the left or right, the policy reorients its body and performs a sideways climbing maneuver (d). When the goal is located farther across the top surface, the robot climbs onto the box, crawls forward toward the target, and then stands up (e). If the goal is on the other side of the box, the robot climbs up, crawls forward, then steps down (f). Similarly, different motions can be generated for getting down from a box given different heights and goal commands (g-i). These examples demonstrate that our unified generalist policy does not simply associate a terrain category with a fixed motion primitive, but jointly interprets environment geometry and goal commands to synthesize appropriate contact patterns and whole-body motions online.
The unified policy further generalizes to unseen and composite terrains, where multiple terrain types and interaction modes are encountered sequentially, as shown in Figure
5
B. In these scenarios, the robot must not only execute individual skills but also autonomously determine how to connect them as the terrain and goal evolve. The policy synthesizes appropriate motion transitions between behaviors without manually designed transition motions, explicit skill-switching mechanisms, or augmentation of the motion dataset for specific terrain compositions. For example, it can transition continuously from walking to climbing, crawling, standing, or other contact-rich behaviors as required by the local geometry and the user-specified goal. In Figures
5
B-a and
5
B-b, only one goal is specified. For the unstructured terrains shown in Figures
5
B-c and
5
B-d, these goals are provided as manually specified intermediate waypoints to guide local traversal. (Global navigation is beyond the scope of this work.) The resulting policy successfully traverses diverse unseen terrains while maintaining its original ability without requiring additional reference motions or terrain-specific motion augmentation. This capability allows a single policy to compose previously learned interaction strategies into continuous whole-body locomotion over terrain configurations not represented in the original motion dataset. Together, these results demonstrate precise, robust, and goal-conditioned whole-body humanoid locomotion that generalizes beyond both the motions and terrain configurations encountered during training. Simulation-based Evaluations
We use simulation to examine whether contact commands provide sufficient guidance for whole-body tracking, how learned contact plans transfer beyond the reference terrains, and how goal-reaching RL fine-tuning and attention-based planning contribute to this generalization (Figure
7
).
We distinguish three terrain groups by their usage in different training stages.
Reference-anchored terrains
are associated with reference motions used in Stage 1/2, and test retention of demonstrated behaviors.
Goal-reaching terrains
are the procedurally generated terrains used for reference-free fine-tuning in Stage 3 and provide a zero-shot transfer test for Stage-2 policies.
Unseen terrains
introduce obstacle composition, task-irrelevant distractors, and surface roughness to test skill transitions, rejection of irrelevant geometry, and traversal of irregular support surfaces, respectively.
The first two groups each contain four categories, defined by support density and the body parts required for support. Dense foot-only terrains provide continuous support for walking, such as stairs and slopes; sparse foot-only terrains require precise foot placement, as on stepping stones and narrow beams. Dense whole-body terrains provide broad surfaces for additional hand or knee support, as in box climbing and get-up transitions; sparse whole-body terrains offer only discrete contacts for multiple links, as in ladder climbing and vaulting. This division distinguishes the placement precision required by sparse support from the multi-limb coordination required by whole-body interactions. Training and evaluation terrain definitions are provided in the
supplementary training details
and
supplementary evaluation details
,
respectively.
Category-level comparisons pool 3,000 episodes per method and category across three evaluation seeds. The terrain-specific comparisons in Figure
7
E use 1,000 episodes per method and radar axis, with the ladder axis pooling four variants. The eight curated composite courses are evaluated separately from the unseen-terrain benchmark. For category-level evaluations, success requires reaching within 0.5 m of the active goal horizontally; for sitting, standing, and get-up transitions, the criterion is instead a vertical error below 0.1 m. On the curated courses, success additionally requires reaching the target height and passing through the prescribed course without entering the pit or leaving the traversal lane.
Contact placement error measures the Euclidean distance between commanded and realized contact positions at contact onset, averaged over valid contact events. We report Wilson 95% confidence intervals for success and episode-cluster-robust 95% intervals for contact error. These quantify evaluation uncertainty rather than variability across training runs. Episodes with invalid policy outputs count as failures and are excluded from contact error. Sensor noise, physics randomization, and action delay are disabled to isolate terrain-dependent performance.

Goal-reaching fine-tuning extends skills learned from motion data to terrains without corresponding reference motions. Discussion
Our results suggest that contact can serve as a general interface for humanoid mobility, bridging motion data, sensory observation, and whole-body control. Unlike full-body trajectories, contacts only specify where, when, and with which body part the robot should interact with the environment without prescribing how the entire motion should be executed. This abstraction allows demonstrations to provide structured guidance during training while leaving reinforcement learning the flexibility to explore behaviors on new terrain. As a result, a single policy can compose and transition between diverse whole-body behaviors without reference trajectories, skill labels, or manually designed transitions at deployment.
The attention-based contact planner plays an important role in terms of the generalization capability of our framework. Building on attention-based map encoding
[
12
,
58
]
, the planner selectively attends to terrain regions relevant to future contacts conditioned on proprioception and goal commands. Rather than coupling a particular terrain configuration to a specific motion, the policy learns to reason about the local geometry that supports each interaction. This allows contact strategies acquired from demonstrated motions to adapt to new terrain geometries and to be recombined on unseen terrain compositions. Goal conditioning further enables different contact strategies to emerge on the same terrain depending on the desired position and orientation. Together, selective terrain attention and explicit contact prediction provide a structured representation that helps transfer whole-body behaviors beyond the terrain in the reference data encountered during training.
Several limitations remain. First, our current perception and contact representations primarily target terrain-centric 2.5-D interactions. Although the LiDAR-based mapping pipeline captures fine geometric structures such as ladder rungs, more general interactions including overhead contacts, hanging, and manipulation will require richer 3D perception and contact representations. Second, the current system also addresses only local goal-conditioned locomotion rather than global navigation. Additionally, the current pipeline cannot handle aerial motions that do not have distinguishable contact sequences. For example, the contact sequences of a backflip and a vertical jump are essentially the same, despite their substantially different whole-body motions, and therefore cannot be distinguished by our current contact representation.
Future work could extend the contact interface to vision-based and general 3D scene representations, allowing contacts with arbitrary surrounding structures rather than predominantly terrain surfaces. Combining such representations with semantic or global planners could enable humanoids to autonomously select goals and interaction strategies over larger environments. Semantic task inputs could also complement the contact representation in cases where different behaviors share indistinguishable contact sequences, providing additional information to specify the intended motion. Ultimately, walking, climbing, crawling, recovery, and manipulation can all be viewed as different sequences of body-environment interactions. Contact therefore offers a common physical abstraction through which humanoids may compose known interaction strategies into new behaviors in previously unseen environments.
Materials and Methods
Motivation
Developing generalizable whole-body motion control exposes a fundamental tradeoff. Pure RL excels at robust, foot-dominant locomotion, but scaling it to whole-body interactions requires complex reward engineering. Conversely, reference-tracking methods provide strong kinematic priors but bind the policy to the source data, necessitating online trajectory generation during deployment. This dependency creates a bottleneck on sparse or unstructured terrains, where precise environmental interactions must rapidly adapt to unseen geometric constraints.
Bridging these approaches does not require transferring complete reference trajectories. Inspired by biological studies showing that human visual attention prospectively targets future foot placements
[
28
]
, we propose that the essential information lies strictly in the spatial, temporal, and anatomical distribution of environmental interactions. Contact thus serves as a compact intermediate representation. It retains the geometrically critical structure of demonstrated motions while leaving the high-dimensional kinematics underconstrained, allowing a single contact sequence to specify highly complex behaviors.
Motivated by this, we use future whole-body contacts as the interface between perception, planning, and control (Figure
2
A). During training, motion data exposes the robot to coordinated interaction strategies, which an attention-based contact planner learns to predict directly from terrain geometry, robot proprioception, and goal commands. Subsequent RL fine-tuning randomizes the terrain without requiring corresponding reference augmentation. This formulation strictly separates what interactions should occur from how the robot should realize them. The contact planner provides geometrically precise, goal-dependent interaction targets, while RL synthesizes the robust motion required between contacts. Consequently, reference motions act solely as training guidance and are entirely eliminated at deployment, enabling a single onboard-sensing policy to autonomously execute and transition between diverse whole-body behaviors.
To support this framework, we developed two enabling pipelines. First, a constrained motion-retargeting tool extracts diverse contact strategies from human data, preserving key environmental interactions while respecting the robot’s kinematic limits. Second, because precise contact planning on sparse structures like ladder rungs demands high-fidelity perception, we introduce a LiDAR-based neural mapping pipeline that reconstructs detailed local geometry to provide the planner with a consistent terrain representation. Together, these components provide diverse contact-rich training data and sufficiently detailed terrain observations for precise whole-body contact planning in real-world environments.
Contact-Informed Whole-Body Tracker
To provide whole-body reference motions for training, we utilize contact-aware motion retargeting
[
61
]
. It transfers recorded human behaviors to the target humanoid while accounting for differences in morphology, kinematic constraints, and, importantly, body–environment interactions. Direct joint-angle mapping is generally infeasible because human motion data and the robot differ substantially in their kinematic structures and body proportions, often resulting in joint-limit violations, ground penetration, and physically inconsistent contacts. Such artifacts are particularly problematic for contact-rich behaviors such as climbing, crawling, vaulting, etc where the semantics of the motion are largely determined by which body part establishes contact, when the contact occurs, and where it occurs in the environment. We therefore explicitly extract the contact sequence together with the robot kinematics from the dataset.
This retargeting tool first converts human motions from different sources into a unified floating-base and Cartesian landmark representation, followed by spatial rescaling and temporal normalization. For each frame, it solves a nonlinear IK problem over the robot base pose and joint configuration. Position objectives track corresponding body landmarks, including the hips, knees, ankles, toes, shoulders, elbows, hands, chest, and head, while orientation objectives align individual robot limb segments with the corresponding directions in the human skeleton. The optimization additionally constrains the robot within its joint limits and enforces unilateral ground constraints on the feet to prevent penetration. For motions involving richer environmental interactions, minimum-distance constraints against the robot and environment geometry further prevent physically invalid intersections with obstacles such as boxes, stairs, and ladder rungs. Temporal regularization toward the previous solution suppresses frame-to-frame discontinuities, producing smooth trajectories while maintaining consistent contact configurations over time.
In parallel with kinematic retargeting, we explicitly detect and record body–environment contacts at every frame, involving the pelvis, knees, feet, elbows, and hands, which are identified from the simulated contact geometry and associated with the corresponding environmental objects. We record both the active contact sequence and contact locations in the world frame, preserving the temporal contact schedule and spatial relationship between the robot and the environment.

Attention-based Whole-Body Contact Planner
At every control step, the planner outputs a contact plan for the nine contact-active bodies of the humanoid: the two feet, two knees, two hands, two elbows, and the pelvis, so that the plan can describe genuine multi-contact behavior rather than footstep sequences alone. For each body the plan gives a target contact position, expressed in a gravity-aligned frame centered at the robot base and rotated with its yaw so that it is invariant to the robot’s world position and heading, together with a binary occupancy flag indicating whether that body is expected to establish a new contact within the planning horizon.

Starting from the learned contact planner and whole-body contact tracker, we fine-tune the policy on procedurally altered variants of the original terrains, with randomized obstacle poses, geometries, and configurations. Through this process, the policy learns to adapt both its contact strategy and whole-body motion to terrain variations while retaining the behaviors acquired from the original motion data.
Hindsight Contact Labeling
The planner’s targets come from the policy’s own successful experience rather than from the motion dataset, so that it learns contacts the tracker can actually realize. After each completed episode we scan its recorded trajectory backward to identify the next contact onset for each body part. We identify contact onset from the vertical contact force after discarding contact segments shorter than ten consecutive control steps, thereby filtering out brief or intermittent contacts. LiDAR-based Neural Mapping
To provide the controller with accurate height map observations, we design a
LiDAR-based neural mapping pipeline, illustrated in
Figure
8
. The pipeline builds on the depth-based neural
mapping method of Zhang et al.
[
58
]
, adapted to the sensing characteristics of
LiDAR to handle perception noise. We convert each frame’s point cloud into
local grids and use a neural network to predict local elevations with
associated uncertainty. The predictions are fused into a global map, which
the locomotion controller queries during deployment.
Network design.
The main difference from Zhang et al.
[
58
]
lies in the network design. Unlike
depth cameras, which provide a roughly fixed region of interest, our
head-mounted MID-360
[
24
]
LiDAR provides a panoramic view
with sparse hits. Rather than directly predicting a dense reconstruction,
we have the network select one of three modes for each grid:
keep the exact measured height, use the average of the neighborhood, or
discard the value and leave the grid empty. This allows the model to
generalize to arbitrary scan sparsity. Moreover, the disagreement among
the mode logits, interpreted as probabilities for sampling modes, serves
as an uncertainty estimate that accounts for sensing noise. Only non-empty
predictions are processed during fusion.
Fusion prior for overhanging structures.
Since the mapping must handle overhanging structures such as ladders, we
introduce a heuristic prior in the global fusion. When a new prediction falls in the
same grid as an existing confident prediction (uncertainty
<
0.15
<0.15
m) and lies more than 0.15 m
below it, the new point is discarded unless its elevation angle is above
−
40
∘
-40^{\circ}
. This ensures that if an earlier scan observes an
overhanging ladder rung while a later close-by scan only observes the floor beneath
it, the rung is not erased from the global map. Despite this ladder-targeted prior, the mapping module stays effective for all tested terrains.
Training and implementation.
We train on the same meshes as Zhang et al.
[
58
]
, augmented with random
overhanging bars and random ladders leaning against boxes to ensure
performance on sparse overhanging structures. We also simulate per-point
positional noise and ray-divergence
noise
[
33
]
according to the
LiDAR specifications. Since training is formulated as mode
classification, we derive labels from the ground truth and the generated
noisy grids, and train the CNN with a cross-entropy loss. Local grids
cover

[
−

with a grid resolution of 3 cm. The pipeline runs onboard on the

It is also worth noting that, since the LiDAR is head-mounted, occlusion is
