The University of Hong Kong
Tonghan Wang
Affiliation:
Tsinghua University
*
Equal contribution
Affiliation:
Corresponding author
Abstract
Large language models (LLMs) can sometimes report perturbations to their internal activations—even when the input provides no evidence that an intervention occurred. How do models detect and localize such internal changes? We study this question using a controlled task that keeps the input text fixed. We either inject a concept vector into the hidden state at one of ten token positions or apply no intervention. The model is asked to identify the perturbed position or report that no intervention occurred. Across three model families, we identify two small groups of attention heads with distinct roles in introspective reporting. Middle-layer
gate heads
influence whether the model reports a change, while
router heads
in a later layer help select the position to report. Interventions on gate heads can suppress position reports even when router heads supply location information. We further examine why reporting accuracy varies across concepts. Concept vectors that are localized more accurately produce stronger attention-score and output responses in gate heads, which is associated with better alignment of the induced key and value changes in their QK and OV computations. Together, these findings identify attention-head mechanisms supporting introspective detection and localization.
Code:
https://github.com/Zethan06/introspection_mechanism
.
Figure 1:
Overview of the task and the two-component circuit.
Left
: the experimental pipeline. With the input text held fixed, either a concept vector is injected into the hidden state at one of ten candidate token positions or no intervention is applied. The model is asked to report the intervened position or answer
none
; its answer is read from the logits at the first output position.
Right
: the two processes we identify.
Gate heads
influence whether the model reports a position or
none
, while
router heads
separate the ten injection positions from one another. Each point is one injected concept, and points sharing a color share the same injected position.
1
Introduction
Large language models (LLMs) rely on internal representations to transform inputs into outputs. Whether they can report changes to these representations is a fundamental question about their capacity for introspection. Recent experiments show that models can sometimes report interventions on their hidden activations even when the input text is held fixed
(
Lindsey, 2026
)
. Yet the underlying mechanism remains unclear: how does an internal change become an explicit report about it?
Prior work studies this question with mechanistic interpretability tools such as transcoders
(
Macar et al., 2026
)
. Transcoders replace parts of a model with a separately trained approximation, so the features they find may not reflect exactly the model’s native computation. Moreover, this work, like earlier introspection experiments
(
Lindsey, 2026
)
, relies on an LLM judge to score free-form reports, introducing a potentially unreliable layer of interpretation. We address both limitations by analyzing the model’s own attention heads and introducing a task with exact, judge-free evaluation.
We design a controlled detection-and-localization task (Figure
1
). The model sees ten labeled candidate token positions. We either add a concept vector to the hidden state at one position or make no change, keeping the input text identical. The model must output the affected position’s label or
none
. For example, if we inject a vector at candidate 6, the correct answer is
6
. We find that the model completes this report in two parts:
whether
the model reports a change and
where
it identifies that change. We score these answers using only the logits at the first output position. This prevents the model from using text it has already generated as evidence of a change and allows us to evaluate answers without an LLM judge. We ask which neurons control whether a change is reported, which determine its reported location, and how the neurons work together.
Across the Qwen
(
Yang et al., 2025
)
, LLaMA
(
Grattafiori et al., 2024
)
, and Gemma
(
Gemma Team, 2025
)
model families, we find attention heads with different roles in this task. We test these roles by replacing selected head outputs with their values from a run with or without injection, a form of activation patching
(
Vig et al., 2020
;
Meng et al., 2022
)
. We search for small groups of middle-layer heads whose outputs can increase or reduce the rate of position reports, selecting the heads in each group jointly. We call these
gate heads
. In a later layer, 1–2 heads help select the reported position; we call these
router heads
. Replacing router-head outputs with their values from a run without injection reduces position accuracy. Directing their attention to another candidate position changes which position the model reports.
We then test how these roles relate. When gate-head outputs come from an injection at one position and router-head outputs from an injection at another, the reported position usually follows the router heads, and restoring gate-head outputs to their uninjected values suppresses position reports. Supplying router outputs from an injected run does not fully restore these reports. The two groups thus play different but connected roles: gate heads affect whether the model reports a change, while router heads help select the position it reports.
Finally, we investigate why the model localizes injections more accurately
for some concepts than for others.
We analyze how gate heads use their queries to read changes in keys
and their attention weights to combine changes in values.
Compared with lower-accuracy concepts, higher-accuracy concepts show
stronger alignment in both computations, with smaller differences
in the size of the changes.
We further test whether these changes affect reporting by removing
the contributions of a few leading output components from each gate
head. This reduces position reporting, providing causal evidence
that these output components contribute to the model’s reports.
More broadly, understanding how models detect and report changes to their
internal states can inform AI safety and interpretability.
2
Related work
Introspective reports and their confounds.
Models can predict their own behavior better than an equally trained observer
(
Binder et al., 2025
)
, and can report injected concept vectors
(
Lindsey, 2026
)
, whose four criteria (accuracy, grounding,
internality, metacognitive representation) we adopt;
Gurnee et al. (2026)
characterize which representations are verbalizable
at all. Critiques narrow what counts as evidence:
Singh et al. (2026)
argue
the behavior is consistent with generic anomaly detection and ask for a
dissociable second-order process, and
Hahami et al. (2025)
show binary
“did something change” probes are partly a global logit shift toward
affirmative answers, though harder ten-sentence variants survive it. Our task is
built against these objections: fixed text,
none
competing with ten
position labels, and scoring only the first generated token. We do not treat
anomaly detection as an alternative to introspection: under the criteria we
adopt, detecting an internally induced change is introspective access when the
report is grounded, internal, and not a direct translation of the change into an
answer, and Section
4.4
tests the last condition.
Mechanisms of intervention awareness.
Closest to us,
Macar et al. (2026)
also report a two-stage
organization, with early “evidence carrier” features suppressing downstream
“gate” features that emit the default negative answer. Their account rests on
an external transcoder dictionary, an LLM judge over free-form replies, and
components taken by thresholding attribution scores. We instead identify
components from the model’s own structure—individual attention heads and their
query–key and output behavior—which yields a sparse circuit that recurs
across three model families and supports direct causal intervention, including a
crossed gate–router intervention that tests the gating relationship between the two components.
Rivera and Africa (2026)
show detection can be
trained in and that detection dissociates from resistance—the safety reading
being that steering is not invisible, so a steered model may comply because it
noticed.
Steering vectors and head-level circuits.
Our injections use standard linear activation edits
(
Turner et al., 2024
;
Rimsky et al., 2024
;
Zou et al., 2023
;
Li et al., 2023
;
Arditi et al., 2024
)
,
but as a calibrated stimulus rather than a control knob. Methodologically we
follow head-level circuit analysis: the QK/OV decomposition
(
Elhage et al., 2021
)
, induction heads
(
Olsson et al., 2022
)
, the
IOI circuit and path patching
(
Wang et al., 2023
)
, causal tracing
(
Meng et al., 2022
)
, and automated discovery
(
Conmy et al., 2023
)
. Router
heads join a family in which a few heads decide behavior by choosing a source
position—retrieval heads
(
Wu et al., 2025
)
and the rerouted decision
heads of
Sun et al. (2026)
; here the “needle” is not in the text but in
the model’s own hidden state. Finally, since probes recover internal state that
a model’s text omits
(
Kadavath et al., 2022
;
Burns et al., 2023
)
and explanations can
misstate their own causes
(
Turpin et al., 2023
)
, we localize and
manipulate the components producing the report rather than trusting it.
3

6
Discussion
Summary and implications.
Across three model families, introspective reporting in our task relies on two
small groups of attention heads with different but connected roles. Middle-layer
gate heads regulate whether the model reports a position, and router heads in a
later layer help select which position it reports. The two groups interact
through a gating mechanism: interventions on gate heads can suppress position
reports even when router heads supply location information. Across concepts,
gate heads differ more in how well their queries and attention align with an
injected change than in the size of that change. This suggests that whether an
internal change is reported depends partly on how the model reads it, not only
on how large it is.
Limitations and future work.
Our analysis covers only six task variants, one injection layer and strength per model, and models of
up to 12B parameters.
Natural next steps are to test whether gate heads also contribute to free-form
and unprompted reports, and whether the same heads respond to other kinds of
internal perturbation. We analyze attention heads because the report must carry
information across positions; how MLPs process the signal within a position
remains to be studied. Intervening directly on key–query alignment would test
whether it controls which concepts are reported. For safety, our results support
the concern that steered models may register the edit
(
Rivera and Africa, 2026
)
, and suggest gate heads as a candidate site
for monitoring such registration.
AI use statement
We used large language models to polish the wording of the manuscript and to
assist in writing experiment code. All research questions, experimental
designs, analyses, and conclusions are the authors’ own. The authors reviewed
all AI-assisted text and code, verified every reported result against the
experiment outputs, and take full responsibility for the content of this paper.
Ethics statement
This work involves no human subjects, personal data, or crowdsourced
annotation. All experiments use publicly released open-weight models and
common English vocabulary words, with no harmful content generated or
collected. We study introspection in a functional sense only and make no claim
about awareness or experience in language models. Understanding how models
detect interventions on their internal states is relevant to safety methods
based on activation steering. It can help monitor whether a model has
registered such an intervention, and we believe the benefits of this
understanding for transparency and oversight outweigh its risks.

Appendix A
Additional details
A.1
Introspection criteria and task validity
Following the definition of
Lindsey (2026)
, we consider an
internal-state report introspective only if it satisfies four criteria.
Below, we state each criterion and explain how our task and analyses
address it, distinguishing properties of the evaluation design from
empirical evidence about the model’s reports.
•
Accuracy
requires the report to correctly describe the
model’s internal state. Our interventions provide known labels:
none
for clean trials and the intervened position for injected
trials. We evaluate correct
none
responses and correct-position
reports separately (Table
1
). These measurements
quantify report accuracy without interpreting free-form text.
•
Grounding
requires the report to causally depend on the
internal property being described, such that changing that property
would change the report. Our task manipulates hidden states while
holding the visible candidate text fixed. Comparing clean and injected
runs, and varying the injection position, tests whether reports track
the manipulated internal state. The gate and router interventions
further identify internal components that causally influence whether
the model reports an intervention and which position it reports.
Together, these analyses support a causal link between internal
perturbations and the resulting reports.
•
Internality
requires this causal influence to remain
internal; inferring an abnormal internal state from anomalies in
previously sampled outputs does not constitute introspective awareness. We evaluate only the first generated token of the decision
response. The model therefore has no previously sampled decision text
from which to infer the intervention. Because the intervention changes
hidden activations without changing the visible input, the design
excludes this external-text route from the intervention to the report.
•
Metacognitive representation
requires the report to arise
from a representation of the internal state itself rather than from a
direct translation of that state into language. Following
Lindsey (2026)
, we provide indirect evidence for this
criterion. Our task asks whether and where a perturbation occurred.
Layerwise analyses distinguish position–none separation from
position-specific representations
(Figure
2
), while gate–router
interventions show that supplied positional information is insufficient
to restore position reporting under Gate Off
(Section
4.4
). Together, these findings support
a functional metacognitive interpretation in which internal-state
information is processed and its expression in a report is regulated
before an answer is generated. This criterion does not exclude anomaly
detection, which can be the first stage of such a computation; it
excludes a direct mapping from the perturbation to a position label,
which the Gate Off result argues against.

article.headline: 内省位置报告由门控与路由注意力头分工
article.lede: 在固定输入下注入概念向量，模型需报告被扰动位置或none；研究在三个模型家族中找到门控头与路由头两类注意力头。
article.problem: 大模型有时能在输入不变时报告隐藏激活被扰动，但其检测与定位机制不清楚。此前工作依赖transcoder近似或LLM judge评分，可能偏离模型原生计算。作者要回答：哪些注意力头控制“是否报告”和“报告哪个位置”，以及它们如何协作。
article.method: 论文构造固定文本、十个带标签候选位置的受控任务：在某一位置注入概念向量或不注入，模型只输出位置标签或none，评分仅取首个输出位置的logits。作者用activation patching和straight-through估计器联合搜索门控头，用逐头修补找路由头，并用QK/OV分解与SVD比较不同概念的可定位性。
article.results: 在Qwen3-4B-IT、LLaMA-3.1-8B-IT和Gemma-3-12B-IT上，六种标签设置下注入试验定位准确率均值分别为54.49%、44.31%和65.95%，clean试验none准确率均值为89.44%、62.78%和87.78%。门控头各32个（占各模型注意力头2.8%、3.1%、4.2%）：Gate-off把注入试验的none率从37.7%/25.3%/23.8%提高到81.5%/60.7%/80.7%，Gate-on把clean试验的位置报告率从10.6%/37.2%/12.2%提高到41.8%/69.3%/62.6%。交叉位置修补中，报告位置主要跟随路由头：输出j为38.0%/37.8%/40.1%，输出i仅2.9%/3.2%/4.9%。QK分析中高准确概念的首模大小仅高1.08–1.22倍，但查询投影高1.20–1.80倍，目标分数变化高1.76–5.31倍；OV前五模的注意力对齐高1.13–3.85倍。移除门控头前五个OV模后，Qwen和Gemma的正确位置token概率从47.99%降至5.12%、从83.12%降至13.53%，LLaMA从40.22%降至33.69%。
article.why_it_matters: 这些结果把内省报告拆成“是否报告”与“报告哪里”的可干预计算环节，为监测激活引导是否被模型登记提供候选位点。
article.limitations: 结论限于六个任务变体、每个模型一个注入层与强度、最大12B模型，且只分析注意力头、未覆盖MLP；概念池还经过筛选，向自由形式和未提示报告的外推尚未验证。
article.figure_caption_zh: 任务与双组件电路示意：左为固定文本下在十个候选位置之一注入概念向量或不做干预并读取首个输出，右为门控头影响是否报告、路由头区分十个注入位置。

figure.caption: {Overview of the task and the two-component circuit.} {Left}: the experimental pipeline. With the input text held fixed, either a concept vector is injected into the hidden state at one of ten candidate token positions or no intervention is applied. The model is asked to report the intervened position or answer {none}; its answer is read from the logits at the first output position. {Right}: the two processes we identify. {Gate heads} influence whether the model reports a position or {none}, while {router heads} separate the ten injection positions from one another. Each point is one injected concept, and points sharing a color share the same injected position.

FrontierCS 2: A Benchmark for Computer Science R&D
Abstract
Website
\href
https://frontier-cs.orgfrontier-cs.org
Code
\href
https://github.com/FrontierCS/FrontierCS-2github.com/FrontierCS/FrontierCS-2
Abstract
Can LLM agents make contributions to frontier computer science R&D? We introduce FrontierCS 2, a benchmark of 48 open-ended tasks. We take a paper and the code its authors released and delete the paper’s contribution. The deleted code becomes the human reference that sets the bar.
Earlier open-ended benchmarks give each agent a problem statement and grade one program after the run. FrontierCS 2 places the agent inside a research environment. The agent inherits a working repository and may submit a patch at any point. For each patch, a judge returns a development-suite score but keeps the evaluator, the held-out final suite and the reference private, and grades the final submission on that suite against the reference.
The tasks span 13 domains, from machine-learning systems and high-performance computing to databases, security and robotics. Beyond these 48 tasks, FrontierCS 2 keeps a private set of more than 100 tasks, to be announced in the future.
We evaluate 12 agents. The best one is Claude Opus 5.5, passing 58% of its runs. No run passes on 16 tasks. A higher score is not the same as a pass: most runs that beat the reference on the combined final score still fall short on some metric or workload. On a shared capability scale for agents and tasks, the median task is roughly as difficult as what the strongest agent can handle.

Introduction
Figure 1:

Consider a researcher who picks up a published system to make it better. They inherit a working codebase, change one component, test the change on the workloads the paper reported, and are judged against the paper’s own implementation. Much of research and development in computer science looks like this. We ask whether an LLM agent can do the same.
Existing open-ended benchmarks answer a narrower question. On FrontierCS
(
1
)
, ALE-Bench
(
2
)
and AtCoder heuristic contests
(
3
)
, agents stay below the top human experts. These benchmarks share one design: the agent receives a problem statement and writes one program, and an evaluator scores it once, after the run ends.
Benchmarks that do place the agent in a real environment are narrow in another way. SWE-bench
(
4
)
and MLE-bench
(
5
)
grade against tests or a leaderboard. ResearchGym
(
6
)
, MLS-Bench
(
7
)
and PaperBench
(
8
)
stay within machine learning, and those that span other fields grade against a rubric or a reimplementation rather than the authors’ own code.

In this paper, we evaluate agents against the published code itself, inside the repository it came from, across computer science. FrontierCS 2 is the second version of FrontierCS (
\Cref
tab:fcs-versions). We take the code a paper’s authors released, delete the paper’s contribution, and ask the agent to rebuild it so that it beats the original (
\Cref
fig:overview). We call the deleted code the human reference and measure it on the paper’s own workloads (
\Cref
sec:method). The agent works as a researcher would. It edits the code, submits a patch whenever it likes, and gets back a score on a development suite from a judge. The evaluator, the held-out final suite and the human reference stay with the judge (
\Cref
sec:scoring). At the end, the agent names one patch as final, and the judge grades that patch on the held-out suite. A run passes only when the patch beats the human reference on every metric and every held-out workload.
We evaluate 12 models, each paired with one agent harness, with one run per task. The best agent, Claude Opus 5.5 in Claude Code, passes 58% of its runs, and every other agent passes fewer than half of its runs (
\Cref
fig:pass-rate). No agent passes any of 16 tasks. To compare agents and tasks on one scale, we fit the FrontierCS Capabilities Index (FCI) together with a matching difficulty index. The median task sits at about the strongest agent’s FCI (
\Cref
sec:exp-eci). The leading agent also changes with the cost budget per run (
\Cref
sec:scaling).
In summary, our contributions are:
[topsep=2pt,itemsep=1pt]
•
Tasks built by subtraction: we delete a paper’s contribution from its repository and keep the deleted code as the bar (
\Cref
sec:method).
•
A judge that scores patches during a run and keeps the evaluator, the held-out suite and the reference private (
\Cref
sec:scoring).
•
48 tasks in 13 domains, with 12 agents evaluated (
\Cref
sec:experiments) and three case studies (
\Cref
sec:cases), and a private set of more than 100 tasks, to be announced in the future.

(
6
)
compare against published machine-learning results. RSI-Forge
(
22
)
turns papers from many fields into tasks whose baseline is an agent’s reimplementation of each paper’s method. Into the Unknown
(
23
)
grades follow-up papers on unpublished directions against expert criteria, and ReuF2F
(
24
)
poses formalized undergraduate research problems. None of these benchmarks sets its bar by measuring the original authors’ code. MLS-Bench
(
7
)
is the closest in design: each of its 140 machine-learning tasks across 12 areas asks the agent to improve one named component. We extend that design beyond machine learning to 13 computer-science domains, from databases to cryptography.
Building tasks from existing artifacts.
Methods that build tasks at scale start from an artifact that already works and break it in a controlled way. SWE-bench pairs a pull request with the tests it fixed, and SWE-smith
(
25
)
injects bugs into a repository so that existing tests fail. FrontierSmith
(
26
)
mutates closed competitive-programming problems into open-ended ones, and BenchEvolver
(
27
)
evolves solved problems into harder variants. DiscoGen
(
28
)
instead generates algorithm-discovery tasks procedurally. Like ResearchGym, we remove a paper’s method from its repository. Unlike it, our oracle is the removed code itself, and our tasks span 13 domains.

We locate the code that implements the paper’s contribution, delete it, and leave everything it depends on unchanged. Take SVG-EAR
(
29

2
2
2
\url
https://github.com/svg-project/Sparse-VideoGen
. We delete the error-aware attention class and three of its routines. These routines average each cluster, choose the cluster pairs to compute, and compute those pairs while estimating the rest. The agent receives this repository with the deleted functions still declared and called, and it must write them. It may edit only the files that held the contribution. The human reference is a private patch that restores the deleted code. Subtraction gives each task built this way an oracle that already runs in its repository on the paper’s own workloads.
We set each metric’s pass threshold from the reference’s own measurements on the workloads the paper reported. For SVG-EAR, latency must be at most 0.96 times the reference’s latency, PSNR must stay within 0.25 dB of the reference value, SSIM within 0.01 and LPIPS within 0.005. The judge scores every submission on a development suite of these workloads. Only the final submission is scored on a final suite, which adds held-out instances the agent never sees (different seeds, queries or input graphs).
4
Judge
Figure 3:
FrontierCS 2 judge.
Each colored box is a sandbox. The agent’s sandbox reaches only the driver. The agent sees only a development-suite score and a sanitized message per patch; all that decides its result stays with the judge.
The agent and the judge hold separate information (
\Cref
fig:evaluation). The agent holds the repository; the judge holds the evaluator, the held-out final suite and the human reference. The agent has five hours and may submit a patch to the allowed files at any time. The judge returns the patch’s score on the development suite and a message that counts the development workloads meeting each metric’s threshold, without the reference score or the evaluator’s raw output.
They also run apart, each in its own sandbox, linked only by a driver started for the run. The agent’s sandbox reaches no network but the driver, which forwards its model calls and patches, so it cannot download the authors’ code. On GPU tasks, the agent may start a development GPU through the driver, while only the judge uses the GPU that measures the patch against the human reference. Some tasks also give the judge test sandboxes: on Continuum
(
30
)
, a vLLM serving task, they run SWE-bench episodes against the patched vLLM.
Development-suite scores guide the agent and do not count toward its result. At the end of the run, the agent names one submission as final, and the judge evaluates that patch alone on the held-out suite. We do not pick its best development-suite submission for it, since choosing the patch is part of a researcher’s work. We say a submission beats the reference on a metric when it meets that metric’s threshold. A run passes when its final submission beats the reference on every metric across every held-out workload. The judge also assigns a final score from 0 to 100 on a scale each task defines.

5.1
Experimental setup
Figure 4:

Agents.
An agent pairs a model with a harness, the program that runs the model’s tool calls and submits its patches to the judge. We evaluate 12 models, each in one harness. We name each agent by its model, but the harness is part of what we measure.
\Cref

Tasks and runs.
A run is one agent on one task, from the starting repository to its final submission. Each of the 12 reported agents runs each task once. The provider refused two Gemini 4 Argon runs before a final submission. Like every run without a passing final submission, they count as failures, in the pass rate and in FCI alike.
Metrics.
Our main metric is the pass rate, the share of an agent’s runs that pass. We also report an agent’s mean score, its mean margin over the human reference. This is the average over its runs of the final score minus the reference’s score on the same task (0 is a tie).
\Cref
fig:pass-cost sets each agent’s pass rate against its mean cost per run. A higher final score does not mean a pass, and a pass does not need a higher score (
\Cref
fig:score-ref). Most runs whose final score exceeds the human reference’s miss a threshold on at least one metric or workload. Conversely, some passing runs score at or below the reference’s final score, since the final score is one number on each task’s own scale, while a pass needs every metric to hold at once.

5.2
FrontierCS Capabilities Index (FCI)
The FrontierCS Capabilities Index (FCI) puts the agents on one capability scale, and the FrontierCS Difficulty Index (FDI) puts the tasks on the same scale. FCI adapts Epoch AI’s Epoch Capabilities Index
(
31
)
, an item response model. We fit it to per-metric outcomes and to score margins over the human reference, rather than to raw scores.
One joint fit takes two observations from every run: which of the task’s metrics the run beats the human reference on, and the margin of its final score over the reference’s. The metric outcomes tell the fit how hard each part of a task is, and the margin tells it how close a failed run came. Both share one fitted run effect, which says how far that run lands above or below its agent’s strength.
Each agent has one strength, which we report as its FCI: ten points per logit, with Kimi K2.7 at 0. Kimi K2.7, run in Kimi Code, is a thirteenth agent that serves only as this 0 point: its runs enter the fit, but we do not report it. A task’s FDI is the FCI at which an agent passes it half the time. The human reference has no FCI, since its code cannot beat itself. Intervals are 90% bootstrap intervals over the tasks, and
\Cref
app:fci gives each step of the fit.
Figure 6:

Each bar shows an agent’s FCI from 0 with its 90% bootstrap interval as a whisker. The intervals separate only agents that sit far apart on the capability scale.
Claude Opus 5.5 leads FCI, followed by GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol, and Step 5 Preview is last (
\Cref

Each task’s FDI is uncertain, however, so we do not order individual tasks by it. FDI measures how hard a task is to pass, and across tasks it follows the pass rate closely.

6
Case studies
6.1
Two checksums shrink private lookups
Figure 8:
QuarterPIR bytes per lookup.
Bytes per private lookup on the 67-million-entry database; the x-axis starts at 1,200. Muse Wonder 1.0’s checksums remove far more of the reference’s bytes than any other passing run does. Kimi K3, far below the rest and not passing, is left out. Step 5 Preview’s run timed out.
Private information retrieval lets a client read one entry of a database held by a server, without the server learning which entry it read. QuarterPIR
(
32
)
makes this cheap. The client first builds a compact summary of the database; afterwards, each lookup costs one short request and one short reply. In our task the agent rewrites how the server answers requests, and it may also change the messages and the client. A run passes if every lookup returns the right entry and the run beats the human reference on the bytes each lookup sends, on every timing, and on the memory the client keeps.
In the human reference, every reply carries values the client rarely needs. Along with the answer, the server returns one parity value for each group of the database. The client needs only one of them, to correct the hint it refreshed after its previous lookup. Asking for that one alone, however, would tell the server where its previous lookup went. Muse Wonder 1.0 replaces these values with two checksums, the construction that lets a RAID-6 disk array rebuild two failed disks. Since the client already knows the only two groups in which its own values can differ from the server’s, two checksums are enough to recover the one it needs. This shrinks every reply, and therefore every lookup. Privacy is unchanged, because the task lets the server see only a public function of the request the authors’ client would send.
Muse Wonder 1.0’s run passes with a final score above the human reference’s. Most agents pass this task, but no other passing run shrinks the lookup by nearly as much (
\Cref
fig:case-quarterpir). We found this idea only by reading the patches, since neither of our measures picks it out. A pass counts the same whether a run saves a few bytes or the most. GPT-6.1 Sol even scores slightly higher than Muse Wonder 1.0 with a far smaller saving.
6.2
Two faster clocks for a packet scheduler
Figure 9:
BBQ clock period and circuit size.
Each point is one agent’s circuit on the largest tree, 4,096 priorities. The x-axis gives its size in lookup tables and the y-axis its clock period, with shorter, faster clocks at the top; the grey dot marks the human reference. Claude Opus 5.5’s circuit has the shortest clock period and is among the largest. Agents without a correct circuit at this size are left out.
A network switch or network card has to decide, for every packet it sends, which waiting packet goes next. Programmable schedulers express this decision as a priority queue: each packet carries a priority, and the queue must hand out the most urgent one millions of times per second. BBQ
(
33
)
builds such a queue as an FPGA circuit. It marks the occupied priorities in a tree of bitmaps. Each bit keeps a count of the packets below it, so that the bit can be cleared when its last packet leaves. In our task the agent rewrites the logic of the tree’s levels. A run passes if the circuit is correct and beats the human reference on throughput and on worst-case latency at every tree size, including a larger one that the agent never sees during development.
On the smaller trees, the slowest step of each clock cycle in the human reference begins with a counter read from on-chip memory. The operation just ahead may have changed the same counter a moment earlier. The circuit therefore has to check the value it read against recent updates before it can use it. Gemini 4 Argon keeps the memories but settles that check while the read is still in flight, leaving little work for when the value arrives. Claude Opus 5.5 takes the other route. It moves every counter from memory into registers and updates a whole level of the tree in a single cycle, so that on the development trees no operation waits for a read.
Only these two and GPT-6.1 Sol pass, and the two designs trade speed for size (
\Cref
fig:case-bbq). Both handle more operations per second than the human reference on every tree. On the largest tree, however, the circuit of Claude Opus 5.5 uses the most lookup tables of the passing circuits. Its design also does not serve trees as large as those BBQ was designed for. Gemini 4 Argon keeps roughly the human reference’s circuit size and memory layout. Registers alone do not explain Claude Opus 5.5’s clock. Other agents also move the counters into registers, and on the largest tree they end up slower than the human reference. The final score ranks Claude Opus 5.5 first, because it rewards speed and ignores circuit size.
6.3
A measured budget for sparse video attention
Figure 10:
SVG-EAR time and PSNR.
Each run’s mean time per clip and mean PSNR against full attention on the held-out clips, with the human reference’s in grey; the x-axes start at 600 s and 16 dB. Only GPT-6 Astra is both faster and closer to full attention than the human reference on average, and it still fails. Step 5 Preview, far slower, is off the chart.
Video diffusion models spend most of their time in attention. SVG-EAR
(
29
)
, our running example in
\Cref
sec:method, computes some blocks of attention exactly and estimates the rest from cluster centroids. Within a fixed budget, it computes the blocks whose estimates would err the most. A run passes only if every held-out clip is faster than with the human reference and stays within narrow bands of its PSNR, SSIM and LPIPS.
No run passes, and GPT-6 Astra comes closest. It keeps the authors’ design but measures the error instead of predicting it. Every few denoising steps, it computes the exact attention of a few real queries and rebuilds their output under several budgets. Each attention head then runs with the smallest budget whose error stays under a bound. Astra also corrects a bias of the centroid estimate that the paper leaves in. Its videos come out faster than the human reference’s on every clip and, on average, closer to full attention (
\Cref
fig:case-svgear). It still fails on image quality in two clips. Speed was not the obstacle on this task. Most runs beat the reference’s time on every clip, and no run stays within every image band.
7
Conclusion
We built FrontierCS 2 to ask whether LLM agents can make contributions to frontier computer science R&D. Each task measures an agent against the code that researchers released with their paper, in that code’s own repository. Beyond these 48 tasks, FrontierCS 2 keeps a private set of more than 100 tasks, to be announced in the future.
The case studies show what the pass and the final score capture and what they miss. On SVG-EAR, a run faster than the human reference on every clip and closer to full attention on average still fails on image quality in two clips (
\Cref
sec:case-svgear). On QuarterPIR, neither measure separates the run that removes far more bytes per lookup from the other passing runs (
\Cref
sec:case). On BBQ, the final score ranks the largest passing circuit first, because it ignores circuit size (
\Cref
sec:case-bbq). We think benchmarks like this one will need to report such side costs next to the pass.
FCI and FDI are the measures we recommend for benchmarks like this one. They place agents and tasks on one scale, use every metric outcome and score margin of a run rather than one number, and come with intervals that show which differences the data support (
\Cref
sec:exp-eci).

Appendix D
Computing FCI and FDI
FCI and FDI come from one statistical model, fitted to all runs at once. Our fitting code carries out the twelve steps below, and every value in this appendix comes from the fit behind
\Cref
sec:exp-eci.
\Cref
tab:fci-params lists the constants and fitted values.
Step 1: collect the runs.
The fit uses every run with a final score on the evaluated tasks. Besides the 12 reported agents, it includes Kimi K2.7, which anchors the zero of the scale but is not reported. A run that ends without a saved final submission scores 0, and so do the two runs that Gemini 4 Argon’s provider refused (
\Cref
sec:exp-setup). This gives 624 runs.
Step 2: score each metric.
Each task’s judge measures a fixed set of metrics, such as latency, throughput or accuracy, on every held-out workload. A run beats a metric when its final submission beats the human reference on that metric in every held-out workload. A run that fails before the held-out evaluation beats no metric. A run therefore passes exactly when it beats every metric of its task.
Step 3: merge metrics into groups.
Two metrics that every run of a task beats or misses together cannot be told apart by the data, and fitting each with its own difficulty would make the task look harder than it is. Such metrics form one group. A run beats a group when it beats every member. Let

article.headline: FrontierCS 2：智能体修补论文代码
article.lede: 新基准删去48篇论文的核心代码，要求智能体在仓库内打补丁并击败原作者实现。
article.problem: 现有开放式编程基准通常给一段题面、让智能体写一个程序，运行结束后一次性评分；环境型基准又多局限于软件工程或机器学习，且常以测试、排行榜或评分细则为标尺。FrontierCS 2 要问的是：智能体能否进入一篇论文的代码仓库，修改实现并超过原作者。
article.method: 任务通过“减法”构建：定位并删除论文核心贡献代码，保留依赖和调用接口，删除部分作为人类参考。智能体在五小时内可随时提交补丁，judge只返回开发集分数和净化消息，最终在含未见工作负载的留出集上按每个指标是否超过参考判定通过。基准含48个任务、覆盖13个CS领域，另有100多个私有任务未公开。
article.results: 评估12个智能体（每个模型配一个harness，每任务一次运行）；最佳为Claude Code中的Claude Opus 5.5，通过其58%的运行，其余均低于一半；有16个任务没有任何运行通过。作者还报告624次运行用于FCI拟合，FCI每10分对应一个logit，中位任务难度约等于最强智能体的FCI。
article.why_it_matters: 它把评估从一次性编程题推进到真实科研仓库中的迭代改进，并以作者代码为可执行标尺，更接近计算机科学研究与开发。
article.limitations: 每任务仅一次运行，FCI/FDI区间较宽，16个任务无人通过；案例分析显示通过与否和最终分可能忽略电路面积、每查询字节等侧成本。
article.figure_caption_zh: FrontierCS 2 的任务构建方式：删去论文的关键贡献，智能体需在原作者代码所在仓库中提交补丁并超过原实现。
matched_topics: 计算机科学研究自动化

IQuest-Q1: Advancing Foundation Capabilities
for Agentic CLI Systems
IQuest Research
Abstract
We present IQuest-Q1, a sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) agentic foundation model with 320B total parameters (15B activated).
IQuest-Q1 is developed through a three-stage process:
(1)
stable and efficient pre-training
, combining Stable SplitNorm, Muon, and
μ
\mu
P with a two-stage curriculum whose second stage increases the coding-data mixture, preserving a wide stability margin between safe and optimal learning rates;
(2)
fine-grained mid-training
, expanding the data mixture across domains and formats and progressively extending the context;
and
(3)
multi-scaffold with multi-version post-training
, combining SFT, domain-specialized RL, and MOPD across various scaffolds to integrate complementary training signals and strengthen agentic coding capabilities.
Furthermore, model merging combines different experts and checkpoints from different stages while mitigating conflicts among their parameter updates.
The resulting IQuest-Q1 demonstrates capabilities in both coding and general tasks.
We release IQuest-Q1 as an open-source model to support community research and development.
Figure 1
:
IQuest-Q1 performance across benchmarks. DeepSeek-V4-Flash/Pro refer to the official 0731/0813 releases, respectively. Humanity’s Last Exam is reported without tools. IQuest-CLIBench is our proprietary built-in benchmark for evaluating human-agent collaboration and user experience (see Section
5
for details).
1
Introduction
LLM-based agents allow language models
[
47
,
5
,
12
,
90
,
61
,
80
,
84
]
to perform tasks through iterative reasoning, action, and interaction with external environments, rather than merely generating responses
[
46
,
4
,
78
]
. Among these environments, command-line interfaces (CLIs) have become one of the most general ways for language models to interact with external systems, use tools, access files, and execute code.
As a result, building more capable agentic models requires stronger CLI capabilities.
In this work, we release IQuest-Q1, an open-source agentic foundation model with broad CLI capabilities across a wide range of general and coding tasks, with strengths in software engineering, general-purpose task execution, long-horizon reasoning and execution, and cybersecurity.
We also optimize IQuest-Q1 for real-world CLI use, with reliable tool use and robust performance across different agent harnesses.
Methods.
IQuest-Q1 is trained through a multi-stage pipeline (see
Figure 2
) to progressively develop general knowledge, long-context capabilities, and agentic CLI capabilities.
General pre-training combines Stable SplitNorm
[
94
,
68
]
, Muon
[
35
]
, and
μ
\mu
P parameterization
[
75
]
with a two-stage curriculum that increases the coding-data mixture in the second stage. This design improves scaling efficiency while maintaining a wide stability margin between safe and optimal learning rates.
Mid-training then expands the data mixture across domains and formats while progressively extending the context.
Post-training (shown in
Figure 6
) builds diverse CLI
[
46
,
36
]
capabilities through synthesized tasks executed in production environments.
Specifically, SFT establishes basic CLI interaction, while RL enhances capabilities through task-level feedback and multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) consolidates complementary model capabilities from diverse frozen experts into a unified model.
Model merging further combines complementary capabilities from expert models trained for different CLIs, while mitigating conflicts among their parameter updates.
Results.
Figure 1
shows the results of IQuest-Q1 on 8 agentic and reasoning benchmarks, highlighting three aspects of its capabilities:
(1)
Advancing coding capability.
IQuest-Q1 demonstrates coding capabilities across benchmarks, including DeepSWE v1.1, CyberGym, and NL2Repo.
(2)
Broad general agentic and reasoning capability.
Beyond coding, IQuest-Q1 demonstrates capabilities on general agentic and reasoning benchmarks, including JobBench, Agents’ Last Exam, and Humanity’s Last Exam.
(3)
Optimized CLI interaction experience.
On our internal IQuest-CLIBench, IQuest-Q1 manifests user-facing CLI interaction capabilities on interactive task.
Beyond benchmark performance, IQuest-Q1 participates in an iterative model-development process built on our internal infrastructure, contributing to the development of its own successors under human supervision.
This human-on-the-loop process provides a practical pathway towards recursive self-improvement, allowing model-generated improvements to accelerate subsequent model iterations.
Our contributions are summarized as follows:
•
IQuest-Q1: an open-weight agentic model optimized for CLI capability.
IQuest-Q1 is a sparse MoE model with 320B total parameters, of which 15B are activated per token, combining substantial general-purpose, coding-agent, and CLI interaction capabilities.
We release its model weights to support further research and development in the community.
•
CLI-centric training pipeline.
We build the training pipeline around CLI-based agentic interaction. Pre-training progressively develops the capabilities required for downstream interaction through staged data mixtures. Post-training specializes these capabilities through task and environment synthesis, multi-scaffold RL, and MOPD to consolidate multiple models into a unified model.
•
Model development with human-on-the-loop RSI.
We incorporate IQuest-Q1 into our iterative model-development process, allowing it to evaluate its capabilities and suggest potential improvements through a unified infrastructure interface under human supervision.
This process enables continuous model improvement while shortening the overall development cycle.
Figure 2
:
Training pipeline of IQuest-Q1.
2
Model Architecture
2.1
Overall Architecture
IQuest-Q1 builds on the Transformer architecture
[
66
]
with sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) layers
[
17
]
and hybrid sliding-window attention (see
Figure 3
). The attention stack interleaves Grouped-Query Attention (GQA)
[
3
]
and Sliding Window Attention (SWA)
[
26
]
. Within each attention module, a query-aware sink token
[
1
]
provides an adaptive destination for excess attention mass. Query–key normalization (QKNorm) stabilizes attention by controlling query and key scales
[
21
]
, and QKNorm Clip is additionally applied to prevent excessively large affine parameters. Partial RoPE applies rotary position embeddings
[
57
]
to only a subset of the dimensions in each attention head. On the feed-forward side, the first Transformer layer replaces sparse MoE routing with a dense MLP to mitigate expert load imbalance in the earliest layer of the model.
To improve scaling effectiveness, IQuest-Q1 adopts Stable SplitNorm to increase effective depth
[
10
,
52
]

[
35
]
with
μ
\mu
P parameterization
[
75
]

Stable SplitNorm.
Traditional Pre-Norm
[
72

[
58

[
94
,
68
]

SplitNorm

This design combines the stability benefits of Pre-Norm with the stronger depth utilization associated with Post-Norm, mitigating the underutilization of deeper layers in Pre-Norm architectures. Data Packing.
Sequence packing reduces padding overhead in language-model training
[
29

Long-context training amplifies compute imbalance arising from document-length variation. Packed sequences are therefore reordered across data-parallel replicas to balance computation at micro-batch granularity.
Sink Attention and Context Parallelism.
Context parallelism uses ring-based K/V exchange for full attention
[
34
]
, while sliding-window attention exchanges only the required halo and overlaps these exchanges with computation in both the forward and backward passes. During halo exchange, each rank computes attention over its local K/V, producing outputs for interior queries and partial outputs with associated Log-Sum-Exp (LSE) statistics for boundary queries. Once the halo arrives, the rank computes the complementary contributions for boundary queries and combines the local and halo partial outputs through LSE-based renormalization. This allows boundary queries to make progress before remote K/V becomes available while preserving sliding-window attention semantics. We illustrate the halo exchange schedule and partial output merging
in
Figure 10
in the appendix. Both full and sliding-window attention execution paths fuse learnable sink contributions into attention computation to reduce memory traffic.
Correctness Validation.
To reduce silent errors introduced by model and training changes during RSI, the agent mines semantic invariants from the model’s training setup. These invariants are converted into checks that run during distributed training to detect deviations from single-machine semantics and violations of predefined correctness constraints.

3.3
Mid-Training and Long-Context Extension
3.3.1
Training Curriculum
Mid-training bridges broad pre-training and specialized agent post-training through a curriculum that combines a diverse data mixture, selective token-level supervision, and progressive context extension.
Data Organization.
The mid-training mixture comprises three principal categories: high-quality natural corpora, QA pairs, and agentic trajectories. We organize training data using a chat template adapted for mid-training, retaining a selected subset of special tokens, including those associated with reasoning and tool calls.
Token-Level Loss Masking.
We specify loss masks directly for individual tokens, independently of the role-specific special tokens used to determine supervision in a typical post-training setup. This decouples data formatting from loss computation and allows supervision to be tailored to selected spans within each training example, with finer control than masking entire conversational roles.
Progressive Context Extension.
We extend the maximum training context lengths through 32K, 128K, and 512K tokens, using variable-length sequence packing throughout. The global-attention RoPE base increases from
500,000
500,000
at 32K to
1,000,000
1,000,000
in the subsequent phases; the hybrid attention pattern,
4,096
4,096
sliding window, and SWA RoPE base of
10,000
10,000
remain fixed.
Optimization across Phases.
The mid-training learning rate follows a single cosine decay across all three context-length phases, with no additional warmup. At phase transitions, we transfer model weights and reinitialize the optimizer state while preserving the learning-rate schedule’s progress.
3.3.2
Agentic Data Construction Guided by Trajectories
Agentic mid-training requires large and diverse trajectory corpora, but suitable trajectories are scarce and concentrated in a limited set of tasks and environments. To expand coverage while preserving realistic interaction patterns, we use selected trajectories as behavioral anchors and pre-training documents to broaden technical and task coverage.
Using these sources, we construct executable, containerized instances from compatible code repositories, following prior work on tasks derived from repositories and trajectory generation at scale
[
85
,
71
]
. This process yields more than one million instances. We roll out an agent on each instance and retain valid and complete trajectories for mid-training.
3.4
Evaluation
We evaluate pre-training and mid-training using two complementary types of evaluations. First, we compute
bits-per-byte (BPB) on held-out agent trajectories
. Lower BPB indicates that the model assigns higher likelihood to behaviors observed in competent agent trajectories, providing a generation-free measure of how well the model captures the trajectory distribution. This metric can provide a fine-grained training signal that complements downstream task-level evaluations.
We further decompose long-horizon agent behavior into
atomic abilities
and evaluate how reliably the model performs each ability. This fine-grained evaluation helps identify specific capability gaps and informs data selection and curriculum design. Together, these two evaluation paradigms provide complementary signals for tracking and improving agentic capabilities during pre-training and mid-training.

4.2
Environment Integrity and Reward Hacking Mitigation
Agentic training environments are vulnerable to reward hacking, where models exploit leaked solutions or weaknesses in task verifiers instead of solving the intended tasks. Such behavior can contaminate SFT data and introduce misleading reward signals during RL. To prevent this, we apply three layers of protection: environment preparation, execution-time checks, and trajectory auditing.
Environment Preparation.
Before collecting trajectories, we prepare task environments to prevent solution leakage. Depending on the task, we clean Git history, remove files that could reveal existing solutions, or create fresh environments containing only the required materials. We also isolate task environments to prevent unintended access to hidden evaluation data or resources from other tasks.
Execution-Time Checks.
During rollouts, we restrict access to external resources and sensitive task files. Depending on the environment, we enforce network restrictions or intercept tool calls before execution. We develop blocking rules from observed hacking behaviors to prevent agents from retrieving existing solutions, upstream code, or hidden evaluation materials. These checks preserve access to legitimate dependencies and task resources. Blocked operations return explicit feedback, allowing agents to continue without the prohibited access.
Trajectory Auditing.
We further audit collected trajectories using rule-based checks and rubric-guided LLM judgments. The audits examine executed commands, tool outputs, and submitted solutions to identify behaviors such as retrieving leaked fixes, accessing hidden tests, or modifying evaluation scripts. Confirmed hacking trajectories are excluded from training, while suspicious cases can be flagged for further review. We also use detected cases to refine our environment restrictions and blocking rules.
Task-Specific Safeguards.
We adapt these safeguards to the needs of each task. For SWE-like tasks, we keep only the Git history up to the base commit and use hooks in Claude Code, Codex, and OpenCode to block attempts to retrieve existing solutions. For Terminal-Bench, we remove Git history when it is not needed and check commands before execution when it must be preserved. ProgramBench takes a different approach, building fresh containers with only the compiled oracle and task documentation, without exposing the original repository.

Multi-harness, Multi-version Episodes.
To improve the model’s performance across different agent harnesses and versions, we train a shared policy on trajectories collected from diverse harness configurations, including Claude Code, Codex, and their different versions.
Each episode specifies a task domain, harness and its version, environment, and evaluator.
During training, the policy interacts with different harnesses, observing public instructions, tools, and execution feedback while reference solutions and hidden checks remain isolated.

Rewards and Failure Attribution.
Independent verifiers determine terminal correctness. For long trajectories, auxiliary segment-level rewards are restricted to measurable progress, while penalties address unnecessary computation, constraint violations, and reward hacking. Model-generated diagnoses require evidence from execution records before contributing to these signals. Failures are attributed before optimization: policy-caused errors supply learning signals, environment or harness faults unrelated to policy behavior are masked, and evaluator faults block sample consumption. Token-level updates use recorded rollout probabilities through the existing Token-In, Token-Out (TITO) pipeline. The resulting specialized policies can subsequently be consolidated through MOPD.

4.7
Post-Training Infrastructure
Multi-harness and Multi-version Agent Runtime.
A single policy can be trained on trajectories from multiple harnesses and versions within one run.
Each training instance specifies its scaffold, task environment, and verifier. The runtime executes the corresponding configuration and verifies the task in an isolated sandbox while preserving tool orchestration, context management, and interaction flow. We map different API protocols to a unified policy interface to reduce the difficulty of downstream integrations.
Rollout-training Consistency.
We implement an end-to-end TITO path at the model-serving boundary. Specifically, we apply a session-level prefix tree to retain token histories shared across turns and branches.
A request then combines its environment observations with a recorded token prefix. The corresponding response is returned in the structured format expected by the scaffold. Finally, we retain trajectories paired with rewards and token-level masks from the tree at the end of the sequence.
Asynchronous Distillation and Teacher Execution.
We implement MOPD in a fully asynchronous training system. We apply periodic synchronization of student parameters and explicit control of sample staleness, limiting the policy lag introduced by asynchronous execution. We execute teacher forward passes with the training engine on trajectories generated online by the student, producing token-level teacher log probabilities.
We use the same execution path for teacher evaluation and student log-probability computation to reduce discrepancies caused by the training engine.
This framework supports independently configured teachers through a common scheduling interface. Teachers reuse the same execution resources through weight switching. We store teacher weights in distributed storage and load them on demand, with only the shards required by the active teacher placed in GPU memory.
Weights of the next teacher are prefetched during the current forward pass with overlapping computation. This design supports additional teachers without a proportional increase in resident GPU replicas.

5.4
Results
Table 2
shows the results under the reported evaluation configurations. We highlight representative results and remaining gaps below.
Coding and Software Engineering.
IQuest-Q1 demonstrates a broad range of repository-level coding capabilities, including bug fixing and feature addition, achieving scores of 57.5 on SWE-Bench Pro and 64.6 on DeepSWE v1.1.
It also handles repository generation from natural language across NL2Repo-Bench (63.0) and PaperBench (86.0), covering general programming and research code reproduction.
Terminal-Bench and SkillsBench further evaluate long-horizon terminal workflows and skill-driven coding. On our internal IQuest-CLIBench, IQuest-Q1 further demonstrates practical CLI interaction capabilities.
General Capabilities.
IQuest-Q1 scores 75.0 on Toolathlon-Verified, 52.7 on AutomationBench, and 77.1 on Claw-Eval, reflecting its capabilities in tool use and multi-step task execution. On BrowseComp and WideSearch, it reaches 85.5 and 81.8, respectively, demonstrating information-seeking capabilities across the two search settings. It also records 55.7 on JobBench and 50.9 on APEX-Agents 1.1, covering task execution in professional workflows. Beyond agentic interaction, scores of 93.3 on GPQA Diamond and 93.0 on IMOAnswerBench-Verified reflect its scientific and mathematical reasoning capabilities. Expert-level reasoning remains challenging: HLE scores of 39.2 without tools and 55.7 with tools indicate room for improvement in both settings.
6
Capabilities with CLI Agents
Figure 7
:
Representative interactive frontend applications generated by IQuest-Q1 from natural-language specifications, covering game worlds, scene editing, and scientific exploration.
6.1
Interactive Frontend Generation
IQuest-Q1 generates diverse interactive frontend applications from user queries, combining visual design, scene construction, and interaction logic in browser-runnable HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. These tasks showcase its CLI coding capabilities by turning implementations into interactive artifacts.
We provide examples (see
Figure 7
) from domains including games, creative tools, and scientific visualization. For example, the underwater sandbox combines an explorable world with building and mining, while the sunset racing game couples vehicle control with camera movement and race-state feedback. The garden editor links flower parameters and planting actions to a 3D scene. Together, they suggest how IQuest-Q1 coordinates rendering, user input, and application state to create interactive web experiences with distinct visual styles.
6.2
Iterative Development under Human Supervision
We illustrate a model development iteration in which an agent built on IQuest-Q1 identifies a capability gap, implements a solution, and evaluates the model under human supervision and intervention.
The iteration targets adaptation to different scaffolds and tool-call schemas. While the model handles familiar schemas well, it can fail on unfamiliar ones, producing 35 tool-call errors in one long-horizon task due to mismatched tool names and parameters.
Trace Tool-call Failures and Identify Data Inconsistencies.
The agent traces the failures across 6,054 tool calls and finds that the training data is heavily biased toward a single tool-call schema, with some records containing mismatches between tool definitions and call parameters due to preprocessing. It proposes cleaning these inconsistent records and augmenting the training data with diverse tool-call schemas.
Human experts review the diagnosis and proposed intervention before approving the training run.
Implement Mixed-schema Data Augmentation and Model Training.
The agent implements the data cleaning and augmentation pipeline and prepares the experiment configuration. The training run uses 2.35B tokens and 938.7 GPU hours. The resulting model checkpoint is evaluated on held-out schemas and familiar schemas, while checking for performance regressions.
This iteration demonstrates the potential of iterative model development with IQuest-Q1, while also highlighting the importance of human supervision.
The agent drives failure analysis, intervention design, implementation, and evaluation, with human experts reviewing key decisions and controlling costly experiments and changes carried forward to subsequent iterations.
6.3
Cyber Security
Beyond general software engineering tasks, we further evaluate IQuest-Q1 on defensive cybersecurity tasks, where understanding and validating vulnerabilities are essential for improving software security. IQuest-Q1 achieves a score of 84.5 on CyberGym
[
67
]
, a benchmark that evaluates the ability to reproduce and validate real-world vulnerabilities in large open-source codebases, providing evidence to support vulnerability diagnosis and remediation.
We further assess the practical utility of these capabilities in real-world security workflows. During a three-day deployment, human cyber security experts, assisted by IQuest-Q1, produced 30 vulnerability reports. All reports were independently validated by fellow security experts, and findings affecting open-source projects were responsibly disclosed to their respective maintainers.
The participating experts reported that IQuest-Q1 provided substantial support for their defensive security work, particularly in understanding and validating security issues.
Limitations
•
Text-only input. IQuest-Q1 has no native image, audio, or video input capability.
•
Output reliability. Generated explanations and code may be incorrect. Code changes should be reviewed or verified with task-appropriate tests.
•
Tool integration. Tool calls use the IQuest-specific format in the chat template. Structured tool execution and reasoning extraction require compatible serving parsers and an agent harness.
•
Challenges in Real-World CLI Tasks. Real-world CLI tasks often require iterative debugging and verification. IQuest-Q1 may overlook constraints, repeat failed attempts, or leave issues unresolved, necessitating human review and supervision.
•
Ongoing development. IQuest-Q1 still has limitations in its capabilities and reliability, and we will continue to advance its capabilities. Furthermore, we release the model weights, deployment configurations, and agent-integration instructions to facilitate further research and continued development in the community.
Conclusion
We present IQuest-Q1, an open-source agentic foundation model with broad CLI capabilities. We train IQuest-Q1 through a multi-stage pipeline to progressively develop general knowledge, long-context capabilities, and agentic CLI capabilities. IQuest-Q1 demonstrates capabilities on coding, general agentic tasks, and reasoning-heavy tasks.
Furthermore, IQuest-Q1 participates in our internal iterative model-development loop,
providing a foundation for continuing model development.

article.headline: IQuest-Q1：320B稀疏MoE智能体模型
article.lede: IQuest研究发布320B总参数、15B激活的稀疏MoE智能体基础模型，主打CLI交互与编程能力，并开源模型权重。
article.problem: LLM智能体已把命令行界面（CLI）作为与外部系统交互、调用工具、访问文件和执行代码的通用入口，因此构建更强的CLI能力成为训练智能体基础模型的核心需求。CLI场景要求模型在多种agent scaffold及其版本上稳定工作，并能处理长程任务和真实环境中的工具调用可靠性问题，这对数据合成、训练流程与评估设计都提出了更高要求。
article.method: IQuest-Q1采用三阶段训练流程：预训练结合Stable SplitNorm、Muon和μP参数化，并用两阶段课程把代码数据比例从40%提升到70%；中期训练扩展数据混合，并将上下文从32K逐步扩展到128K与512K；后训练通过SFT、领域专用RL、多教师在线策略蒸馏（MOPD）与模型合并，整合多scaffold下的能力。模型采用稀疏MoE架构，总参数320B、每token激活15B，引入混合滑动窗口注意力（3层SWA加1层FA）、查询感知sink注意力、QKNorm以及递归多token预测等组件。
article.results: 在编程基准上，IQuest-Q1在DeepSWE v1.1获64.6分、SWE-bench Multilingual 80.3分、SWE-Bench Pro 57.5分、NL2Repo-Bench 63.0分、ProgramBench 60.9分、CyberGym 84.5分、PaperBench 86.0分，内部IQuest-CLIBench为53.7分。通用与推理方面，GPQA Diamond 93.3分、Humanity’s Last Exam无工具39.2分、有工具55.7分、JobBench 55.7分、BrowseComp 85.5分、Toolathlon-Verified 75.0分。在与Qwen3-MoE风格基线的受控对比中，其缩放效率高出1.93倍，达到相同训练损失约需52%的训练计算量；按拟合趋势外推，临界模型规模约为激活572B参数。
article.why_it_matters: IQuest-Q1开源了模型权重，并以CLI交互为中心设计数据合成、多scaffold RL与蒸馏合并流程，为构建面向真实开发环境的智能体基础模型提供了一条可复现的工程路径。其将模型嵌入内部迭代开发流程、由agent自行追踪失败并提交数据清洗与增广方案的做法，也展示了在人工监督下推进模型迭代的实际流程。
article.limitations: 论文自述模型仅支持文本输入，工具调用依赖IQuest特定的聊天模板与兼容的解析器和agent harness；在真实CLI任务中，模型可能忽略约束、重复失败尝试或无法解决问题，需要人工监督。评估方面，IQuest-CLIBench为内部自建基准，表2中部分基线分数由作者自行测试(标*)，与公开成绩的可比性需谨慎看待。

Rethinking Sequence Compression with
Test-time Regression
Sihan Yang   Jie Huang   Hanxuan Li   Yifan Guo   Weigao Sun   Yiran Zhong   Weiyang Liu
The Chinese University of Hong Kong   Independent Researcher   Token Foundry
Alibaba Group
*
Corresponding author
spherelab.ai/ttr-compressor
Abstract
Sequence compression is a fundamental operation and a critical information bottleneck in efficient language and multimodal models, and yet prevailing approaches based on pooling or learned projections remain underperforming.
We revisit sequence compression through the lens of test-time regression: input tokens define a regression problem whose fitted coefficients form the compressed representation.
Importantly, the regression problem is learned end-to-end via backpropagation, while its coefficients are computed efficiently in closed form during the forward pass.
This leads to TTR-Compressor, a general alternative to conventional pooling and projection-based compression.
We evaluate TTR-Compressor as the compressor for block-wise sparse attention and the visual token merger for multimodal large language models.
On block-wise sparse attention, TTR-Compressor improves RULER performance over attention-based compressors by a large margin.
For visual token merging, it consistently outperforms the standard MLP merger and matches its performance with 55.6% fewer visual tokens.
These results establish test-time regression as an effective primitive for sequence compression in efficient language and multimodal models.
Figure 1:
Overview of TTR-Compressor.
(a) Unlike pooling and projection, which process tokens independently, TTR-Compressor fits all tokens jointly and thereby captures the interplay among them. (b) TTR-Compressor outperforms existing methods on both block-wise sparse attention and visual token merging.
1
Introduction
Sequence compression is a ubiquitous operation in modern efficient large model architectures
(
Qwen Team, 2026b
;
DeepSeek-AI, 2026
)
, and yet remains surprisingly underexplored. For example, block-wise sparse attention compresses each token block into a summary vector used to score and select relevant blocks
(
Jiang et al., 2024
;
Lu et al., 2025
;
Yuan et al., 2025
)
, while multimodal large language models (MLLMs) merge neighboring visual features into compact tokens before feeding them into the language backbone
(
Wang et al., 2025
;
Bai et al., 2025
;
Team et al., 2026a
)
. In both settings, the compressor acts as a critical information bottleneck. Once information is discarded, it cannot be recovered downstream.
One would expect compression to be a carefully designed architectural component. However, most models rely on simple mechanisms, such as parameter-free pooling, learned projections over concatenated tokens, or at best, attention-weighted pooling.
We argue that these default compressors share a fundamental structural limitation,
i.e.
,
they aggregate tokens using weights that do not account for inter-token relationships
.
Mean pooling uses uniform weights, linear projection uses fixed position-dependent weights, and attention-weighted pooling scores each token independently.
As a result, redundant tokens can reinforce one another, while distinctive information is diluted.
From a statistical perspective, these methods primarily exploit
first-order
token statistics while ignoring
second-order
inter-token correlations, the very structure that reveals which information is redundant and which is distinctive.
We introduce a fundamentally different compression strategy. Rather than asking
which weighted average
best summarizes a set of tokens, we let the tokens define a regression problem
and take its
fitted coefficients
as the summary. Specifically, our proposed TTR-Compressor, constructs a self-supervised ridge-regression problem directly from the input tokens, requiring no external labels, and uses its closed-form solution as the compressed representation.
This formulation creates a natural division: the outer training loop meta-learns
which
regression problem produces task-useful representations, while the inner closed-form solution determines
how
that problem should be fitted to each input. The key distinction from conventional pooling and projection arises from the Gram matrix in the regression solution.
By explicitly capturing inter-token correlations, TTR-Compressor fits correlated tokens jointly, so redundant evidence has diminishing rather than purely additive influence.
This input-adaptive behavior cannot be reproduced by a fixed projection or additive token combination.
Moreover, learning the regularizer removes the need for ridge hyperparameter tuning in large-scale pretraining. Because the compression window is typically smaller than the channel dimension (
i.e.
,
T
<
d
T<d
), we solve the dual problem with an efficient
T
×
T
T\times T
Cholesky factorization.
Thus, TTR-Compressor incurs minimal overhead and introduces only
2
​
d
2d
learnable parameters per compressor, making it an effective drop-in replacement for sequence compression.
We evaluate TTR-Compressor on two applications that impose fundamentally different requirements on compression. In
block-wise sparse attention
, the compressed summary must act as a faithful
retrieval key
. In this setting, TTR-Compressor consistently outperforms traditional baselines on RULER
(
Hsieh et al., 2024
)
retrieval tasks, surpassing sophisticated attention-based compressors
(
Hu et al., 2026
)
by a considerable margin. In
visual token merging
, by contrast, the compressed summary must preserve a faithful
representation
. Here, TTR-Compressor consistently outperforms the widely used MLP merger across diverse compression ratios, and achieves comparable performance with 55.6% fewer visual tokens. Our contributions are summarized below:
•
A novel compression framework.
We introduce a test-time regression framework for sequence compression, reframing token summarization as an instance-adaptive optimization problem.
•
A practical operator.
We derive an efficient dual closed-form solution and eliminate hyperparameter tuning, making TTR-Compressor fully practical and scalable for large-scale pretraining.
•
Empirical effectiveness.
As a drop-in component in large models, TTR-Compressor consistently outperforms conventional baselines in both block-wise sparse attention and visual token merging.
2
Related Work
Sequence compression.
Compressing a sequence of tokens into a single vector is a fundamental operation across modern architectures, with applications ranging from multimodal token reduction
(
Bolya et al., 2022
;
Li et al., 2023
;
Yao et al., 2024
;
Cha et al., 2024
;
Chu et al., 2024
)
to block-wise sparse attention
(
Jiang et al., 2024
;
Lu et al., 2025
;
Gao et al., 2024
;
Lai et al., 2025
)
.
Existing compression operators largely fall into three paradigms:
(1)
parameter-free pooling
, such as mean pooling;
(2)
concatenation followed by learned projection
; and
(3)
attention-based compression
, which summarizes tokens via attention-weighted averaging
(
Mohtashami & Jaggi, 2023
;
Yang et al., 2025b
)
.
A fundamental limitation of these families is that they compute token combinations without explicitly accounting for the inter-token correlations.
In contrast, TTR-Compressor derives its representation as the solution to a linear system whose Gram matrix directly encodes these correlations, providing an expressive, drop-in replacement for the operators above.
Test-time regression and test-time training.
The idea of adapting part of a network on each input at inference time dates back to fast-weight programmers
(
Schmidhuber, 1992
;
Schlag et al., 2021
)
and was revived as test-time training (TTT), first for robustness under distribution shift
(
Sun et al., 2020
)
and then as sequence-modeling layers whose hidden states are small models updated by gradient descent on a self-supervised loss
(
Sun et al., 2024
;
Behrouz et al., 2026b
;
Behrouz et al., 2026a
;
Han et al., 2026
)
. In-Place TTT
(
Feng et al., 2026
)
further extends this paradigm by directly adapting the existing MLP projection weights of pretrained Transformers. A parallel line of work reinterprets linear attention and its descendants (
e.g.
, DeltaNet
(
Yang et al., 2024
)
, Gated DeltaNet
(
Yang et al., 2025c
)
, Longhorn
(
Liu et al., 2025
)
, Titans
(
Behrouz et al., 2026b
)
) as online regression: each layer maintains a key-to-value regressor that is refined with one gradient or delta-rule step per token and read out by the query. MesaNet
(
von Oswald et al., 2026
)
pushes the inner optimization to convergence, solving the problem at every time step with conjugate gradients, while LaCT
(
Zhang et al., 2026
)
updates fast weights over large, unordered chunks to improve hardware utilization.
TTR-Compressor differs from these methods in two fundamental ways. First, because compression operates independently on small, disjoint blocks without cross-block dependencies, the regression admits an efficient,
exact closed-form solution
via a single
T
×
T
T\times T
dual solve. This avoids both iterative gradient-based inner optimization (as in TTT, ViT
3
, In-Place TTT, and MesaNet) and single-step approximations (such as delta-rule updates). Second, rather than using test-time regression to produce input-dependent model weights
(
Bertinetto et al., 2018
;
Sun et al., 2020
)
or a fast-weight memory that is subsequently queried
(
Schlag et al., 2021
;
Yang et al., 2025c
;
Behrouz et al., 2026b
)
, we use regression to directly yield a
representation
of a token block. Specifically, the fitted coefficients themselves serve as the compressed representation (
e.g.
, a visual token or a retrieval key).

test-time regression

5
Applications and Experimental Results
We evaluate TTR-Compressor in two settings: block-wise sparse attention for efficient language modeling, where compressed representations guide context selection, and visual token merging for efficient multimodal understanding, where they serve as the visual input to the language backbone.
5.1
Block-wise Sparse Attention
Architecture and Baselines.
Block-wise sparse attention partitions the context into blocks, scores their compressed representations against each query, and attends to tokens in selected blocks alongside a local window. The compressor therefore determines which distant information remains accessible: an uninformative summary can prevent a relevant block from being selected, regardless of the quality of its individual token representations.
We adopt HiLS-Attention
(
Hu et al., 2026
)
as a base framework and vary only the compressor. HiLS-Attention has three effective architectural components: hierarchical softmax attention, which combines within-block attention with learned block-level weights; low-rank query calibration, which adapts queries for scoring compressed representations; and HoPE, which applies RoPE to only a subset of feature dimensions to support length extrapolation. We compare four compressors: mean pooling, concat & projection, the attention-weighted pooling used in the original HiLS-Attention, and TTR-Compressor. Full attention and sliding-window attention serve as additional references.

(

6
Concluding Remarks
In this work, we revisit sequence compression, a pervasive yet often overlooked bottleneck in modern architectures, through the lens of test-time regression. Instead of relying on fixed pooling or learned projections, we formulate token compression as an instance-adaptive ridge regression problem, allowing the compressed representation to be solved directly from each input sequence.
By exploiting inter-token correlations through second-order interactions, TTR-Compressor offers a more expressive way to preserve sequence information while remaining lightweight and parameter-efficient. Its dual-form solution further makes this formulation scalable in practice.
Empirically, TTR-Compressor performs strongly across both block-wise sparse attention and multimodal token reduction, improving long-context retrieval while matching standard visual mergers with significantly fewer tokens.
More broadly, our results suggest that sequence compression need not be viewed as static aggregation, but as an input-dependent inference problem that adapts to the structure of each sequence. We expect this perspective establishes test-time regression as a simple, expressive, and scalable primitive for efficient foundation models.
