article.headline: 用测试时回归重做序列压缩
article.lede: TTR-Compressor把token块压缩写成测试时岭回归，用闭式对偶解替代池化与投影，并在稀疏注意力和视觉toke
article.problem: 块稀疏注意力和多模态大模型都依赖序列压缩，但常用池化、拼接投影或注意力加权池化在聚合token时不显式建模token间关系。结果是冗余token相互叠加、独特信息被稀释，而压缩一旦丢弃信息便无法在下游恢复。
article.method: TTR-Compressor把每个token块构造成自监督岭回归：归一化token作为回归键，标量目标由可学习投影（可选局部卷积）给出，回归系数即压缩表示。外层用任务损失端到端学习目标投影和可学习对角正则，内层利用T≪d，通过对偶T×T Cholesky分解精确求解，基础压缩器仅增加2d个参数。
article.results: 在345M语言模型的块稀疏注意力实验中，TTR-Compressor在RULER上的平均分为0.5092，高于注意力加权池化的0.3920，带卷积变体为0.5144；原文称其比最强基线高12.24个百分点。视觉token合并中，2×2压缩把平均分从MLP的54.93提高到55.92（卷积变体56.03），3×3卷积变体比MLP平均高2.58分，并在OCRBench、InfoVQA、ChartQA上分别高4.10、4.54、3.56分。附录的1B模型/100B token设置下，TTR平均0.7996，对比注意力加权池化0.735。
article.why_it_matters: 序列压缩是长上下文与多模态模型的关键信息瓶颈，TTR把压缩从固定聚合变成输入相关的推理问题，且只增加少量参数，具备作为即插即用模块的潜力。
article.limitations: 实验规模仍有限：主实验为345M语言模型和Qwen3-4B视觉设置，1B/100B仅与注意力加权池化对比。长上下文检索仍有明显失败模式：TTR在RULER上平均0.5092，MK-NIAH 32K仅0.110，且方法依赖T≪d以控制T×T求解成本。
article.figure_caption_zh: TTR-Compressor总览：内层把token块压缩为岭回归并用对偶Cholesky闭式求解，外层用任务梯度学习回归目标与对角正则，Gram矩阵使冗余token影响衰减。

figure.caption: {Overview of TTR-Compressor.} (a) Bilevel learning: The inner solve formulates sequence compression as test-time ridge regression with an exact dual Cholesky solve to obtain the representation $ {h}^*$, while the regression parameters are learned end-to-end via task gradients. (b) Input-dependent second-order adaptation: By jointly coupling tokens through the Gram matrix, TTR naturally diminishes the relative influence of redundant tokens compared to additive pooling. For intuitive illustration, we set $ {D}= {I}$ and uniform targets $ {v}= {1}$; as typically learned in practice, a smaller regularizer $ {D}$ further amplifies this deduplication effect, yielding an even higher relative share for distinct tokens.

page_papers.content:
Abstract
Reliable multi-view forecasting requires videos from different cameras to describe the same evolving 3D scene.
To this end, we introduce Video-Point Model (VPM), a world model that conditions on multi-view video histories and a language instruction to jointly forecast future videos from arbitrary viewpoints and the 3D trajectories of persistent scene points.
We extend a pretrained world model with camera-conditioned multi-view processing that integrates complementary observations across cameras, and add a trajectory head that predicts how physical points move through time.
Each trajectory tracks a single point across all views, and supervising these trajectories alongside video generation therefore anchors appearance changes in every camera to a shared description of 3D motion.
To support training and evaluation, we build VPM-Data, a simulation corpus pairing synchronized multi-view videos with persistent point trajectories, and VP-WorldBench, a forecasting benchmark spanning simulated and real environments.
We further extend VPM to robot control by adding robot actions as a token modality in the generator.
Action tokens share the point-supervised backbone and are denoised jointly with future videos, thereby grounding the policy in the same 3D-aware representation.
On VP-WorldBench and existing 4D generation benchmarks, point supervision improves both video
fidelity and 3D motion accuracy over a video-only counterpart, and in simulated and real-robot experiments, it also raises the manipulation success of the action-enabled model.

Introduction
World models aim to anticipate how scenes evolve from past
observations. Recent models pursue this goal by predicting
future videos and, for robot interactions, the associated
actions
(
Agarwal et al., 2026
)
.
However, visual plausibility alone does not establish whether
these forecasts describe coherent 3D motion.
Multi-view histories provide richer evidence for predicting
this motion by revealing scene structure and ongoing dynamics
that may be obscured in individual cameras
(
Rajič et al., 2025
)
.
To exploit this evidence, a model must relate observations
across cameras to a common prediction of scene evolution.
Its forecasts from arbitrary viewpoints should therefore
depict the same future event, despite differences in
perspective and visibility.
To connect these predictions, we build on geometric
supervision
(
Lee et al., 2026b
)
for video modeling, including pointmap prediction
and trajectory-derived representation
alignment
(
Liu et al., 2026
;
Yang et al., 2026
)
.
Specifically, we investigate jointly forecasting future images
and persistent 3D point trajectories. Because each trajectory
follows the same scene point over time, it provides a common
description of motion across cameras. Learning this motion
alongside image generation encourages the model to relate
appearance changes to the movement of identifiable points.
Unlike conventional tracking, both predictions extend beyond
the observed history, requiring the model to anticipate
correspondences without access to future frames.
Our hypothesis is that learning where scene points will move
helps the visual predictor produce more faithful forecasts.
Accordingly, we introduce
VPM
,
a multi-view video–point world model built on
Cosmos 3
(
Agarwal et al., 2026
)
.
Given posed video histories and a language instruction,
VPM predicts future videos from arbitrary viewpoints
together with the trajectories of points selected from
observed frames. To integrate information across cameras,
we process their video tokens in a shared sequence, using
ray-based embeddings to encode camera geometry and a view
axis in positional encoding to distinguish camera streams.
A trajectory forecasting head is optimized jointly with
video generation, allowing explicit point-motion supervision
to shape the representation used for visual prediction.
To support this learning objective, we construct
VPM-Data
, a simulation corpus covering tabletop
manipulation and urban dynamics. Each sequence pairs synchronized
multi-view videos with persistent point trajectories, camera
geometry, visibility annotations, and language descriptions,
providing aligned supervision for future appearance and motion.

Setup.
We test whether point supervision also benefits robot control
using the action-enabled extension of VPM (

Section

Simulation experiments follow each benchmark’s standard protocol
with three synchronized views: one wrist camera and one or two
third-person cameras on either side of the robot.
In the real world, we use the DROID platform (a Franka Research 3 arm
with a Robotiq 2F-85 gripper) and train only on an 89K-trajectory subset of DROID dataset.
We evaluate three pick-and-place tasks of varying difficulty,
with 24 trials each. We provide more details in Appendix
A.3
.

results show point trajectories benefit both generation and action. We next
examine why.
Why 3D point trajectory forecasting helps multi-view video generation.
The trajectory head predicts point motion from the generator’s intermediate
features, which the remaining blocks process into future
frames, so point supervision directly shapes the representation from which
videos are generated.

Conclusion and Limitations
We presented VPM, a multi-view world model that jointly forecasts future
videos and persistent 3D point trajectories from posed video histories and
language instructions. With VPM-Data and VP-WorldBench, our experiments show
that supervising where scene points will move improves visual forecasting on
simulated and real benchmarks and carries over to robot action learning.
Limitations remain. Our point supervision covers only the
robot and annotated objects rather than the full scene; skeletal annotations
also omit independent cloth and hair motion. VPM assumes known camera
intrinsics and poses at inference, and its cost grows with the number of
views, as all camera streams share one token sequence. Future work includes
deriving trajectory supervision from real multi-view videos at scale,
extending it to denser, non-rigid content, and relaxing the need for
calibrated cameras.

article.headline: 多视角世界模型同时预测视频与3D点轨迹
article.lede: VPM 以多视角视频历史和语言指令为条件，联合预测未来视频与场景点的3D轨迹，并把点监督反哺到生成表示，还扩展到机器人动
article.problem: 世界模型通常只以视觉逼真度衡量，但画面合理并不等于预测描述了一致的3D运动；单相机还常看不到遮挡下的场景结构与动态。要让不同视角的未来预测指向同一件事，模型必须把各相机的观测关联到共同的场景演化描述上，而现有视频生成模型缺乏这种跨视角的几何约束。
article.method: 作者在 Cosmos 3 基础上构建 VPM：把各相机视频 token 放进同一序列，用基于射线的嵌入编码相机几何，并在位置编码中加入视角轴以区分相机流。生成器之外增加一个轨迹头，预测从观测帧中选出的持久场景点在所有视角下的未来3D轨迹，并与视频生成联合优化，使外观变化锚定到共享的3D运动描述。作者还构建了配对的仿真数据语料 VPM-Data 与预测基准 VP-WorldBench，并通过把机器人动作作为 token 模态加入生成器，将模型扩展到策略学习。
article.results: 在 VP-WorldBench 和既有 4D 生成基准上，同时使用视频与轨迹监督的 VPM（V+T）优于仅视频版本（V）。消融显示：在 Simulation General 上加入序列损失使 FVD 从 101.37 降到 91.92，再加入深度损失使 Real-world Robot 的 δ3D_avg 从 54.69 升到 59.94；同时去掉视角轴、Plücker 嵌入与相机相关旋转三项后，Simulation General 的 FVD 由 81.92 恶化到 140.06，补回 Plücker 嵌入则从 128.41 降到 84.60。真实机器人实验在 DROID 的 89K 轨迹子集上训练，三个抓放任务各做 24 次试验，文中称点监督在每个基准上都提升了成功率，但具体成功率数字论文未给出具体数字。
article.why_it_matters: 它把「点往哪里动」作为跨视角的共同监督信号，为多视角视频世界模型提供了一个可验证3D一致性的抓手，并让同一套3D感知表示直接服务于机器人策略。
article.limitations: 点监督只覆盖机器人和被标注物体而非整个场景，骨骼式标注也忽略了布料与头发的独立运动；推理时假定相机内外参已知，且所有相机流共享一个 token 序列，计算代价随视角数增长。
article.figure_caption_zh: 给定带位姿的多视角历史视频与任务指令，VPM 预测未来视频以及从观测帧中查询点的轨迹，3D 点跟踪器迭代精化点位置与深度后再提升到 3D，联合点监督塑造生成器表示，动作扩展版本还会输出机器人动作块。

Abstract
Despite recent progress in dexterous reference tracking, existing models focus primarily on single-hand manipulation and a limited range of interactions, leaving the bimanual dexterous behaviors common in real life unaddressed. The scarcity of contact-rich bimanual manipulation data and the increased complexity of coordinating contacts make developing a generalist bimanual tracker particularly challenging. Therefore, we present
1)
DONIC
, the first generalist bimanual tracker jointly trained across operation categories and human-motion sources, together with
2) BiHOI
, a multi-view dataset of
1,575
1{,}575
sequences spanning
229
229
objects and emphasizing sustained bimanual interaction, where reconstructed interactions are retargeted into robot references.
DONIC
combines proximal policy optimization with behavioral cloning in a feedback loop that recycles verified successful executions into training demonstrations. An object-centered per-hand reward maintains object-motion feedback while supervising each hand according to its reference contact role. Clip-Centered Advantages remove reference-dependent advantage offsets while preserving within-trajectory differences. Together, these designs enable one single policy to learn coordinated manipulation across heterogeneous references. Without fine-tuning, a single checkpoint achieves
86.79
%
86.79\%
success on unseen trajectories of training objects and
57.32
%
57.32\%
on held-out objects, surpassing the state-of-the-art bimanual tracking baselines by
77.36
77.36
and
45.73
45.73
percentage points.
Generalist Dexterous Bimanual Tracking Control from Human Demonstrations

DONIC
.

DONIC

reference-tracking tasks.
1
Introduction
Dexterous manipulation supports household assistance, industrial assembly, and assistive care. Unlike gripper-based manipulation, it requires precise coordination of finger motions and changing hand–object contacts to grasp, reorient, and reposition objects
[
28
,
2
,
8
,
33
]
. Generalizing across objects and behaviors is challenging, especially when human demonstrations must be retargeted to robot hands with different kinematics
[
26
,
19
,
38
]
. Simulation-ready objects
[
4
,
5
,
6
]
and synthetic trajectories
[
12
,
40
]
enable large-scale interaction data, but may not fully capture natural human manipulation. Recent trackers therefore learn from human hand–object motion
[
19
,
38
,
1
]
, yet remain largely limited to single-hand tasks. Many everyday tasks instead require asymmetric bimanual coordination: one hand stabilizes an object while the other opens, rotates, or repositions it
[
9
,
41
,
43
]
. This motivates a generalist bimanual reference tracker that learns from diverse human motion to control different objects and tasks with one policy.
Developing such a tracker poses two challenges. First, public datasets include bimanual manipulation
[
9
,
41
,
20
,
10
]
, but fully tracked hand–object sequences with sustained two-hand contact remain scarce, limiting the available coordination patterns. Second, a shared policy must learn trajectories with changing hand roles and contact timing. Hand-pose accuracy alone does not ensure successful object manipulation, while requiring both hands to satisfy contact conditions can mask one hand’s progress. Unequal clip difficulty also creates advantage offsets that can weaken updates for useful actions in harder sequences. Shared training therefore needs feedback grounded in object motion and each hand’s reference contacts, alongside advantages that preserve differences among transitions within each clip.
We address these challenges with
DONIC
, a generalist bimanual reference tracker, and BiHOI, a multi-view hand–object interaction dataset. BiHOI contains
1,575
1{,}575
sequences spanning
229
229
objects and
14.77
14.77
hours, captured from
32
32
calibrated RGB views. It covers symmetric manipulation and asymmetric coordination. We reconstruct both hands and the object, then retarget hand motion to robot references paired with the object trajectory. Combined with public references, BiHOI broadens the training objects and coordination patterns.
DONIC
learns one policy for both hands through proximal policy optimization (PPO)
[
31
]
and behavioral cloning (BC) on verified demonstrations. Trajectory-specific policies optimize screened references, while successful shared-policy executions are verified and reused. At inference, one checkpoint tracks new references without further training. Our
object-centered per-hand reward
maintains object-motion feedback and supervises each hand’s reference contacts, including asynchronous engagement. Our
Clip-Centered Advantages (CCA)
subtract each clip’s mean estimated advantage before PPO updates, removing clip-dependent offsets while preserving within-clip differences. On held-out trajectories and objects from public datasets,
DONIC
exceeds the stronger bimanual baseline by
77.36
77.36
and
45.73
45.73
percentage points in success rate, respectively.
Our contributions are:
•
To our knowledge,
DONIC
is the first bimanual reference tracker jointly trained across operation categories and human motion datasets; a single checkpoint is evaluated on unseen trajectories and objects without fine-tuning.
•
We introduce BiHOI, a multi-view hand-object interaction dataset emphasizing coordinated bimanual manipulation, and reconstruct its recordings into robot motion references.
•
We propose an object-centered per-hand reward and CCA to support joint PPO training across bimanual references with different contact roles and difficulty.
•
On our two public-data evaluation splits,
DONIC
outperforms bimanual adaptations of DexTrack and Dexplore in success rate and completion, reaching
86.79
%
86.79\%
and
57.32
%
57.32\%
success on unseen trajectories and objects, respectively.
2
Related Work
From human references to executable manipulation.
Human trajectories provide motion targets, but retargeting alone cannot ensure successful contact. Sequence-specific policies commonly use reinforcement learning to correct retargeted motion. ManipTrans
[
15
]
reuses a general hand-motion imitator but learns a task-specific residual policy for interaction. DexMachina
[
23
]
learns from individual demonstrations by gradually removing virtual object assistance. CHORD
[
44
]
guides sequence-specific learning through contact-wrench matching, while ConTrack
[
17
]
trains one policy per clip with an adaptive balance between object tracking and motion fidelity. We instead learn one generalist bimanual policy that tracks diverse references without per-reference training or fine-tuning at test time.
Generalist manipulation policies.
Generalist policies share knowledge across objects, motions, or skills, predominantly in single-hand settings. UniDexGrasp++
[
33
]
generalizes grasping across object geometries, UniCross
[
42
]
unifies multiple manipulation skills, and ArtManip
[
39
]
learns category-level articulated in-hand manipulation. For reference tracking, DexTrack
[
19
]
combines reinforcement learning with demonstrations mined by trajectory-specific controllers. Dexplore
[
38
]
expands exploration around reference motions, while AdaDexTrack
[
1
]
combines specialist distillation with online reference modulation. Bimanual tracking must coordinate complementary hand roles and contact timing. Existing work explores narrower generalization: BiDexHD
[
43
]
distills teachers into a separate trajectory-conditioned policy for each operation category and evaluates new object–tool combinations and instances within categories; PhysGraph
[
16
]
transfers task-trained policies to new tool and object geometries. We jointly train one bimanual reference tracker across operation categories and human motion datasets, and evaluate it on unseen trajectories and objects without fine-tuning.
Bimanual hand–object interaction datasets.
GRAB
[
32
]
records whole-body grasping with detailed contact information, while ARCTIC
[
9
]
captures the coupled motion of two hands and articulated objects. OakInk2
[
41
]
organizes bimanual manipulation into primitive and complex tasks, and TACO
[
20
]
covers diverse tool–action–object compositions. GigaHands
[
10
]
further expands the scale and diversity of bimanual activities with language annotations. Complementing these motion collections, H2O
[
13
]
and HOI4D
[
21
]
support egocentric interaction understanding, while HOT3D
[
3
]
and HO-Cap
[
34
]
provide recordings and annotations for hand–object reconstruction and tracking. Capture and annotation conventions differ, and human kinematics do not ensure executable robot actions. We harmonize, retarget, and screen zero-residual feasibility to form a common bimanual reference pool for joint training.

To expand limited bimanual training data, we introduce
BiHOI
, a multi-view hand–object interaction dataset. We describe its capture system and composition, then the annotation and retargeting pipeline that converts recordings into robot references.
3.1
Multi-View Capture and Dataset
Multi-view capture system.
We record hand–object interactions with
32
32
calibrated RGB cameras surrounding a tabletop workspace, at a resolution of
1920
×
1232
1920\times 1232
pixels and a frame rate of
30
30
fps. Complementary views support reconstruction under occlusion; calibration supplies a common metric coordinate system.
Dataset composition.
BiHOI contains
1,575
1{,}575
interaction sequences covering
229
229
objects and
14.77
14.77
hours of unique interaction. The objects span household items, containers, utensils, tools, and electronics. Participants perform natural object-centric interactions rather than following fixed motion templates. The recordings include symmetric bimanual manipulation, asymmetric bimanual coordination, and coordinated multi-object manipulation.
Table
1
compares BiHOI with commonly used hand–object interaction datasets.
Our collection emphasizes sustained two-hand interaction. Among frames with at least one hand in contact,
65.91
%

have both hands in contact, exceeding H2O, the highest analyzed public subset at
38.57

27.34

3.2
Annotation and Reference Construction
Reconstruction and annotation.
We reconstruct metric hand–object trajectories from synchronized RGB recordings.
SAM3 provides object masks
[
7
]
, while multi-view Depth Anything 3 provides spatially consistent depth that we align to metric scale using the calibrated camera extrinsics
[
18
]
.
MV-SAM3D reconstructs a canonical object mesh from first-frame views and masks
[
14
]
; back-projected depth determines its physical scale.
FoundationPose then recovers 6-DoF object motion
[
37
]
, using multi-view pose consensus to handle occlusion and re-registration when consensus fails.
For each participant, triangulated calibration keypoints are used to estimate metric hand scale and calibrate a participant-specific MANO shape.
WiLoR provides per-view hand observations
[
24
]
; these observations are triangulated, temporally smoothed, and fitted with the MANO hand model
[
29
]
, with shape held fixed across the sequence.
Joint refinement against multi-view metric depth combines geometric alignment with reconstruction and temporal regularization, producing bimanual MANO parameters, a metric object mesh, and its 6-DoF trajectory in a common world frame.
Reconstruction and refinement details appear in Appendix
B.2
.
Retargeting.
We map the reconstructed human motion to the Wuji robot hands through frame-wise kinematic fitting, following standard retargeting practice
[
11
,
27
,
19
]
.
After wrist-frame alignment, we fit hand keypoints to robot links under joint limits, initializing and regularizing each frame against the preceding solution. Smoothing occurs only before retargeting. The resulting wrist and finger references are paired with the object trajectory.
4

). Its object-centered per-hand reward supports complementary roles and asynchronous contacts while maintaining object-motion feedback. CCA removes reference-dependent offsets after generalized advantage estimation (GAE)
[

Subtracting the clip mean preserves pairwise advantage differences among its transitions while removing their common empirical offset. The adjustment is applied after GAE; the learned critic and temporal advantage estimation remain unchanged.
Groups are defined by reference identity rather than by environment instance or temporal phase, allowing parallel rollouts of the same reference to contribute to a common baseline. Unlike batch-wide centering, CCA removes an offset specific to each reference instead of applying one shared shift to all clips. We subtract only the group mean, without dividing by a per-clip standard deviation, preserving the scale of within-clip advantage differences. This adjustment acts on the policy’s learning signal; it does not modify the reward or the critic’s regression targets.

6
Conclusion, Limitations and Future Work
We presented
DONIC
, a generalist bimanual tracker, and BiHOI, a multi-view bimanual interaction dataset. Object-centered per-hand rewards and CCA support iterative PPO+BC training, yielding one checkpoint that generalizes to unseen trajectories and objects without fine-tuning and substantially outperforms adapted baselines. Ablations support both learning signals and the benefit of additional BiHOI data.
However, our quantitative evaluation focuses on simulated single-object interactions and relies on reconstructed, retargeted motion references.
We aim to extend
DONIC
to longer-horizon and multi-object manipulation, evaluate on an independent benchmark, and investigate transfer to physical bimanual systems.

Appendix A
Additional Related Work
Executable human references and shared control.
Human demonstrations provide motion targets but do not directly specify robot actions: differences in hand kinematics and simulated contact can make a kinematically plausible reference physically difficult to execute. Reference-based trackers address this gap through closed-loop control. DexTrack
[
19
]
combines trajectory-specific demonstration generation with generalist learning; Dexplore
[
38
]
expands exploration around reference motions; and AdaDexTrack
[
1
]
combines specialist distillation with reference modulation. Our reference-conditioned action interface and iterative reinforcement–imitation learning loop build on this line of work. Our contributions within that loop are the object-centered per-hand reward and Clip-Centered Advantages (CCA), designed for shared bimanual tracking across heterogeneous references.
What generalization means here.
Generalization across grasped objects, manipulation skills, and complete reference trajectories imposes different requirements. UniDexGrasp++
[
33
]
studies generalizable dexterous grasping, while BiDexHD
[
43
]
learns trajectory-conditioned bimanual policies within operation categories. Our controller is jointly trained across operation categories and human-motion sources. We evaluate new trajectories of training objects and trajectories involving held-out objects with the same checkpoint. These two splits test reference and object generalization; they do not, by themselves, establish generalization to held-out operation categories or arbitrary manipulation goals.
Interaction capture and usable control data.
GRAB, GigaHands, OakInk2, TACO, and H2O provide complementary sources of hand–object interaction
[

,
10
,

,

]
. HOI4D and HO-Cap further broaden capture settings and annotation tools
[
21
,
34
]
. Our comparison distinguishes the inventory of a source dataset from the subset retained for robot training. A clip enters our bimanual pool only if the required hand and object tracks are available and both hands contact the object at some point. This allows sequential as well as simultaneous hand participation. BiHOI complements these sources with a higher measured proportion of simultaneous bimanual contact in the analyzed recordings.

Following DexTrack’s reinforcement–imitation loop
[
19

, specialist training covers all references retained by replay screening. Each trajectory-specific controller seeks an executable realization of its reference; successful rollouts are exported and replay-verified before admission to the demonstration library. The shared controller is periodically evaluated on the training pool, and its verified successes supplement the library for subsequent PPO+BC updates. Held-out references are excluded throughout.
Verification checks object displacement and, when required by the reference, lifting. An exported rollout must succeed again on replay. This admission procedure selects executable supervision and is distinct from the trajectory-fidelity metrics in Section
D.2
. Each BC minibatch samples 4,096 observation–action pairs independently of the PPO minibatch.
A versioned action/reference contract records the action parameterization, reference version, and retargeting fingerprint. Changes to this contract invalidate incompatible stored actions.

article.headline: DONIC：单策略实现双臂灵巧参考跟踪
article.lede: 提出通用双臂灵巧跟踪器DONIC与BiHOI数据集，单一检查点零微调成功率86.79%和57.32%。
article.problem: 现有灵巧参考跟踪模型大多聚焦单手操作和有限交互类型，难以覆盖日常生活中常见的双臂协同。接触丰富的双臂操作数据稀缺，且双手角色与接触时序的协调使通用跟踪更困难。
article.method: 作者构建BiHOI多视角数据集，含1575条序列、229个物体、14.77小时、32路RGB视角，并将重建的人手—物体交互重定向为机器人参考。DONIC用PPO与行为克隆的反馈循环训练一个共享双臂策略，成功执行经核验后回灌为示范。其物体中心逐手奖励分别监督双手接触角色，Clip-Centered Advantages在GAE后减去每条参考的均值以保留轨迹内差异。
article.results: 在零微调、单一检查点设置下，DONIC在训练物体未见轨迹上成功率86.79%、完成度67.62%，在留出物体上57.32%、54.69%；比更强的双臂基线Dexplore-bi分别高77.36和45.73个百分点。加入全部1575条BiHOI序列后训练池从1845增至3420条，成功率升至88.68%和59.76%，未见物体平移误差从15.74降至13.96厘米。消融中移除CCA使成功率降至81.13%和48.17%，移除接触门控降至81.13%和48.78%。腕部平移误差在未见轨迹和未见物体上分别从21.88降至3.96厘米、从19.46降至4.58厘米。
article.why_it_matters: 这项工作把人类双臂演示转成可执行机器人参考，并展示单一策略跨轨迹和物体泛化，为家庭辅助等双臂灵巧操作提供了数据与训练范式。
article.limitations: 定量评估限于仿真中的单刚体物体参考跟踪，依赖重建重定向轨迹，尚未在物理双臂系统或独立基准上验证，也未覆盖长时程、多物体和留出操作类别。接触监督使用净力与距离代理，重建流程没有显式接触或碰撞损失。
article.figure_caption_zh: DONIC总览：BiHOI采集经重建与重定向后，与公开数据参考共同构成训练池；共享双臂策略在PPO+BC迭代循环中通过仿真交互和核验示范学习，物体中心逐手奖励、CCA与行为克隆提供互补学习信号。

Abstract
Online reinforcement learning (RL) fine-tunes diffusion models with black-box rewards, but reverse-process methods such as Flow-GRPO are limited in efficiency by poor credit assignment, while forward-process methods such as DiffusionNFT are efficient yet unstable without carefully tuned exponential-moving-average (EMA) off-policy training. We show that NFT-style objectives contain
a hidden forward–reverse consistency force
that joint positive–negative training cancels only partially, and that EMA stabilizes training through
restoration
rather than off-policy rollouts. We introduce
DiffusionART
(
Diffusion
Reinforcement with
A
ggregation-First
R
eward
T
ilting), which aggregates each prompt’s rewards into a shared reward-improving direction for reverse-process states, removing the consistency force by construction, and adds a trust-region-masked second update for drift-adaptive restoration without EMA tuning. It requires no differentiable reward model, remains effective with fewer samples per prompt, and supports pairwise reward models (DiffusionART-Pairwise). Across image and video generation, DiffusionART trains efficiently and stably without per-task tuning. In particular, on HunyuanVideo-13B with equally weighted visual and motion quality rewards, DiffusionART reaches the late-stage mean reward levels of DiffusionNFT and Flow-GRPO-Fast with
12.02
×

and
11.72
×
11.72\times
fewer GPU hours, respectively, while achieving 28.8% and 53.0% higher mean training rewards.

Introduction
Visual diffusion and flow-matching models
1
1
1
We use “diffusion” as a general term. Our paper targets rectified-flow with linear data–noise interpolation
[
Lipman et al., 2022
]
, which shares the core principles of diffusion.
are typically trained to fit the data distribution by regressing noise or velocity targets rather than to optimize downstream criteria such as visual quality, motion quality, or human preference, making reward-guided fine-tuning central to recent image and video generation tasks
[
Xu et al., 2026a
,
Gao et al., 2025
]
. We focus on online diffusion Reinforcement Learning (RL), which, unlike differentiable reward-model optimization such as ReFL
[
Xu et al., 2023
]
or offline preference learning such as Diffusion-DPO
[
Wallace et al., 2023
]
, evaluates clean samples from the evolving generator and can use black-box rewards. Because these rewards arrive only after a complete output is generated, online diffusion RL faces a credit-assignment problem: costly output-level feedback must be translated into effective updates across many denoising states
[
Liu et al., 2025a
,
Zheng et al., 2025
]
.
Within this paradigm,
reverse-process RL
[
Black et al., 2023
]
, such as Flow-GRPO and its variants
[
Liu et al., 2025a
,
Xue et al., 2025
,
He et al., 2025
,
Wang et al., 2026
]
, optimizes sampled denoising transitions via group-based endpoint reward feedback. It trains on states actually visited by the generator but requires ODE-to-SDE conversion for tractable likelihoods, and its policy gradient updates each selected transition along its own transition-level sampling noise, weighted by a trajectory-level advantage that this transition only partly determines, resulting in poor credit assignment and limiting training efficiency.
Forward-process RL
, such as DiffusionNFT
[
Zheng et al., 2025
]
, instead applies forward noising to the generated clean samples and regresses velocities with reward-weighted positive and negative objectives. It needs no transition likelihoods and is highly efficient, but it is unstable without two stabilizers: joint positive–negative training and an exponential moving average (EMA) rollout policy whose lag must be tuned for each task
[
Zheng et al., 2025
]
. Neither family is thus both efficient and stable without per-task tuning. In this paper, we focus on studying the instability of forward-process RL and developing a scalable algorithm which is both stable and efficient.
We first examine NFT-style training, starting from a puzzle: its positive and negative branches share the same ideal reward-improving direction, so either alone should suffice, yet each alone collapses (Figure
2
(a)). We find that NFT’s targets, built from forward-noised endpoints, implicitly assume that the model’s sampling velocity equals the ideal forward velocity induced by its own endpoints. The two differ in practice, and the gap introduces a hidden non-reward-improving
forward–reverse consistency force
: the positive branch pulls each state’s velocity toward the ideal forward velocity and the negative branch pushes it away. Joint training can cancel this force but only partially, since reward centering balances rewards across samples rather than at each state. The residual can destabilize training and slow the reward optimization. We further show that EMA stabilizes NFT through the
restoration force
of its lagged reference, not through off-policy rollouts, but the EMA trick must be tuned per task.
Driven by these insights, we introduce
DiffusionART
(
Diffusion
Reinforcement with
A
ggregation-First
R
eward
T
ilting). It borrows supervised velocity regression from forward-process training but applies updates to states and actions during reverse-process rollouts. It first aggregates each prompt’s samples and rewards into a shared reward-improving direction
G

(
c

G(c)
, then regresses each visited state’s action toward its guided target (Section
4.1
). As this target never involves the forward velocity, the consistency force is removed by construction rather than by cross-sample cancellation, and each state receives an explicit reward-improving direction instead of a scalar advantage passed through likelihood ratios. A second update with a trust-region mask mechanism on each rollout adds a restoration force proportional to each state’s drift, replacing EMA with no schedule to tune (Section
4.2
). We summarize our main contributions as follows:
Main Contributions
1. Diagnosing the instability of NFT-style training.
The NFT objective implicitly contains a harmful forward–reverse consistency force that joint training cancels only partially (Section
3.1
).
2. Identifying restoration as the key stabilizer.
EMA stabilizes NFT through restoration rather than off-policy data, but requires per-task tuning (Section
3.2
).
3. Aggregation-first reward tilting with adaptive restoration.
DiffusionART removes the consistency force by construction, eliminating the need for EMA with drift-adaptive restoration (Section
4
).
4. Efficient and stable training.
DiffusionART matches the strongest baseline’s efficiency on SD3.5-M without EMA or per-task tuning.

6
Conclusion
We studied why NFT-style forward-process diffusion post-training can be unstable and found that its objective can introduce an implicit forward–reverse
self-consistency force that is not reliably canceled across states, while stronger restoration can improve stability at the cost of slower reward optimization. DiffusionART presents a simple but effective way to systematically cancel the unstable force by aggregating endpoint reward guidance before assigning it to reverse-rollout states, and then using a second update with a trust-region mechanism to provide drift-adaptive restoration for stabilization. Experiments on image and video generation show efficient, stable reward improvement, including with pairwise feedback and small rollout groups. Beyond the algorithm, our work provides insights into forward-process training, offering a clearer understanding of diffusion reinforcement learning and a path toward scalable diffusion post-training for visual generation.

A.6
Trust-Region Masking for Image Generation
We remove only the trust-region mask, retaining normalized covariance guidance, timestep weighting, and two disjoint MSE updates. On the three SD3.5-M benchmarks and FLUX.1-dev, training remains effective without masking and can improve slightly faster (Figure
12
). On FLUX.1-dev, the no-mask run reaches a training GenEval score of 0.971 by step 180. The benefit of masking is more pronounced for video generation (Figure
8
); Appendix
A.7
examines its stabilizing effect beyond reward curves.

A.7
Trust-Region Masking Diagnostics
We further inspect the matched HunyuanVideo comparison with VQ:MQ weights of
1
:
1
1{:}1
. Without masking, training exhibits larger late-stage gradient and
velocity-drift spikes (Figure
13
), complementing the
reward curves in Figure
8
(a–b).
Although the mask constrains only the second update of each rollout, its stabilizing effect extends to subsequent first updates. Over the shared first 300 training steps, the maximum first-update gradient norm is 1.96 with masking, compared with 3.33 without it. The velocity drift measured before second updates, which reflects displacement caused by the first update, also shows much larger spikes without masking (Figure
13
). With masking, the velocity drift score stays a healthy level. These observations suggest that restricting second updates helps keep later first updates well behaved, rather than merely suppressing gradients at the masked update.

article.headline: 聚合优先的扩散模型强化微调
article.lede: 提出 DiffusionART，先聚合每个提示的奖励为共享引导方向，再用漂移自适应恢复替代 EMA，在图像和视频生成上更
article.problem: 在线扩散强化学习中，Flow-GRPO 等反向过程方法因信用分配差而效率受限；DiffusionNFT 等前向过程方法高效，却依赖逐任务调参的 EMA 才能稳定。作者进一步指出，NFT 目标隐含一个前向-反向一致性力，正负分支联合训练只能部分抵消它。
article.method: DiffusionART 先把每个提示的 K 个 rollout 端点与奖励聚合成归一化协方差引导 G(c)，直接施加到反向 rollout 访问的状态上，从构造上移除一致性力。随后把每个 rollout 拆成两个不相交小批，各做一次 MSE 更新；第二次更新按每个状态的漂移提供恢复力，并用 trust-region mask 抑制过大策略变化。
article.results: 在 HunyuanVideo-13B、VQ:MQ=1:1 权重下，DiffusionART 达到 DiffusionNFT 与 Flow-GRPO-Fast 的后期平均奖励水平所需 GPU 小时分别少 12.02 倍和 11.72 倍，平均训练奖励分别高 28.8% 和 53.0%。T2V 评估 VQ 与 MQ 达 8.970 和 4.224，比最强基线高 31.4% 和 57.4%；I2V 达到 MQ 6 用 45.8 GPU 小时，对比 Flow-GRPO-Fast 的 220.3 小时，减少 4.8 倍。成对奖励下 K=2 的 400 步耗 260.8 GPU 小时，K=8 为 883.3 小时，减少 3.4 倍。
article.why_it_matters: 它为扩散与流匹配模型的后训练提供了一条不依赖可微奖励模型、也无需逐任务 EMA 调度的稳定路径，并可扩展到视频生成和成对偏好奖励。

page_papers.content:
Abstract
Video diffusion models have learned rich 3D/4D priors, making them promising for scene generation and video re-rendering. However, their use in these spatial tasks is limited by imprecise camera control, spatial and temporal inconsistencies, and the entanglement of camera motion with scene dynamics. Existing approaches, such as task-specific fine-tuning and post-process warping, often introduce visual artifacts, generalize poorly, or incur high computational costs. We propose WorldForge V2, which aims to achieve accurate camera control while preserving the generative capabilities of pretrained video models. We first develop a training-free guidance framework using warped references to iteratively refine generation along a target camera path. Optical-flow analysis identifies motion-related latent channels for selective guidance, helping separate motion control from appearance. A dual-path strategy further compares guided and unguided predictions to correct artifacts from imperfect references. Together, these components guide viewpoint changes while preserving scene appearance and object motion. To reduce refinement costs, v-cache approximates the correction using the preceding denoising prediction, avoiding an additional model evaluation. We further extend motion localization from latent channels to network blocks and introduce Trajectory LoRA, which concentrates adaptation on blocks most responsive to trajectory guidance. A two-stage training strategy teaches these adapters to denoise the states encountered during guided generation, using limited supervision effectively. This enables reliable camera control with very little training data, with a single training scene already supporting generalization to unseen scenes. Quantitative and qualitative evaluations across multiple datasets show that our method achieves state-of-the-art generation quality and trajectory accuracy in camera-controlled video generation.
Index Terms:
Camera control, video diffusion models, 3D/4D generation.
I

Introduction
Fig. 1:
Comparison with existing methods. With limited training data and iterations, our method achieves state-of-the-art visual quality and trajectory accuracy in camera-controlled video generation.
Recent video diffusion models (VDMs) can synthesize videos with coherent motion, consistent scene content, and plausible viewpoint changes over time
[
1
,
2
,
3
]
. Trained on large-scale video data, these models acquire strong spatiotemporal priors, making them powerful backbones for spatial-intelligence tasks such as 3D/4D generation, video re-rendering, and world modeling
[
4
,
5
,
6
,
7
,
8
,
9
,
10
,
11
]
. In these applications, the camera trajectory determines how a scene is observed over time, which regions become visible, and how viewpoint changes relate to scene geometry. Effective trajectory control is therefore essential. The generated video should follow a specified camera path while preserving scene content, object motion, temporal coherence, and visual quality.
To realize such control, existing approaches broadly follow two directions. One direction adapts VDMs for camera control through additional trainable modules, pose-aware conditioning interfaces, or model fine-tuning
[
12
,
13
,
14
,
15
,
5
,
16
]
. These methods provide explicit camera control but often require large-scale trajectory–video supervision or careful fine-tuning. With limited supervision, such adaptation may weaken the visual and temporal priors of the pretrained model. Recent work has therefore explored training-free alternatives that keep the pretrained VDM fixed and inject trajectory cues only during inference
[
6
,
17
]
, including the zero-shot variant of Warp-as-History
[
18
]
. A representative route is
warping-and-repainting
, which warps already observed content along the target camera path and uses the pretrained video model to synthesize newly revealed regions. This route enables direct camera control at inference time while preserving the pretrained model, making it well suited to downstream spatial-intelligence tasks.
Despite these advantages, warping-and-repainting can introduce a denoising-state mismatch during diffusion sampling. When warped visible regions are directly combined with model-generated regions in a noisy latent, the two parts may correspond to different noise states. The warped regions are associated with externally sampled noise, whereas the generated regions follow the model’s own denoising trajectory. We refer to this mismatch as a
denoising-state domain gap
. It can lead to boundary discontinuities, geometric artifacts, noisy patches, and texture degradation. The key challenge is therefore to inject useful trajectory evidence from warped references while reducing the denoising-state gap introduced by their fusion.
To address this problem, we propose
WorldForge V2
, a camera-trajectory-control framework that helps VDMs use imperfect warped trajectory signals more effectively while preserving generation quality.
WorldForge V2 follows the warping-and-repainting route.
First, it addresses the incompatibility introduced by warped-reference fusion: direct fusion in noisy latents mixes externally noised warped regions with generated regions following the model’s current denoising state.
WorldForge V2 reduces this mismatch by fusing the warped reference into the model-predicted clean estimate and mapping the fused result back to the current denoising state, enabling training-free trajectory-aligned video generation.
Second, clean-estimate fusion provides a reliable way to inject warped references into the denoising process by reducing noisy-state mismatch.
To further improve its sampling efficiency, we introduce v-cache, which approximates the clean-estimate correction directly in noisy latents.
In this way, warped-reference guidance can retain the benefit of clean-estimate fusion while reducing the extra sampling overhead.
Finally, full-model fine-tuning and large trainable control modules involve optimizing a large number of parameters, making it difficult to use limited training data efficiently. To address this problem, we build on our pipeline and further investigate an optimization-based approach to camera-trajectory control. Since different layers in VDMs specialize in different functions, we extend the motion-channel localization used in FLF to model adaptation. We identify trajectory-sensitive blocks and apply LoRA only to these blocks. This selective adaptation provides a data-efficient alternative to broad model tuning.
First, we address the denoising-state incompatibility caused by warped-reference fusion. In direct noisy-space fusion, the warped visible regions and the model-generated regions may follow different denoising states, causing geometric artifacts, boundary discontinuities, and noisy patches. To mitigate this mismatch, Intra-Step Recursive Refinement (IRR) fuses the warped reference with the model-predicted clean estimate under the visibility mask and then re-noises the fused estimate to the current timestep. This fuse-then-renoise process associates all regions with the same Gaussian noise realization, thereby reducing their denoising-state gap.
Camera-trajectory control also faces a typical motion–appearance disentanglement problem, as enforcing camera motion may inadvertently alter object and scene appearance. To address this problem, Flow-Gated Latent Fusion (FLF) uses optical-flow cues to locate channels that are highly correlated with motion and injects trajectory guidance only into these channels, thereby reducing appearance distortion.
Finally, artifacts or misalignment in the warped reference may degrade the quality of the generated video. To mitigate this issue, we propose Dual-Path Self-Corrective Guidance (DSG). Inspired by classifier-free guidance
[
19
]
, DSG compares the trajectory-guided and unguided denoising directions. Their difference captures the update introduced by trajectory guidance, which DSG uses to suppress unreliable deviations while retaining useful trajectory constraints. Together, IRR, FLF, and DSG enable training-free trajectory-aligned video generation while reducing the adverse effects of incompatible denoising states and unreliable reference signals.
Second, the fuse-then-renoise process in IRR provides an effective way to reduce the denoising-state gap introduced by warped-reference fusion. We further improve the efficiency of this process with v-cache. Our key observation is that the correction induced by clean-estimate fusion can be approximated directly in noisy latent space from a denoising prediction already available during sampling. Based on this observation, v-cache applies the approximated correction during warped-reference fusion, allowing trajectory guidance to remain on the original denoising path. This avoids an additional model evaluation and reduces inference latency.
Finally, we further develop an optimization-based extension of our pipeline for camera-trajectory control. Existing optimization-based methods often fine-tune the full model or introduce large trainable control modules, making inefficient use of limited supervision. Since camera control mainly depends on motion-related representations, we extend the motion-channel localization idea of FLF to model adaptation. Leveraging the functional specialization of different VDM layers
[
20
]
, we identify trajectory-sensitive blocks, apply LoRA only to these blocks, and train the adapters with a two-stage optimization strategy tailored to our pipeline. This selective adaptation provides a data-efficient alternative to broad model tuning. In our experiments, we find that training data from a single scene is sufficient to enable effective trajectory following.
Our main contributions are summarized as follows:
•
To address denoising-state mismatch, motion–appearance entanglement, and unreliable warped references, we develop a training-free guidance pipeline with IRR, FLF, and DSG, enabling trajectory-aligned video generation with fewer artifacts and less appearance distortion.
•
To retain the benefit of clean-estimate correction with lower sampling cost, we introduce v-cache, which approximates the correction in noisy latent space and avoids an additional model evaluation, thereby reducing inference latency.
•
To avoid data-inefficient full-model tuning, we identify trajectory-sensitive blocks, adapt only these blocks with LoRA, and optimize them using a two-stage strategy tailored to our pipeline; training data from a single scene is sufficient to enable effective trajectory following.
•
Comparative experiments on multiple public datasets demonstrate accurate camera-path control and high-quality video generation.
A preliminary version of this work was published at
CVPR 2026
[
21
]
. The source code is available at
https://github.com/Westlake-AGI-Lab/WorldForge
.
Fig. 2:
Overview of WorldForge V2.
Given a single image or video frame and a target camera trajectory, the scene geometry is reconstructed and rendered into trajectory-aligned warped frames.
WorldForge V2 first performs training-free trajectory guidance in the predicted clean latent space using IRR, FLF, and DSG.
Building on this framework, we further introduce an efficient route that directly fuses trajectory information in the noisy latent space with V-Cache, together with a trajectory-sensitive lightweight LoRA scheme for camera trajectory control using only limited training data.
The resulting video follows the specified camera path while preserving the generative capability of the pretrained video diffusion model.
II

Camera Control in Video Diffusion Models
Existing camera-control methods broadly follow two directions. Training-based methods introduce pose-aware conditioning interfaces, additional control modules, or model fine-tuning to learn camera-controlled generation
[
12
,
13
,
15
,
14
,
5
,
44
,
16
,
45
]
. These methods provide explicit camera control but usually require substantial trajectory–video supervision; when training data are limited, model adaptation may weaken the visual and temporal priors learned during pretraining. Recent work has therefore increasingly explored training-free inference-time control and lightweight adaptation, which preserve most or all of the pretrained model and inject trajectory cues through initial noise, latent transformations, rendered references, or history frames
[
8
,
6
,
17
,
46
,
47
,
18
,
48
]
. Across training-based and training-free methods, warping-and-repainting warps observed content along the target camera path and uses a VDM to generate newly revealed regions
[
49
,
50
]
. This route provides explicit geometric correspondence and integrates naturally with depth estimation, point-based rendering, and visibility masks. WorldForge V2 adopts this route and studies how warped references can be used more effectively for camera-trajectory control while reducing the artifacts introduced during denoising. Related motion-control work also uses entity-specific 3D trajectories to control object motion
[
51
]
.
II-C
Guidance and Correction Strategies in Generative Models
Guidance methods steer diffusion or flow models toward desired outputs by modifying their sampling directions. Classifier-free guidance (CFG) combines conditional and unconditional predictions to improve alignment with semantic conditions
[
19
]
. Subsequent methods further adjust the guidance direction through negative or auxiliary branches, differential predictions, adaptive rescaling, resampling, and iterative repainting
[
52
,
53
,
54
,
55
,
56
,
57
,
58
]
. In 3D/4D generation, guidance is also widely used to enforce viewpoint consistency from rendered or warped observations
[
59
,
60
,
6
,
17
,
8
]
. However, conventional guidance does not directly address the artifacts introduced by noisy warped references. WorldForge V2 explores correction strategies for warping-guided generation, including correcting warped-reference fusion in noisy latent space and using the difference between guided and unguided predictions to refine the denoising process. Together, these strategies improve the quality of trajectory-controlled videos generated under warping guidance.
II-D
Parameter-Efficient Adaptation for Camera Control
Model adaptation commonly uses trainable control branches or parameter-efficient fine-tuning. ControlNet and T2I-Adapter introduce lightweight conditioning modules, while LoRA adapts pretrained models through low-rank parameter updates
[
61
,
62
,
63
]
. These lightweight adaptation strategies have also been applied to motion learning, sparse-view synthesis, and trajectory-controlled generation with limited training data
[
64
,
65
,
18
,
45
]
. Related studies further show that motion- and camera-related representations are concentrated in particular latent channels or network layers
[
20
,
66
]
. Based on these findings, WorldForge V2 uses optical-flow cues in FLF to localize motion-related latent channels and reduce appearance interference. We further extend this idea to model adaptation by identifying trajectory-sensitive blocks and applying lightweight LoRA only to these blocks, enabling effective trajectory alignment with very limited training data.
III

Method
WorldForge V2 (Fig.
2
) aims to control camera trajectories while preserving the video priors of pretrained generation models. Given a source image or video and a target camera path, geometric warping first produces a trajectory reference and its visibility mask. WorldForge V2 then uses these signals to guide denoising and generate videos that follow the target path. Sec.
III-A
introduces the required notation and background. Sec.
III-B
presents the training-free guidance pipeline: IRR reduces the denoising-state gap through clean-estimate fusion, FLF restricts trajectory injection to motion-related latent channels, and DSG corrects the guided prediction using the model’s original denoising path. Sec.
III-C
derives a noisy-latent correction that reduces the denoising-state gap with fewer model evaluations. Finally, Sec.
III-D
identifies trajectory-sensitive network blocks and adapts them with LoRA using limited supervision, enabling data-efficient trajectory control for VDMs.
III-A

Experiments
Our experiments examine how rendered-reference guidance combines camera control with the scene priors of pretrained video models. We first evaluate the training-free framework in static 3D generation and dynamic 4D re-rendering, then study V-Cache correction and data-efficient LoRA adaptation. Transfer experiments examine the reuse of the learned control, and ablations establish the roles of guidance, block selection, and training. We denote the IRR–FLF–DSG framework as
Ours (Training-Free)
and the adapted models as
Ours (LongCat)
and
Ours (H3)
.
IV-A

Experimental Setup

Metrics
We evaluate visual quality and camera accuracy together. The training-free experiments use FID and CLIP similarity for static scenes, and FVD and CLIP-V similarity for dynamic videos. For Trajectory LoRA, we additionally evaluate target-view reconstruction with pixel-level metrics, PSNR and SSIM, and the perceptual metric LPIPS. Vis-LPIPS and Disocc-LPIPS assess preservation of visible content and completion of newly exposed regions, respectively. ATE measures overall trajectory agreement, while RPE-T and RPE-R measure local translation and rotation errors. Metric implementations are specified in the supplementary material.
IV-B
Inference-Time Camera-Trajectory Control
We evaluate whether warped-reference guidance can follow a prescribed camera path while retaining the scene priors of a frozen video backbone. For static 3D generation, we compare with See3D
[
49
]
, ViewCrafter
[
4
]
, ViewExtrapolator
[
17
]
, TrajectoryAttention
[
15
]
, TrajectoryCrafter
[
5
]
, and NVS-Solver
[
6
]
. For dynamic 4D re-rendering, we compare with ViewExtrapolator, TrajectoryAttention, and TrajectoryCrafter using matched source videos and target trajectories. ReCamMaster
[
14
]
does not directly accept warped reference videos as trajectory inputs and is therefore included only in the qualitative comparison.

Method

Conclusion
We presented WorldForge V2 for accurate camera control while preserving the generative capabilities of pretrained video models. Our training-free guidance uses warped references to iteratively refine generation along the requested camera path, with motion-aware channel selection and self-correction preserving scene appearance and object motion. Building on this guidance, v-cache reuses denoising predictions to approximate the refinement correction, reducing sampling cost. Trajectory LoRA extends motion localization from latent channels to network blocks and combines selective adaptation with two-stage training, enabling pretrained video models to learn reliable trajectory control from very few trajectory–video pairs. Quantitative and qualitative evaluations across multiple datasets demonstrate state-of-the-art generation quality and trajectory accuracy in camera-controlled video generation. Future work will explore long-horizon, real-time streaming generation with camera control to support the development of interactive world models.

article.headline: WorldForge V2：免训练相机轨迹控制
article.lede: 将变换后的参考帧融入模型预测的干净估计再重加噪，WorldForge V2 在冻结主干时实现相机轨迹控制。
article.problem: 现有相机控制方法要么依赖大量轨迹—视频监督进行微调，要么在推理期采用 warping-and-repainting，但把变换后的可见区域直接拼进噪声潜变量会带来去噪状态不匹配。论文将这一问题称为去噪状态域间隙，表现为边界不连续、几何伪影、噪声块和纹理退化。此外，相机运动容易与物体及场景外观纠缠，且变换参考本身可能不可靠，错误会沿采样过程累积。
article.method: WorldForge V2 用 IRR 把变换参考与模型预测的干净估计在可见性掩码下融合，再重加噪到当前时间步，使所有区域共享同一高斯噪声实现，从而缩小去噪状态间隙。FLF 借助光流定位与运动相关的潜通道，只在这些通道注入轨迹引导以减轻外观畸变；DSG 则比较有引导与无引导的预测方向，抑制不可靠参考带来的偏差。效率方面，v-cache 复用前一次去噪预测在噪声潜空间中近似校正，避免额外模型评估；进一步地，Trajectory LoRA 只适配对轨迹敏感的模块，并用两阶段训练策略利用有限监督。
article.results: 论文称在多个数据集上取得相机控制视频生成的 SOTA 生成质量与轨迹精度，并称来自单个训练场景的数据即可支持泛化到未见场景。但材料中的定量表格未列出 FID、FVD、CLIP/CLIP-V、ATE、RPE-T、RPE-R、PSNR、SSIM、LPIPS 等指标的具体数值，论文未给出具体数字。
article.why_it_matters: 相机轨迹控制是视频扩散模型进入 3D/4D 生成、视频重渲染与世界模型的关键接口。WorldForge V2 试图以免训练引导加轻量 LoRA 的方式，在不破坏预训练时空先验的前提下复用这些模型。
article.limitations: 论文把长时程、实时流式生成列为未来工作，说明当前方法尚未覆盖这些场景；v-cache 只是对校正的近似，其精度损失与延迟收益在材料中未量化。此外，材料未给出定量结果，“单场景训练即可泛化”仍需更系统的跨场景验证。
article.figure_caption_zh: 不同参考插入策略下的噪声状态一致性：直接插入会在可见区域与模型生成区域之间留下噪声均值和对数方差的间隙，并伴随噪声块与结构断裂；IRR 缩小这些间隙，V-Cache 在保持连续表面和清晰几何细节的同时近似其校正。

figure.caption: Noise-state consistency under different reference-insertion strategies. Direct Insertion leaves gaps in the inferred-noise mean and log-variance between visible and model-generated regions, accompanied by noisy patches and broken structure. IRR reduces these gaps, and V-Cache approximates its correction while retaining continuous surfaces and clear geometric detail.

BeNice! Closing Looping’s Inference-Memory Gap via KV-Sharing
Hayden Prairie
Affiliation:
University of California, San Diego
Affiliation:
Together AI
Jacob M. Ryan
Affiliation:
University of California, San Diego
Taylor Berg-Kirkpatrick
Affiliation:
University of California, San Diego
Daniel Y. Fu
Affiliation:
University of California, San Diego
Affiliation:
Together AI
Abstract
Looped architectures scale quality while keeping parameter count fixed by repeatedly passing activations through the same block of layers.
During inference, each recurrence generates independent
KV-caches
, causing memory to grow linearly.
To address this challenge, prior work has proposed KV-sharing (i.e., sharing KV-caches across depth),
finding that, in some cases, the KV-cache of the final recurrence can be shared with the earlier recurrences
without quality loss
, a property we denote as
KV-shareability
.
However, the mechanisms underlying KV-shareability remain poorly understood, with even identically trained looped architectures not consistently exhibiting it.
In this paper, we study how
KV-shareability
can be enabled in looped models.
We propose a two-stage method: in the first stage, we use
stochastic depth
during pretraining, which induces contractive residual dynamics that drive representations toward a common limit across recurrences. In the second stage, we propose BeNice!, a post-training method that broadcasts the final recurrence’s KV-cache into the first recurrence, training it to produce compatible residuals while preserving the original model’s quality.
As a result,
BeNice!
enables KV-shareability while matching standard finetuning’s unshared validation perplexity.
Using
BeNice!
, we show that KV-sharing is complementary to alternative KV-compression methods, composing with memory-efficient sequence mixers (e.g., multi-latent attention, Kimi delta attention) and low-precision KV-cache quantization (e.g.,
fp8
,
mxfp8
,
nvfp4
).
Finally, in simulated low-memory, long-context inference, KV-sharing improves cache hit rates by up to 31.4%, increases throughput by up to 23.6%, and reduces p90 time-to-first-token by up to 83.6%.

Introduction
As inference deployments move to the edge
[
43
,
45
]
and take up a large portion of compute
[
67
]
, looped architectures create a new, predictable avenue to scale quality while keeping parameter count fixed
[
20
,
50
,
41
]
.
Unfortunately, while looped architectures keep the memory overhead of parameters capped, they still create
KV-caches at each recurrence
[
50
,
80
,
19
]
,
causing memory overhead to still
grow linearly
with recurrence count at inference time.
One potential direction to reduce inference-memory overhead is KV-sharing (i.e., sharing KV-caches across recurrences).
Specifically, some recent looped models have been shown to support reuse of the final recurrence’s KV-cache for all prior recurrences with
minimal impact to quality
[
20
,
21
]
, a property we term
KV-shareability
(
Figure
1
[
right
]).
Unfortunately, the mechanisms underlying KV-shareability remain poorly understood, with more recent work reporting significant quality degradation with KV-cache reuse
[
80
,
19
]
.
Moreover, even models trained under identical setups can differ in whether they exhibit KV-shareability (see
Table
1
).
In this paper, we hypothesize that contractive recurrent dynamics drive residual states toward fixed points, whose agreement under shared and unshared KV-caches enables
KV-shareability
.
To encourage contractive residual dynamics, we train with
stochastic depth
, randomly sampling depth throughout training (
Figure
1
[
left
]).
By requiring low-loss predictions across multiple depths, stochastic depth discourages residual drift and promotes convergence across recurrences.
Contractive residual dynamics are what allow KV-shareability, which we formally analyze and empirically validate by showing that replacing intermediate caches with the final cache perturbs the attention output by a term bounded by the difference between their input residuals (see
Section
3.1
).
Unfortunately, even though
stochastic depth
creates contractive residual dynamics, it does not guarantee that residual states converge to the same fixed point with and without KV-sharing. Instead, KV-sharing sometimes introduces token-independent residual errors in the first recurrence, shifting the model’s fixed point and harming downstream quality (see
Section
3.2
).
To enable KV-shareability, we pair stochastic depth pretraining with a targeted correction of the residual errors introduced by KV-sharing. We propose a two-stage method: first,
stochastic depth
pretraining to induce contractive residual dynamics; second,
BeNice!
to correct first recurrence residual errors created from KV-sharing.
Specifically,
BeNice!
jointly optimizes both the first recurrence with KV-cache reuse and the final recurrence without reuse (
Figure
1
[
middle
]), balancing KV-shareability and base-model quality.
To further study KV-sharing with other KV-compression techniques, we extended
BeNice!
to memory-efficient sequence mixers, including multi-latent attention (MLA)
[
13
]
and Kimi delta attention (KDA)
[
65
]
, by reusing the final recurrence’s latent or state, respectively.
Overall,
BeNice!
unlocks near-lossless KV-cache reuse across recurrences, facilitating predictable quality scaling using extended looping
[
50
]
while keeping parameter count and KV-cache memory constant as depth grows.

Stochastic Depth,
BeNice!
, and KV-Shareability.

In this section, we study

in looped architectures.
To evaluate KV-shareability, we compare

6
Conclusion
In this work, we study the emergence and failure points of
KV-shareability
, finding that contractive residual dynamics drive KV-caches towards a common shareable limit. To enable
KV-shareability
, we propose a two stage method: first, we use stochastic depth to induce contractive residual dynamics across recurrences; second, we provide
BeNice!
, a post-training method that corrects residual errors in the first recurrence to ensure that models approach a common limit with and without KV-sharing. KV-shareability composes with both memory-efficient sequence mixers and KV-quantization, detaches inference memory overhead from test-time recurrences, and improves throughput and TTFT in memory-constrained settings.

Appendix B
Extended Literature Review
Looped architectures have been and continue to be explored by a growing body of work. We focus on architectural differences. Here, we discuss the main categories of architectural differences, as well as other works on memory efficiency in looped models.
Middle-Looped Models.
This framework of models utilizes three blocks: a prelude block (
𝒫
\mathcal{P}
) that performs representation extraction using transformer layers, a recurrent block (
ℛ
\mathcal{R}
) that recurrently updates activations, and a coda block (
𝒞
\mathcal{C}
) that turns activations into outputs.
Bansal et al. [7]
,
Geiping et al. [20]
,
McLeish et al. [41]
, and
Prairie et al. [50]
all train middle-looped models with stochastically sampled recurrence depth during pretraining.
Schwethelm et al. [58]
trained middle-looped models with fixed recurrence depth. These architectures tend to be trained with implicit halting mechanisms to determine when to stop looping
[
7

20
,

,
58

[

,
58

Bae et al. [4]
is trained with a middle-looped architecture, but uses an explicit halting mechanism of lightweight routers to decide recurrence depth.
Fully Looped Models.
This regime of looped models loops the entire model every recurrence. While not strictly a requirement, this regime of architecture tends to pull from
Graves [23]
work on adaptive compute time (ACT), using explicit halting mechanism to determine when to stop looping.

article.headline: BeNice! 实现循环模型 KV 共享
article.lede: 两阶段训练让循环语言模型在推理时复用最终循环的 KV 缓存，缓解内存随循环深度线性增长。
article.problem: 循环架构重复使用同一组层，能在参数固定下提升质量，但推理时每个 recurrence 都会生成独立 KV-cache，使内存随循环次数线性增长。此前的 KV-sharing 只在部分模型上有效，机制不清，且相同训练的模型也不一定具备该性质。
article.method: 作者先用 stochastic depth 预训练，诱导收缩的残差动力学，让不同循环的表示趋向共同不动点；随后提出 BeNice! 后训练，把最终 recurrence 的 KV-cache 广播到第一个 recurrence，并联合优化共享与不共享路径以纠正首个循环的残差误差。该方法也扩展到 MLA 和 KDA 等高效序列混合器。
article.results: 在 Parcae 模型上，BeNice! 使共享设置下的 Core 和 Core-extended 分数最多提升 8.35 和 4.56 分；相比标准微调，共享时验证困惑度改善 9.75 分，非共享质量持平。模拟长上下文推理中，KV-sharing 将 1.3B 模型 HBM 占用从 63.82 GB 降到 21.60 GB（66.2%），缓存命中率最多提升 31.4%（8.1 个百分点），吞吐量最多提升 23.6%，p90 TTFT 最多降低 83.6%（2 req/s 时从 139.2 s 降至 23.2 s）。
article.why_it_matters: 若成立，循环模型可通过增加测试时循环次数提升质量，而不让 KV-cache 内存随深度增长，对长上下文和内存受限部署尤其重要。
article.limitations: KV-shareability 并非所有循环模型天然具备，stochastic depth 单独不足，仍需 BeNice! 后训练；实验集中在 Parcae 架构和模拟推理负载，真实部署与其他架构的泛化尚待验证。
article.figure_caption_zh: 预训练循环模型的定点收敛：在已发布的 Parcae 模型和 Huginn 中，循环残差状态与注意力模式的相对变化随循环深度增加而下降。

Abstract
Activation steering provides a lightweight and flexible way to control large
language model (LLM) behavior. However, effective steering requires more than inducing the intended behavior:
it should also limit unintended changes and remain robust across inputs and training data.
Existing evaluations cover these dimensions only in fragments. As a result, the trade-offs between efficacy and side effects have not been systematically characterized.
We introduce
SteerScope
, a two-axis,
multi-dimensional evaluation suite that jointly characterizes
steering
outcomes
and
method properties
through 15 metrics. We score
target efficacy and side effects on language quality, task capabilities,
and safety and reliability, and further assess generalization and data
dependence through steering-specific metrics for sample efficiency and sample
sensitivity.
Rather than comparing methods at a single operating point, we characterize their efficacy–side-effect trade-offs.
Under matched models, tasks, and evaluation protocols, we benchmark 23 methods spanning 4 families, including prompting, LoRA, and SFT as
baseline methods, and release the suite as an extensible codebase.
We find that current activation steering methods do not yet surpass the Prompt Steering baseline in their overall balance between steering efficacy and side effects:
across both model scales, no evaluated activation steering method achieves higher efficacy without incurring greater composite side effects.
We further uncover a
consistent coupling between steering efficacy and side effects. Under OOD
prompts, target efficacy is often preserved, whereas side effects tend to become
more pronounced, particularly through declines in instruction relevance and
fluency. Methods also exhibit sharply different sample-efficiency profiles.

liangmingpan@pku.edu.cn

1
Introduction
As large language models (LLMs) are deployed across diverse tasks and
applications, fine-grained control over their behavior has become increasingly
important
(
Ouyang et al., 2022
)
. Prompting and fine-tuning are widely used
for this purpose. However, prompting lacks an explicit mechanism for continuously
adjusting the strength of a desired behavior, while fine-tuning requires
additional training and parameter updates
(
Wu et al., 2025a
)
. Recently,
activation steering
has emerged as a promising approach to behavioral control. It intervenes in internal
representations, such as the residual stream, to induce or suppress specific
concepts, styles, and safety-related behaviors
(
Turner et al., 2023
;
Zou et al., 2023
;
Rimsky et al., 2024
)
. By keeping
the backbone parameters frozen and allowing intervention strength to be adjusted,
activation steering is more lightweight and adjustable.
However, the effects of steering are not always confined to the intended target.
Prior work has reported multi-dimensional side effects across language quality,
task capabilities, safety, and reliability. These include degraded generation
quality and task performance, as well as changes in bias, refusal, and jailbreak
susceptibility
(
Stickland et al., 2024
;
Bhalla et al., 2024
;
Sprejer et al., 2026
;
Li et al., 2026d
)
. Existing evidence suggests that
these side effects may arise from concept entanglement, whereby concepts
are not behaviorally independent and steering one can unintentionally alter
others
(
Durmus et al., 2024
;
Siu et al., 2026
;
Li et al., 2026d
)
. Beyond these side effects, steering outcomes may vary across
input distributions. They may also depend on the amount and composition of the
data used to construct the intervention
(
Tan et al., 2024
;
Braun et al., 2025
;
Ding et al., 2026
)
. Together, these challenges motivate a
comprehensive evaluation framework organized around two questions:
what steering
changes
and
when those changes hold
.
Recent work has begun to establish benchmarks for evaluating LLM steering, such as
AxBench
(
Wu et al., 2025a
)
,
SteeringSafety
(
Siu et al., 2026
)
,
FaithSteer-BENCH
(
Ding et al., 2026
)
, and
CLaS-Bench
(
Gurgurov et al., 2026
)
. However, existing benchmarks cover the relevant dimensions only in fragments, leaving an incomplete picture of what steering changes and when its effects hold. For example, AxBench limits side-effect evaluation to instruction following and
fluency. SteeringSafety centers on safety entanglement, while CLaS-Bench
specializes in cross-lingual language control. FaithSteer-BENCH focuses on deployment-time reliability, but evaluates each
method at a single calibrated operating point and does not cover side effects
on language quality or safety.
Fig.
1
(right) illustrates these gaps in coverage.
Figure 1:
Overview of the SteerScope evaluation suite and benchmark coverage.
Left: our hierarchical evaluation taxonomy. Right: coverage matrix of existing
steering benchmarks, where rows denote taxonomy nodes and columns denote
evaluation works (last column: SteerScope). A
✓
indicates a corresponding metric,
✗
indicates none, and
△
\triangle
indicates that the dimension is considered indirectly but
not measured independently.
To bridge this gap, we introduce
SteerScope
, a comprehensive, multi-dimensional evaluation suite for LLM steering.
1.
Systematic evaluation taxonomy.
SteerScope organizes 15 metrics into a hierarchical taxonomy with two complementary axes (Fig.
1
, left).
Steering Outcomes
examines what steering changes, covering target efficacy and side effects on language quality, task capabilities, and safety and reliability.
Method Properties
examines when steering effects hold, covering generalization under cross-lingual prompt shifts and dependence on training data.
2.
Broad method coverage.
We evaluate 23 methods spanning 4 families on 2 models.
These include diverse activation steering methods alongside prompting, LoRA, and SFT baselines.
3.
Efficacy–side-effect trade-off characterization.
We characterize each adjustable method through its efficacy–side-effect trade-offs, revealing how unintended effects change alongside target efficacy.
Our central finding is that
current activation steering methods do not outperform the Prompt Steering baseline in the efficacy–side-effect trade-off on either evaluated model
.
Although some activation steering methods outperform this baseline on existing benchmarks, none achieves higher target efficacy without greater composite side effects under our default aggregation.
On Gemma-2-9B-it, for example, A-PSR improves the Concept Expression score by 1.30 points but incurs an average normalized degradation of 0.12.
Consistent with this, steering efficacy and side effects generally increase together as intervention strength grows.
Nevertheless, activation steering remains useful because its adjustable intervention strength provides access to high-efficacy operating points.
Among activation steering approaches, methods with learned interventions tend to achieve more favorable trade-offs than optimization-free methods.
We further find that target efficacy is often preserved under out-of-distribution prompts. In contrast, side effects tend to become more pronounced, particularly through declines in instruction relevance and fluency.
Finally, sample efficiency varies substantially across methods, reflecting
different levels of dependence on training-data size.
2
Related Work
Representation-Based Activation Steering.
Representation-based activation steering controls model behavior by intervening on
internal activations at inference time. Early methods often modeled target concepts
with linear directions, motivated in part by the linear representation hypothesis
(
Bolukbasi et al., 2016
;
Elhage et al., 2022
;
Park et al., 2024
;
Nanda et al., 2023
)
. Existing methods span
contrastive directions, subspaces, latent representations,
geometric transformations, hypernetworks, and nonlinear interventions
(
Turner et al., 2023
;
Zou et al., 2023
;
Marks & Tegmark, 2024
;
Wu et al., 2024
;
Pham et al., 2026
;
Sun et al., 2025
;
Wu et al., 2025b
;
Jin et al., 2026
;
You et al., 2026
;
Zhao et al., 2026
)
. We organize the methods evaluated in this
work by their underlying mechanisms in Section
4
.
Benchmarks for Activation Steering.
Existing benchmarks have begun to standardize the evaluation of activation steering, but each covers only a subset of the relevant evaluation dimensions. AxBench
(
Wu et al., 2025a
)
evaluates 500 steering targets across activation steering, prompting, and fine-tuning methods, but its off-target evaluation is limited to instruction following and fluency. SteeringSafety
(
Siu et al., 2026
)
studies behavioral entanglement across nine predefined safety perspectives within a curated safety concept set. FaithSteer-BENCH
(
Ding et al., 2026
)
focuses on deployment-time reliability, evaluating clean controllability, capability preservation, and robustness under changing conditions at a single calibrated operating point. SteerEval
(
Xu et al., 2026
)
broadens evaluation across behavioral domains and concept granularities, while CLaS-Bench
(
Gurgurov et al., 2026
)
extends steering evaluation to 32 languages and cross-lingual transfer.
Complementary studies have identified specific steering side effects, including degradation in generation coherence
(
Bhalla et al., 2024
)
, capability–behavior trade-offs
(
Sprejer et al., 2026
)
, and sensitivity to individual samples and prompt conditions
(
Tan et al., 2024
)
.
Overall, existing evaluations cover safety entanglement, deployment reliability, cross-lingual control, and other aspects, but remain fragmented across evaluation dimensions and steering methods.

Sample Efficiency.
Sample Efficiency measures how much of a method’s full-data Overall improvement

4
Steering Methods
We evaluate 23 representative methods and baselines, plus a Random control. The methods span diverse steering mechanisms while avoiding redundant variants and enabling both method- and mechanism-level analysis. A broader catalogue is provided in Appendix

4.1
Optimization-Free Steering Methods
Concept Directions.
These methods construct steering directions from activation patterns associated
with a target concept.
DiffMean

and negative mean representations to model activations at inference
time
(

;
PCA
extracts the first principal component
from positive-example activations
(
Wu et al., 2025a
)

LAT
applies PCA to contrastive activation
differences
(
Zou et al., 2023
)
. As a control,
Random

DiffMean after randomly partitioning the training examples, removing
concept-specific label alignment.
Structured Interventions.
These methods introduce geometric, latent-space, or unit-level interventions.
Spherical Steering
performs norm-preserving geodesic rotation toward a target direction, aiming to better respect the geometry of the model’s representation space
(
You et al., 2026
)
.
HiDRA
performs steering in a higher-dimensional feature space, where discriminative structure can be captured
(
Pham et al., 2026
)
.
AUSteer
steers in discriminative LLM components and assigns adaptive strengths
(
Feng et al., 2026
)
.
SAE-Based Methods.
SAE-based methods use decoder directions from a sparse-autoencoder dictionary
(
Huben et al., 2024
)
.
SAE
uses a concept-associated feature, while
SAE-A
selects the feature with highest target-discriminative AUROC
(
Wu et al., 2025a
)
.
4.2
Directly Optimized Steering Methods
Learned Steering Directions.
Several methods learn interventions using supervised training.
Linear Probe

(

;
Wu et al., 2025a
)
.
SSV

(
Wu et al., 2025a
)
, and
ReFT-r1

(
Wu et al., 2025a
)
.
Learned Subspace and Adaptive Interventions.
LoReFT
learns a low-rank intervention subspace over hidden representations
(
Wu et al., 2024
)
.
PSR
combines a learned steering direction with an activation-dependent gate, allowing intervention strength to vary across tokens
(

)
. We evaluate its all-layer variant (
A-PSR
) and single-layer variant (
S-PSR
).
RePS

(
Wu et al., 2025b
)
.
ODESteer

(
Zhao et al., 2026
)
;

4.3
Hypernetwork-Based Steering Methods
These methods use shared auxiliary networks to generate steering interventions conditioned on natural-language targets.
HyperSteer
trains a transformer-based hypernetwork that maps a natural-language steering target and the model’s internal activations to a dynamically generated steering vector
(
Sun et al., 2025
)
.
FLAS
instead trains a transformer-style FlowBlock to parameterize a concept-conditioned velocity field over activation space
(
Jin et al., 2026
)
.
4.4
Non-Representation-based Steering Methods
Four baseline methods that do not operate directly on model representations are included: two prompting baselines and two parameter-update baselines.
Prompt Steering
uses an LLM to convert each target concept into a short steering context, whereas
Simple Prompt Steering
uses a fixed concept-conditioned instruction; both prepend the resulting context to the original instruction. The prompt templates are provided in Appendix
C.5
. We further evaluate
Supervised Fine-Tuning
(SFT)
(
Ouyang et al., 2022
)
and
Low-Rank Adaptation
(LoRA)
(
Hu et al., 2022
)
as the two parameter-update baselines.
